The eight branches: kāyacikitsā, śālākya, śalya, viṣa/agada, bhūtavidyā, kaumārabhṛtya, rasāyana, vājīkaraṇa (Ca Sū 30.28; Su Sū 1.7; AHS Sū 1.5: body, child, seizers, above the clavicle, surgery, fangs, old age, virility).
The eight limbs: restraints, observances, posture, breath-regulation, sense-withdrawal, concentration, meditation, samādhi (2.29), whose practice destroys impurity (2.28).
Tamil aṭṭāṅka yōkam: iyamam, niyamam, ātaṉam, pirāṇāyāmam, pirattiyākāram, tāraṇai, tiyāṉam, camāti (TM 552), commended by Kaṭuveḷi (31).
A song of eight stanzas with refrain, set to a named rāga and tāla — the twenty-four songs of the Gīta Govinda; in Kerala the name of the Gīta Govinda singing tradition itself.
The eight protections of the Liṅgāyata: guru, liṅga, jaṅgama, pādōdaka, prasāda, vibhūti, rudrākṣa and mantra; several appear as sub-sthalas of the bhakta-sthala in the SSM (5.27–30).
Freedom from desire for what is not one's own (YBh 2.30); when established, all jewels present themselves (2.37).
One of the common duties of all (MDh 10.63).
The fifth tissue: supports the body and nourishes marrow (Su Sū 15.5).
The life-breath that leaves at death (the fathers 'have gone to asu', RV 10.15.1); the one life of the gods arose from the waters (10.121.7).
Viewing the body as hair, flesh, blood, bone, bile, excrement and so on, cultivated to abandon lustful passion (NBh 4.2.3).

cross_language.note: same term; the Buddhist practice has its own contexts and lists

definitions.definition: The karma of the yogin (4.7): not white, since he renounces the fruit; not black, since he does not take it up (YBh 4.7); others' karma is black, white-and-black, or white.
In the Ṛgveda a lord of mysterious power, applied to Varuṇa and other gods ('great is the one asura-ship of the gods', RV 3.55); later the gods' opponents.

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan ahura.

definitions.definition: Hypocrisy, arrogance, pride, anger, harshness and ignorance, leading to bondage (BhG 16.4–5); its bearers deny truth, foundation and a Lord (16.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who follow Kṛṣṇa's teaching with faith and without carping (anasūyantaḥ) are freed from actions (3.31); those who carp at it and do not follow it are lost (3.32).
The imperishable tree with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns, to be cut with the axe of non-attachment (BhG 15.1–4); 'among trees I am the aśvattha' (10.26).
The eternal fig tree with roots above and branches below, which is brahman, the immortal, in which all worlds rest (KU 2.3.1).
The twin horsemen, divine physicians and rescuers, praised by Ghoṣā (RV 10.39–40).
Repeated contraction and expansion of the anus.
The renunciant's continual wandering, not staying long in one place.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna calls the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra ātatāyinaḥ, and says sin would come upon them for killing even these aggressors (1.36).
The six supports (āṟu ātāram) of the body: mūlātāram, cuvātiṭṭāṉam, maṇipūrakam, anākatam, vicutti, ākkiñai; the Siddha counterpart of the cakras, burnt away by the guru's grace in Aḻukaṇṇi's song.

equivalents.note: the six ātāras correspond to the six cakras

definitions.definition: The primordial fire-priest who churned out Agni (RV 6.16.13); with the Aṅgirases, the seers of the Atharvaveda.

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan āθravan (priest).

definitions.definition: The old name of the Atharvaveda, pairing its auspicious (ātharvaṇa) and fierce (āṅgirasa) portions.
The gift of oneself to the Lord, whose fruit is final non-return, as against ordinary gifts of cows, land and gold.
The extension of the procedure of an archetype to an ectype ('the ectype is to be performed like the archetype'), in general (adhyāya 7) and in particular (adhyāya 8).

literal: one who has passed beyond what is to be cultivated

definitions.definition: One of Vyāsa's four kinds of yogin (YBh 3.51): One whose sole aim is the dissolution of the mind, with the sevenfold final insight.
Servitude — the soul's being the Lord's servant, and the service it owes 'at all times without break' (TVM 3.3.1); the Āḻvārs call themselves aṭiyēṉ, 'your servant'.

equivalents.note: aṭimai is the servant-state; kaiṅkarya the service done from it
the Bhāgavata's dāsya is one of nine forms; for the Āḻvārs servitude is the soul's very nature

definitions.definition: Name given by the Śaiva scriptures to the Pāśupata and Lākula (and skull-observing) division of Śaivism: knowledge 'beyond the states of the intellect', 'beyond the world'.
In the Mantramārga's own scriptures, the ascetic Śaiva path (Pāśupata and Lākula) ranked above Vedic and 'spiritual' religion but below the Mantramārga.

notes: U17 owns lin:atimarga and its own account; this is the Mantramārga's classification.

definitions.definition: A Tamil Śaiva monastic house (maṭha) headed by a paṇṭāra-caṉṉiti, e.g. Tiruvāvaṭuturai and Dharmapuram, custodians of the Meykaṇṭa tradition and of temples.
Enduring the three sufferings without remedy while keeping one's rule; the supreme austerity.
The guest, whose honouring is the sacrifice to men (MDh 3.70).
The deities who conduct the departed soul along the path of light.
The airy (vāyavīya) body that the dead takes immediately upon leaving the gross body.
The knower beyond castes and stages of life.
Performing the prescribed acts as the Lord's command; the supreme worship.
The Lord's servants, his devotees; the Āḻvārs hold the servants of his servants, of any birth, to be their masters.
'Those at the feet': Śiva's devotees, to be served and revered as Śiva himself.
The freed soul should join the true devotees (meyyaṭiyār) and revere their garb as Śiva.
The Śrīvaiṣṇava's customary way of saying 'I', expressing servitude.
Giving oneself over to the Lord's protection — the principal (aṅgin) of prapatti in Deśika's account, the sixth of the six in the Ahirbudhnya verse.
The renouncer's own funerary offering, among the eight śrāddhas.
Inquiry into the self: 'Who am I? How did this world arise? Who is its maker? What is its material?' (Aparokṣānubhūti 12); inquiry, not action, attains the Real (VC 11).
The highest dharma, attained by yoga (YS 1.8).
The eight virtues — compassion, patience, freedom from envy, purity, calm, auspiciousness, generosity, freedom from greed — without which the forty sacraments do not lead to Brahman (GDh 8.22–25).
The highest of the means to the supreme good, foremost of all sciences, by which immortality is gained (MDh 12.85).

The self: in the Upaniṣads the innermost reality of a person — the seer of seeing that cannot be seen (BAU 3.4.2), the inner controller (BAU 3.7), the light of a person (BAU 4.3.6) — which is declared to be brahman (BAU 1.4.10, 2.5.19; ChU 6.8.7; MāU 2). The word also means body or oneself in narrative passages (ChU 8.8.4).

Breath and self: Sūrya is the self of what moves and stands (RV 1.115.1); the dead man's breath (ātman) goes to the wind (10.16.3); Vāta is the self of the gods (10.168.4); knowing the wise, ageless, young self one does not fear death (AVŚ 10.8.44).

The embodied self, unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain (BhG 2.20); to be raised by the self, being its own friend or enemy (6.5–6); the Lord as the self in the heart of all beings (10.20).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The self in which the one of steady wisdom is content — in the self alone, by the self (2.55) — and in which one who has nothing to do delights and is satisfied (3.17); knowing what is beyond the understanding (which 3.42 calls only 'he', saḥ; the commentators take it as the self), one steadies the self by the self (ātmānam ātmanā, 3.43). Also used reflexively and for one's person, nature or mind (vidheyātmā 2.64; vimūḍhātmā 3.6, 3.27; ātmavān 2.45; kāmātmānaḥ 2.43). The embodied one of 2.12–30 is called dehin or śarīrin, not ātman.

An eternal substance distinct from body, senses, mind and cognition, known by the marks desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition (NS 1.1.10); the knower, the one who remembers (NS 3.2.40).
An all-pervading substance marked by breath, eye-movements, life, mind's movement, desire, effort etc. (VS 3.2.4 C); many (VS 3.2.16 C); perceived by yogins (VS 9.13).
The substrate of cognition; two kinds: the supreme self (the one omniscient Lord) and the individual self, distinct in each body, all-pervading and eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The inner self (pratyag-ātman): pure, self-luminous consciousness, the witness of the three states, not the body, senses, mind or ego; identical with Brahman.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda, Caraka): the supreme self is changeless, eternal, the cause of consciousness with mind, elements and senses, the seer (Sū 1.56); beginningless, the knower of the field, all-pervading, witness, known by the marks of life (breath, blinking, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, effort, consciousness, memory, ego-sense) (Śā 1.59-85); knows only through its instruments (Śā 1.54-55).
Suśruta: the knowers of the field in Āyurveda are eternal but not all-pervading (Su Śā 1.16).

In ritual contexts the body or trunk (of the altar, of the sacrificer) that the rite constructs; in the teachings of Śāṇḍilya and Aśvapati the inner self 'made of mind, with breath for body' (ŚB 10.6.3).
The self to be seen by yoga (YS 1.8), its own witness (MDh 8.84), one in all beings though appearing many like space in pots (YS 3.144).
The one self of the deity of which the many gods are limbs (Nirukta 7.4).
The self, distinct from body and cognition, known to itself, shown by desire, memory and recognition; taught by negation ('not this, not this') (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
Distinct from cognition, senses and body; all-pervading, permanent, many; manifested as the subject in cognitions of objects (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Eternal, the agent and enjoyer who reaps the fruits of rites in another world; known through reasoning and made firm by the Upaniṣads (ŚV ātmavāda 148).

The eternal self, distinct from body, senses and intellect, known through the I-cognition and memory (SSM 5.55–60); dwelling in the heart like the hundredth part of a hair-tip, shining like a lamp (18.5–7).
The self is consciousness (Śiva Sūtra 1.1); the bound self is the mind (3.1); the self is a dancer (3.9).
U04 usage: the Self in the body-temple, identical with Brahman; threefold as outer, inner and supreme self in the Ātma Upaniṣad.

cross_language.note: the Buddhist texts deny a permanent attā; same word, opposed doctrine

definitions.definition: Complete self-surrender to the Lord, the ninth form of devotion.
Giving one's life over to the Lord who owns release (TVM 1.2.1).
Having offered self, world and Veda to the Lord, the devotee has no anxiety at worldly loss (NBS 61); self-offering is one of love's eleven forms (NBS 82).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The condition of the person who delights in, is satisfied in and content in the self alone, for whom nothing remains to be done and who depends on no being for any purpose (3.17–18).
Private worship by an initiate in the liṅga given by the guru or on a ground-altar, for one's own fruit.
Worship of Śiva for oneself, obligatory daily for the initiate.
The direct experience of one's own self as distinct from matter, the fruit of karma- and jñāna-yoga and prerequisite for bhakti-yoga.
One who sacrifices knowing that each rite builds a limb of his own (new) self, and who so sheds the mortal body like a snake its skin (ŚB 11.2.6.13).
One who sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, and so attains self-rule (MDh 12.91).
Renunciation in mortal danger, by mind and speech.
Absence whose counterpositive is delimited by a relation for all three times ('no pot on the ground').
Final, without recurrence — of the cessation of suffering in kaivalya (SK 1, 68).
Liberation understood as a dissolution: knowledge cuts the ego-knot and the self abides in itself; dissolution into the eternal Brahman (VP 6.8.1).
Beyond the stages of life: the Pāśupata observance so described by revelation.
The Pāśupata state: the initiate leaves the rules of his former āśrama and follows the restraints and observances of the state beyond the āśramas.
Name used by Śaiva scripture for the Pāśupata branch of the Atimārga.
One beyond the stages of life, to whom Śvetāśvatara declared brahman (ŚU 6.21).
Propriety, appropriateness of every element to rasa and context; for Kṣemendra the life of poetry.
A Nāth initiate who has received the first initiation (mantra, top-knot cut, black thread) but not yet the ear-splitting.
A name for Aghora ascetics; in Aghora usage the one who has passed beyond all distinctions.
Bhāskara's form: difference of soul from Brahman is due to real limiting adjuncts (upādhi); non-difference is natural.
The relation of word and meaning, not created by any person (MS 1.1.5); known from the beginningless usage of elders (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Delimitation: consciousness delimited by the intellect, like the space enclosed by a pond; its identity with the whole is taught by the great sayings.
The Goddess appears divided by adjuncts like the space in pots.
Delimitation: the jīva as consciousness delimited by the inner organ, as space by a pot.
The property (or relation) by which a property or relation is specified — e.g. potness delimits the counterpositiveness of 'absence of pot'.
In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the prasādi stage.
One who has 'shaken off' all worldly ties, a liberated wanderer who behaves like a child, madman or dullard; the teacher of King Yadu.

Defined syllable by syllable: a — free of the noose of hope, ever in bliss; va — free of vāsanās, living in the present; dhū — dust-grey limbs, cleansed mind, free of concentration and meditation; ta — held to truth, free of anxiety, darkness and ego.
The renouncer who has shaken off saṃsāra, beyond castes and stages, without marks or rules; etymologized syllable by syllable.
The yogī who has 'shaken off' all conventions and bonds and abides in the supreme state; the ideal described in the sixth upadeśa of the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati; addressed in Hindi as 'avadhū'.
In the Mahānirvāṇa, the saṃnyāsa of the Kali age (8.221); four kinds, complete (paramahaṃsa) and incomplete (14.142-149).
The vīra renunciant who holds 'I am Śiva, the bliss of Bhairava' (Nirvāṇa Tantra 14.6).
The 'avadhū' whom Kabīr addresses in many songs — the Nāth yogī, challenged to find the Lord within rather than in yogic garb and feats.
The protective 'veiling' of the deity or offering, made with the right fist and extended index finger turned around.
Inviting the deity into an image for worship; not done for the iṣṭaliṅga, in which Śiva already abides from initiation (SSM 10.44–47).
The kapha in the chest that supports the trika and heart and the other seats of kapha (AHS Sū 12.15-16; Su Sū 21.14 describes the function without the name).
Being held in contempt by all beings, sought by the second-stage ascetic.

An 'enclosure' of the Śrīcakra: each of its nine concentric parts, from the square to the point, with its presiding goddess (cakreśvarī), class of yoginīs, attendant deities and mudrā, worshipped in turn (navāvaraṇa-pūjā).
The veiling power of māyā that covers knowledge.
The veiling power of ignorance, which hides the self as a small cloud hides the sun from the viewer.
The practitioner's fixed stations until the gain: manifest, unmanifest, conquest, cutting, completion.
Tamil avattai: the five states among the ninety-six principles — cākkiram, coppaṉam, cuḻutti, turiyam, turiyātītam.
State of the soul: waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth and beyond the fourth.
Avattai: the soul's states; also the three great conditions kēvalam (isolation with āṇava), cakalam (embodied) and cuttam (purified).
Change in the strength or condition of a present property (e.g. impressions of stilling growing strong; a pot's newness turning to age) (3.13, YBh 3.13, 3.15).
Viṣṇu's manifestation of his own eternal body of consciousness and bliss, not a birth of flesh; the avatāras are wholly identical with him and flawless.
The Lord's coming into being age after age by his own māyā to protect the good, destroy evil-doers and establish dharma (BhG 4.6–8); the noun itself is not used in the Gītā.
The Lord's successive manifestations (prādurbhāva), foretold by Nārāyaṇa to Nārada (MBh 12.326.72–94).

A descent of the Lord in a form for the protection of the world; innumerable, the principal ones listed as twenty-two (BhP 1.3), ten (Agni, Garuḍa) and in other lists; all are portions and parts, but Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān himself (BhP 1.3.28).
The incarnations come from the regions of Kāl to maintain order in the creation; the Saints come from the highest region to take souls home and are above them.
Kabīr's descents in the four ages are not avatāras of Viṣṇu but comings of the Sat Puruṣ's messenger; Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheś are Kāl's sons.
The Lord's real descent in a body of pure sattva by his own will, not from karma.
The uprooting of desire (Kuṟaḷ ch. 37), desire being the seed of all births.
(1) A member of the demonstrative statement — proposition, reason, example, application, conclusion (NS 1.1.32); (2) a part of a whole.
A part, in which the whole (avayavin) inheres.
A new substance over and above its parts, inhering in them and perceived (NS 2.1.31–37, 4.2.4–17).
The notion of the whole form (e.g. 'woman', 'man') with its embellishments that causes the faults (NS 4.2.3; NBh).
A rival account of liberation rejected by Rāmakaṇṭha: possession [of the soul by the Lord's qualities].
Among the siddha's powers: he 'enters all' and none can enter him (sarvāṃś cāviśati ... anāveśyaḥ).
Viṣṇu's special presence in a soul (as distinct from an avatāra); one must know which beings are his avatāras and which are only his āveśas.
Vijñānabhikṣu: non-separation — souls and prakṛti are not separate from Brahman, their substrate, though distinct; his preferred name for the relation.
The released soul's non-separation from Brahman (BS 4.4.4).

Taking the impermanent, impure, painful and non-self as permanent, pure, pleasant and self (2.5); the field of the other afflictions (2.4) and the cause of the conjunction (2.24); not the absence of knowledge but a contrary cognition (YBh 2.5).

Ignorance: in Śaṅkara, superimposition itself (the non-discrimination of self and not-self); in later Advaita, a beginningless, positive, indescribable power that veils Brahman and projects the world, removed by knowledge alone.
One positive ignorance having pure consciousness as its locus and object.
Ignorance residing in the individual selves (many, one per jīva), with Brahman as its object.

In the Tattvasamāsa, the five-jointed avidyā = the five errors (Tattvasamāsa 12; Kramadīpikā). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra denies that bondage is caused by an avidyā that is unreal (SS 1.20–26) or that avidyā is the world's material cause (SS 5.65).

Ignorance: those living in it think themselves wise and go round like the blind led by the blind (KU 1.2.5; MuU 1.2.8); Īśa 9-11 pairs it with vidyā (read by some as rites); the perishable is avidyā (ŚU 5.1); the teacher takes one across to the far shore of avidyā (PrU 6.8).
VP 6.7.11: taking non-self for self and what is not one's own as 'mine'; VP 1.5.5: fivefold avidyā arising first in creation; VP 6.7.61: the third, 'avidyā-karma' śakti.
A real, beginningless covering in each soul, twofold: one covering the soul's own nature and qualities, one covering (the soul's knowledge of) the Supreme; removed only by the Lord.
Defective cognition arising from defects of the senses and from impressions (VS 9.25–26 C); doubt, error, indefinite cognition and dream (Praśastapāda).

Not an indescribable cosmic ignorance but karma (the third power 'avidyā-karma' of Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.61) and the ignorance it causes in the soul — the contraction of its knowledge and the mistaking of body for self.
The beginningless ignorance covering the jīvas (Kulārṇava 1.9).
Ignorance, which Jñāneśvar's Amṛtānubhava argues cannot exist in the self-luminous reality at all.

equivalents.note: Used interchangeably in Advaita texts (Vedāntasāra prefers ajñāna).

notes: Not the cosmic ignorance of Advaita.

definitions.definition: Unmodified transformation: Brahman becomes the world without any change in itself, as gold in ornaments.
Kāśī, where Rudra gives the tāraka to the dying; located in the body between brows and nose.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: That by which all this is pervaded is indestructible (2.17); the knower knows the embodied one as indestructible (2.21).
Non-abstention: the mind's greed for contact with objects (YBh 1.30).

Manifestation and concealment: Brahman's being, consciousness and bliss are manifest or concealed in its forms; creation and dissolution are manifestation and concealment, not origination and destruction.
The five subtle elements, which lack the calm, turbulent and dull differentiation (SK 38).
The second level: the five tanmātras and I-am-ness alone (2.19, YBh 2.19).
Inference proceeding by difference, negating (the alternatives) — the śeṣavat kind (Vācaspati on SK 5).
Uttering meaningless, repetitive or self-contradictory words.

notes: From the sūtra 'api tad bhāṣeta'.

definitions.definition: Acting as one who cannot tell pure from impure, fit from unfit (e.g. handling sticks and clods), without breaking the restraints.

notes: From the sūtra 'api tat kuryāt'; Ratnaṭīkā: apitatkaraṇa.

definitions.definition: The failure to discriminate puruṣa from prakṛti, the cause of their conjunction and so of bondage (SS 1.55); beginningless, removed by discrimination like darkness by light; bondage is non-discrimination alone (SS 6.12–16). The manifest and unmanifest are 'non-discriminating' (SK 11).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The embodied one is called unmanifest (2.25); beings have an unmanifest beginning and end and are manifest only in the middle (2.28).

Prakṛti in its unmanifest state: uncaused, eternal, pervasive, inactive, one, unsupported, non-merging, partless and independent — the opposite of the manifest (SK 10) — and known through its effects (SK 8, 14–16).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): in Caraka the self as knower of the field, and one of the eightfold prakṛti (Śā 1.61-63); in Suśruta the uncaused cause of all beings, threefold in guṇas, support of many knowers of the field (Su Śā 1.3).
The unmanifest: higher than the great self, below the person (KU 1.3.11, 2.3.8).

The unmanifest: from which beings emerge at Brahmā's day (BhG 8.18); another eternal unmanifest beyond it is the Imperishable (8.20); worshipped by some (12.1–5); in the Mokṣadharma the field, prakṛti (12.294.38).
'The unmanifest' (Kaṭha 1.3.11), which the sūtras deny to be Sāṃkhya's pradhāna (BS 1.4.1); Brahman is also called unmanifest (3.2.23).
A name of māyā, the unmanifest power of the Lord (VC 108).

notes: Whether this is the Sāṃkhya pradhāna is debated (Brahma Sūtra 1.4.1).

definitions.definition: The second-stage ascetic who hides his Pāśupata sign while his conduct is manifest.
The second stage, in which birth and sign are hidden and the ascetic courts dishonour among people.
A property that occurs in a locus only in part (e.g. monkey-contact in a tree), coexisting with its own absence — a test case for definitions of pervasion.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of that by which all this is pervaded, which no one can destroy (2.17), and of the self known as indestructible and unborn (2.21).
'This self is Brahman' (Māṇḍūkya 2): the practice sentence (abhyāsa-vākya), mahāvākya of the Atharvaveda and of Jyotirmaṭh.
The temple (built by another) where the first-stage practitioner lives; the Ratnaṭīkā says it stands for the teacher.

notes: Homonym of the Buddhist technical term āyatana (sense-base).

definitions.definition: Beings (bodies) not born from wombs exist, also on the evidence of the Veda (VS 4.2.9 C).

The science in which the wholesome and unwholesome, happy and unhappy life, what is good and bad for life, and its measure are taught (Ca Sū 1.41); so called because in it life is found or by it one attains life (Su Sū 1.15); it makes life known by its own marks (Ca Sū 30.23). It is beginningless and eternal (Ca Sū 30.27), an upāṅga of the Atharvaveda (Su Sū 1.6). Synonyms: śākhā, vidyā, sūtra, jñāna, śāstra, lakṣaṇa, tantra (Ca Sū 30.31).

cross_language.note: Tibetan rendering of āyurveda (recalled)

definitions.definition: The union of body, senses, mind and self; its synonyms are dhāri, jīvita, nityaga and anubandha (Ca Sū 1.42); the continuance of consciousness (Sū 30.22); fourfold as happy or unhappy, wholesome or unwholesome (Sū 1.41, 30.24); in Śārṅgadhara the union of body and breath (Pūrva 5.52).
Rites and hymns for long life (AVŚ 8.1–2; VS 3.62).
Souls bound in saṃsāra by beginningless karma, their knowledge contracted.
In the Dāsbodh: The bound person sunk in the world, first of the four conditions.

The three states of processed mercury in the doctrine: swooned it removes disease, 'dead' it revives, bound it gives sky-going (Rasārṇava 1.19; Rasahṛdaya 1.3); the same said of breath. RESTRICTED: the tests and processes are not recorded.
A pseudo-reason whose probandum's absence is known by another means of knowledge ('fire is not hot').
Sublation: the cancellation of a cognition by a later one that shows its object never was as it appeared (the snake by the rope-cognition); the criterion of the three levels of reality.
The lapse of transferred details that serve no purpose in the ectype, e.g. husking for gold pieces (MS 10.1.1–2).
A later cognition that the object is otherwise, which (with knowledge of a causal defect) alone sets aside a cognition's validity.
The eighth Mahāvidyā; the one-faced Mahārudra, destroyer of the world, is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.14); matched with Kūrma (10.9); goddess of paralysing (stambhana).
The first five limbs; even the inner three are outer relative to seedless samādhi (3.8).
The external power, māyā, which produces the material world and covers the souls turned away from the Lord.
Outer worship, e.g. of the Śrīcakra on a physical support; the Yoginīhṛdaya's 'aparā' worship, performed even by Śiva (YH 3.3).
External worship of the deity in liṅga, image, maṇḍala or fire.
Second kind: triple staff, ochre, eight mouthfuls from many houses.
An alternative verse to the Raudrī Gāyatrī for expiation and recitation (usually taken as the Aghora mantra).
The ten capacities, operating in the present and presenting objects to the three internal ones (SK 33).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): innate, seasonal/age-born and acquired (Ca Sū 11.36); identified with ojas (Su Sū 15.19).
Bālā Tripurasundarī, the Goddess as a young girl, whose three-syllable vidyā is imparted first at initiation (PKS 1.39).
Devotion to the teacher, clarity of mind, conquest of opposites, merit and vigilance.
Kuṇḍalinī as the young ascetic widow seated between the Gaṅgā (iḍā) and Yamunā (piṅgalā), to be seized by force (HYP 3.109–110).
The offering of a victim to the Goddess, taught in the Kālikā Purāṇa's offering chapter with its substitutes and restrictions (67). Restricted: summary only.
Food set out daily for beings (bhūtayajña) (ŚB 11.5.6.2); offerings 'not into fire' (ĀśGS 1.1.2).

A lock that contains the breath: mūla (root), uḍḍiyāna (abdominal) and jālandhara (throat), together the 'three locks' practised by the great Siddhas (HYP 3.74–76); applied at the end of inhalation and of retention (2.45–46).

Bondage comes from error (SK 44) and belongs to prakṛti, which binds herself by seven forms (SK 62–63); it is threefold — to prakṛti, to the modifications, and through gifts (Tattvasamāsa and Kramadīpikā).
The self's threefold connection with the world: the body (seat of experience), the senses (its instruments) and the objects (what is experienced) (Śāstradīpikā).
A lock: uḍḍiyāna, jālandhara and mūla are among the five seals whose knower is fit for success (GŚ 32–37).
The three locks — root, abdominal, throat.

The hidden correspondence the Brāhmaṇas establish between an element of the rite, the cosmos and the person (e.g. the bricks of the altar = the days and nights of the year = the joints of Prajāpati); knowing the bandhu is what makes the rite effective.
The twelve sub-orders of the Nāth yogīs, said to have been set in order by Gorakhnāth (six from Śiva's and six from Gorakh's panths in one telling).
A disciple of the Kartābhajā, who pays dues through a Mahāśay to the Kartā.
The devotional rāga songs of Śaṅkaradeva and Mādhavadeva in Brajabuli.
The strewn grass on which the gods are invited to sit.
'The present': what is here and now, verifiable in the living body; the Bāuls call themselves bartamān-panthī, followers of the present.

equivalents.note: Like perception, bartamān is direct knowledge, but it is specifically the body's own experience and is set against scripture as such.

definitions.definition: The second cleansing act: washing the colon by drawing in water while squatting in navel-deep water (jala-basti); the GS adds a 'dry' basti on the ground.
Medicated enema (decoction or oil), the chief remedy for vāta (AHS Sū 1.25; Ca Sū 25.40 'best of vāta-removers').
A 'madman' (of God): a practitioner who has abandoned convention to seek the Man of the Heart; the word appears in the Caitanya-caritāmṛta (Antya 19) for the God-mad.
Allama's Kannada word for the void — open space without enclosure — in which the devotee, the liṅga and the world disappear.

equivalents.note: Kannada and Sanskrit words used side by side for the void in Allama's vacanas

definitions.definition: The enigmatic, paradoxical vacanas (beḍagina vacana) especially of Allama Prabhu.
The 'city without sorrow' of Ravidās's song: no grief, tax, fear or ranks; the goal and the ideal community of the Ravidāsīs.
The auspicious, prayed for in intention, hearing and seeing (RV 1.89.1, 1.89.8).
A form of Kālī widely worshipped (in Kerala and elsewhere) as the fierce protectress; in the Kālīkula one of Kālī's forms.
The six excellences whose possessor is Bhagavat: aiśvarya, vīrya, yaśas, śrī, jñāna, vairāgya.
Partial implication: the mode by which 'that' and 'thou' are understood as their common consciousness, dropping the opposed features, as in 'this is that Devadatta'.

equivalents.note: the Rāma Gītā names it bhāga-lakṣaṇā after rejecting jahatī and ajahatī; later Advaita manuals call the same jahad-ajahal-lakṣaṇā

definitions.definition: Object of a meditation on the self, reported by Yāmuna as the Kāpāla means to nirvāṇa (restricted; opponent's report).
The scriptural duties as the Lord's commands, which the surrendered still obey (ājñā), and further services allowed but not required (anujñā).
The Lord as possessing the six qualities (knowledge, power, lordship, strength, virility, splendour) without limit.

literal: the one possessing the six excellences

definitions.definition: The one possessing the six excellences - lordship, valour, fame, fortune, knowledge and detachment - who knows the origin and end of beings, knowledge and ignorance; properly Vāsudeva; with Brahman and Paramātman one of three names of the non-dual reality.
The Lord (Bhagavān), speaker of the Gītā ('śrībhagavān uvāca') and object of the Bhāgavatas' devotion; the Pañcarātra's whole knower is 'the Lord himself' (12.337.63).
The Lord as possessor of the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya).
A devotee of the Lord; the Bhāgavata Purāṇa; devotees are themselves tīrthas (BhP 1.13.10).
A worshipper of Bhagavat (Vāsudeva); the Nārāyaṇīya says Sāṃkhyas together with Bhāgavatas enter Saṃkarṣaṇa on the path of liberation (12.332.16).
A follower of the Pāñcarātra; opponents held the Bhāgavatas/Sātvatas to be a low temple-serving class, Yāmuna that they are brahmins so named for a quality.
Offence against the Lord's devotees, including judging them by birth — graver than offence against the Lord.
The practices of devotion to Bhagavān, to be undertaken from childhood (BhP 7.6.1).
Livelihood of the first and third stages - whatever falls into the bowl.
The deity of the Kāpālikas in hostile portraits (Mahābhairava worshipped with liquor and alleged human offerings); the skull-bearing form of Śiva.
The supreme Śiva as the Trika names him; his true form is indescribable fullness identical with the Goddess, not the forms with parts described for meditation (VBT 7-16).
In the Śiva Sūtra the upsurge of awareness (udyama) is Bhairava (1.5).
The state said to arise in the Kula rite, with the vision of sameness everywhere (Kulārṇava 5.74).
The fifth Mahāvidyā (Tripurabhairavī); Dakṣiṇāmūrti is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.11); matched with Balabhadra (10.10); in the Bṛhaddharma Satī herself is Bhairavī.
The circle of Kaula worship in which all castes are twice-born and all are equal to Śiva, but separate again when it ends (Kulārṇava 8.96-97; Mahānirvāṇa 8.151-154). Restricted: summary only.
The Atharvaveda's healing rites and hymns against fever, consumption, jaundice, leprosy, worms and demons.
Devotional song and worship; the Sants' songs are sung as bhajan in satsaṅg.
In Sant Mat also the technical name of listening to the inner sound current.
Congregational singing of abhaṅgas and the name with cymbals and drum, the daily and nightly practice of Vārkarī groups.
Devotional song to Rāma sung in company.
Worship in general; also the second, inner instruction given after śaraṇ (usage to verify).
Devotional singing, typically congregational, of songs and names of the deity, from 'bhaj' (to share in, worship).

equivalents.note: duplicate id (Hindi form) used by U27; to be merged

definitions.definition: Performance of devotional practice under a guru — the third stage.
A devotee; also the resident monks of a sattra; as bhakta, one of the four real things.
The first sthala: one in whom devotion to Śiva has arisen; its dharma is taught in fifteen sub-sthalas (SSM 5.26–30).
One devoted to the Lord; the four kinds of devotee (BhG 7.16) and the devotee dear to him (12.13–20); 'my devotee never perishes' (9.31).
The Lord's dependence on his devotees — 'I am subject to my devotees, as if not free' (BhP 9.4.63).
The Lord who 'did as he was told' (Tirumaḻicai), who takes whatever form his devotees love (MT 44).
In the Gīta Govinda Kṛṣṇa pleads to place Rādhā's foot on his head (GG 10).

Firm love for Viṣṇu exceeding all other love, preceded by knowledge of his greatness; the sole means of liberation, to which all other practices are subsidiary, and itself eternal bliss in liberation.
Devotion as the Āḻvārs sing it (Tamil pattu/patti): love (aṉpu), longing (ārvam) and a melting heart offered to Tirumāl, given by his grace as 'knowledge-and-love', lived as service and refuge.
Supreme love (parama-prema) for the Lord, of the nature of nectar (NBS 2–3); supreme attachment (parānurakti) to Īśvara (ŚBS 2); not desire, not knowledge, not an act — the fruit itself.
Devotion to the Lord, by which he is known, seen and entered (BhG 11.54); supreme devotion is attained by one who has become Brahman (18.54), and by devotion one knows him in truth (18.55).
One-pointed devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to Nārāyaṇa, 'the one devoted solely, intent on Nārāyaṇa' (MBh 12.336).
Devotion: the natural, motiveless inclination of the senses and mind toward the Lord, greater than liberation; by it alone the Lord is attained; it purifies even outcastes.
Loving devotion to Rāma, the lamp without which knowledge does not shine and the cause of liberation; open to men, women and even animals.
Devotion to the Goddess, the easiest of the three paths, graded by the guṇas and culminating in supreme devotion.

Devotion to Śiva, ninefold (SSM 9.2–3), outer and inner (9.6–9), arising from grace and giving rise to grace (9.11–12); its presence, not birth, makes one a bhakta (9.4–5); in the six-bhakti scheme it rises from faith to samarasa.

Unmotivated, uninterrupted love and service directed to the Lord, the highest dharma (BhP 1.2.6); graded by the guṇas and beyond them (3.29); ninefold in practice (7.5.23-24); the one means that 'wins' the Lord (11.14.20-21).
Meditation that has become love: knowledge in the form of supreme affection (prīti) for the Lord, the means to liberation prescribed by the Upaniṣads.
Devotion: 'to one who has the highest devotion to God and to his teacher as to God, these matters shine forth' (ŚU 6.23).

Devotion as the relish of identity with Śiva; for the one rich in devotion Śiva manifests without meditation or procedure (Śivastotrāvalī 1.1); the intense devotion of the dispassionate is Śaṅkara's power (VBT 121).
Tamil patti: 'devotion is the highest thing on earth' (Kaṭuveḷi 18); the Siddhars' devotion is to the Lord within and to the guru, not to temple images.

cross_language.note: as in 'pattuṭai aṭiyavar', TVM 1.3.1

definitions.definition: The relish of love for Kṛṣṇa, when the permanent emotion of love combines with its excitants, effects, bodily signs and transient emotions; the highest rasa.
The scriptures of devotion, to be reflected upon (NBS 76).
Serving the Lord with unswerving devotion, by which one passes beyond the guṇas and becomes fit for Brahman (BhG 14.26); the theme of ch. 12.
Exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to Nārāyaṇa-Vāsudeva, the highest dharma (Nārāyaṇīya).
The yoga of devotion, fitting one in whom faith in the Lord's stories has arisen, who is neither disgusted with nor too attached to the world.
The loving meditation of the Upaniṣads, the direct means to the Lord, prepared by karma-yoga and jñāna-yoga and supported by the seven aids.
The teachers of devotion named in NBS 83 (Kumāra, Vyāsa, Śuka, Śāṇḍilya, Garga, Viṣṇu, Kauṇḍinya, Śeṣa, Uddhava, Āruṇi, Bali, Hanumān, Vibhīṣaṇa and others), who declare the same without fear.
'Vessel and universe': 'what is in the vessel (body) is in the universe' — the correspondence of body and cosmos.

cross_language.note: cf. 'yat piṇḍe tat brahmāṇḍe' in Nāth and haṭha usage

definitions.definition: The demon born from the ashes of Kāma burnt by Śiva, slain by Lalitā with her powers (LSN 25-33; Lalitopākhyāna).
The 'whirling cave', the fourth region above Mahāsunn, where the flute is heard.
The staging of an aṅkīyā nāṭ in the nāmghar as an act of worship.
The principal act of prapatti: placing the burden of one's protection and its fruit on the Lord; often performed through a teacher.
The region south of the Himālaya and north of the ocean, the one land of action (karma-bhūmi), where the gods wish to be born.
The fullness of Bhairava's state (bharitākārā, VBT 15) and of the practitioner (VBT 24, 72, 117).
Dramatic allegorical folk song in which a village character (scorpion-bitten man, Jogī, madwoman) carries a hidden spiritual meaning; perfected by Eknāth.
Ash, so called because it reproaches sins; bathing in ash is the supreme 'fire-bath' (SSM 7.4–5; 7.23–25).
Ash consecrated with the mantras, used for bathing thrice daily, lying on, re-bathing and initiation; the sign of the first stage.
The Atharvaśiras identifies all the elements with ash: 'fire is ash ... all this is ash'.
The ash of a cremation, smeared by a Kāpālika (Sattasaī) and listed by Yāmuna among the six Kāpāla insignia.
Sacred ash worn by Śaivas (often as the tripuṇḍra), praised in the Śiva Purāṇa.

Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra / later Āyurveda): the calcined preparation of a metal, mineral or gem used as medicine; the texts insist that only properly purified and processed material is used, the impure being life-destroying (RRS 5.47-48, 5.73). RESTRICTED: no processes recorded.
Sacred ash from the sacred fire, smeared on all the limbs in the Pāśupata yoga.
Ash used in the Virajā initiation (Śiva Gītā).
Tirunīṟu, the sacred ash: mantra, medicine and the mark of Śiva's devotee.

notes: Also: vibhūti
alt_notes: Homonym: sacred ash of the Śaiva ascetics.

definitions.definition: Sacred ash, prepared with mantras; worn in the pāśupata vow and the tripuṇḍra.
Bathing the body in consecrated ash at the three junctures of the day.
The retention preceded by forceful bellows-breathing through the nose; it is said to awaken kuṇḍalinī and pierce the three knots.

The eight dispositions of buddhi — virtue, knowledge, dispassion, power and their opposites (SK 23) — innate, natural or acquired (SK 43), which perfume the subtle body (SK 40) and by seven of which prakṛti binds herself (SK 63).
A name of Rudra, paired with Śarva (AVŚ 11.2).
The practitioner's disposition that governs the mode of worship: paśu, vīra or divya; the Kālīvilāsa assigns them to the ages and allows only paśu in the Kali age (4.2-3; 6.10-16).
Emotion: the stage after attachment in Rūpa's sequence, pure sattva that softens the heart; in the Ujjvalanīlamaṇi also the name of mahābhāva's threshold.

Emotional state; so called because, with speech, body and sattva, it 'brings into being' (bhāvayati) the meaning of the poem (NŚ 7.1–3); of three kinds — eight stable, thirty-three transient, eight involuntary; love directed to gods, gurus and kings remains a bhāva (KP 4).

literal: state, feeling; 'that which brings into being'
notes: Disambiguated from trm:bhava (used by other units for Sāṃkhya's bhāvas, Rudra's name 'Bhava' and the Gauḍīya stage 'bhāva').

definitions.definition: Devotion as emotion: the first sprouting of love, a ray of the sun of prema that softens the heart.
The state of the bodiless and those merged in prakṛti, which has becoming as its cause (1.19); Vijñānabhikṣu glosses bhava as birth.
Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka's power of poetic language to 'make present' its content in generalized form (reported by Abhinavagupta).

literal: the liṅga of feeling / of pure being

definitions.definition: The liṅga in which feeling (bhāva) itself dissolves, grasped by devotion and worshipped with flowers of feeling, superior to liṅgas of clay or stone (SSM 15.37–44); in the vacana triad iṣṭa–prāṇa–bhāva the third, beyond form.

notes: SSM 6.49–50 names the third liṅga of the triad tṛptiliṅga.

definitions.definition: Cultivation: of the meaning of the praṇava (1.28), of the four attitudes (1.33), of the opposites of harmful thoughts (2.33); Vyāsa: equanimity toward the wicked is not a cultivation (YBh 3.23).

The operation of the one who brings about, expressed by the verbal suffix: verbal (śābdī) bhāvanā — the prompting power of the injunctive — and objective (ārthī) bhāvanā — the person's activity toward the result; each expects what (sādhya), by what (karaṇa) and how (itikartavyatā).
Contemplative identification: the body as Śrīcakra and worship as non-difference (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad); its firmness brings the power of command (PKS 1.13); the Goddess is 'reached by bhāvanā' (LSN 41).
VP 6.7.48-51: the three contemplations of beings - of Brahman, of action, and of both.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What the unyoked lack; without it there is no peace (2.66). Commentators gloss it as steady contemplation, dwelling on the self, or conviction.
The impression produced by experience that causes memory; resides only in the self (Tarkasaṅgraha).

equivalents.note: both are sustained meditative identification

notes: Glossed by the commentators as meditation or as intent absorption in knowledge of the self.
alt_notes: Homonym: in Buddhist and yoga contexts bhāvanā means cultivation / meditation.

definitions.definition: Ignorance as a positive entity (not a mere absence of knowledge), held by the Vivaraṇa line and later Advaita, proved by the experience 'I am ignorant'; rejected as un-Śaṅkaran by Satchidanandendra (recent).
A non-initiate or one averse to the conduct of the path; the SSM bids the devotee refuse goods sent by bhavis (9.30–32).
Real difference, which is the very nature (svarūpa) of each thing, grasped together with the thing itself; not a separate negation (anyonyābhāva). Fivefold and eternal between God, souls and matter.
Difference-and-non-difference: Brahman is at once one with and different from souls and world (one as cause, many as effect).
Natural difference-and-non-difference of cit and acit from Brahman, like snake and coils.
Held to be inconceivable (acintya) in the relation of the Lord and his powers.
Taking the mendicant's garb: the Bāul initiation into renunciation (with the ālkhāllā robe), after the first initiation (dīkṣā).
The yogī's garb and, by extension, the Nāth order as a body ('the bhekh of the twelve panths').
The sectarian garb and marks of ascetics (ochre, matted locks, earrings, beads, ash), which the Sants reject as display.
A remedy — plants, waters, amulets and spells; Rudra has a thousand (RV 7.46.3); 'the waters are the remedy for all' (10.137.6).
Food begged by the renouncer; five kinds; better than unsolicited food.
Living by begged food, part of the renunciant discipline Cakradhar enjoined.
Living on alms, the mendicant's life (BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22; cf. MuU 1.2.11).
One who lives on alms; four kinds in the Bhikṣuka Upaniṣad.
Experience, which buddhi accomplishes for puruṣa (SK 37); with liberation, one of the two purposes for which prakṛti acts (commentaries on SK 21).

Experience: a cognition that fails to distinguish sattva and puruṣa (3.35); determining the guṇas as desired or undesired without discrimination (YBh 2.18); one of the two purposes of the seen (2.18).
Enjoyment, which in the Kula dharma 'becomes yoga' (Kulārṇava 2.24).
The freed soul's equality with Brahman in the enjoyment of bliss, not in cosmic function.
The regions other than Bhārata, where beings only enjoy the fruits of past deeds.
The soul at the stages of prasādi and prāṇaliṅgi, correlated with the subtle body and the prāṇaliṅga.
The body, as the locus in which the self experiences pleasure and pain.
Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka's power of poetic language to make the rasa enjoyed in a state pervaded by sattva, akin to tasting Brahman (reported by Abhinavagupta).
Puruṣa as experiencer, one proof of its existence (SK 17); experience culminates in consciousness (SS 1.104).
The enjoyer: the self joined with body, senses and mind (KU 1.3.4); enjoyer, enjoyed and impeller as the threefold brahman (ŚU 1.12).
The pitta in the skin that gives lustre (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.14).
Delusion — above all the sectarian delusions of Hindu and Turk and the belief in outward means; 'bhram bidhauṃsaṇ' is its destruction.
The 'bee's cave' in the head, a place of inner absorption in Hindi Nāth and Sant songs.
The retention with a bee-like humming on inhalation and exhalation (HYP); in the GS a nocturnal practice of listening to the inner sounds with the ears closed, the means to nāda-samādhi.
Erroneous vision: false knowledge (YBh 1.30).
Humility — the attitude of a servant toward Śiva and his devotees (dāsōhaṃ).
The point between the eyebrows where gaze and mind are fixed; the HYP calls it the place of Śiva where the mind dissolves.
The twofold fruit that all four pādas of Śiva's scripture serve.
The double fruit of Kaula practice (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 9.15; Kulārṇava 3.11).
Plenitude: that in which one sees, hears and understands nothing else; it is happiness and immortal, established in its own greatness (ChU 7.23-24).
A stage of knowledge (seven) or of ignorance (seven); also the four stages of yoga.
The outer square of the Śrīcakra with three lines and four gates, the first enclosure (trailokyamohana).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Beings, whose beginning and end are unmanifest and middle manifest (2.28), and who arise from food (3.14).
From saṃyama on the five forms of the elements (3.44).
The fourteenfold creation of beings: eight divine, five animal, one human (SK 53; Tattvasamāsa 18).
Scriptures of the western stream (Sadyojāta) for controlling and expelling spirits.
Ahaṃkāra in its tāmasa aspect, from which the subtle elements proceed (SK 25).
The five 'heats' of earth, water, fire, air and space that digest the corresponding elemental qualities of food (Ca Ci 15.13).
Elemental space, extended in the ten directions, the support of wind and clouds.
An arthavāda neither contradicted nor already established by another means (e.g. 'Indra raised the thunderbolt against Vṛtra').
The ritual-meditative dissolution of the body's elements into their sources and the re-creation of a pure, divine body before worship (the Kāmika's 'self-purification' corresponds in function).
Purification of the elements performed before worship of Bhagavān.
Performed by the tantri in the preliminary sequence of Kerala worship.

The branch for those whose minds are seized by gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, ancestors, piśācas, nāgas and grahas, treated by pacificatory rites and offerings (Su Sū 1.8); 'graha' in AHS Sū 1.5. Summary only.
The fourth Mahāvidyā; Tryambaka is her Bhairava, who delights in her in heaven, earth and the underworld (Toḍala 1.9-10); matched with Vāmana (10.10).

Seed-syllable: a monosyllabic mantra (often ending in the nasal bindu) that contains a deity or element in seed form — e.g. laṃ vaṃ raṃ yaṃ haṃ for the elements, hrīṃ, śrīṃ, klīṃ, aiṃ for goddesses; in the threefold bindu, bīja is Śakti (ŚT 1.8–9).
Seed-waking: the first pure, nameless stirring of consciousness, the seed of the future names 'jīva' and the like.
God as the original of which the soul is the reflection; the Lord in one's heart contemplated as 'you are the bimba, I am the reflection'.
The prototype or original of a reflection; in the Vivaraṇa, Īśvara/Brahman as the original of which the jīva is the reflection.

The vital essence (semen; with rajas in women), identified with the moon (Amṛtasiddhi); 'death by the fall of bindu, life by holding bindu' (HYP 3.88); its control is a sign of success (2.78); mind, breath and bindu are made steady together (4.28). Cosmologically bindu is Śiva and rajas Śakti (SS 1.92); Śiva's nature is nāda, bindu and kalā (HYP 4.1).

The central point of the Śrīcakra, abode of Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī, the ocean of nectar (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 8); in the Kāmakalāvilāsa the great point in which Śiva's light is reflected in the mirror of self-awareness, and the pair of white and red points.
The vital drop (semen/seed) whose retention is life and whose fall is death (HYP 3.88); arising from the mind as ghee from milk (Candrāvalokana).
The 'point' arising from nāda (ŚT 1.7), which divides into bindu, nāda and bīja — Śiva, their union and Śakti (ŚT 1.8–9); in mantras the nasal dot (anusvāra).
The point of Oṃ; the seed-essence (white and red) whose retention the haṭha passages seek; identified with mind.
The point arising from Nāda in the Śāradātilaka's account of emanation.
The point of light seen or meditated (VBT 36-37) and a subtle phase of a mantra's utterance (VBT 42, 90).
Pure māyā (śuddha-māyā, mahāmāyā, kuṭilā): the pure material cause of the pure universe, of the bodies of pure beings and of sound; distinct from Śiva, who does not change.

cross_language.note: the drops of the Vajrayāna subtle body

equivalents.note: the white bodhicitta/drop of Buddhist tantra in the Amṛtasiddhi's milieu; functional analogy, not an identity asserted by either tradition

notes: Contribution from U08; U31/U28 own bindu.

definitions.definition: The kapha in the tongue that makes taste known (AHS Sū 12.17).
The first knot; when pierced in the beginning stage, bliss from the void and tinkling inner sounds arise (HYP 4.70).
The hour before dawn for waking and reflecting on dharma, artha and the meaning of the Veda (MDh 4.92).
The innermost path by which breath and kuṇḍalinī rise (HYP 2.46, 3.69); in the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa the channel within citriṇī.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What one attains who abides in the brahmic state even at the time of death (2.72); first use of the term in the text.
The goal reached by one established in the brāhmī state even at death (BhG 2.72) and by sages free of faults, delighting in the welfare of beings, for whom it lies near on every side (5.24–26).

notes: Recurs at BhG 5.24–26 (outside this chunk).

equivalents.note: the Gītā's compound shares the word nirvāṇa with Buddhist usage; whether and how the meanings relate is disputed and each tradition defines its own term

definitions.definition: The liberated self after the final renunciation, no longer perceived, without mark (Ca Śā 1.155; 5.21).

The state of the yogin at peace who has become Brahman (BhG 5.24, 6.27); having become Brahman, serene, he attains supreme devotion (18.54); fitness for it (brahmabhūya) comes from devotion (14.26) and discipline (18.53).
Practice of Brahman: thinking of it, speaking of it, awakening one another to it and being wholly devoted to it.
The wheel of brahman, in which the goose (haṃsa) wanders (ŚU 1.6) and which God's greatness turns (6.1).
The Vedic student, praised in AVŚ 11.5 as quickening both worlds by fuel, girdle, toil and tapas.
Restraint of the generative organ with the senses guarded (YBh 2.30); when established, vigour is gained (2.38).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the third support of life (Ca Sū 11.35); 'the best of paths' (Sū 30.15); among the qualities of good conduct (Sū 8.29) and of the one who lives on constant rasāyana (Ci 1.4.30); required of the initiated medical student (Vi 8.13).
Vedic studentship, by which the debt to the seers is paid (TS 6.3.10.5); the student is withheld from Death if he brings fuel and begs daily (ŚB 11.3.3).
The student's stage in the teacher's house, with chastity, begging and service; temporary or lifelong (naiṣṭhika).

The life of a student of the Veda, celibacy: what people call sacrifice is really brahmacarya (ChU 8.5); the brahma-world belongs to those who find it by brahmacarya (ChU 8.4.3); preparatory year of austerity, celibacy and faith (PrU 1.2).
The vow of celibacy of the meditator (BhG 6.14) and of those desiring the Imperishable (8.11); bodily austerity (17.14); Sanatsujāta's four quarters of brahmacarya (MBh 5.44).

cross_language.note: In Pali the holy life in general

definitions.definition: The sin incurred by Bhairava/Śiva in cutting off Brahmā's head, whose penance - wandering with the skull - the Kāpālika vow imitates.
The desire to know Brahman, i.e. the inquiry into Brahman, with which the Brahma Sūtras open.
The inquiry into Brahman undertaken after acquiring the four means, not after the inquiry into ritual.

The world of brahman: reached by the path of the gods (BAU 6.2.15) and by brahmacarya (ChU 8.4-5); described with its lake, river, tree, city and palace (KauU 1.3-5; ChU 8.5.3); in BAU 4.3.32 the ocean-like non-dual seer 'is the world of brahman'.
The world of the conditioned Brahman (Hiraṇyagarbha), reached by meditators on the qualified Brahman, where they are liberated at the end of the cycle.

In the Ṛgveda, the potent sacred formulation or prayer and the power in it (Bṛhaspati/Brahmaṇaspati is its lord); in the Atharvaveda and Yajurveda, the highest principle: 'that is brahman' (VS 32.1), 'homage to the highest Brahman' (AVŚ 10.8.1), 'those who know Brahman in man know the Supreme' (10.7.17), Brahman entered the golden city of the body (10.2.33).

The ultimate ground: that from which beings arise, by which they live and into which they go (TU 3.1.1); being, one without a second (ChU 6.2.1); truth, knowledge, infinite (TU 2.1.1); understanding and bliss (BAU 3.9.28); described also by negation (BAU 2.3.6). Also the name of the formula or sacred word in older usage.
That from which the origin, sustenance and dissolution of the world proceed, known from the Upaniṣads (BS 1.1.2–4).
The one reality without a second: existence–consciousness–bliss, attributeless (nirguṇa) in itself, identical with the inner self; associated with māyā it is Īśvara, the world-cause.

In Dvaita the word applies primarily to Viṣṇu alone, 'full' (pūrṇa) in qualities; defined as that from which come creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, knowledge, ignorance, bondage and release.
In the Brāhmaṇas: the sacred formulation and the Veda; also the first principle — 'in the beginning this was Brahman' (ŚB 11.2.3.1), 'Brahman the self-existent' (ŚB 10.6.5.9; 13.7.1.1; GB 1.1.1).
The supreme reached by self-knowledge and seeing the self in all (MDh 12.125); 'the one syllable is the supreme Brahman' (VDh 10.5).

The imperishable supreme (BhG 8.3), beginningless, neither being nor non-being (13.12), with hands and feet everywhere (13.13); also the Veda from which ritual action arises (3.15) and the prakṛti called 'great Brahman', the Lord's womb (14.3); 'na mama' is the eternal Brahman (MBh 12.13.4).
In the Purāṇas the supreme reality, identified with Viṣṇu (VP), Śiva (ŚiP), or the Goddess (DBhP); one of three names of non-dual knowledge (BhP 1.2.11).
The supreme reality, Nārāyaṇa, great in essence and qualities and making others great; qualified (saviśeṣa) by souls and matter, never an attributeless consciousness.
The liṅga itself, so named for its vastness and expanding (SSM 6.36–38); the liṅga of light by whose light all shines (12.38–41).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.72 in the compounds brāhmī sthiti and brahmanirvāṇa (the state and goal of the one of steady wisdom). In 3.15 'brahma' arises from the imperishable and is the source of action, and the 'all-pervading brahman' is established in sacrifice; commentators take brahma in 3.15 as the Veda or as prakṛti.
U04 usage: the one reality realized as 'so'ham'; the soundless beyond nāda; the goal of renunciation; named as Nārāyaṇa, Śiva, Rāma or the Goddess in the sectarian Upaniṣads.
Sundardās: the one without a second, known at the end of the path as one's own self.
Brahm is the ruler of Trikuṭī and the universal mind, the highest god of the Vedas but within Kāl's domain; Pārbrahm is the region above it.

cross_language.note: used in Pali mostly for the deity Brahmā or as 'excellent'

notes: U01 contribution: the Saṃhitā senses. The Upaniṣadic and Vedānta definitions are contributed by other units.

equivalents.note: Advaita holds Brahman and the inner self identical; other Vedānta schools deny strict identity.

definitions.definition: The priest who oversees the whole rite in silence and repairs its faults; Vāc makes whom she loves a brahmán (RV 10.125.5).

notes: The Atharvavedic tradition claims this office for Atharvavedins (dsp:atharvaveda-status).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.46 the 'knowing brāhmaṇa', for whom all the Vedas are of as much use as a well amid a flood.
Whatever in the Veda is not mantra (MS 2.1.33): the injunctions, arthavādas and the like.
The prose portion of the Veda that enjoins rites and explains them; 'Veda is the name for mantra and brāhmaṇa' (ĀpŚS 24.1.31–32).

notes: The social class 'brāhmaṇa' is under trm:varna.

definitions.definition: The cosmos, and the body so named because it contains the cosmos (SS 1.91, 2.6; the thousand-petalled lotus is outside the body called brahmāṇḍa, SS 5.151).
The cosmic egg within which the fourteen worlds lie, enclosed by sheaths of the elements; broken up in the elemental dissolution.
The cosmic egg — the universe, all of which is found within the body (piṇḍa).
Established in Brahman: having direct knowledge of the self, the second qualification of the teacher.
A name of suṣumnā (HYP 3.4) and the subtle opening within it; kuṇḍalinī sleeps at its mouth (SS 4.14); fixing the mind there frees from sin (SS 5.141, recalled).
The aperture of Brahman at the crown; place of the space-concentration that opens the door of liberation (GŚ 73) and through which the jīva departs when the skull splits (KJN 20.2).
The opening at the crown; seat of the state beyond the fourth; exit of the breath that does not return.
The opening at the crown through which the yogin departs.
'Relation with Brahman': the initiation in which the disciple dedicates body, senses, mind, family and wealth to Kṛṣṇa, removing the five kinds of faults (Siddhāntarahasya).

'Twin brother of tasting Brahman': Viśvanātha's description of rasa (SD 3.2), following Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka's comparison of aesthetic enjoyment with the tasting of the supreme Brahman — akin to it, not identical with it.
The women named in the Bṛhaddevatā as speakers of Vedic verses.

checks.note: Confirmed: the term and the Bṛhaddevatā list (2.82–84).

definitions.definition: Knowledge of brahman, 'the foundation of all knowledge', taught by Brahmā to Atharvan (MuU 1.1.1); to be taught only to those who performed the head-vow (MuU 3.2.10).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The state of the one of steady wisdom described in 2.55–71; having attained it one is no longer deluded, and abiding in it even at death one attains brahmanirvāṇa (2.72).
The state of the one of steady wisdom, attaining which one is not deluded (BhG 2.72).
The ritual exchange of riddles on cosmic matters (VS 23.9–12); RV 1.164 is composed in this manner.
A formal verbal contest on the hidden meaning of the rite and the cosmos, as between Yājñavalkya and Śākalya (ŚB 11.6.3) or Uddālaka and Svaidāyana (ŚB 11.4.1).
The literary song-language (a blend of Maithili with Assamese or Bengali) used for bargīts and aṅkīyā nāṭs, and in Bengal for Vaiṣṇava lyrics.
Lord of sacred speech (brahmaṇaspati), who smelted the worlds like a smith (RV 10.72.2) and is addressed in the hymn on knowledge (10.71).
The other principal sāman of the soma rite, paired with the rathantara (AVŚ 15.3).
In Mādhva usage the tomb-shrine of an ascetic saint, where the tradition holds the saint to remain present (e.g. Rāghavendra at Mantrālaya, Vyāsatīrtha at Nava Brindāvana).
Nourishing therapy against emaciation and depletion (Ca Sū 22).

literal: one wishing to enjoy / one wishing to be liberated

definitions.definition: The two orientations of Mantramārga initiates: seeking powers and enjoyments in the higher worlds, or seeking liberation; the Mantramārga caters for both.
In the Vasiṣṭha–Karāla dialogue, the twenty-sixth, the ever-awakened (MBh 12.296.7, 12.296.11).

notes: U05's definition (the epic Sāṃkhya usage); the Buddhist sense is defined by the Buddhist units.

definitions.definition: Not different from apprehension and knowledge (NS 1.1.15); a non-eternal quality of the self, not an eternal inner instrument (against Sāṃkhya, NS 3.2.1–9).
The cause of all usage; memory or experience (Tarkasaṅgraha).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The understanding declared 'according to sāṃkhya' and 'according to yoga', joined with which one casts off the bondage of action (2.39); when resolute it is single, when irresolute many-branched (2.41); it must cross the thicket of delusion and stand immovable in samādhi (2.52–53); it is destroyed after the loss of memory (2.63) and becomes steady in serenity (2.65); higher than the mind (3.42) and one of the seats of desire (3.40). Arjuna asks why action is urged if buddhi is superior (3.1).

The determining faculty (adhyavasāya, SK 23), whose sāttvika form is virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power and whose tāmasa form is their opposite; the door-keeper among the instruments (SK 35), which accomplishes all experience for puruṣa and discriminates puruṣa from pradhāna (SK 37).
The instrument of cognition (the 'power of seeing') whose apparent identity with the seer is I-am-ness (YBh 2.6); neither the same as the puruṣa nor wholly different (YBh 2.20).
The understanding, higher than mind (BhG 3.42); resolute and one in the yogin (2.41); its destruction follows loss of memory (2.63); threefold by the guṇas (18.29–32).
Intellect: the inner organ as deciding; the seat of the reflected consciousness and of the ego's agency.
Intellect: the charioteer (KU 1.3.3); higher than mind, below the great self (KU 1.3.10); it does not stir in the highest state (KU 2.3.10).

notes: Distinct from the Sāṃkhya-Yoga buddhi (mahat), a principle of prakṛti.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The discipline of action yoked with understanding: action is far inferior to it (2.49); yoked with it one casts off good and evil deeds (2.50) and the wise, abandoning the fruit of action, are freed from the bondage of birth (2.51); introduced as the 'yoga' form of the teaching at 2.39.
Action guided by the resolute understanding that is free from attachment to fruits (BhG 2.49–50); the Lord gives it to his loving devotees (10.10) and Arjuna is told to resort to it (18.57).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What the wise should not cause in the ignorant who are attached to action (3.26; cf. 3.29 'should not unsettle').
Ear, skin, eye, tongue and nose (SK 26), whose function is mere awareness (ālocana) of sound and the rest (SK 28); later called jñānendriya.
The twenty-fifth as unawakened yet awakening (MBh 12.294.43; 12.296.3–10).
Consciousness as the self (Śiva Sūtra 1.1); Kṣemarāja: the absolute freedom of knowing and doing.
The guru within the heart: the Lord as Paramātman guiding from within.
'Dying without dying': the death of ego and the mortal body while living, by which death is conquered (Aḻukaṇṇi 9; Rāmatēvar 2; Kuṭampai 13).

A centre of the subtle body along the central channel; the texts differ in number and attributes — six plus the thousand-petalled lotus (ṢCN; GŚ), nine (Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati), with sixteen supports (ādhāra), three targets and five voids in the Nāth body-maps.
A centre (wheel/lotus) of the body; Nāth texts count six (Yogaviṣaya, GŚ), nine (SSP) or eleven (KJN).
A centre of the subtle body; six (or nine) in the Yoga Upaniṣads; also the Śrīcakra.

In the Tamil Siddha texts the centres are usually called ātāram (supports), six in number, with the crown-space above them; cakkaram names also the worship-diagram (the Meru of forty-three triangles, Caṭṭaimuṉi 1).
Centres through which the power rises (VBT 29); the Netratantra names six wheels, sixteen supports, three targets and five voids (Netra 7.1).

cross_language.note: the Vajrayāna channel-wheels (usually four or five)

definitions.definition: The image for the knower's continued embodiment by residual momentum (SK 67; SS 3.83).

The presiding goddess of each enclosure of the Śrīcakra: Tripurā, Tripureśī, Tripurasundarī, Tripuravāsinī, Tripurāśrī, Tripuramālinī, Tripurāsiddhā, Tripurāmbā and, at the centre, Mahātripurasundarī.
One of the Haṭharatnāvalī's eight cleansing acts, a cleansing of the anus.
The litany of petitions 'and … for me' (TS 4.7; VS 18).
Harmony, equal flavour: Tāyumāṉavar's reconciliation of Vedānta and Siddhānta (vētānta cittānta camaracam), later taken up by Vallalar.
Wonder, the life of rasa (SD 3.3); for Abhinavagupta the self-relishing of consciousness in aesthetic experience; for Viśvanātha's ancestor Nārāyaṇa the reason why the marvellous is the one rasa.
The wondering relish of consciousness in itself; in the Śiva Sūtra 'wonder' marks the stages of yoga (1.12).
Kālī's name after slaying Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (DM 7).
The fierce Goddess of the Devī Māhātmya.
The moon in the head / at the root of the palate, made of nectar, raining downward (GŚ 57–58; SS 2.6–9); the left channel; in the Amṛtasiddhi identified with bindu.
The moon at the root of the palate, made of nectar, raining downward (GŚ 57–58); the left side and left nostril (AmŚ 71).
Where the Kubjikā teaching was first given (Kubjikāmata 1, 'Candradvīpāvatāra'; 2.21).
Where the Kaula scripture came down, brought by Matsyendra (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 22.12).
The penance in which food follows the waning and waxing moon (MDh 11.216) — restricted content.
Bhagavad Gītā 18.66, read as the Lord's command to surrender to him alone, with the promise of freedom from all sins.
A school of Vedic study and ritual practice, often coextensive with a śākhā and its sūtras.

The 'four moons': coded name for four bodily substances whose secret handling under a guru belongs to Bāul body practice; recorded only as a name (restricted), with the tradition's warnings that it is secret and ruinous without a guru.

notes: RESTRICTED: no method or substance-handling details are recorded.

definitions.definition: The four things of the dharma: the name (nāma), God (deva), the guru and the community of devotees (bhakta).
The Kaula sacrificial food (caru) of the non-dual rite (caru-advaita), including substances ordinarily forbidden; restricted, summary only (KJN 11).
'Chewing': the relishing through which rasa exists — for Abhinavagupta rasa is not a thing produced but consists in this relishing and lasts as long as it lasts.
The series of acts from ash-bathing to feigned folly; threefold as gift, worship and austerity; twofold as vows and doors; the second means to the gains.
Conduct: the first of the four pādas (and a section of each Āgama) — rules of life and service.
Cariyai: temple service — cleaning, lamps, garlands, singing — the servant's path (dāsa-mārga), leading to sālokya.
Caste (birth-group), which the Siddhars declare baseless — 'is there a difference in flesh, skin and bone?' (Sivavākkiyar); 'the castes called unequal are one' (Kaṭuveḷi 32).

equivalents.note: Tamil form of jāti (in the social sense)

definitions.definition: The sixty-four Bhairava tantras in eight groups of eight (Śrīkaṇṭhīya).
The sixty-four tantras 'of the Mothers' named in the Vāmakeśvara, by which Paśupati 'beguiled the world' before revealing the Goddess's own tantra (Saundaryalaharī 31).
The circle of sixty-four yoginīs worshipped in hypaethral circular temples (Hirapur, Ranipur-Jharial, Bheraghat, Mitaoli); their names differ between lists.
The four verses spoken by the Lord to Brahmā (BhP 2.9.32-35), held to be the seed of the whole Bhāgavata.
The fourfold order created by the Lord according to the division of guṇas and actions (BhG 4.13).
The four pillars of treatment — physician, medicine, attendant, patient — each with four qualities (Ca Sū 9.3-9; AHS Sū 1.27).
The square ritual ground and rite (caukā āratī) of the Dharamdāsī Kabīr Panth, performed for initiation and for the dead, with coconut, betel and lamps.
The round of 8.4 million species of birth through which the soul wanders; the human birth, rare within it, is the only chance to be freed.
The true or perfect reality — the Real, Śiva; in the Kuṟaḷ the reality to be seen for birth to end.
A red calcined preparation of a metal or mineral.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: Sentient dependent beings: Lakṣmī (eternally untouched by sorrow) and all souls, divided by their relation to sorrow and their fitness.
Puruṣa is conscious; the manifest and unmanifest are unconscious (acetana) (SK 11); the unconscious liṅga appears conscious through conjunction (SK 20).
Countering a statement by supposing an alternative meaning; verbal, generalizing and figurative (NS 1.2.10–17).
Vedic metre; the metres came from the Puruṣa sacrifice (RV 10.90.9).

Metre, the 'feet' of the Veda (PŚ 41); so called because the gods covered (chad) themselves with the metres against death (ChU 1.4.2). In Pāṇini, also the Vedic language as opposed to ordinary speech.

The cutting of the tongue's frenum prescribed, together with 'moving' (cālana) and 'milking' (dohana), in the preparation for khecarī. RESTRICTED: recorded as a term only; the procedure is not reproduced.
The fourth stage, ending in the cutting [of bonds], in the cremation ground.
The sixth Mahāvidyā; her Bhairava is Kabandha, by whose worship one becomes lord of all powers (Toḍala 1.12-13); matched with Nṛsiṃha (10.9).
The semblance or reflection of consciousness in the intellect, which makes the inner organ appear conscious; together with the kūṭastha it constitutes the jīva.
The space of consciousness: the knower within and without all beings that reveals existence; mind-space and elemental space arise from it.
'The space of consciousness': Chidambaram (Tillai), where Śiva dances in the 'small hall' (ciṟṟampalam); also the heart-space.
The bliss of consciousness gained by unfolding the centre, which, made firm, is liberation in life (PH 16-17).
'The play of consciousness': the name later given to Jñāneśvar's teaching in the Amṛtānubhava that the one reality sports as the world without change or second.
The mode of worship of Tārā/Nīlasarasvatī learned in Mahācīna; Vasiṣṭha was sent there by the Goddess and taught the Kula way by the Buddha (Rudrayāmala 17; Tārā Tantra 1).
The palace of wish-gems at the centre of Śrīnagara, whose four doors are the four transmissions (PKS 3.10; LSN 22; SL 8).
Sentient reality: the individual souls, eternal, atomic knowers, bound, freed or eternally free; one of the three realities.
Consciousness: self-luminous awareness, the nature of the self and of Brahman, never an object.
The conscious reality: the souls, one of the three realities.
Consciousness-power: the Goddess as the power of the sentient, who is also the power of the insentient (LSN 90).
Śiva's power of consciousness, inseparable from him, identified with Umā and with the supreme ether; the world subsists in it subtly.
Consciousness as free power, the cause of the universe (PH 1); contracted, it is the individual and the mind (PH 4-5); its essence is reflexive awareness (ĪPK 1.5.13).
The puruṣa as the power of consciousness: unchanging, not passing over into objects, pure and infinite (YBh 1.2); kaivalya is its establishment in its own form (4.34).
Vācaspati's name for puruṣa as consciousness, to which suffering is disagreeable (on SK 1, 5).
Yama's recorder of the deeds of beings, consulted at judgment.
A subtle channel within suṣumnā (within vajrā, per the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa), 'dear to Śiva', in which is the brahmarandhra (SS 2.18).

literal: mind; that which is conscious (as if)

definitions.definition: The mind, a product of prakṛti made of the three guṇas, whose activities are to be stilled; it is seen, not self-luminous, and exists for the sake of the puruṣa; one, having many objects, and enduring (YBh 1.32). Commentators gloss it as the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

Thought: a rung above intention in Sanatkumāra's ladder (ChU 7.5); with whatever thought one has one enters breath at death (PrU 3.10); 'the mind alone is saṃsāra' (cittam eva hi saṃsāraḥ, MaiU 6.34).
The inner organ as remembering and reflecting (in the fourfold Advaita division); in general usage, mind.
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda, Bhela): citta rests in the heart and is the cause of all cognitions and actions; those of good citta go the good path (Bhela Ci 8).
Consciousness descended and contracted by the knowable (PH 5); turned inward, it becomes consciousness again (PH 13).
The bound self is the mind (Śiva Sūtra 3.1); the mind is mantra (2.1).

equivalents.note: Nāgeśa glosses citta as antaḥkaraṇa; Yoga uses citta for the whole inner organ (buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas together) rather than naming its parts.

definitions.definition: The five levels of the mind — scattered, stupefied, distracted, one-pointed, stilled (YBh 1.1).
The clearing of the mind that results from the four attitudes; the clear mind becomes one-pointed (1.33, YBh 1.33).

cross_language.note: Buddhist 'serenity/confidence of mind'

definitions.definition: Purification of the mind, the proper result of selfless action, which makes one fit for knowledge.
The name of the nine obstacles (1.30); called impurities of yoga and adversaries of yoga (YBh 1.30).
The space of mind: the creator pervading all through its conceiving.
For the Siddhars, Civam is the supreme within the body, identical with love ('love is Civam', TM 270) and reached by inner knowledge rather than temple ritual.
Śiva as the auspicious absolute (neuter), identified with love in Tirumantiram 270.

The statement that impels to action (Śabara); the injunction, which alone makes known dharma, including what is future, subtle or remote. Śabara on MS 2.1.5 also uses 'codanā' for the apūrva the injunction makes known.

equivalents.note: codanā is the older (sūtra/bhāṣya) word; vidhi is the manual term, which also names one of the five kinds of Vedic sentence

definitions.definition: Light, flame: the Lord seen as light within ('the light mingled within', Sivavākkiyar; 'like the inner light of a ruby', Aḻukaṇṇi; 'the supreme light' parañcōti).
Simply being still: the silent guru's instruction 'be still' (cummā iru) and the state of mind at rest that Tāyumāṉavar holds harder than every power.

equivalents.note: stillness of mind, of which outer silence is one form

definitions.definition: A lime-like calcined preparation, held very potent.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: A herbal powder.
Purification: the processing by which toxic minerals, metals and plants are said to be rendered usable; the tradition insists that unpurified substances are poison. Term only; no procedure.

The fifth state of the afflictions, in one whose affliction-seeds are burnt by reflection, who is 'skilled' and in the last body (YBh 2.4); burnt-seed impressions give rise to no cognitions (4.28, YBh 4.28).
The small (space): 'in this city of brahman is a small lotus-dwelling, within it a small space; what is within that is to be sought' (ChU 8.1.1).
The small space of the heart where the Samayin imagines and worships the Śrīcakra (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 8; Bhāskararāya on LSN 37).
The small space in the lotus of the heart (Chāndogya 8.1), identified with Śiva as the supreme ether and the seat of meditation.

equivalents.note: the dahara is the space within the heart, not the heart itself

definitions.definition: Fate: in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha nothing but one's own former effort (prāk-pauruṣa); a name given to the fruit of one's deeds, without form, act or power of its own; relying on it is delusion.
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): one's own deed of a former body (Ca Vi 3.30; Śā 1.116; 2.44); balanced against present effort (Vi 3.29-36).
The divine or fated factor, the fifth cause of action (BhG 18.14); which does not bear fruit without human effort, as a seed without a field (MBh 13.6.7).
Mantra, herbs worn, gems, auspicious rites, offerings, gifts, oblations, observances, expiation, fasting, benedictions, prostration and pilgrimage (Ca Sū 11.54; Vi 8.87).
The set of virtues — fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in knowledge and yoga, non-harm, truth, compassion and the rest — that leads to liberation (BhG 16.1–3, 16.5).
Skill and effective will; Vasiṣṭha pleads that his fault was 'not my own will (dakṣa)' (RV 7.86.6); Dakṣa is also the god born of Aditi (10.72.4).
The sacrificial fee and gift to the priests; the givers of gifts stand high in heaven and partake of immortality (RV 10.107.2).
The gift to the officiating priests, the 'human gods', as oblations go to the gods (ŚB 2.2.2.6); it does not reach the world attained by knowledge (ŚB 10.5.4.16).
The right-hand conduct; the Goddess 'abides on the right and left paths' and is 'worshipped by the dakṣiṇa and non-dakṣiṇa' (LSN 169-171).
The fourth mode: 'right-hand' worship of the Goddess without the Kaula substances (or with substitutes); in Bengal the usual mode of Kālī worship.
The southern fire, associated with the fathers and protection.
The four-armed Kālī on Śiva as a corpse, with sword and severed head, fear-dispelling and boon-giving hands (Kālī Tantra as quoted in the Tantrasāra); consort Mahākāla (Toḍala 1.3).

literal: Kālī 'of the south' / the propitious Kālī

definitions.definition: The Southern transmission; in the later scheme the cult of Kāmeśvarī / Tripurasundarī (Śrīvidyā).
Breath (Persian dam), as the vehicle on which the Man moves; the subject of coded breath practice (restricted, summary only).
Self-restraint, a mark of the divine endowment (BhG 16.1) and one of the three 'horses of Brahman' (MBh 11.7.19); taught by the Haṃsa (12.288).
Self-control: restraining the outer organs and turning them back to their sources.
Self-restraint: the gods' 'da' (BAU 5.2); among the virtues of BAU 4.4.23 (dānta); foundation of the upaniṣad with austerity and work (Kena 4.8).
Giving of wealth and food; the giver's wealth does not waste away, and 'who eats alone has only sin' (RV 10.117).
Giving, sāttvic when given because it ought to be given, to one who makes no return, at the right place and time to a worthy recipient (BhG 17.20).
