Made of mind: the self within the breath-self (TU 2.3); also the person made of mind in the heart (TU 1.6; BAU 5.6; ChU 3.14.2).
The sheath of mind: mind with the five organs of knowledge, the seat of doubt and desire.
The sixth kind of samādhi in the GS (7.6, 7.16), and in the HYP the effect of mūrcchā retention (2.69).
Dissolution of mind, 'with form' in the jīvanmukta and 'without form' in the videhamukta.
Dissolution of the mind: the mind's ceasing to take on forms, practised by the knower for stable abidance.
The steadiness of mind when the breath moves in the middle (HYP 2.42); the one state (3.54); saluted as a goddess (4.64).
Synonym of unmanī and samādhi (HYP 4.3); also a name of Śakti (KJN 20.11).
The end of sound and of mind; the goal of nāda-yoga; also a measure of the sixteen-measured praṇava.
'Jewel of the mind' — the supreme goddess as mother and light in the Siddhar worship; in yoga texts also the name of the state beyond mind (manonmanī).
The 'kingdom of the mind': fancy or day-dream, which in the stories (Śukra, Lavaṇa) creates whole lives.
A circle: (1) the three circles of fire, sun and moon among the ninety-six principles; (2) in Siddha medicine a fixed course of treatment (commonly forty or forty-eight days).
Walking as if one's foot were injured.

notes: SDS reads mandana.

definitions.definition: A Vedic verse or formula used in rite and recitation; its meaningfulness was defended by Yāska against Kautsa (Nirukta 1.15–16); in the Saṃhitā 'common be your mantra (counsel)' (RV 10.191.3).
The portion of the Veda recited during the rite as prompting its performance; the rest is Brāhmaṇa (MS 2.1.32–33). Mantras have meaning like ordinary sentences (MS 1.2.40).
Mantras are meaningful by reminding the performer of items connected with the performance; an unseen purpose for their recitation is assumed only where no seen purpose is possible.
The Saṃhitā portion of the Veda — verses, formulas and chants — which, with the Brāhmaṇa, makes up the Veda (ĀpŚS 24.1.31); to be recited with exact accent (PŚ 52) and understood (Nirukta 1.15–18).

A sacred formula made of the letters (mātṛkā), each with its seer, metre, deity, seed, power and pin; mantras proper have male deities, vidyās female; they are male, female or neuter by their endings (ŚT 2.57–59) and fiery or lunar (ŚT 2.60–63).
Śiva's powers present as sound-forms through which ritual acts; the perfected mantras paralyse and destroy the soul's bonds in initiation.
The mind is mantra (Śiva Sūtra 2.1); mantras rest on the strength of spanda and dissolve in it with the worshipper's mind (SK 2.1-2).

Tamil mantiram: the Siddhars use seed-syllables (the three letters of Vālai, the five letters) yet ask 'for those who stand in the true tantra, why mantra?' (Kuṭampai 7) and prize the unspoken mantra.

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan maθra.
alt_notes: Contribution from U08; U31 owns mantra theory.

definitions.definition: The 'consciousness' or life of a mantra: without it a mantra is only letters; it is awakened by the guru's transmission, purification and the practitioner's absorption.

equivalents.note: the Śaiva 'potency of mantra' (Śiva Sūtra 1.22, 2.3)

definitions.definition: A defect of a mantra (cut, obstructed, powerless, asleep and forty-five more, ŚT 2.64–70) that makes it fail to protect the practitioner.
The knower at the level of śuddhavidyā.
The ten purifications of a mantra — generation, enlivening, striking, awakening, consecration, cleansing, strengthening, satiation, kindling, guarding (ŚT 2.112–113).
Success or perfection in a mantra, when after purification and puraścaraṇa the mantra 'awakens' and gives its fruit — enjoyment and liberation.
The first and lowest of the four yogas: placing the mātṛkā letters on the body and repeating a mantra; fit for the mild (mṛdu) practitioner, who succeeds in twelve years (DYŚ 11–13; SS 5.11).
The first of the four yogas; repetition, or the natural haṃsa reversed.
The knower at the level of Sadāśiva.

The initiatory division of Śaivism whose scriptures (Siddhānta and non-Saiddhāntika tantras) give both powers/enjoyment and liberation through initiation, mantra-worship and yoga; the fifth and highest stream after the worldly, Vedic, spiritual and Atimārga paths.
The other great division of Śaivism, beside the Atimārga, whose scriptures (Siddhānta and Bhairava tantras) describe and outrank the Atimārga.
The division of the Bhairava tantras centred on a male Bhairava, chiefly Svacchandabhairava.
Experienced by attending to the great lake (Śiva Sūtra 1.22); in PH 20 the perfect I-ness is the potency of the great mantra.
The knower at the level of Īśvara.
Progenitor and law-giver presiding over a manvantara; the present is the seventh, Vaivasvata; the eighth will be Sāvarṇi (the Devī Māhātmya's Suratha).
Worship of the human: God is served and found in the human being, above all in the guru.
The Kartābhajā maxim 'worship the human'.
The period of one Manu, seventy-one ages of the gods (MDh 1.79).
The period ruled by one Manu, about 71 cycles of the four yugas; fourteen make a day of Brahmā; each has its own Manu, Indra, gods, seven sages and avatāra.

The two kinds of music: mārga, the 'sought-out' divine music fixed by Brahmā and Bharata that gives well-being when performed before Śiva, and deśī, regional music that delights people (ŚR 1.1.22–23; Bṛhaddeśī 13).
Gnosis: the fourth and inmost of the four ways (after śariyat, tarikat, hakikat) by which Bāul-Fakirs place their path beyond the law — recorded as context (Sufi vocabulary).
The image, attached to the Teṅkalai, of the kitten carried by the mother cat: the Lord saves without the soul's effort.

notes: As for trm:markata-nyaya.

definitions.definition: The image, attached to the Vaṭakalai, of the baby monkey that clings to its mother: the soul must make the act of surrender.

literal: the maxim of the young monkey
notes: Label used in the dispute literature and modern accounts; the schools' own texts argue in other terms.

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): one hundred and seven vital points of five kinds — of flesh (11), vessels (41), ligaments (27), bone (8) and joints (20) (Su Śā 6.3-4); the three great marmas are head, heart and bladder (Ca Sū 29.3). (Marma in depth: U58.)
The eighteen vital points of the body through which the breath is moved in one kind of withdrawal (Yoga Yājñavalkya; Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā).
One of eighteen vital points through which breath and attention are moved in pratyāhāra; 'cut' in the Kṣurikā.
The storm-gods, sons of Rudra (RV 2.33.1).
The path of rule: devotion and liberation pursued through scriptural discipline and means.
Rāma as the supreme person who keeps every bound of dharma — as son, brother, husband and king.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Kṛṣṇa's teaching (me matam), which those who follow with faith are released from actions and those who cavil at are lost (3.31–32).
The palmyra-stem 'horse' ridden through the streets by a spurned lover to shame the beloved; Tirumaṅkai's heroine threatens to ride it, though convention reserved it for men.
The ninth Mahāvidyā; Mataṅga (Dakṣiṇāmūrti) is her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.15); matched with Rāma (10.10); also worshipped as Ucchiṣṭa-Mātaṅgī.
The gross body, which perishes (SK 39); in the Kramadīpikā made of six sheaths — hair, blood and flesh from the mother, sinew, bone and marrow from the father.
A name of the One named in RV 1.164.46; the messenger who brought fire.
The yogin's small secluded hut, whose place and construction the HYP (1.12–13) and GS (5.5–7) prescribe.
A Nāth monastery (Gorakhpur, Tilla Jogian, Kadri, Dhinodhar, Asthal Bohar and others).
'Goodness of understanding': the knowledge-and-love 'free of delusion' that the Lord graciously gave Nammāḻvār (TVM 1.1.1); the commentators take it as knowledge that has taken the form of bhakti.

cross_language.note: commentarial gloss

equivalents.note: as glossed by the commentators: knowledge become love

literal: having me as the highest; intent on me

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One should sit disciplined, intent on Kṛṣṇa, having restrained all the senses (2.61).
Vowel quantity: short, long and prolated (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.27); one of the six topics of phonetics (TU 1.2).
A measure of Oṃ: a, u, m and the half-measure; twelve measures in the Nādabindu, sixteen in the Nāradaparivrājaka.

literal: contact of the senses with objects

definitions.definition: The contacts of senses and objects giving cold and heat, pleasure and pain, transient and to be endured (BhG 2.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Sense-contacts give cold and heat, pleasure and pain; they come and go, are impermanent, and are to be endured (2.14).
The ground of limited knowledge (Śiva Sūtra 1.4); the groups of letters are presided over by Māheśvarī and the other mothers of the bound (3.19).
The letters from A to KṢA in their natural order as the emanation of the tattvas (Parātrīśikā 5-9).

The 'little mothers': the fifty (or fifty-one) letters from a to kṣa, manifestations of śabda-brahman through kuṇḍalinī (ŚT 1.14), the body of the Goddess and of every mantra; placed on the body in mātṛkā-nyāsa.
The fifty letters as the 'little mothers', matrix of mantras; the Goddess is of the form of the fifty seats (LSN 156); mātṛkā is placed on the disciple's body at initiation (PKS 1.39).

literal: the 'little mother': the power of the letters

definitions.definition: The will or pleasure of the Supreme (and of the Master), to which the disciple surrenders; everything happens by the Mauj.
'Mother': the Vārkarīs' name for Viṭṭhala and for Jñāneśvar, expressing God and the saint as mother to the devotee.
Silence, part of mental austerity (BhG 17.16) and mark of the dear devotee (12.19); 'of secrets I am silence' (10.38); for Sanatsujāta, the true muni's silence (MBh 5.42–43).
Tamil mauṉam: silence — Pattirakiriyār's 'taking the form of a mute' (19); the silent guru of Tāyumāṉavar.
The state of the muni, by which the sages were 'exhilarated' and mounted the winds (RV 10.136.3).
The wondrous creative power by which Varuṇa measured out the earth (RV 5.85.5) and Indra goes in many forms (6.47.18); the wise see the bird 'anointed with the asura's māyā' (10.177.1).
The notion of self in the non-self by which saṃsāra is imagined; it has the powers of projection and veiling.
The Goddess's own inseparable power, neither real nor unreal nor both; conventionally called ignorance, in truth not other than her.
The power by which all that is grasped by mind and senses is a perishable mental creation; bondage and liberation are said by reference to its guṇas.
The Lord's beginningless, indescribable power, consisting of the three guṇas, known from its effects, by which the one Brahman appears as the world; neither real nor unreal (VC 108–109).
In Vidyāraṇya's usage, prakṛti with pure sattva, the adjunct of Īśvara, as distinct from avidyā with impure sattva, the adjunct of the jīva.

The Lord's power: by his own māyā he comes into being (BhG 4.6); his divine māyā made of the guṇas is hard to cross except by taking refuge in him (7.14); by it he moves beings as if on a machine (18.61).

Śiva's power through which he takes names and forms (SSM 1.9) and by whose concealment difference in Śiva is imagined (14.8–9); the Vīramāheśvara keeps it away (5.17–18). Allama: gold, woman and land are not māyā — the desire before the mind is.
The Lord's power by which what is not real appears (BhP 2.9.33); the gross and subtle forms are fashioned by its guṇas (1.3.30).

Power, magic, illusion; deceit: Indra goes about in many forms by his māyās (BAU 2.5.19); know prakṛti to be māyā and the great Lord the māyin (ŚU 4.10); the cessation of all māyā (ŚU 1.10); in PrU 1.16 māyā is deceit.
In Madhva's usage chiefly God's will (icchā) or wisdom, and also prakṛti; not an indeterminable illusion. The 'māyā' of the Advaitins is identified polemically with the Buddhist saṃvṛti.
Not an illusion-producing ignorance but prakṛti, called māyā because it produces manifold wonderful effects, and the Lord's wonderful power; the world it produces is real.
The Goddess's own power by which she becomes and veils the world; she is 'of the form of both knowledge and ignorance' (LSN 87) and 'the substratum of the illusory world' (LSN 142).

Sixth tattva: the Lord's power of concealment - 'the supreme freedom of Maheśa which accomplishes the impossible' (Paramārthasāra 15) - making the knowable appear as separate; real as a power, not an inexplicable illusion.

The great swindler (mahāṭhaginī) with the noose of the three qualities, who takes a different form in every house (Lakṣmī, Bhavānī, idol, pilgrim-water) and binds the world; also 'gold and woman' (kanak-kāminī).
Māyā, the material power ruling the lower regions under Kāl.
One, eternal, insentient, real substance: the material cause of the impure universe (and, as bindu or mahāmāyā, of the pure). Not illusion.
'I and mine, you and yours': the power that holds all beings; a painting without colour on the void, neither simply true nor false.

notes: Other lineages (Advaita, Śaiva, Buddhist) contribute very different definitions of māyā; the Vedic sense is creative, wondrous power. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (2.5.19) quotes RV 6.47.18.

equivalents.note: Identical in the Vivaraṇa and Saṃkṣepaśārīraka usage (one entity under two aspects); distinguished by Vidyāraṇya (pure vs impure sattva).
māyā as material cause vs māyā as bond

alt_notes: Advaita commentators read māyā as the principle of appearance; the Vaiṣṇava commentators as the Lord's real power (prakṛti).

definitions.definition: Dvaita's name for Advaita Vedānta (its adherents 'māyins'), whose tenets — the world's falsity, the indeterminable, identity of soul and Brahman — are refuted.
Māyēyam: the products of māyā (bodies, organs, worlds, objects), counted as the fourth of the five malas.
The possessor of māyā, the great Lord who projects the world (ŚU 4.9-10).
The impurity of difference: the appearance of the knowable as separate (ĪPK 3.2.5).
The bond of māyā: the body, instruments, worlds and objects given to the soul from māyā, which both bind and help it by awakening its powers partly.

notes: Same name as in the Śaiva Siddhānta, where the impurity is held to be a real substance.

definitions.definition: 'The dark one' / 'the wondrous one': the Saṅgam and Āḻvār name of Viṣṇu-Kṛṣṇa, dark-hued, of wondrous deeds (māyam).

literal: the dark one; the one of wonders

equivalents.note: Māyōṉ stresses darkness and wonder; same Lord

definitions.definition: The fourth tissue: gives unctuousness, sweat and firmness and nourishes bone (Su Sū 15.5).
Wisdom and retentive intelligence, invoked as a goddess by students (AVŚ 6.108; 1.1).
Rejuvenatives that promote the intellect — maṇḍūkaparṇī, liquorice, guḍūcī and above all śaṅkhapuṣpī (Ca Ci 1.3.30-31).
Festival gathering of Bāuls and fakirs (Joydeb-Kenduli at Pauṣ Saṃkrānti; Lalon's festival at Cheuṛiyā), for singing, sādhu-sevā and teaching.
A parent scale under which rāgas are grouped; Veṅkaṭamakhin's scheme of seventy-two melas.

notes: Disambiguated from trm:mela (festival).

definitions.definition: A waxy preparation, often containing mineral ingredients.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: The golden axial mountain at the centre of Jambudvīpa, with the cities of the gods on its summit; the VP gives it 84,000 yojanas above ground and 16,000 below.

notes: Also: sumeru

definitions.definition: Realization of the truth (Kuṟaḷ ch. 36).
Investigation of the meaning of the Veda; the school founded on Jaimini's sūtras (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā), distinguished from the Uttara Mīmāṃsā (Vedānta).
Prakṛti, in which sattva is mixed with rajas and tamas; the material of bodies and worlds; it veils the soul's knowledge.

Moderate diet: smooth, sweet food eaten to please Śiva, leaving a quarter of the stomach empty (HYP 1.58); chief of the yamas (HYP 1.38; DYŚ 30); without it yoga brings disease (GS 5.16); half food, a quarter water, a quarter air (GS 5.22).
Moderate, sweet, unctuous food leaving a quarter of the stomach empty; chief of the yamas.
Śrī and Nārāyaṇa together as the one object of surrender and of service.

False: what appears but is sublated by knowledge; defined as indescribable, as the counterpositive of absence in its own locus in all three times, as removable by knowledge, or as other than the real (five definitions in the Advaitasiddhi).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One who restrains the organs of action but sits recalling sense objects in the mind is called a hypocrite (3.6).
The root of the series leading to pain (NS 1.1.2); its forms include 'there is no self', taking the non-self for the self, pain for pleasure, the impermanent for the permanent (NBh 1.1.2).

equivalents.note: Yoga's avidyā (YS 2.5) is likewise taking the impermanent, impure, painful and non-self as permanent, pure, pleasant and self; Nyāya's list overlaps but belongs to a different account of self.

definitions.definition: The Advaita claim that the world is false; Dvaita refutes the proposed definitions and the inferences from perceivability, insentience and limitedness.
Varuṇa's companion, god of alliance; 'may we look on one another with the eye of Mitra (a friend)' (VS 36.18).

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan Miθra.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The steadfast are not bewildered by the passage to another body (2.13); understanding must cross the thicket of delusion (mohakalila, 2.52); delusion (saṃmoha) arises from anger and leads to loss of memory (2.63); one who attains the brāhmī sthiti is not deluded (2.72); desire deludes the embodied one (3.40).
The second error, eightfold (SK 48): attachment to or self-assertion for the eight powers, through which even gods like Indra fall back (Gauḍapāda; Kramadīpikā).
The worst of the faults, since the others arise only in the deluded (NS 4.1.6).
Delusion born of anger (BhG 2.63) and of the pairs of opposites (7.27); destroyed by the teaching, as Arjuna declares (18.73).

Absolute dissolution of the threefold bond (body, senses, objects), when dharma and adharma are exhausted and no new body arises; not an enjoyment of pleasure (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 105–108; Śāstradīpikā).
The absolute ending of embodiment caused by the complete exhaustion of dharma and adharma; the self remains in mere being, without cognition or bliss (Prakaraṇapañcikā).

The soul's enjoyment of its own intrinsic bliss in the Lord's presence, in eternal difference from and dependence on him, graded by fitness, with bhakti continuing; forms: sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya.

In Sāṃkhya, release belongs to prakṛti, not puruṣa (SK 62); it is threefold in the Tattvasamāsa commentaries — by increase of knowledge, calming of passion, and total exhaustion of virtue and non-virtue (Kramadīpikā); it is not the manifestation of bliss (SS 5.74).
When adṛṣṭa is absent, no contact (with a body) and no new appearance (VS 5.2.20 C); quiescence like a fire whose fuel is burnt (Praśastapāda).
Absolute cessation of pain qualified by the experience of eternal pleasure (Bhāsarvajña — a minority view).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda, Caraka): the complete cessation of all feeling (Śā 1.137); separation from all conjunctions through the absence of rajas and tamas and the exhaustion of strong karma — non-return (Śā 1.142); disengagement (nivṛtti), the supreme, tranquil, imperishable brahman (Śā 5.11).

Release: rare as a noun in the early prose Upaniṣads, which speak of immortality (amṛtatva); 'freed, he is freed' (KU 2.2.1); release (vimokṣa) for one who has a teacher (ChU 6.14.2); the cause of saṃsāra and mokṣa (ŚU 6.16); 'the mark of liberation' (MaiU 6.20); 'desiring liberation (mumukṣu) I go for refuge' (ŚU 6.18).
Liberation, from which there is no return (BS 4.4.22).
Liberation: not produced but the eternal, bodiless nature of the self, realized when ignorance is removed by knowledge; the attainment of bliss and cessation of sorrow.
Release from karma and saṃsāra after the fall of the body, reaching Vaikuṇṭha and eternally serving the Lord, with individuality kept and knowledge fully expanded.
Liberation, on which one sets the mind after paying the three debts (MDh 6.35–37), reached by renunciation, yoga and self-knowledge (MDh 6.74, 12.85).
Pursued with dharma in old age (Kāmasūtra 1.2.4).
Not an abode or a going elsewhere, but the manifestation of one's own power by cutting the knot of ignorance (Paramārthasāra 60); one, whatever the means (TĀ 1.165-166).
Oneness with Brahman after death, when the adjuncts fall away.
Attainment of the Lord's nature and non-separation from him, with difference preserved.
Held lower than loving service; puṣṭi devotees do not seek it.
Made to seem trivial by pure devotion; below prema, the fifth aim.
Equality with Śiva, free of bonds.

equivalents.note: Pārthasārathi's 'cutting off of all specific qualities of the self' parallels the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika apavarga; Mīmāṃsā grounds it in the exhaustion of ritual karma

definitions.definition: The four gatekeepers at the door of liberation: peace (śama), inquiry (vicāra), contentment (santoṣa) and holy company (sādhusaṅgama); mastering one brings the others.

literal: gatekeeper of the door of liberation

definitions.definition: The teaching on liberation, title of the third part of Bhīṣma's instruction (MBh 12.168–353).
Death as a power with its own path (RV 10.18.1) and fetters (AVŚ 8.1); 'may I be freed from death, not from immortality' (RV 7.59.12).
Death personified; identified with the year, which wears away mortals' lives by days and nights (ŚB 10.4.3.1); his claims are limited by knowledge and rite.
Death, as a power and as a person: death covered all at the beginning (BAU 1.2.1); death as weariness seizing the functions (BAU 1.5.21); Yama, Death, is the teacher of Naciketas (KU).
The conquest of death by the nectar meditations (KJN 5).
The stupefied mind, the second level (YBh 1.1).
Gladness cultivated toward the virtuous, one of the four attitudes that clarify the mind (1.33, YBh 1.33). Saṃyama on it yields its strength (3.23).

cross_language.note: one of the four brahmavihāras (immeasurables); in Buddhism radiated to all beings

definitions.definition: In haṭha, a bodily technique that seals and redirects breath, bindu and kuṇḍalinī — ten in the HYP (3.6–7), twenty-five in the GS (3.1–3); to be kept secret and learned from a guru (HYP 3.8–9, 3.129).
Seal: the ten mudrās of the Śrīcakra worship (sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī to trikhaṇḍā), one for each enclosure plus the tenth; the Goddess is 'worshipped with the ten mudrās' (LSN 179).
A seal of body, gaze or attention (mahāmudrā, khecarī, śāmbhavī, vaiṣṇavī, ṣaṇmukhī); also the renouncer's inner 'seal'.
Seals such as Karaṅkiṇī, Krodhanā, Bhairavī, Lelihānā and Khecarī (VBT 77; TĀ 32); an āṇava support (karaṇa).
Tamil muttirai: seals of yoga and ritual, declared needless for one who remains awake in awareness (Kuṭampai 6).
Among the five tattvas, mudrā denotes parched grain eaten in the rite, not the hand-gesture (Mahānirvāṇa 5.22).

A gesture 'giving joy' (mudaṃ rāti) to the deity, made by joining the fingers, which are the five elements; the invocation series, dhenu, mahāmudrā and others are shown at fixed points of worship and are not to be shown to the uninitiated.
Hand gestures shown to the deity and in purificatory acts during worship.
Ear-ornament (or necklace), rucaka, earrings, crest-jewel, ash and sacred thread, with skull and khaṭvāṅga as sub-insignia; knowing and wearing them is said to bring release (Yāmuna's report).
A unit of 30 kalās; thirty muhūrtas make a human day and night (VP 1.3.8).
'The mute's tasting': the image of love's inexpressibility (NBS 52).
Primary devotion — love itself, one though it appears in eleven forms (NBS 82); the one-pointed devotees (ekāntin) are 'chief' (mukhya, NBS 67).
Vāyu as the chief vital breath presiding in all bodies; name under which he is worshipped (Hanumān shrines of the tradition).

equivalents.standpoint: Dvaita reads the Upaniṣadic chief breath as the deity Vāyu
equivalents.note: The Upaniṣadic 'mukhya prāṇa' is, for Dvaita, the highest soul Vāyu presiding over breath.

definitions.definition: The three 'faults' or vital humours — vaḷi (vātam), aḻal (pittam), aiyam (kapam) — whose balance is health and whose excess or deficiency causes disease (Kuṟaḷ 941).

equivalents.note: equal in function to Āyurveda's tridoṣa; the Siddha tradition claims independent origin

definitions.definition: Souls released from saṃsāra who have reached Vaikuṇṭha and serve the Lord eternally.
The upsurge of Śiva's bliss in the Śivayogin in whom the world has dissolved (SSM 14.15); the supreme knowledge of the self dissolved in sāmarasya (14.42–44).
The absolute cessation of pain, i.e. a destruction of pain not contemporaneous with any prior absence of pain in the same self (Muktivāda).
Souls whose intrinsic nature fits them for liberation: gods, sages, ancestors, rulers and the best humans (the 'sāttvika' souls).

equivalents.note: Jain 'bhavya' (capable of liberation) is analogous to 'mukti-yogya'; Dvaita grounds it in intrinsic nature and grace.

definitions.definition: Root-ignorance: the beginningless causal ignorance that is the material cause of the world-appearance, as distinct from the particular ignorances (tūlāvidyā) of objects.
Contracting the root so that apāna rises; by it prāṇa and apāna, nāda and bindu become one (HYP 3.61–65).
The root lock drawing apāna upward (GŚ 37).
The principal fixed image in the sanctum.
The principal installed liṅga or image.
The root mantra of the Goddess (the Śrīvidyā); she is 'of the nature of the root mantra' (LSN 36).
Primal nature, identified with Sītā, who creates, preserves and dissolves by Rāma's mere presence and performs the deeds superimposed on him.
The unmanifest root nature as the Lord's power resting in him (Īśvara Gītā 2.7.30).
The root Purāṇa-saṃhitās: Romaharṣaṇa's and those of his three saṃhitā-making disciples (four in all).
The root centre: the Goddess's sole dwelling (LSN 38); where the Samayin worships Samayā with Navātman (SL 41).
The first centre at the perineum/anus, four-petalled, of earth (LAṂ), seat of sleeping kuṇḍalinī and of the triangular yoni with the self-born liṅga (GŚ 10–12; ṢCN 4–13).
The base centre at the anus, with the triangle where kuṇḍalinī lies.
Any of the 28 root Siddhānta scriptures, as distinct from their sub-divisions (upāgama/upabheda); installation rites should be done with a mūlāgama.

The root: the lowest support (mūlātāram) where the fire and the goddess Vālai are placed; in the Tirumūla ñāṉam also the letter 'a' as the ground of all. 'To know that root is liberation' (Kaṭuveḷi 13).
Prakṛti as the uncaused root of all modifications, itself not a modification (SK 3); 'the rootless root' (SS 1.67).
Medicinal herb; the first of the three classes of Siddha drugs (mūlikai — plants, tātu — minerals and metals, jīvam — animal products).

The ten fundamental topics of the Ṣaṣṭitantra: pradhāna's existence, oneness and purposiveness; puruṣa's distinctness; being for another; plurality of puruṣas; separation; conjunction; the remaining function (persistence of the body); non-agency (lists differ slightly in order).
A bound soul seeking liberation — either the isolation of the self (kaivalya) or the Lord; the latter are bhaktas or prapannas.
In the Dāsbodh: The seeker who has turned from the world and longs for freedom.
Longing for liberation: the desire to be freed from bondage by knowing one's true nature.
The garland of severed heads worn by Kālī (Kālī Tantra dhyāna); later Bengali interpretation reads its fifty heads as the fifty letters (moderate confidence).
The silent sage of the Keśin hymn, wind-girdled and clad in soiled brown, ecstatic with munihood (RV 10.136).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The sage of steady mind is not agitated in sorrows and is free of passion, fear and anger (2.56); the seeing sage is awake in what is night for all beings (2.69).
Silent sage: 'having done with learning and childhood he becomes a muni' (BAU 3.5.1); 'knowing it one becomes a muni' (BAU 4.4.22).
The sage of steady mind whom sorrow does not agitate (BhG 2.56); 'among sages I am Vyāsa' (10.37).
The secret 'three salts' of Siddha alchemy, said to be the key to fixing mercury and to the deathless body; its composition is deliberately veiled. Summary only.

notes: Restricted subject (alchemy): no identification or process recorded.

definitions.definition: The retention, with a very firm throat lock, that makes the mind faint (HYP 2.69); in the GS the 'swoon of the mind' with the attention between the brows (manomūrcchā).
A sequence of the seven notes of a grāma beginning from each note in turn, basis of the ancient modes.
A luminous opening inside the skull; saṃyama there gives sight of the perfected beings (3.32, YBh 3.32).
The guru (Arabic-Persian term) in Bāul-Fakir usage; Madan Bāul sings that guru and murśid stand in the way when they become institutions.
'The first Āḻvārs': Poykai, Pūtam and Pēy, who met at Tirukkōvalūr and sang the first three antātis.
Fills the bladder and carries away moisture (Su Sū 15.5).
The navel wheel, locus of concentration (YBh 3.1) and of saṃyama giving knowledge of the body's arrangement (3.29).
Keeping the tongue turned upward and the breath held wherever one is (GS 3.9); in the Gorakṣaśataka's list of five seals.
The Nāciketa fire, the fire-altar leading to heaven taught by Yama as the second boon; one who piles it three times crosses birth and death (KU 1.1.14-18).

The inner sound heard in the purified suṣumnā; laya rests on it (HYP 4.29); its stages and sounds mark the four stages of yoga (4.69–77, 4.84–86); whatever is heard as nāda is śakti, the soundless is the supreme Brahman (4.101–102).
Inner sound, manifesting when the channels are purified (GŚ-Briggs 101); with bindu and Śakti one of three objects of meditation (KJN 5.31).

Sound, on which song, instrument, dance, speech and the world depend (ŚR 1.2.1–2; Bṛhaddeśī 16–17); born of the union of breath (na) and fire (da) (ŚR 1.3.6); twofold, struck and unstruck, and fivefold by its places in the body.
The sounds that manifest the sphoṭa and plant their seeds in the intellect (VP 1).
The second emanation after Śakti (ŚT 1.7), and in the threefold bindu the union of Śiva and Śakti (ŚT 1.8–9).
The unstruck inner sound, heard in stages, in which the mind dissolves; 'no mantra higher than nāda'.
Musical sound; one who knows the vīṇā, the microtones and rhythm reaches liberation without effort (YS 3.115).
The resonance arising from Śakti in the unfolding from the supreme Lord, from which Bindu arises.
Resonance: one of the subtle phases of the mantra's final sound, between rodhinī and nādānta (Varivasyārahasya).
The subtle resonance of a mantra and the self-arising sound which is itself the mantra repeated (VBT 42, 145).

notes: Nāda doctrine at large → U31/U28.
alt_notes: Contribution from U08; U31 owns nāda.

definitions.definition: Brahman as sound: the consciousness of all beings unfolded as the world, bliss without a second, worshipped through nāda (ŚR 1.3.1–2); Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the supreme Śakti and Śiva are its forms (Bṛhaddeśī 17–18).
Holding attention on the inner sound; it destroys vāsanās.

The channels of the subtle body carrying the breath: seventy-two thousand arise from the bulb (GŚ 16; HYP 1.39, 4.18), of which ten (or fourteen, SS 2.13, which counts 350,000 in all) are principal and three chief — iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā. When clogged with impurities the breath cannot enter the middle (HYP 2.4).
The hundred and one channels of the heart, one (suṣumnā) going to the crown, by which the knower departs at death with the help of Hari in the heart; the suṣumnā 'shines' in the seated worshipper.
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): a synonym of srotas (Ca Vi 5.7); in Śārṅgadhara the pulse-vessel at the root of the thumb, 'witness of life' (Pūrva 3.1).
Channel: 101 channels of the heart, one leading to the crown (KU 2.3.16; ChU 8.6.6); 72,000 branch channels (PrU 3.6); the suṣumnā (MaiU 6.21).
Channel of breath; 72,000 arise from the kanda; ten or fourteen are principal.
Tamil nāṭi means both the channels of the subtle body (ten principal ones in the ninety-six) and the pulse, the chief of the eight examinations, read at the wrist for the three humours.
Channels whose withdrawal is a yogic attainment (Śiva Sūtra 3.5).

cross_language.note: the channel in Vajrayāna subtle-body teaching

definitions.definition: Diagnosis by the gait of the pulse — leech or snake for vāta, sparrow, crow or frog for pitta, swan or pigeon for kapha (Śārṅgadhara Pūrva 3.1-5); absent from the classical saṃhitās' lists of examinations.

The cleansing of the channels, prerequisite to breath-control (HYP 2.4–10; GS 5.35–36: with seed-mantra, samanu, or by the cleansing acts, nirmanu); its signs are slimness, radiance, kindled fire, holding the breath at will and manifestation of nāda (HYP 2.19–20).
Worship of nāda: through it Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara are worshipped (ŚR 1.3.2); the unstruck nāda by sages on the guru's path, the struck nāda through music (ŚR 1.2.165–167).
Worship through sound and music, joined to devotion (Tyāgarāja).
Minor breath causing belching (SS 3.8, one of the five beginning with nāga).
Acts enjoined on an occasion (e.g. the birth of a son, an eclipse); for the seeker of release they are to be performed like the obligatory ones.
The dissolution of the three worlds at the end of Brahmā's day, while the creator sleeps on Ananta.
Freedom from hope or expectation, called the highest happiness by Piṅgalā.
Freedom from hope or expectation, 'the highest happiness', learned by Piṅgalā (MBh 12.168.52).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: A person does not attain naiṣkarmya by not undertaking actions (3.4).

Freedom from the binding power of action, not attained by abstaining from action (BhG 3.4) but, as supreme perfection (naiṣkarmya-siddhi), by an understanding unattached everywhere through renunciation (18.49).
The final cure, without upadhā, which ends suffering altogether — renunciation of all grasping (Ca Śā 1.94-95); 'naiṣṭhikī' also qualifies the true understanding in Śā 5.26.
One of the twenty-seven (or twenty-eight) star-groups through which the moon passes, used to fix the times of rites (Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa; ŚB 2.1.2.3 on the Kṛttikās).

notes: Later astral use → U32.

definitions.definition: 'Gift of the Name': initiation by the living Master, with the names for simran and instruction in dhyān and bhajan.
Congregational worship in the nāmghar by singing the name and verses of the Kīrtana-ghoṣā and Nām-ghoṣā, led by a nām-lagowā.
The Lord's name, whose utterance, even indirect, destroys sins and is the supreme expiation and the dharma of the age.
The noun, whose chief meaning is being (sattva) (Nirukta 1.1); all nouns derive from verbs according to Śākaṭāyana (1.12).

The name 'Nārāyaṇa', found after long searching, which gives family, wealth, heaven, grace and strength and removes devotees' suffering, more than a mother (PTM 1.1); its sweetness is worth more than Indra's kingdom (Tirumālai 2).
The Lord, being sung of, quickly manifests himself and makes his devotees experience him (NBS 80).
The Lord's name, non-different from him, a wish-fulfilling gem, fully empowered and manifesting itself on a tongue turned to service.
The names of Kṛṣṇa given at the first initiation (the refuge mantra) and sung in kīrtan.
The name of God ('Viṭṭhala', 'Rāma Kṛṣṇa Hari'), the easy means that needs no rule of time, place or caste; standing a moment at God's door with the name wins the four liberations.
Rāma's name, greater than both his formless and embodied forms and the one support in Kali.
The name of Kṛṣṇa, first of the four real things and the chief means of the single refuge.
The Name of the Lord (usually Rām), whose inward remembrance is the Sants' chief practice; not the spoken syllables only but the Name revealed by the guru and dwelt on with the mind.
Nām = Śabd: the creative Word, the inner sound and light, to which the names given at initiation connect the soul; distinguished from 'varṇātmak' (spoken) names.
The true Name (sat nām) given at initiation with the pān-parvānā, by which the soul passes Kāl.
Recitation of the Goddess's names; she 'delights in the recitation of her names' (LSN 141), and the Rudrayāmala places it at the summit of a long ladder of births (Saubhāgyabhāskara).
Name and form, which are placed in the Remainder (AVŚ 11.7.1).

Name and form: the unmanifest became manifest by name and form (BAU 1.4.7); being entered and differentiated name and form (ChU 6.3.2); space accomplishes name and form (ChU 8.14.1); the knower is freed from name and form (MuU 3.2.8).
Name and form: the empirical world as distinct from being–shining–dear; the adjuncts through which Brahman appears as many.

cross_language.note: Buddhist sense: mentality-materiality

definitions.definition: The semblance of the name: the name uttered without full attention or intent (e.g. by Ajāmila); destroys sin and gives liberation, but not love.
A word in an injunction that names the rite rather than enjoining a quality (e.g. udbhid, citrā, agnihotra, śyena) (MS 1.4.2–5).
Meaningful by delimiting what is enjoined; a word is taken as a name for four reasons — avoiding secondary meaning, avoiding a split sentence, another text supplying the quality, and comparison.
The Śatarudrīya, named from its repeated 'namaḥ' (homage).
An offence against the name; ten are listed (from the Padma Purāṇa), and they block the name's fruit of love.
One of ten offences that obstruct the fruit of chanting the name, listed from the Padma Purāṇa by later Vaiṣṇava authors.
The two 'great monsters/spirits' of Brahman by which it descended into the worlds; as far as name and form extend, so far extends the universe (ŚB 11.2.3).

cross_language.note: In Buddhism a link of dependent origination, a different doctrinal sense

definitions.definition: Homage to the Lord as part of the offering; for the Ratnaṭīkā a mental act.
The village prayer hall where the community gathers for the name (nām-prasaṅga), reading, drama and council.
Kṛṣṇa's cowherd bride in the Tamil tradition, whom the girls of the Tiruppāvai wake to plead for them; read by the commentators as Nīḷādevī and as the mediator (puruṣakāra).
The twin seers born in Dharma's house who perform austerity at Badarī (MBh 12.332.19), identified in the epic with Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument: varṇa-mixture leads family-destroyers and the family to hell (1.42); those whose family dharmas are uprooted dwell in hell for an indefinite time, as 'we have heard' (1.44).

A place of torment for the dead, below the earth in the south within the three worlds, ruled by Yama; twenty-eight are named in BhP 5.26; the VP also calls heaven what pleases the mind and hell its opposite.

cross_language.note: Buddhist hells (U36)

literal: resting-place of beings / of the waters

definitions.definition: Name of Viṣṇu most used by Madhva in his invocations: full of qualities, free of defects, known only through the true scriptures.
The supreme Lord of the Nārāyaṇīya, also present as the ṛṣi at Badarī; the culmination of every system of knowledge (MBh 12.337.63–67) and the goal of the ekāntins (12.336.3–4).
Named by Bhīṣma in his hymn to Kṛṣṇa (12.47) and as the one attained by the Sāṃkhya follower (12.290).
The proper name of the supreme Brahman: both the abode of all souls and things and the one who abides in them; Brahmā and Śiva are souls in his body.
Nāraṇaṉ: the Lord's name for the Āḻvārs, the creator of Brahmā (NMT 1) and the saving name found by Tirumaṅkai (PTM 1.1.1).
In the Vaiṣṇava and several yoga and renunciate Upaniṣads, the supreme Lord from whom Brahmā and Rudra arise, the Person in the solar orb, the one inner self.
The rite performed for one who died a bad or untimely death so that the normal rites can take effect.
Fixing the gaze on the tip of the nose, prescribed with the seated postures, in breath-control and as a laya signal.
One who reviles the Veda and relies on reasoning against it, to be expelled by the good (MDh 2.11).
Denial of the Veda's authority and of the self and afterlife; Kumārila's effort is to lead Mīmāṃsā away from a Lokāyata reading onto the āstika path (ŚV pratijñā 10, ātmavāda 148).
Medication through the nose for the head; a daily practice in small measure (AHS Sū 2.6).

'Lord'; the title of the perfected masters of the tradition (Ādinātha, Matsyendranātha, Gorakṣanātha) and the name-ending taken by initiated yogīs; in the Kaulajñānanirṇaya the jīva itself is called the lord (nātha), the all-pervading Śiva.
Drama, the 'fifth Veda' made by Brahmā for all classes, the representation of the moods of the three worlds (NŚ 1.12, 1.107).
The cleansing act of turning the belly rapidly to right and left with the shoulders bent; called laulikī in the GS and 'the crown of the haṭha practices' in the HYP.
The nine centres of the body taught in the SSP (2).

The 'nine connoisseurs' whom Sahajiyā tradition counts as its exemplary masters, each with a female partner (e.g. Caṇḍīdās and Rāmī, Jayadeva and Padmāvatī, Vidyāpati and Lachimā, Bilvamaṅgala and Cintāmaṇi); the list varies.

notes: Membership of the list recalled with low confidence.

definitions.definition: The nine means of devotion taught to Śabarī: holy company, talk of Rāma's stories, singing his qualities, expounding his words, guileless service of the teacher as Rāma, virtuous conduct with steady worship, worship through his mantra, honouring devotees and seeing him in all with dispassion, and inquiry into his nature.
The nine forms: hearing, singing, remembering, serving the feet, worship, obeisance, servitude, friendship and self-offering (BhP 7.5.23-24).

Tulsī's own list to Śabarī: saints' company, love of the Lord's stories, service to the guru, singing his qualities, mantra repetition, self-control, seeing the world full of him, contentment, and guileless trust.
The Bhāgavata's nine, each expounded in the Dāsbodh's fourth daśaka, culminating in self-offering.
The nine forms, of which hearing and singing are foremost.

notes: The Bhāgavata's nine forms (7.5.23: hearing, singing, remembering ...) are a different list.

definitions.definition: The body, in which the self-controlled embodied one dwells neither acting nor causing action (BhG 5.13).
The nine pāṣāṇams from which, the tradition says, Bogar made the Palani image of Murukaṉ.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: The nine-night worship of the Goddess, especially in autumn (the 'great worship' of DM 12).
The nine nights of the Goddess's worship in autumn and spring (Devī Bhāgavata 3.26), each night associated with one of the nine Durgās (Devī Kavaca).
The nine-syllable mantra of Caṇḍikā used with the Saptaśatī. (Syllables not recorded.)
Kubjikā's consort Bhairava (also Kujeśa, Śrīnātha), addressed as 'Kujeśvara' in the Kubjikāmata.
The nine relations of Lord and soul: father–son, protector–protected, master–servant, husband–wife, knower–known, owner–owned, support–supported, self–body, enjoyer–enjoyed.
The nine 'wombs' (triangles) of the Śrīcakra — four of Śiva (śrīkaṇṭha) and five of Śakti (śivayuvatī) (SL 11; Tripurā Upaniṣad 2).
'Leader, master': title of the sixty-three canonized Śaiva saints (plural Nāyaṉmār).
The heroine of love poetry, classed by her situation (waiting, wronged, quarrelled, going to the tryst, holding her lover in her power...); Rādhā passes through these states in the Gīta Govinda.
The poet's taking the voice of the heroine in love with the Lord — Parāṅkuśa-nāyakī (Nammāḻvār), Parakāla-nāyakī (Tirumaṅkai); the commentators' term for the Āḻvārs' bridal mode.

equivalents.note: the Āḻvārs' bridal voice is Tamil akam convention, not rasa theory; Gauḍīya madhura-rasa classifies the same love aesthetically

definitions.definition: Heart-mind; the Āḻvārs address it as a companion to be exhorted ('O my mind, worship and rise', TVM 1.1.1) and as the place where the Lord is held (PTA 75).
The cleansing act of passing a fine thread in through a nostril and out through the mouth.
In the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, the form of the practice of the principles: discrimination comes by giving up (each principle) with 'not this, not this' (SS 3.76).

'Not so, not so': the instruction (ādeśa) about brahman/the self, for there is nothing beyond this 'not so' (BAU 2.3.6); the self is 'not this, not this' — ungraspable, indestructible, unattached (BAU 3.9.26, 4.2.4, 4.4.22, 4.5.15). In BAU 3.2.11 and 4.5.3 the same words are an ordinary double negative.
'Not so, not so' (BĀU 2.3.6): negating all specifications of Brahman by adjuncts, not Brahman itself (BS 3.2.22).
The oil-drop sign: a drop of oil on the urine spreading like a snake indicates vātam, like a ring pittam, staying like a pearl kapam.
The cause of disease, the first of the five means of knowing it; synonyms occasion, cause, basis, condition, origin (Mādhava Nidāna 1.4-5).
The closing portion of a sāman, sung by all three chanters.
Contemplation: the flow of like ideas (of the self as Brahman) excluding unlike ones, removing contrary habitual notions; for the Bhāmatī the principal means.

equivalents.note: Advaita distinguishes nididhyāsana (dwelling on the known truth of the self) from upāsanā (meditation on a supported object, an act enjoined); Maṇḍana and the Bhāmatī bring them closer.

definitions.definition: Sleep: the activity whose support is the cognition of absence (1.10); a cognition, since it is recollected on waking, and to be stilled in samādhi (YBh 1.10).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): one of the three supports; one sleeps when the tired mind and senses withdraw from their objects; happiness, strength, knowledge and life depend on it (Ca Sū 21.35-36); seven kinds, of which night-born sleep is the 'nurse of beings' and tamas-born sleep the root of sin (Sū 21.58-59).
Repeating the proposition on the ground of the reason (NS 1.1.39).
The traditional list of Vedic synonyms, obscure words and deity names on which the Nirukta comments.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Beings follow their own nature; what will suppression accomplish? (3.33).
Occasion for rebuke in debate: misunderstanding or non-understanding (NS 1.2.19); twenty-two kinds (NS 5.2.1).
One without a guru, who 'goes away thirsty' from the nectar-well (Gorakh Bānī); its opposite is sagurā.
Attained from knowledge of the truth of the sixteen categories (NS 1.1.1); in the science of the self it is the attainment of liberation (NBh 1.1.1).
One of the two results of dharma, beside prosperity (VS 1.1.2).
The highest good, secured by Vedic recitation, austerity, knowledge, sense-restraint, non-injury and service of the teacher, above all by self-knowledge (MDh 12.83–85).
The highest good with which what injunction makes known joins a person (Śabara on MS 1.1.2); for Āpadeva and Laugākṣi Bhāskara, the fruit of dharma done as an offering to Govinda/Īśvara.
The Supreme's own power, the first to come forth in the origin of the body (SSP 1).
The inner grove of Vṛndāvana where the pair's eternal play goes on.
The grove (kuñja) of the eternal pair, focus of the Haridāsī worship.
Worship of the eternal pair in the grove as a sakhī, through song and inner service.

equivalents.note: worship of the divine couple in the Nimbārka school; the Haridāsīs stress the grove and the sakhī stance

definitions.definition: Epithet of Rudra in the Śatarudrīya (TS 4.5.1; VS 16.8).
Tārā as goddess of speech, the deity of the Bṛhannīla Tantra.
The closing phase of Śaṅkara's pulse (SK 1.1).
The efficient cause: Śiva alone, who does not change by causing.
A cause other than the inherent and non-inherent (loom, weaver); the Lord is the efficient cause of the world.
Arthavāda that blames what is prohibited (e.g. the story of Rudra's weeping, supplementing 'silver is not to be given on the barhis').
'Without a side': Dādū's impartiality, belonging neither to Hindu nor Turk.
The supportless mind, body or awareness through which Bhairava is reached (VBT 80, 82, 91, 108).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Objects turn away from the embodied one who does not feed on them, all but the relish (2.59).
Without support: the mind made supportless at the end of retention (HYP 2.77) or when kuṇḍalinī wakes (3.3); 'one god is the supportless' (3.54); a synonym of samādhi (4.4).
'Spotless': the supreme free of all stain and states, abiding subtly within the mind (AmŚ 39–40); one of the synonyms of the highest state (HYP 4.4).
The spotless one beyond the centres, known by piercing them (Yogaviṣaya 10).
The stainless state reached by devotion to Śiva the guru (HYP 4.1), a synonym of samādhi (4.4), in which mind and breath dissolve (4.105).
The stainless formless ultimate, the name of God for the Nirañjanīs, as for the Nāth yogīs ('alakh nirañjan').
The stainless one whom Dādū salutes first in his Vāṇī.
In the Dharamdāsī literature, Nirañjan is Kāl, the fallen creator of the three worlds (see trm:kal-niranjan).

cross_language.note: in Bengal also a name of the deity Dharma

equivalents.note: The same name is the highest for Nāths, Nirañjanīs and Dādū, and a lower, deceiving power for the Kabīr Panth and Sant Mat; see dsp:status-of-niranjan.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna is to fight free from expectation and 'mine', having renounced all actions in Kṛṣṇa (3.30).
The seeing faculty of the soul, paired with surat (hearing faculty): surat hears the sound, nirat sees the light.
In Kabīr: absorption or detachment paired with surati.
Samādhi when even the impression of truth-bearing insight is stilled (1.51); the three inner limbs are outer limbs relative to it (3.8).

Initiation in which the post-initiatory observances are purified away for those unable to keep them (children, the foolish, women, the old, the sick), their liberation coming through devotion; contrasted with sabīja ('with seed') initiation for the capable.

notes: The Kiraṇa passage teaches the practice without using the word.

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu's freedom from every defect, even in his avatāras, whose apparent sufferings are shown to delude the unfit.

literal: free from the pairs of opposites

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One of the qualities Arjuna is told to have when free of the three guṇas (2.45).
Without attributes: Brahman in itself, free of all qualities, relations and distinctions (BS 3.2.11, 3.2.14 as read by Śaṅkara).
Without qualities: said of the one God (ŚU 6.11), an early occurrence.
Read by Dvaita as 'free of the qualities of prakṛti (sattva, rajas, tamas)'; the Advaita reading 'without any attributes' is rejected as against scripture and reason.
In the Sants: the Lord beyond the three qualities and beyond form, image and incarnation, yet the object of love and remembrance ('nirguṇ rām'); not an abstraction to be merely known.
Dādū's Rām, formless and stainless (nirañjan), the one God of Hindu and Turk.
The formless, qualityless Brahman, not different from the embodied Rāma; the name mediates between them.
The formless Brahman beyond the elements, known by discrimination.
Attributeless devotion: the fourth, highest devotion beyond the tāmasa, rājasa and sāttvika forms, by which one transcends the guṇas.
The unbroken flow of the mind to the Lord on merely hearing of his qualities, like the Gaṅgā into the sea (BhP 3.29.11-12).

Loving devotion to the attributeless Lord through the Name, the guru and inner remembrance, without images or avatāras; the defining stance of the Sants (a scholarly label that the Sants' own 'nirguṇ rām' supports).
The Lord's grace as uncaused by any act of the soul.
Urine signs: examination of the urine's colour, density, smell, froth and deposit.
What has been offered to Śiva, which purifies the mind (SSM 11.6–11); the nirmālya of fixed (temple) liṅgas is not to be used by Vīraśaivas (9.33–35).
Flowers taken down from the image, worn to increase devotion and show the sign.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Without the sense of 'mine': the one who attains peace (2.71); Arjuna is to fight nirmama (3.30).
Minds created from I-am-ness alone (4.4), directed by one mind (4.5); only the meditation-born is without residue (4.6); the first knower taught Āsuri through a created mind (YBh 1.25).
The mind the first knower assumed in order to teach (saying quoted in the Yoga Bhāṣya on YS 1.25).
Determination of a thing after deliberation by thesis and counter-thesis (NS 1.1.41).

The stilling of the mind's activities, achieved by practice and dispassion (1.2, 1.12); as a transformation it is the mind's being joined to the moment of stilling as impressions of stilling overpower those of emergence (3.9); Nāgeśa calls it a supersensible effort of restraint that dissolves the activities.
In the Nārada Sūtra: the laying down (nyāsa) of all worldly and Vedic activity in the Lord; devotion is 'of the nature of nirodha', hence not desire (NBS 7–8).
Absorption in the Lord through forgetting the world, brought about by his play (the theme of the tenth canto).

cross_language.note: in Buddhism the cessation of suffering / of perception and feeling; different doctrinal frame

notes: Distinct from Yoga's citta-vṛtti-nirodha; related to (not identical with) Vallabha's nirodha as forgetting the world through attachment to Kṛṣṇa.
alt_notes: Homonym: Yoga Sūtra 1.2 uses nirodha for the stilling of mind-activities; Vallabha's nirodha is absorption of attachment in Kṛṣṇa — no equivalence asserted.

definitions.definition: The mind's being joined to the moment of stilling as impressions of emergence are overpowered and those of stilling appear (3.9); its peaceful flow comes from impressions (3.10).
Destruction and misfortune personified, from whose lap and fetters one is rescued (RV 10.18.10; AVŚ 8.1.3).
The stilled mind, in which asamprajñāta samādhi occurs (YBh 1.1).
The science of explaining Vedic words, chiefly by deriving them from verbal roots — the completion of grammar (Nirukta 1.15).
The correlation of relational properties that define each other (e.g. causehood determined by effecthood).
Life-span karma that ripens slowly, like a rolled-up wet cloth (3.22, YBh 3.22).
The explanation of a word by relating it to a root and a meaning; one should always attend to the meaning and never fail to give one (Nirukta 2.1).

In the Purāṇas the calm of the mind freed of object like a flame going out (BhP 3.28.35), the end of the delusion of object-knowledge-action (11.14.46), Maheśa's state (LiP 1.8.5), and the self's nature (VP 6.7.22).
The liberating initiation that purifies the six paths (adhvan) and burns past and future karma, leaving only the karma that sustains the present body, which is exhausted by experience.
The liberating initiation: the guru, as Śiva, purifies the six paths and burns the disciple's bonds; liberation follows at death, prārabdha continuing till then.
The subtlest power in the crown centre within which is the abode of Śiva (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa 49-50).
Disgust or disenchantment with worldly aims, the sword that cuts the noose of hope; for the Bhikṣu a raft sent by the Lord.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: When understanding crosses the thicket of delusion, one reaches nirveda towards what is to be heard and what has been heard (2.52).
Despondency, world-weariness: the first of the thirty-three transient states (NŚ 6.18), made by Mammaṭa the stable emotion of śānta.
Coalescence with subtle objects free of such delimitation; its lucidity brings inner clarity (1.44, 1.47).
The thought-free condition repeatedly invoked in the dhāraṇās (VBT 26, 43, 45, 108).
Absorption in which the mental mode in the form of Brahman remains, unmanifest, with no distinction of knower and known, like salt dissolved in water; distinct from sleep because the mode persists.
The first bare awareness of an object, like an infant's or a mute's, born of the pure object (ŚV pratyakṣa 112).
Perception without a qualifier ('this is something'); read by Vācaspati into 'avyapadeśya' in NS 1.1.4.
Not itself perceived but inferred as the first stage of determinate perception.
Coalescence in which, memory purified, the object alone shines as if empty of its own form (1.43); the highest perception, seed of testimony and inference (YBh 1.42).
A sentence that turns a person away from an act that brings harm; one of the five kinds of Vedic sentence.
Acts forbidden by the Veda, whose performance produces demerit; the seeker of release avoids them.
Śiva as partless Brahman, worshipped in the formless liṅga.
Viṣṇu's partless highest form (represented by the fixed image, receiving only flowers) and his partite, gross form (represented by the movable image, receiving full worship).
Śiva as partless (niṣkala), partite (sakala) and both (sakala-niṣkala, e.g. the liṅga).
The supreme Lord as sakala, from whom Śakti, Nāda and Bindu arise.
Acting without desire for results, offering all acts to Hari as their real doer; with flawless service and fitness, a condition of seeing Hari.
Later name for the Gītā's teaching of acting without attachment and without desire for the fruit (BhG 2.47–48, 3.19, 18.23).

notes: The compound is a commentarial and later label; the Gītā speaks of abandoning attachment (saṅga) and the fruit (phala).

definitions.definition: The fourth stage: rudragranthi pierced, flute and vīṇā sounds, the mind one — rājayoga (HYP 4.76–77); it gives both enjoyment and liberation (DYŚ 147).
Fourth stage: natural yoga; liberation while living.
The waveless state to which the 112 teachings lead (VBT 129, 139).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The twofold commitment declared by Kṛṣṇa of old: by the yoga of knowledge for the sāṃkhyas and by the yoga of action for the yogins (3.3).
Steadiness in practice, free from the obstacles of sleepiness, distraction and the like — the fifth stage.
In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the māheśvara stage. The SSM's māheśvara is marked by steadfastness in the liṅga (liṅganiṣṭhā, 10.21–22).
The fifth stage: complete cessation of all the practitioner's activity; its place is Rudra alone.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna is told to be free of the three guṇas, which are the domain of the Vedas (2.45).
Niṭṭai: abiding in Śiva, the fourth step of jñāna after hearing, reflection and clarity.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Epithet of the embodied one (2.18, 2.20, 2.21, 2.24).
'The eternal ones': the fifteen goddesses of the lunar days (Kāmeśvarī to Citrā) around Tripurasundarī, the sixteenth (Mahānityā); they are the unfolding of time (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
One of the fifteen lunar goddesses of Tripurā.
Eternal servant: the soul's constitutional nature.

Acts enjoined for life (e.g. the Agnihotra 'as long as one lives'); performing them destroys earlier sin and averts the demerit of omission (Tantravārttika), and the seeker of release must perform them (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 110).
Performed because enjoined; the command itself, not a fruit, is what prompts the performer (Prābhākara view as generally reported).
Obligatory daily rites (e.g. sandhyā), whose omission incurs sin; performed without desire they purify the mind.
Lakṣmī (Śrī, Ramā), the one dependent sentient being who is eternally untouched by sorrow and never bound.
The continual arising and perishing of all beings, carried off by the current of time.
Souls unfit both for liberation and for blinding darkness, who remain forever in transmigration (the middling humans); Tattvasaṅkhyāna calls them 'sṛti-saṃsthita', Tattvaviveka 'nityāvarta'.

equivalents.note: Jain 'abhavya' souls, never able to attain liberation, are analogous to Dvaita's souls unfit for liberation; the grounds (karma-theory vs innate fitness) differ.

definitions.definition: The Lord's eternal domain, Vaikuṇṭha or Paramapada, made of pure sattva, beyond prakṛti and time, where the eternal and freed souls serve him.
The eternal love-play of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in the groves of Vṛndāvana, without separation, birth-story or departure.
The eternal play of the natural pair in the nikuñja.
Souls never bound, such as Ananta (Śeṣa), Garuḍa and Viṣvaksena, eternally serving the Lord in Vaikuṇṭha.
Desireless action preceded by knowledge, leading beyond the elements to the supreme good (MDh 12.89–90); abstention, which bears great fruit (MDh 5.56).
The five observances: purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, devotion to Īśvara (2.32).
The second limb: VP study, purity, contentment, austerity; ŚiP purity, contentment, austerity, japa, praṇidhi; MkP freedom from anger, service to the teacher, purity, light food, study.
Non-anger, service of the teacher, purity, lightness of diet and vigilance.
Ten observances (austerity … vows); non-injury is called chief of the niyamas in the Yogatattva.
The particular (means of dharma) for each life-stage (NBh 4.2.46).
An injunction that fixes one means where the end could be reached optionally by several (e.g. husking to remove the husk).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The action Arjuna is told to perform, action being better than inaction (3.8); commentators take niyata as 'prescribed/obligatory'.

notes: The commentators take it as obligatory (daily) rites or one's appointed duty.

definitions.definition: Fixed order, necessity: listed among the candidate causes in ŚU 1.2.
Kañcuka: restriction of cause and place ('only this, here').

notes: The same word names the Ājīvika doctrine of necessity (U33); the ŚU names no school.

definitions.definition: The appointment of a widow or wife to bear a son by a brother-in-law or sapiṇḍa; permitted and then condemned in Manu (9.59–68).
The command conveyed by the injunctive, which by itself prompts the qualified person, independent of his desire for the fruit.
A vow of observance: fasting from certain foods, bathing before dawn, abstaining from adornment and harsh speech, and giving alms (TP 2).
Dance according to the dramaturgical rules, offered to the Lord; a bodily act.
Pure dance, movement without representational meaning; with song and instrument part of saṅgīta (ŚR 1.1.21).
Expressive dance that conveys bhāva through gesture and glance.

Placing: the installation of letters, mantras and deities on parts of the body by touch and visualization (mātṛkā-nyāsa, ṛṣyādi-nyāsa, the six-limbed nyāsa), making the body divine before worship and japa.
Placing mantras (e.g. the five brahma-mantras and six limbs) on the body and on the image to make them divine.
Placing mantras on the body (and, in another sense, 'depositing' oneself — see trm:nyasa-surrender).
Placing of mātṛkā and deity mantras, as taught in the Prapañcasāra and Śāradātilaka.
Placing mantras and deities on the body; Śrīvidyā uses many sets (karaśuddhi, the vāgdevatā-nyāsa, the sixfold ṣoḍhā-nyāsa and others), taught in the Vāmakeśvara and the Kalpasūtra.

notes: Homonym: see trm:nyasa-surrender.

definitions.definition: Surrender of oneself to the Lord, which alone attains what other means cannot; equated with the six-limbed śaraṇāgati.

equivalents.note: AS 37 treats nyāsa and śaraṇāgati as one

definitions.definition: The examination of things by the means of knowledge (NBh 1.1.1); also the five-membered demonstration.
An interpretive principle established in an adhikaraṇa and applied elsewhere (e.g. the viśvajit maxim that heaven is the fruit where none is stated).

notes: Mīmāṃsā sense ('maxim'); distinct from Nyāya as a school.

definitions.definition: The seat named because the Goddess 'flew up' (oḍḍitā) there (Kubjikāmata 2.40); the 'body' (piṇḍa) level of the fourfold yoni (11.7).
Uḍḍīyāna, where Satī's thighs fell (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.41).
One of the four great seats (pīṭha), which in the Yoginīhṛdaya are transformations of the four fused powers and are located in the subtle body.

notes: Shared with the Kaula pīṭha lists (U24).

definitions.definition: A 'stream' of gurus; Śrīvidyā worship honours three: the divine (divyaugha), the perfected (siddhaugha) and the human (mānavaugha) teachers, forming the circle of gurus.

The supreme essence (tejas) of the tissues from rasa to semen, identical with strength (bala) (Su Sū 15.19; AHS Sū 11.37); seated in the heart, pure, slightly reddish-yellow, ghee-coloured, sweet, smelling of parched rice, the first thing produced in the body, whose loss is death (Ca Sū 17.74-75); the 'supreme' (para) ojas in the heart as distinct from the ojas carried by the ten great vessels (Ca Sū 30.7-9, as the commentators read it).

The one-syllabled Brahman to be uttered at death while remembering the Lord (BhG 8.13); the praṇava in all the Vedas (7.8); the first of the threefold designation 'oṃ tat sat' with which the expounders of Brahman begin their rites (17.23–24); 'among words I am the one syllable' (10.25).
The syllable made by Prajāpati from the sounds a, u, m drawn out of the three utterances (AB 5.32); expounded at length in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa.
The imperishable syllable, Brahman and Prajāpati, recited with the utterances and the Sāvitrī (MDh 2.76–84; VDh 10.5).

The syllable Om: the udgītha (ChU 1.1.1); brahman and all this (TU 1.8; MāU 1); the word all Vedas proclaim (KU 1.2.15); the bow (MuU 2.2.4); the higher and lower brahman (PrU 5.2); its measures A, U, M and the measureless (MāU 8-12).

The sacred syllable, which in the Saṃhitā layer appears at the close of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā ('Oṃ, kratu, remember'; 'Oṃ, the void is brahman', VS 40.15–17) and as the first of the four quarters of speech in one reading (Nirukta 13.9).
Uttered and prolonged, with the void contemplated at its end (VBT 39).

notes: U05's definition (the Gītā usage); Oṃ in the Upaniṣads and mantra-śāstra is defined by U03 and U31.

definitions.definition: The threefold designation of Brahman by which the brāhmaṇas, Vedas and sacrifices were ordained; Oṃ begins the rites, 'tat' marks acts done without seeking fruit, 'sat' denotes reality, goodness and praiseworthy action (BhG 17.23–27).
The object of meditation, with fixation in the heart, in the third stage.
The syllable Oṃ, explained in the Atharvaśiras as that which raises the breaths; its measures correspond to worlds, Vedas, fires and deities.
Temple singers who sing the Tirumuṟai in their paṇs during worship.
The Marathi verse-form of the Jñāneśvarī, Amṛtānubhava and Eknāthī Bhāgavat, also used in women's grinding songs.
The verse form of the classic Mahānubhāva poems.
The pitta between the stomach and the intestine, which digests the four kinds of food and separates essence and waste and supports the other pittas; called 'fire' (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.10-12).
Step, place, quarter (speech has four padas, RV 1.164.45) and, in recitation, the word (as in padapāṭha).
A word, defined as what ends in a nominal or verbal ending (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.14); also a quarter of a verse.
Sounds ending in a case-ending (NS 2.2.60 DCS); its meaning is individual, form and universal (NS 2.2.68).
What possesses denotative power (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The supreme state ('the state') with which the body is brought to one taste (piṇḍa-pada-samarasa); 'param pad' in Hindi.
Meditation, the second of the four (KJN 3.4).
One of the four sections of an ideal Āgama: knowledge (vidyā/jñāna), ritual (kriyā), yoga, and conduct (caryā); all of Śiva's scriptures are said to have the four pādas.
The Pādma Saṃhitā is arranged in the same four pādas (jñāna, yoga, kriyā, caryā).
Patamutti: the 'liberations in a station' — sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya — reached by caryā, kriyā and yoga; not final.
The recitation of a Saṃhitā word by word, with sandhi undone.
The analysed text in which each word is recited separately without sandhi (for the Ṛgveda, Śākalya's).
The categories: substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence (six), with absence as seventh in later works.
The sixteen topics of NS 1.1.1; also 'word-meaning' (NS 2.2.68).
Seven categories (Tarkasaṅgraha, Bhāṣāpariccheda); Raghunātha re-examines the list.
The meaning of a word; the word-meanings, once conveyed, convey the sentence-meaning (Śabara on MS 1.1.25). Also 'category' in ontology (Bhāṭṭas five, Prābhākaras eight).
Sixth stage: objects no longer appear.
Sixth stage: delighting in the Self, one no longer conceives inner or outer objects and understands them only when long prompted by others.
Service of the Lord's feet, the fourth form of devotion.
Serving and dwelling at the Lord's feet — to lie as a step before his sanctum (PT 4.9), to have his feet enter one's eyes (Amalaṉātipirāṉ 1).
A ritual manual systematising the procedures of the Āgamas (e.g. Somaśambhu's, Aghoraśiva's).
The Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati as a principal authority of Kerala temple ritual.

Water sanctified by washing the feet of the guru or jaṅgama, received as one of the eight shields; the SSM also reads it as the oneness of guru ('foot') and disciple ('water') through initiation (19.6–7).

The guru's 'sandals' — the mantra of the guru's feet given before the Bālā (PKS 1.41); the feet are contemplated in the crown each morning (PKS 2.2); immersion in the Goddess's sandals is complete meditation (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
The guru's sandals and the mantra of the lineage's feet; 'there is no mantra beyond the pādukā' (Kulārṇava 12.12).
Religious hypocrisy and empty show; Viśvanāth Siṃh's Bījak commentary is 'the destroyer of pākhaṇḍ'.
That in which the probandum is doubted, e.g. the mountain (Tarkasaṅgraha).
A side or thesis in debate (NS 1.1.41, 1.2.1).

literal: presence of the probans in the subject

definitions.definition: The probans's occurring in the mountain etc.
Absence of certainty (of the probandum in the subject) not accompanied by a desire to infer.
The body ripened by the fire of yoga (opposite apakva).
The body 'ripened' in the fire of yoga (liberated) versus the unripe body subject to karma and rebirth (Yogabīja).
The palanquin carrying the silver sandals (pādukā) of a saint — above all Jñāneśvar's from Āḷandī and Tukārām's from Dehu — at the head of the vārī.
'Many years': Periyāḻvār's benediction for the Lord's long life and safety, the model of maṅgaḷāśāsana.
A melodic mode of old Tamil music to which each Tēvāram patikam is set; some two dozen are used in the Tēvāram.
The consecrated betel-leaf 'passport' given in the Dharamdāsī initiation and death rites, which Kāl's messengers honour.

The five concentrations in which breath and mind are held in the place of each element with its colour, shape, seed and deity; the GS counts them among its twenty-five mudrās, the GŚ calls them the stabilising, liquefying, burning, whirling and drying concentrations.
The fivefold truth: Caitanya, Nityānanda, Advaita, Gadādhara and Śrīvāsa as forms of Kṛṣṇa as devotee.
The five images of a Vaikhānasa temple: fixed (dhruva), movable worship (kautuka), festival (utsava), bathing (snapana) and offering (bali) images.
The five real and eternal differences: soul–Lord, soul–soul, matter–Lord, matter–matter and matter–soul; they hold in all states, including liberation.
Resolve, self-assertion, desire, the task of awareness, and action — the functions of buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas and the two sets of capacities (Tattvasamāsa 8; Kramadīpikā).
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna, one closing each adhyāya of the Sūtra; the Ratnaṭīkā calls them the five purifiers (pavitra).
The five codes: liṅgācāra, sadācāra, śivācāra, bhṛtyācāra and gaṇācāra.
The fifteen-syllable Śrīvidyā mantra in three sections (kūṭa); called the 'full Gāyatrī' and given fifteen meanings in the Varivasyārahasya. (Syllables not recorded.)

equivalents.note: the Gāyatrī read as Śrīvidyā

definitions.definition: The knowledge of the five fires: yonder world, the rain-god, the earth, man and woman as sacrificial fires, into which faith, Soma, rain, food and semen are offered, so that the waters come to be called person at the fifth offering (ChU 5.3-10; BAU 6.2).
The five periods of the Pāñcarātrin's day: abhigamana, upādāna, ijyā, svādhyāya, yoga.
The five cosmic divisions — nivṛtti, pratiṣṭhā, vidyā, śānti, śāntyatīta — into which the principles are grouped and which are purified in initiation.

notes: Not to be confused with trm:pancakala (Pāñcarātra five periods).

definitions.definition: The five purificatory therapies — emesis, purgation, the two kinds of enema (decoction and oil), and nasal evacuation (bloodletting is counted instead by the surgeons) — preceded by oleation and sudation; the best medicines for the bodily doṣas (AHS Sū 1.25; Ca Sū 2, Si). Summary only.
The five sheaths (food, vital air, mind, intellect, bliss) which seem to cover the self; the self is known by discriminating it from each.
The five incarnations of Parameśvara: Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Dattātreya, Cāṅgadeva Rāüḷ, Govindaprabhu and Cakradhar.
The five cosmic acts — creation, preservation, withdrawal, concealment and grace — performed by the Goddess through Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara and Sadāśiva (LSN 63-64; SL 24).
Emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment and grace; the individual performs them too, as manifesting, relishing, reflecting, planting the seed and dissolving (PH 10-11).
Śiva's five acts: emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, grace.
Aintoḻil: paṭaittal, kāttal, aḻittal, maṟaittal, aruḷal — enacted in Naṭarāja's dance.

The mantra 'namaḥ śivāya', designation of Śiva and root of all mantras, at the head of all the śrutis; there is no mantra greater (SSM 8.2–7); whispered into the disciple's right ear at initiation (6.19–21).
The formula 'namaḥ śivāya', which the Śaiva traditions trace to the eighth section of the Śatarudrīya (TS 4.5.8).
Śiva's mantra 'namaḥ śivāya' (six syllables with Oṃ), praised as the essence of the Veda.
Tamil añceḻuttu: the five letters (na-ma-ci-vā-ya); chanting them yields birthless release (Paṭṭiṉattār, Tiruttillai 17).
The five letters na-ma-śi-vā-ya (Tamil namaccivāya): concealment, mala, Śiva, grace, soul; gross form 'namaḥ śivāya', subtle 'śivāya namaḥ'.
Namaccivāya: the devotee's refuge in every danger.

notes: U01 contribution: the Vedic locus only. Śaiva units contribute the mantra's doctrine and practice.

definitions.definition: The five marks of a Purāṇa: sarga, pratisarga, vaṃśa, manvantara and vaṃśānucarita.
The fifth human aim: love of Kṛṣṇa, beyond the four (dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa).
The epic's claim to Vedic status: it calls itself the 'kārṣṇa veda' (MBh 1.1.205).

The five 'M's — wine, meat, fish, parched grain or gesture, and sexual union — said to manifest the bliss that is Brahman's form; used in secret, and exposure leads to hell (PKS 1.12); daily worship continues without them when they are unavailable (PKS 1.24). Summary only.
The five tattvas named by their initial 'm': madya, māṃsa, matsya, mudrā, maithuna. Restricted: summary only.
A seat built over five skulls used for sādhana in Bengal (Tārāpīṭh; Ramakrishna's seat at Dakshineswar in the tradition's account). Restricted: named only.
The five seats founded by the five ācāryas — Rambhāpurī, Ujjayinī, Kedāra, Śrīśaila and Kāśī.

The seat of five 'corpses' — Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and Īśvara as the legs and Sadāśiva as the plank of the Goddess's couch, lifeless without her (LSN 61; PKS 3.10); in SL 94 the four gods become the couch and Śiva its coverlet.

The system of Nārāyaṇa worship called Pañcarātra in the Nārāyaṇīya, 'this great upaniṣad made by Sāṃkhya-yoga' (12.326.100), whose whole knower is the Lord himself (12.337.63); one of the five systems of knowledge (12.337.59).
The scripture and tradition of Bhagavān; the Pādma derives the name from the five other śāstras becoming 'night' before it; other explanations link it to Nārāyaṇa's five-day rite (ŚB 13.6.1).

notes: U05's definition (the early usage); the Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās are covered by U08.

definitions.definition: The five categories that sum up the Pāśupata teaching: effect, cause, union, rule and the end of suffering; also the name of the system ('Pāñcārthika').
The Vaiṣṇava initiation in Pāñcarātra-based Śrīvaiṣṇava usage: branding (tāpa) with discus and conch, the sectarian mark (puṇḍra), a new name (nāma), the mantra, and worship (yāga).
Purification of oneself, the place, the substances, the mantras and the liṅga before worship.
The five kinds of pollution the Liṅgāyatas reject: of birth, of death, of menstruation, of leftovers (ucchiṣṭa) and of caste (jāti).

notes: Membership of the list from memory; verify.

definitions.definition: Wine, meat, fish, mudrā (parched grain) and maithuna, the five 'realities' of Śakti worship (Mahānirvāṇa 1.57; 5.22). Restricted: summary only.
In the Kālīvilāsa's view not to be used in the Kali age, when only the paśu disposition is allowed (Kālīvilāsa 4.2-3).

equivalents.note: two names for the same five

definitions.definition: Sadāśiva's five faces, identified with the five brahma-mantras (Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta), whose combinations yield the Śiva-, Rudra- and Bhairava-tantras.
The twenty-fifth principle, the knower beyond the twenty-four; the unawakened self called 'the one awakening', which on knowing itself becomes alone (MBh 12.294.42–43).

equivalents.note: the twenty-fifth of the enumeration is the puruṣa

definitions.definition: Quintuplication: each subtle element is halved, one half divided into four, and each gross element formed of half of itself and an eighth of each of the other four.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The wise, who grieve neither for the dead nor for the living (2.11).
The simile for the conjunction of puruṣa (who sees but cannot move) and prakṛti (who moves but cannot see) (SK 21).
'Path': an organized following of a Sant (Kabīr Panth, Dādū Panth), with initiation, seats and sādhus — which the Sants' own verses often warn against making sectarian.
A sub-order of the Nāth yogīs; tradition counts twelve (bārah panth).
'The king of paths': Jñāneśvar's name in Jñāneśvarī 6 for the Nāth yoga of kuṇḍalinī's awakening and ascent (summary only).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Sin: Arjuna fears it would cling to them for killing kin (1.36, 1.39, 1.45); Kṛṣṇa says refusing the dharmic battle incurs it (2.33) while fighting with equanimity does not (2.38); those who cook only for themselves eat sin (agha, 3.13); Arjuna asks what drives a person to sin against his will (3.36).
The supreme form of Bhagavān (Para Vāsudeva) in his highest realm, first of the five modes.
The supreme Goddess; in the Kalpasūtra one of the vidyās worshipped (the eighth section, parākrama); the commentators call Mahātripurasundarī Parābhaṭṭārikā.
Supreme devotion to the Goddess beyond the guṇa-graded forms, seeing her in all beings and ending in non-dual knowledge.
Supreme devotion, to which secondary devotion leads (ŚBS, second adhyāya, as recalled).

equivalents.note: the Śrīvaiṣṇava parabhakti is a named stage before parajñāna and paramabhakti; the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra's parā is simply primary devotion as against gauṇī

definitions.definition: The highest of the Trika's three goddesses; Bhairava's own state proclaimed as the Goddess (VBT 17); the power of will (TĀ 1.271-272).
Paramutti: final release, sāyujya, inseparable union with Śiva reached by jñāna.
The supreme body — the first of the bodies emanated from the Supreme before the human body (SSP 1).
The Lord's higher nature that has become the life-element (jīvabhūtā), by which the world is upheld (BhG 7.5).
Freedom from thirst for the guṇas themselves, from discernment of the puruṣa (1.16); only the clarity of knowledge; the means to asamprajñāta samādhi (YBh 1.16, 1.18).
Consciousness as reflexive awareness is supreme speech, arising of itself (ĪPK 1.5.13); higher than paśyantī.
The first, unmanifest level of speech, where it 'sprouts'.
Accepted by Nāgeśa as the fourth, highest level of speech, motionless and unmanifest in the root centre — a level not named by Bhartṛhari.
