The supreme level of speech, identical with the Goddess (Śakti) as consciousness, above paśyantī.
The Lord's highest form in Vaikuṇṭha, seated with Śrī, Bhū and Nīlā, served by the eternal and freed souls.
The higher knowledge: that by which the imperishable is grasped (MuU 1.1.5).
The first of three states Rāmānuja prays for: intense longing that cannot bear separation, arising from knowledge of the Lord.
Śiva, partless, all-knowing, without qualities, being–consciousness–bliss (Kulārṇava 1.7-8).
'Acquaintance': the direct encounter with the Lord (paracā kau aṅg); also the genre of hagiography that makes a saint known (paracaī).

Mercury, so called because it gives the far shore (pāra) of saṃsāra (SDS Raseśvara 1-2), or because adepts proclaim it for others (para-artha) (Rasārṇava 1.35); Śiva's seed (harabīja), also called rasa, sūta, rasendra, rasarāja (Rasārṇava 1.28, 1.34-36).

notes: Restricted subject: no processes recorded.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Another's dharma, even well performed, is worse than one's own deficient dharma and brings danger (3.35).
The dharma of another, which is 'fraught with fear' even when well performed (BhG 3.35, 18.47).
The drum the cowherd girls ask of Kṛṣṇa in the Tiruppāvai — at the end revealed to mean kinship and service to him alone (TP 29).
The second state: direct vision of the Lord granted to the one filled with parabhakti.
Discernment, assaying (as a jeweller tests a gem): the Bījak's key virtue of testing every doctrine and deity as the mind's creation; the basis of the 'Pārakh' school of Bījak interpretation.

Love for one who is not one's spouse, taken as the model of the practitioner's relation with the partner, because it is free of social motive and full of risk and longing — recorded in summary only (restricted context).
Paramour love: love for Kṛṣṇa by those married to others, held by Rūpa (UN 1.21) to be the supreme form in Vraja; its status is the subject of the svakīyā–parakīyā debate.
Arthavāda recounting a deed done by another great person.
The Lord's supreme abode, not illumined by sun, moon or fire, from which there is no return (BhG 15.6, 8.21).
Supreme love: the Nārada Sūtra's definition of devotion (NBS 2).

equivalents.note: both define bhakti as the highest love; the Nārada Sūtra calls it prema and nectar, the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra anurakti (attachment) toward Īśvara
Gauḍīya prema is the ripened stage of a graded path; NBS prema is devotion's own nature

definitions.definition: Supreme separation — the last of the eleven attachments (NBS 82); cf. Nārada's own definition, supreme anguish on forgetting the Lord (NBS 19).
Supreme anguish on forgetting the Lord — half of Nārada's definition of devotion (NBS 19).
The highest heaven, where the syllable rests on which the gods sit (RV 1.164.39), where the dead meet the fathers (10.14.8), and where the overseer of creation is (10.129.7).
The third state: love so intense that separation from the vision would be unbearable; it ripens into attainment.
Fourth kind: no topknot or thread; knowledge as staff; beyond dharma and adharma; attains the world of truth or liberation.
The highest class of renunciant, established in knowledge of the self, beyond ritual marks; the model of the vidvat-sannyāsin.
The supreme ether: Śiva's cit-śakti, the ākāśa of the Upaniṣads read as Brahman.
Viṣṇu's highest step, which the wise ever see and where there is a well-spring of honey (RV 1.22.20, 1.154.5).

notes: The Kaṭha Upaniṣad (1.3.9) names it the end of the road (reference only).

definitions.definition: The eternal, partless, imperceptible ultimate constituent of earth, water, fire and air; of spherical size (VS 4.1.1, 4.1.7, 7.1.26 C).
Division ends in atoms, which lie beyond the truṭi (NS 4.2.16–17); atoms are imperceptible (NS 2.1.37).

equivalents.note: Jain atoms are also partless and eternal but are undifferentiated as to element; the Vaiśeṣika holds four kinds of atoms.

definitions.definition: Cognition of the probans as qualified by pervasion and present in the subject ('this mountain has smoke pervaded by fire'), the instrument of inference.
Kapila, by whom the secret knowledge was expounded (SK 69; Gauḍapāda).
The highest aim — God and liberation — pursued within household life.
The spiritual goal, which the Dāsbodh teaches alongside skilful worldly life.
Ultimately real: never sublated — Brahman alone.
The one reality, consciousness that is both light and reflexive awareness, free, performing the five acts, transcending and containing the thirty-six tattvas.

equivalents.note: Both name a non-dual conscious absolute; the Kashmir Śaivas insist theirs is active (vimarśa, svātantrya) and object to an inactive Brahman and to the world as vivarta

definitions.definition: The supreme person in the body — witness, permitter, supporter, experiencer, great Lord (BhG 13.22); the highest puruṣa (15.17); beginningless and without guṇas, it neither acts nor is tainted (13.31).
In the Bhāgavata one of the three names of the non-dual reality (with Brahman and Bhagavān).
The supreme self whose subtlety the renouncer discerns by yoga (MDh 6.65).
The supreme self, i.e. Brahman as the self of all; not different from the inner self.
The Lord, one and omniscient, as one of the two kinds of self (Tarkasaṅgraha).
'This supreme self is examined here' (NK 1.2).
The supreme Self, whose sovereignty is the reflexive awareness that is supreme speech (ĪPK 1.5.13).

notes: In Nyāya the supreme self is a distinct self, not the self of all.

definitions.definition: The supreme Lord, splendid with being, consciousness and bliss, with parts (sakala), source of Śakti, nāda and bindu (ŚT 1.7).
The one Supreme, distinct from souls, deities and world, who alone grants liberation and incarnates as the five Kṛṣṇas.
The act done in worship with the hand-gesture called mahāmudrā (thumbs interlocked, fingers extended).
Supreme attachment to the Lord: the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra's definition of devotion (ŚBS 2), a form of rāga, the opposite of hatred.

equivalents.note: Rāmānuja makes bhakti a steady remembrance that is knowledge (upāsana); the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra denies that bhakti is knowledge

definitions.definition: The Supreme beyond the supreme; Tāyumāṉavar's address to the ultimate in the refrain of the Paraparakkaṇṇi.
Half of Brahmā's lifetime of a hundred years of such days and nights; the whole life (two parārdhas) ends in the elemental dissolution.
Public temple worship on behalf of king and realm, performed by qualified priests in installed liṅgas.
Temple worship for others, performed by Ādiśaiva priests consecrated for it.
The five-membered statement by which one who has inferred makes another infer.
That aggregates exist for another's sake, proving puruṣa (SK 17); prakṛti's undertaking is for another as if for itself (SK 56, 60).
The mind's entering another body after loosening the cause of bondage and knowing its pathways (3.38); the senses follow it like bees their queen (YBh 3.38).
Śiva as the liṅga itself, with the supreme Śakti as its pedestal (SSM 11.32).
All reality other than Viṣṇu — Lakṣmī, souls, matter, time, the Veda, negations — which exists, knows and acts only as dependent on and controlled by him.
Complete dependence on the Lord for existence, knowledge and action; the Teṅkalai hold it deeper than śeṣatva, excluding any independent act of one's own toward salvation.
Spatial (far/near) and temporal (older/younger) qualities.
The Lord's supremacy — 'he who has the highest good, beyond which there is none higher', lord of the eternal ones (TVM 1.1.1).
The contempt the ascetic courts; the wise one who is insulted becomes complete in austerity.
The third stage: the breath reaches the great void; drum sound; natural bliss (HYP 4.74–75); the breath enters suṣumnā and pierces the centres (DYŚ 97–99; SS 3.60–61).
Third stage, in which kuṇḍalinī enters the suṣumnā.
Possession or grasping, which brings suffering in proportion to how dear the thing is (the osprey).
Testing by the means of knowledge whether a definition fits — the third activity of the śāstra (NBh 1.1.3).
Cause of measuring; four kinds: minute, large, long, short.
The minimal, eternal magnitude of atoms (VS 7.1.26 C).
Real transformation: prakṛti operates through the guṇas by combination and transformation, like water taking on different tastes in different receptacles (SK 16).
Real change of form in the guṇas and their products (3.9–15, 4.14, 4.32–33).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): time, marked by the seasons, called 'transformation'; excessive, deficient or contrary seasons are the third cause of disease (Ca Sū 11.42-43); in Suśruta one of the candidate 'sources' (Su Śā 1.11).
Transformation of a cause into an effect (BS 1.4.27).
Real transformation (as milk into curd); Advaita accepts it only for māyā/avidyā in relation to the world, never for Brahman, which undergoes only apparent transformation (vivarta).
The real change of Brahman's body from subtle to gross in creation, Brahman as self remaining unchanged; opposed to Advaita's apparent transformation (vivarta).
The doctrine that the world is a real transformation of Brahman (through its śakti).
The world is a real transformation of the Lord's power.
Accepted in the form avikṛta-pariṇāma: transformation without change in Brahman.
Accepted as śakti-pariṇāma: the external power transforms, the Lord remains unchanged.
The permanence of the guṇas, whose nature is not destroyed as they transform (YBh 4.33).
Code language: the veiled names the Siddhars gave herbs, minerals, processes and yogic states, so that only the guru's disciple could decode them; glossaries (e.g. Akattiyar paripāṣai) explain some.

cross_language.note: Sanskrit: technical convention

definitions.definition: Inquiry put to the wise, the second way to learn knowledge (BhG 4.34).
The council of learned brāhmaṇas that decides dharma where texts are silent — ten, three, or even one who knows the Veda or the self (MDh 12.108–113; YS 1.9).

An injunction that, where something is obtained both in the stated case and elsewhere, serves to exclude the others (e.g. 'five five-nailed animals may be eaten'); explicit (śrautī) or implied (lākṣaṇikī).
A contemplative exercise in the Upadeśasāhasrī's prose part: reviewing sound and the other objects as not-self and oneself as pure unrelated awareness.
The wandering ascetic; one night in a village, five in a town, the rains in one place.

equivalents.note: Parivrājaka stresses wandering, saṃnyāsin the act of renunciation; the texts use both for the fourth āśrama.

definitions.definition: The rain-god, 'father' beside mother Earth (AVŚ 12.1.12).
The indirect, hidden name or form preferred by the gods — 'the gods love the cryptic and dislike the obvious' (ŚB 10.5.2.20; 14.6.11.2; AB 3.43).
Mediate knowledge: knowing that something is, without its being immediately one's own ('there is a tenth').
Indirect or veiled statement: the Vedic seers speak indirectly and the indirect is dear to the Lord.
A calcined (white) preparation of a mineral, metal or shell.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: The relation by which a number such as 'two' resides in both relata together, not in each singly.
The rotation of the worship of Kṛṣṇa at Uḍupi among the eight maṭhas; now two years per maṭha (a change credited to Vādirāja Tīrtha).

A negation that does not attach to the injunctive but forms a positive injunction of 'not-doing' (e.g. the snātaka's vow not to look at the rising sun), used where a prohibition proper is impossible or would create an option.
The noose of māyā with which the Lord binds the paśus in play.
The bonds are the kalās called effects and instruments, by which the paśus are bound and made subject to sense-objects.

Bond; the eight bonds beginning with disgust whose destruction is liberation while living (Dīpikā on YH 1.86); burned away by the guru at initiation (PKS 1.36); in the Goddess's hand the noose is attachment (LSN 2).
The fetter of Varuṇa (or of death, Nirṛti) that binds the offender (RV 1.24.15, 7.88.7; AVŚ 4.16.6).
The bond of the paśu, loosened by the pāśupata vow.
The bonds: āṇava mala, karma and māyā (with Śiva's concealing power counted as a bond, and bindu for souls in the pure worlds); eternal realities, not appearances.
Pācam: the three (or five) malas that bind the soul; eternal, their power quelled in release.
A 'stone', i.e. a poisonous mineral; the tradition counts 64 (32 natural, 32 prepared).

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: 'The gift of grace': the closing prayer of the Jñāneśvarī for the good of all beings, sung at the end of Vārkarī gatherings.
The Western transmission: the cult of Kubjikā and Navātman (Kubjikāmata 2.21-22).
All selves wandering in saṃsāra, the Lord's 'cattle'.

Every conscious being other than the Lord - with body and organs (sāñjana) or without (nirañjana), including the gods from Brahmā down and those liberated by Sāṃkhya-Yoga - bound by the kalās; so called from 'seeing' (only the body) and 'being bound'.
Used in the same sense in the Śaiva sources that report on the Kāpālikas; no independent Kāpālika definition survives.
The soul dependent on the Lord, its servant at the stage of practice (SSM 10.40); 'who is paśu, who pati?' when māyā dissolves (14.8–9).
The bound 'animal' — one whose tendency is outward, who worships external liṅgas or falls from the pledge (KJN 3.17, 3.31, 11.4).
One bound by the eight fetters (Kulārṇava 13.91).
The jīva bound by ego and the bonds.
The soul: eternal, formless, ignorant, inactive, without qualities or lordship, pervasive, lodged in māyā and bound through kalā, vidyā, rāga, prakṛti and the instruments.
The bound soul; the Goddess's devotee is freed from 'the entanglement of the paśu's bonds' (SL 99).
The bound soul: eternal, countless, by nature a conscious knower and agent (cit), all-pervading, whose powers are covered by beginningless mala; 'tethered animal' of the Lord.
The soul (Tamil uyir, āṉmā, pacu): sadasat, knowing only when made to know, taking on the nature of what it is joined with.
The bound soul, deprived of his glory by the kalās and made the object of the powers of the mass of sounds (SK 3.13).
In Kaula usage the uninitiated or the one in the paśu disposition, from whom Kula knowledge is kept; the guru 'takes up the paśu' as disciple (Kulārṇava 13.79).

equivalents.note: both name the individual embodied soul; for the Pāśupata the paśu is eternal, pervasive and never becomes the Lord

notes: Contribution from U08; U18 owns the Siddhānta definition.

definitions.definition: The first disposition — ritually pure worship without the Kaula substances; 'always pure' (Kālīvilāsa 6.10), the only one allowed in the Kali age by the Kālīvilāsa, and the beginning of the path in the Buddha's teaching to Vasiṣṭha (Rudrayāmala 17.137).
The observance and doctrine taught by Paśupati for the release of the paśus; also a follower of it. The Pāśupata Sūtra opens by announcing 'the Pāśupata rule of yoga'.
In the Purāṇas also the Vedic ash-vow of the Atharvaśiras ('pāśupata vrata'), distinguished by the Kūrma Purāṇa from the non-Vedic Pāśupata scriptures.
Smearing ash with 'fire is ash …' for release from bonds.

The yoga of smearing the body with sacred ash while reciting the 'agnir iti' mantras and meditating on Īśāna as the supreme light, for freeing the bound soul; called the essence of Vedānta and 'beyond the stages of life'.
Epithet of Rudra as lord of beasts, to whom the five kinds of animals are allotted (AVŚ 11.2); also in the Śatarudrīya.
The Lord (Rudra, Maheśvara) as master of all bound souls; he 'reaches' and 'protects' them by infinite knowledge and lordship, and releases them by grace.
The Lord of beings, all-knowing, doer of the five acts; witness who empowers the senses.
A verse-hymn of the Āḻvārs; the unit of the four thousand.

literal: the state of being a paśu

definitions.definition: Bondage: a beginningless lack of lordship (anaiśvarya) and dependence; its complete removal through connection with Maheśvara's lordship is the fifth purification.
The grammarians' highest level of speech; for Somānanda it is only the knowledge-power at the Sadāśiva level, not the ultimate (Śivadṛṣṭi 2.1).

The highest of Bhartṛhari's three levels of speech: undivided, all sequence withdrawn, the inner light of its own form, subtle and imperishable (Vṛtti on VP 1.142); identified by the grammarians with the Word-Brahman.
The second of four levels of speech, above madhyamā and below parā; placed by Nāgeśa and the tantric manuals at the navel.
The second level of speech, where it puts forth two leaves.

equivalents.note: the grammarians treat paśyantī as the supreme; Somānanda and Utpaladeva place parā vāk above it

definitions.definition: The seven netherworlds below the earth (bila-svarga), full of palaces, named differently in the Bhāgavata and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa; also the name of the lowest of them.
Wholesome diet and conduct: that which keeps the balanced tissues balanced and restores the unbalanced (Ca Sū 25.33).
Śiva as Paśupati, lord of the bound selves, who binds them and alone frees them.
The Lord as possessor of unsurpassed powers of seeing and acting, eternally related to that lordship and not acquiring it (SDS ch. 6); he alone is not a paśu.
Mahādeva as the Lord on whom the bound soul depends (SSM 10.40); at union lordship and boundness are seen as imagined by māyā (14.8–9).
The Lord, Śiva: one, eternally free (anādimukta), omniscient and omnipotent, the efficient cause who by his single power performs the five acts for the souls' release; distinct from souls and bonds.
Pati (Tamil pati, iṟai): the Lord who is one with, other than and together with souls; the Real (cat).

equivalents.note: the Pāśupata Pati is the independent efficient cause, not the Nyāya Īśvara who acts in dependence on karma

definitions.definition: In the Prabandham, a decad of hymns (usually ten verses and a signature verse) — each 'tiruvāymoḻi' of the Tiruvāymoḻi is such a decad.
A hymn of (usually) ten or eleven verses, the unit of the Tēvāram, the last verse often naming the poet and promising fruit.
The devoted wife, whose power humbles the angry Kauśika (MBh 3.196–197), whom Sāvitrī exemplifies (3.281), and whose dharma Anasūyā teaches Sītā (Rāmāyaṇa 2.117–119).
The dietary and behavioural restrictions to be kept during a course of Siddha treatment, held strictest for mineral-metal medicines.
A reciter/teacher of the Purāṇas; the six paurāṇikas who learned from Romaharṣaṇa (BhP 12.7.5).

Human effort: mental and bodily activity guided by the instruction of the good and by scripture; by it everything is attained. It is twofold, former (whose fruit is called fate) and present, and the present overcomes the former.

equivalents.note: puruṣakāra, the usual epic/smṛti word for human effort opposed to daiva

definitions.definition: Rites for prosperity (increase of cattle, crops, wealth).
The maidens' vow of the month of Mārkaḻi, kept by the cowherd girls of the Tiruppāvai to win Kṛṣṇa.

notes: The Śaiva Tiruvempāvai (Māṇikkavācakar) is a parallel Mārkaḻi vow-song (prc:tiruvempavai-vow, U18).

definitions.definition: Soma as it flows through the filter; the ninth maṇḍala.
Annual offering of a thread-garland (pavitra) to Śiva in Śrāvaṇa or Nabhasya, removing all defects in the year's worship.
Annual pavitra offering to Viṣṇu with the same function.
The unspoken mantra: the identity of guru and Lord, He and She, known without utterance (Tirumūla ñāṉam 6).

equivalents.note: both name a mantra not recited aloud; the Tamil verse does not mention the breath

definitions.definition: Tamil names of the Lord (Viṣṇu) in the temples; Rāmānuja is 'Emperumāṉār', 'the one who is (like) our Lord'.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One is never entitled to the fruits of action (2.47); those whose motive is the fruit are pitiable (2.49).
The result produced by activity and faults (NS 1.1.20).
The result of a rite. A fruit stated for a subsidiary is praise (MS 4.3.1); where none is stated, heaven is the fruit (MS 4.3.15); for a principal rite the stated fruit is real (Ātreya, MS 4.3.18).
Being of the nature of the fruit: why devotion is higher than action, knowledge and yoga (NBS 26) and is its own fruit (NBS 30).
The Vaiśeṣika view that when a clay pot is baked the pot dissolves into atoms, whose colour changes, and is then re-formed.
The body as the microcosm of the whole cosmos; the SSP's six upadeśas are organised around the piṇḍa (its origin, knowledge, vision, support and samarasa with the pada).
The 'place' among the four (piṇḍa, pada, rūpa, rūpātīta) of the Kula aim (KJN 3.4).
The body as microcosm containing Meru, the continents, stars and gods (SS 2.1–5).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna says that when classes are mixed the ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water (piṇḍodaka-kriyā, 1.42).
The rice-ball offered to the dead and ancestors; the ten daily piṇḍas build the preta's body and the monthly ones feed him on the road.
The rice-ball offered to the father, grandfather and great-grandfather in the ancestral rites.
The body as the place where nāda becomes manifest; hence the Saṅgītaratnākara's section on 'the origin of the body' (piṇḍotpatti) (ŚR 1.2.3).
The first sub-sthala: the embodied soul made fit for the path by the ripening of karma and Śiva's grace (SSM 5.27–30; cf. 5.34–36).

notes: Homonym of piṇḍa, the rice-ball offered to ancestors (other units' definitions).

definitions.definition: Awareness of the body as containing the cosmos (SSP 3).
The firmness of the body, the precondition of jīvanmukti in the rasa doctrine (SDS Raseśvara 1; Rasārṇava 1.11, 1.18).
The body of the preta built up limb by limb by the ten days' piṇḍas, which merges with the airy body.
Discernment of the self as distinct from body, senses and intellect, and of the Lord as distinct from the selves (SSM 5.55–60).
The right channel, of the sun, identified with the Yamunā (HYP 3.110).
The channel on the right, of the sun (GŚ 20, 23).
The right channel, carrying the sun.
Tamil piṅkalai: the right channel (solar), second of the ten nāṭis of the Siddha ninety-six.
Birth, and the round of births the Āḻvārs pray to be freed from — the 'sea of sorrow' (iṭar āḻi).
Seat: the four seats Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara and Oḍḍiyāna, located in the subtle body (YH 1.41-42; LSN 82); the Goddess is 'of the form of the fifty seats', the letters (LSN 156).
A sacred seat of the Goddess where a part of Satī's body fell and Śiva stays as a liṅga (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.46).
The four seats as levels of the supreme yoni (Kubjikāmata 11.6-7).
A seat, used in the haṭha texts as a synonym of āsana (posture): 'the eighty-four seats', 'Matsyendra's seat', 'the lord of yoga-seats'.
Four seats in the body — Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, Uḍyāna.
A sacred seat of the Goddess and yoginīs: Kāmākhyā, Pūrṇagiri, Oḍiyāna, Arbuda with their sub-seats (KJN 8.20–22).
The Naiyāyika view that heat changes the colour of the pot as a whole without its dissolution.
The ancestors, to whose company the dead is joined by sapiṇḍīkaraṇa and who are fed by śrāddha; they dwell in the south below the earth.
The dead ancestors, lower, higher and middle, who have gone to the life-breath and rejoice with Yama in svadhā (RV 10.14–15).
The ancestors, who receive food monthly, svadhā as drink, the moon as their light (ŚB 2.4.2.2).
The primeval deities of several classes (Somasads, Agniṣvāttas, Barhiṣads…) (MDh 3.192–199).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The ancestors, who fall when deprived of the rice-ball and water offerings because of varṇa-mixture (1.42).

cross_language.note: ancestors

definitions.definition: The dark path of smoke, night, the dark fortnight and the southern course, by which one reaches the lunar light and returns (BhG 8.25).

The path of the fathers: through smoke, night, the waning fortnight, the southern course, the fathers' world, space and the moon, and back as rain and food into a womb (ChU 5.10.3-6; BAU 6.2.16; PrU 1.9).
The path of the fathers, one of the two paths 'I have heard of' (RV 10.88.15).
The path of the fathers, taken by performers of rites, leading to the moon and return to earth with residual karma (BS 3.1).

The doṣa of heat and transformation: slightly unctuous, hot, sharp, liquid, sour, flowing and pungent (Ca Sū 1.60); there is no fire in the body apart from pitta (Su Sū 21.9); fivefold as pācaka, rañjaka, sādhaka, ālocaka and bhrājaka (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.10-14).
Tamil aḻal or pittam: the fire humour, second of the three.
The retention in which the belly is filled with air so that one floats on water.
Wealth, polity, the things of life; the Kuṟaḷ's second book (70 chapters).
The specific action of a substance not explained by its taste, potency or vipāka (Ca Sū 26).
Synonym of prakṛti as the principal cause of the world (SK 11, 57); the term under which Vedānta and other critics discuss the Sāṃkhya cause.
The guṇas as the unmanifest source, 'neither being nor non-being' (YBh 2.19); mastery of pradhāna is one of the three 'honey-like' powers (3.48).
Primal matter: the perishable (ŚU 1.10); God is lord of pradhāna and of the field-knower (6.16); like a spider covering himself with threads from pradhāna (6.10).
Primal matter, one of the four forms of Viṣṇu in the VP (with puruṣa, vyakta and kāla).
The principal act, which bears the fruit; its subsidiaries serve it (MS 9.1.1).

cross_language.note: as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

definitions.definition: Absence after destruction: with a beginning, without end.
The Nārāyaṇīya's word for the Lord's appearances: Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma Bhārgava, Rāma Dāśarathi, the appearance at Mathurā, and earlier the Swan and the Horse-headed one (12.326.72–94).
The third form, born from Saṃkarṣaṇa; the liberated, 'becoming mind', enter Pradyumna (MBh 12.326.68; 12.332.15).
The vyūha manifesting lordship and virility; in Śaṅkara's report, identified with mind (manas).

equivalents.note: Pradyumna corresponds to the mind in the Nārāyaṇīya's ascent

definitions.definition: Absence of a product before it arises: beginningless, with an end; an effect is defined as the counterpositive of a prior absence.
The renunciation declaration ('I have renounced'; 'I have risen above the desires for wife, wealth and worlds').

The lord of creatures, named in the last verse of the Hiraṇyagarbha hymn (RV 10.121.10) and in the White Yajurveda as moving unborn within the womb and born in many ways (VS 31.19); in the Atharvaveda Time is his father (AVŚ 19.53.8).

The creator who, alone in the beginning, desired to multiply, heated himself with austerity and emitted the worlds and beings; exhausted and fallen apart after creating, he is the year and is rebuilt in the fire-altar and the sacrifice.
In Manu, the creator-lord who milked the syllables a-u-m and the Sāvitrī from the Vedas (MDh 2.76–77); one of the names by which the one supreme Person is called (MDh 12.123).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The creator who in the beginning created beings together with sacrifice and told them to prosper by it (3.10).
The form of Viṣṇu that presides over deep sleep, in which the soul, covered by tamas, rests in him.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The wisdom that is 'firmly established' in the one who neither rejoices nor hates, withdraws and restrains the senses (2.57, 2.58, 2.61, 2.68); carried away when the mind follows the senses (2.67). Arjuna is said to speak prajñāvāda, words of (seeming) wisdom (2.11).
Insight: the fifth means (1.20); truth-bearing in nirvicāra lucidity (1.48); sevenfold at the final stage (2.27); its light comes from mastery of saṃyama (3.5).

Wisdom, intelligence: the wise brahmin should cultivate prajñā (BAU 4.4.21); Indra as 'breath, the intelligent self' (prajñātman, KauU 3.2); by intelligence one obtains thoughts and desires (KauU 1.7).
Intelligence or cognition, most developed in man, who says and sees what he has known and seeks the immortal (AA 2.3.2).
The self as experiencer of deep sleep, identified with the causal body (counterpart of Īśvara); bound by cause only (GK 1.11).

cross_language.note: Buddhist technical sense differs

definitions.definition: The 'intelligent one', the third quarter of the self, whose field is deep sleep, a mass of cognition, made of bliss (MāU 5); the intelligent self that embraces the sleeper (BAU 4.3.21).

notes: Distinct from prajñā (wisdom); id disambiguated.

definitions.definition: One of Vyāsa's four kinds of yogin (YBh 3.51): One who has mastered the elements and senses and guards what has been cultivated.
Intelligence, cognition: the sixteen faculties of heart and mind are its names; 'the world is guided by intelligence; intelligence is brahman' (AU 3.1.2-3).
A solid mass of cognition: the great being is a mass of understanding like salt dissolved in water (BAU 2.4.12, 4.5.13); the sleeper as prājña is a mass of cognition (MāU 5).
'Consciousness is Brahman' (Aitareya 3.3): the defining sentence (lakṣaṇa-vākya), mahāvākya of the Ṛgveda and of Govardhana (Purī).

literal: offence against (one's own) wisdom; failure of discernment

definitions.definition: The inauspicious act of body, speech or mind done by one whose intellect (dhī), resolve (dhṛti) and memory (smṛti) have lapsed; the provoker of all doṣas (Ca Śā 1.102); wrong knowing and wrong acting of the intellect (Śā 1.109); one of the three causes of disease (Sū 11.43); the source of adharma and so of epidemics (Vi 3.20) and the cause of exogenous insanity (Ni 7.10); all mental disorders are born of it (Sū 7.52).

equivalents.note: both name a root error of understanding behind suffering; prajñāparādha is an act (karma) proceeding from lapsed intellect, not a cosmic ignorance

definitions.definition: A mode: an entity that exists only as the attribute of another (its prakārin) and cannot be known apart from it; souls and matter are modes of Brahman.
What appears in a cognition as qualifying something; its property is prakāratā.

The fourth means of subsidiarity: mutual expectancy between a principal needing a procedure and subsidiaries without a stated fruit; major (of the main rite) and minor (of a subsidiary) (MS 3.3.14; Arthasaṅgraha).
A pseudo-reason in the Nyāya Sūtra's list (NS 1.2.7 DCS).
The light of consciousness by which anything appears; never without vimarśa, else it would be insentient like a crystal (ĪPK 1.5.11).
Light: Śiva's nature, 'whose body is pure light' (KKV 1); the Goddess is its fusion with self-awareness (Dīpikā on YH 1.6); Bhāskararāya's 'great light, seeing which nothing else is seen' (VR 3).
The karma that covers discriminative knowledge, dwindling through prāṇāyāma (2.52) and destroyed by the great bodiless concentration (3.43).
The manifestness of an object produced by cognition; another name for jñātatā.

literal: that which brings forth; nature, source

definitions.definition: The unconscious, productive principle consisting of the three guṇas in equilibrium (SS 1.61), from which mahat and the other principles emerge (SK 22); one and common to all puruṣas (SK 11); inferred from its effects (SK 8, 15–16); it acts for puruṣa's experience and liberation and binds and releases itself (SK 57–63). In SK 3 'prakṛti' also names any principle that produces another (the seven prakṛti-vikṛtis).
Material nature, the seen, of three guṇas; in YS 4.2–3 'prakṛti' (plural) are the material causes whose overflow transforms beings.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) bodily constitution — the doṣa predominating from conception, giving vāta-, pitta-, kapha-, mixed or balanced natures (Ca Sū 7.39-40; Vi 8.95; AHS Sū 1.9-10); (2) the normal state, i.e. balance of the dhātus (Ca Sū 9.4); (3) the eightfold prakṛti of the person's principles (Ca Śā 1.63); (4) for Suśruta 'in medicine' nature, the Lord, time, chance, destiny and transformation are held to be the source (Su Śā 1.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The guṇas born of prakṛti make everyone act (3.5); actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti (3.27); beings deluded by its guṇas are attached to their workings (3.29); one's own nature, which even the knower follows (3.33).

The Lord's nature: the lower, eightfold prakṛti and the higher life-element (BhG 7.4–5); beginningless, the cause of effect, instrument and agency, from which the guṇas arise (13.19–20); all action is done by its guṇas (3.27); under the Lord's oversight it brings forth the world (9.10).
The unmanifest pradhāna of three guṇas, cause and effect in one; in Kapila's teaching it is powerless before the self that sees with knowledge, dispassion and devotion.
Nature whose properties (suffering, ignorance) belong to it and not to the self (VP 6.7.22-24); the Goddess as the primordial unmanifest Prakṛti (DM 4).
Mixed-sattva matter with the three guṇas, eternal and real, the Lord's body, transforming into the twenty-three evolutes; it is also called māyā because it produces wonderful effects.
Nature, primal matter: 'know prakṛti to be māyā' (ŚU 4.10).
The eternal material cause of the world, insentient and dependent, presided over by Lakṣmī (as Śrī, Bhū and Durgā); God is the efficient cause only.

cross_language.note: also renders svabhāva; as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify
also renders svabhāva; as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

equivalents.note: Gauḍapāda lists māyā among the synonyms of prakṛti (on SK 22) and Śvetāśvatara Up. 4.10 equates them, but Sāṃkhya holds prakṛti real and independent, while Advaita holds māyā indeterminable and not a second reality.
In the Yoga texts pradhāna names the unmanifest prakṛti (YBh 2.18–19, YS 3.48).

definitions.definition: A rite whose subsidiaries are all taught in its own context (e.g. the new- and full-moon rites) is an archetype; one that lacks them and takes them by transfer is an ectype.
The dissolution at the end of Brahmā's life when the cosmic egg and all principles return into Prakṛti.

The result of dispassion (without discrimination) (SK 45): a dissolution into prakṛti or its evolutes, taken for liberation, from which one rises again like a diver (SS 3.54); the Kramadīpikā calls it 'bondage to prakṛti'.
Those whose mind, with its task unfinished, is dissolved in prakṛti, experiencing a quasi-kaivalya until it returns (YBh 1.19); Bhoja: those who rest content in I-am-ness samādhi (RM 1.17).
The dissolution of beings or worlds, fourfold: constant, occasional, elemental and final.
A dissolution destroying everything, for which there is no means of knowledge; creation and dissolution are to be understood 'as today' (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 68, 113).
The periodic dissolution of all products into atoms at the end of a Brahmā's lifespan by Maheśvara's desire (Praśastapāda).
Division of wholes does not end in nothingness, because atoms exist (NS 4.2.16).
Dissolution, fourfold: daily (deep sleep), occasional, elemental, and final (liberation).
A soul bound by mala and karma, whose māyic body is dissolved in the cosmic dissolution.
The knower resting in the void, as in deep sleep or cosmic dissolution, with the kārma impurity (ĪPK 3.2.8).
Valid cognition: cognition of an object not already known and not contradicted.
Experience that apprehends, in what has a property, that property as its qualifier (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Correct determination (Udayana, NK 4.5).
Heedlessness, which Sanatsujāta calls death (MBh 5.42.4); a mark of tamas (BhG 14.8, 14.13).
Carelessness: not cultivating the means of samādhi (YBh 1.30); Vyāsa warns that carelessness watches for an opening to revive the afflictions (YBh 3.51).
The first activity of mind: valid cognition, of three kinds — perception, inference and testimony (YS 1.7).
The instrument of valid cognition; four: perception, inference, comparison and verbal testimony (NS 1.1.3). That by which the knower knows; purposeful because it makes action succeed (NBh 1.1.1).
Two only: perception and inference, verbal knowledge being explained as inference (VS 9.18–19 in Candrānanda's recension; Praśastapāda).
The special cause (karaṇa) of a valid cognition; the four khaṇḍas of the Tattvacintāmaṇi follow the four means.
What accords with its object (yathārtha); twofold — valid knowledge itself (kevala) and its means (anupramāṇa).
Three are accepted — perception, inference and reliable testimony — since all others are included in them (SK 4); Vācaspati reduces postulation, absence, inclusion and tradition to these.
Three: perception (sensory and of the self), inference (as-before, from-the-remainder, seen-in-general), and scripture.
A cognition that apprehends what was not apprehended before and is free from defects in its causes and from contradicting cognition (Śāstradīpikā); six in number.
Every experience (anubhūti), as distinct from memory; five in number (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Three are accepted — perception, inference and scripture; all of them apprehend qualified objects, none an undifferentiated reality.

Means of valid knowledge: six in Advaita (perception, inference, comparison, testimony, presumption, non-cognition), all valid empirically and all within the sphere of ignorance; scripture alone reveals Brahman.
The validity of a cognition, which arises and is known from the cognition itself; invalidity comes from outside.
Validity of a cognition, known extrinsically (parataḥ).
Produced by excellences in the causes and known by inference, not by the cognition that apprehends the cognition (Prāmāṇyavāda).
Beings emitted by Śiva, equal to him in splendour and able to create and dissolve worlds, among them Reṇuka and Dāruka (SSM 2.25–27).
The one who acts, impelled by the wish to obtain or avoid, and who knows through a means of knowledge (NBh 1.1.1).

The twelve objects whose true knowledge leads to liberation: self, body, senses, objects, cognition, mind, activity, faults, rebirth, fruit, pain, liberation (NS 1.1.9); other objects (the Vaiśeṣika categories) are acknowledged (NBh 1.1.9).
The knowing that results from a means of knowledge (NBh 1.1.1); it culminates in perception (NBh 1.1.3).
Breath and life-force; in the Atharvaveda Prāṇa is lord of all, death and fever, awake among sleepers (AVŚ 11.4); wind was born from the Puruṣa's breath (RV 10.90.13).

The breath: life is its staying in the body and death its departure (HYP 2.3); as one of the ten vāyus it abides in the heart (SS 3.7); with apāna it pulls the living soul up and down (GŚ 26–29); their union is the aim of mūlabandha (HYP 3.64).

Breath as the vital power: the seers are the breaths (ŚB 6.1.1.1); the breath is the consecrated (KB 7.1); the one god is the breath, called 'that' (ŚB 11.6.3); the breaths are enumerated as five (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna).
The breath impelled by the body's fire that, striking the places of articulation, produces the phonemes (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 6–9).
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at mouth and nose.
The breath expelled and retained in 1.34; the chief of the five vital airs, moving through mouth and nose up to the heart (YBh 3.39).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the first of the five vāyus, seated in the head and moving in chest and throat, upholding intellect, heart, senses and mind and governing breathing, swallowing, spitting, sneezing and belching (AHS Sū 12.4-5); in Śārṅgadhara the breath that rises from the navel, touches the heart-lotus, drinks the nectar of the sky and returns to nourish the body (Pūrva 5.51); the 'prāṇas' also denote the seats of life (Ca Sū 29.3; Śā 7.9).

Breath, life-breath: the eldest and best of the vital powers (BAU 6.1; ChU 5.1); the one god (BAU 3.9.9); the gatherer in the body (ChU 4.3.3); born from the self like a shadow (PrU 3.3); brahman (KauU 2.1) and 'the intelligent self' (KauU 3.2); also the collective name of the five breaths (BAU 1.5.3).

The (in-)breath, offered into apāna in breath-sacrifice (BhG 4.29), fixed between the brows (8.10) or in the head (8.12) at death; the Lord as vaiśvānara joined with prāṇa and apāna digests food (15.14).
The air moving within the body; one, named prāṇa, apāna and the rest by differences of adjunct (Tarkasaṅgraha); inhalation and exhalation are marks of the self (VS 3.2.4 C).
The vital breath; the self in the Brahma Upaniṣad; chief of the ten vāyus; its vibration is a seed of mind.
The breath-power (marudrūpā śakti) whose arising, turning and suspension are contemplated (VBT 24-27, 64); in the āṇava means its five forms carry the seven blisses (TĀ 5).
Prāṇa and apāna prevail in waking and dream, samāna in deep sleep, udāna in the fourth, vyāna beyond (ĪPK 3.2.19-20).
The vibration of the life-breath, one of the two seeds of the mind: when it moves awareness arises, when it rests the mind does not arise.

equivalents.note: shares the word spanda with Kashmir Śaivism, where spanda is the divine self-vibration of consciousness; in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha passage it is the breath's movement; not asserted as the same

definitions.definition: The offering of the first morsels of a meal to the five breaths (prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, samāna, udāna) with svāhā, so that eating becomes an Agnihotra offered in all worlds and selves (ChU 5.19–24; Mahānārāyaṇa Up. = TA 10.69–70; Prāṇāgnihotra Up.).
The meal-rite of the twice-born incorporating the breath-oblations, prescribed in the Dharmasūtras' rules on eating.
Offering food to the five breaths as an inner agnihotra.

The fire-offering into the breaths: in ChU 5.19-24 the first morsels of food are offered to prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, samāna and udāna as an agnihotra into the vaiśvānara self; the name is from later texts (e.g., the Prāṇāgnihotra Upaniṣad).

The subtle liṅga, made of inner contemplation (SSM 6.49–50): the light that arises from the navel-bulb when prāṇa and apāna meet, in which breath dissolves like frost in the sun (12.6–8); the initiation formula also calls the given liṅga 'your prāṇaliṅga, to be borne like your breath' (6.26).

equivalents.note: internal equivalence within the SSM: the inner liṅga is described as the liṅga of light (6.35; 12.6–9)

literal: one who has the liṅga in the breath

definitions.definition: The fourth sthala, where the yoga of knowledge begins: one who knows the liṅga as consciousness-brahman whose power is the breath (SSM 12.2–3).
Made of breath: the self within the food-self, with prāṇa as head (TU 2.2).
The sheath of vital air: the five prāṇas with the five organs of action.
The movement of prāṇa, one of the two seeds of the mind-tree.
The designator of Īśvara (1.27), whose relation to him is fixed, not conventional (YBh 1.27); repeated with contemplation of its meaning (1.28).

The designator of Viṣṇu, eightfold (a, u, m and five further subtle components up to 'atiśānta'), naming his forms Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, Turīya, Ātman, Antarātman, Paramātman and Jñānātman; source of the other mantras.
The single syllable that reveals the partless, second-less Śiva; it arises from 'so'ham' by dropping the 'h' and the 's' (SSM 8.17–22).
Om as the sacred syllable: 'praṇava is the bow' (MuU 2.2.4); the upper fire-stick of meditation (ŚU 1.14).
The syllable Oṃ, whose three measures and half-measure are meditated upon; raised in the heart like a bell's sound.
Oṃ as analysed into measures and taught as the means of meditation, the renouncer's only study, the 'thread' and the tāraka; of three, four, twelve or sixteen measures.
In the tirumantra, a-u-m teach that the soul (m) exists for the Lord (a) alone (u).

Oṃ, the 'tāra', prefixed to mantras; its letters a, u, m are Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, and its subtle phases (bindu, ardhacandra, nirodhikā, nāda, nādānta, śakti, vyāpinī, samanā, unmanā) are traversed in meditative utterance.
The one word from which the Veda's knowledge springs, opposed to no doctrine (VP 1.9, low confidence).

equivalents.note: praṇava is the name of the syllable Oṃ
same syllable; duplicate ids to be merged

definitions.definition: Intimacy: love free of reverence, feeling oneness with the beloved.

Breath-control, practised after posture is firm (HYP 2.1); threefold as exhalation, inhalation and retention (2.71); correct practice destroys disease, improper practice causes it (2.16–17); the Jyotsnā identifies haṭha itself with prāṇāyāma, the union of prāṇa and apāna.
Breath-restraint as a form of sacrifice: offering in-breath into out-breath and the reverse, restraining their courses (BhG 4.29); equalizing the breaths in the nostrils (5.27).
Mastery of the breath, in recaka, pūraka, kumbhaka; with or without support; it burns the faults (BhP 3.28.11) and yields the states of calm and clarity (ŚiP 7.2.39).

The cutting off of the movement of inhalation and exhalation (2.49); external, internal or suspended, regulated by place, time and number (2.50); a fourth transcends both spheres (2.51); it thins the covering of the light (2.52).

Breath-control performed with Oṃ, the utterances and the Gāyatrī with its 'head' — the highest austerity, burning away the faults of the senses as smelting burns the dross of ores (MDh 6.70–72; YS 1.23; VDh 10.5).
Breath-control: first limb of the Maitrī's yoga (MaiU 6.18); ŚU 2.9 describes restraining the breaths and breathing out gently through the nose.
Regulation of breath; inwardly, seeing all as Brahman (exhalation negating the world, inhalation 'I am Brahman', retention steadiness).

notes: The Gītā names no counts or retention durations.

definitions.definition: Ten seats where life resides: the temples, the three vital points (head, heart, bladder), throat, blood, semen, ojas and anus (Ca Sū 29.3); or head, throat, heart, navel, anus, bladder, ojas, semen, blood and flesh (Ca Śā 7.9).
Prostration before the wise, the first of the three ways to learn knowledge (BhG 4.34).
The sevenfold insight of the discerning yogin: four releases regarding what is to be done and three releases of the mind (2.27, YBh 2.27).
Worldly household life; the saints teach that prapañca and paramārtha (the highest aim) can be joined.
Worldly life, to be conducted with vigilance and effort together with the pursuit of the highest.
The world, one of the four eternal realities: made of māyā, distinct from souls, deities and Parameśvara.
The stilling of the world's diversity: an epithet of the fourth (MāU 7, 12).

notes: The same compound appears in the dedicatory verse of Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā (src:mulamadhyamakakarika); see brw:mandukya-madhyamaka-prapancopasama.

literal: one who has come for refuge

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple who has taken refuge in him and asks to be instructed (2.7).
One who has performed (V) or accepted (T) surrender; he has done what is to be done and lives in service.
Taking refuge in the Lord (prapad-): Arjuna 'has taken refuge' as a disciple (BhG 2.7); those who take refuge in the Lord cross his māyā (7.14); 'I take refuge in that primal person' (15.4).
Surrender to the Lord alone, who frees from all sins (BhG 18.66); in the Rāmāyaṇa, Vibhīṣaṇa's refuge (6.18.33).
Surrender to the Lord (with Śrī) as one's sole refuge, the path of those who have no other means.
An independent means (upāya) performed once with its limbs, the occasion (vyāja) for the Lord's grace.
Not a means but the soul's acceptance of the Lord as the already-accomplished means, befitting its dependent nature.
Going for refuge: 'I, desiring liberation, go for refuge (śaraṇam ahaṃ prapadye) to that God' (ŚU 6.18); the verb, not the later noun, is used.
Surrender to the Lord, one of the five means; the refuge of Kṛṣṇa's feet (Daśaślokī 8).
Surrender (śaraṇāgati) with six limbs, underlying all devotion.

equivalents.note: the Gītā uses the verb prapad- and 'śaraṇaṃ vraja'; later Śrīvaiṣṇava usage treats prapatti and śaraṇāgati as synonyms
used interchangeably with śaraṇāgati, nyāsa and bharanyāsa

definitions.definition: Karma that has begun to bear fruit; for the knower it moves the body but does not bind; its exhaustion brings bodiless liberation.
Karma that has begun to fruit and keeps the body of the liberated alive until exhausted (BhP 3.28.38: 'the body ... lives on while its karma lasts').
Karma that has begun to bear fruit in the present body and is exhausted by experiencing it; for the surrendered the Lord may end it at once.
The destiny karma that made the present body; not altered by the Master, only borne with detachment.
Karma that has begun to bear fruit and produced the present body; not destroyed by knowledge but exhausted by experience, like the momentum of a potter's wheel.

Viṣṇu's grace, without which there is no liberation; lowest when won by ritual (giving heaven), middling by hearing etc., highest by fullness of knowledge (giving liberation); it reaches lower beings through the higher.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Attained by the disciplined one who moves among objects with senses free of passion and aversion (2.64); in it all sorrows cease and understanding quickly becomes steady (2.65).

Purity of mind achieved by Śiva's grace; whatever is offered to Śiva is his prasāda, and eating only what has been offered purifies the mind (SSM 11.2; 11.6–11); devotion and grace arise from each other like seed and sprout (9.11–12).

Two senses: the serenity of mind of one who moves among objects free of attraction and aversion (BhG 2.64–65, 18.37); and the Lord's grace, by which one attains the eternal abode (18.56, 18.62), sees the universal form (11.47) and regains memory (18.73).
The Lord's grace (īśaprasāda), by which alone the end of suffering is reached; also listed as the fifth means. As 'clarity of mind' (mateḥ prasāda) it is one of the strengths.

Serenity; grace: 'through the serenity of the constituents' (dhātuprasāda, KU 1.2.20) or 'through the grace of the creator' (dhātuḥ prasāda, ŚU 3.20); by the serenity of knowledge one sees the partless (MuU 3.1.8); by God's grace Śvetāśvatara knew brahman (ŚU 6.21); by serenity of mind one destroys karma (MaiU 6.20, 6.34).
Grace received from the guru met in the unseen.
Parshād: food or grace blessed by the Master.

equivalents.note: Both name divine grace; in Dvaita prasāda is won by knowledge and devotion and graded, so the overlap is partial.

definitions.definition: One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the śaraṇa stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
The third sthala: one whose bonds of sin are destroyed through steadfastness in the liṅga and who attains serenity of mind through receiving Śiva's grace (SSM 11.2).
A subsidiary performed for one principal also incidentally benefiting another, e.g. the animal's prayājas benefiting the animal-cake (adhyāya 12).
The meditation called the cloud of dharma (YBh 1.2); its fire burns the seeds of affliction (YBh 2.2); one who takes no interest even in it attains the cloud of dharma (4.29).
Repeated contemplation of objects (and then of the body) that removes false construction and the I-notion (NBh 4.2.2, 4.2.46).

Repeated meditative contemplation of the Upaniṣadic knowledge to make it direct and to destroy the impressions of difference — required by Maṇḍana, rejected as necessary by Śaṅkara (US 18) and Sureśvara.
The mind's peaceful flow from the impressions of stilling (3.10, YBh 3.10).
The opening portion of a sāman, sung by the prastotṛ.
The three foundations of Vedānta: the Upaniṣads (śruti), the Bhagavad Gītā (smṛti) and the Brahma Sūtras (nyāya).
The Upaniṣads, the Brahma Sūtra and the Bhagavad Gītā, the three canonical sources of Vedānta; the Gītā counts as the smṛti source. BhG 13.4 refers to 'the words of the Brahma-sūtra'.

notes: A later Vedāntic term; the Gītā does not use it.

definitions.definition: A state of the afflictions (2.4): Existing in the mind as mere potency, like seeds (YBh 2.4).
One of Vyāsa's four kinds of yogin (YBh 3.51): The beginner, in whom the light has only begun to shine.
What prevents an effect when present (e.g. a gem or mantra stopping fire's burning); its absence is a cause.
Intuition, forerunner of knowledge born of discrimination, like dawn before sunrise (3.33, YBh 3.33); with divine hearing, touch, sight, taste and smell arising from knowledge of the puruṣa (3.36).

The flash of intuition in which a sentence's unitary meaning is grasped, indescribable even by its possessor; also the instinct by which animals act (the cuckoo's song, nest-building); sixfold by source (VP 2.143–152).
Poetic genius: the cause of poetry (śakti, KP 1.3); for Rājaśekhara twofold, creative (kārayitrī) and appreciative (bhāvayitrī).
Kṣemarāja glosses the 'upsurge' that is Bhairava (Śiva Sūtra 1.5) as the flash of the supreme I-awareness.
The seers' kind of knowledge occasionally arising in ordinary people (Praśastapāda).
Apparently real: existing only while perceived and sublated by ordinary waking cognition — dream objects, the rope-snake, shell-silver.
Puruṣa, reflected in buddhi and taking on its shade, appears to have knowledge and pleasure, while buddhi, taking on the shade of consciousness, appears conscious (Vācaspati on SK 5).

The soul as reflection of God — dependent on its original, similar to it and eternally different from it; the 'adjunct' that makes it a reflection is its own nature, so the reflection is eternal (not produced by an external upādhi as in Advaita).
The universe as a reflection in the mirror of consciousness, appearing distinct yet undivided from it (TĀ 3; Paramārthasāra 12-13).
Reflection: the jīva (or Īśvara) as the reflection of consciousness in an adjunct, like the sun in water (BS 3.2.18).
Awakening: brahman 'known through each awakening' (pratibodhaviditam, Kena 2.4); the commentators interpret it variously.
The portion of a sāman sung by the pratihartṛ.
The statement of what is to be proved (NS 1.1.33).
In the ŚS's pratīkopāsana, one's own reflected image seen first in sunlight and then in the sky.
Meditation on Brahman through a symbol (name, mind, sun, Oṃ); the symbol is not to be taken as the self (BS 4.1.4).
Abstaining from what displeases the Lord; second limb of prapatti.
A substitute offering (e.g. a gourd or sugarcane in place of an animal) as allowed in the Kālikā Purāṇa and later practice.
Countering harmful thoughts by reflecting on their endless fruit of suffering and ignorance (2.33–34).
Return of an effect into its cause: the subtle afflictions are abandoned by it (2.10); kaivalya is the involution of the guṇas (4.34).
A phonetic treatise of a particular Vedic school (śākhā), governing the relation of the word-by-word and continuous texts, sandhi and accent.
Dissolution of the principles into their causes in reverse order, the unmanifest itself not dissolving (Tattvasamāsa 6 and commentaries).
The second of the five marks; in most Purāṇic usage the secondary creation by Brahmā (and by some understood as dissolution and re-creation).
Installation and consecration of liṅga, image or temple, to be performed with a single root āgama.
Consecration of images and temples (e.g. the Hayaśīrṣa's subject).
Installation of the fixed and movable images.
Installation of the seven deities, performed only by the tantri.
That of which something is the absence (the pot, for 'absence of pot'), or the first term of a relation.
Recognition of one's own self as the Lord, shown by revealing his powers (ĪPK 1.1.3); like recognizing a lover standing near (4.17).
Drawing the senses back from objects so they follow the mind, as a tortoise draws in its limbs.
Sense-withdrawal: the senses, disjoined from their objects, imitating the mind's own form (2.54), bringing supreme mastery of the senses (2.55).

Withdrawal: bringing the wandering mind back under the self's control (GS 4.1–2); withdrawing the senses while in retention and seeing all as the self (DYŚ 84–88); the sun's 'drawing in' of the moon's nectar (GŚ 55); moving breath through the eighteen marmas (YY, VS).
Withdrawal of the senses, which burns away attachments (MDh 6.72).
Withdrawal (of the senses): second limb of the Maitrī's yoga (MaiU 6.18); cf. drawing the senses into the heart (ŚU 2.8) and turning the sight inward (KU 2.1.1).
Withdrawal of the senses; five kinds, including seeing all as the Self.
An abbreviation formed from the Māheśvara sūtras by a first sound and a final marker, naming a class of sounds (e.g. aC = the vowels).

notes: Distinct from yogic pratyāhāra (sense-withdrawal), trm:pratyahara.

definitions.definition: The faultless contact of sense and object; sevenfold — the witness (sākṣin) and six senses (five outer and manas).
Cognition arising from sense-object contact, non-verbalizable, non-deviating, determinate (NS 1.1.4).
Arises from the contact of self, sense, mind and object (VS 3.1.13, 9.15 Candrānanda); includes yogic perception (VS 9.13).
Cognition produced by sense-object contact, indeterminate or determinate, through six contacts; also extraordinary (alaukika) perception.

Perception: the mind's activity, coloured by an external thing through the senses, that chiefly ascertains the particular; its result is the puruṣa's awareness of the activity (YBh 1.7). The perception of nirvitarkā samāpatti is the 'highest perception', the seed of testimony and inference (YBh 1.42).
Cognition arising in a person when the senses are in contact with an existing object; it grasps only what is present and so cannot know dharma (MS 1.1.4).
First an indeterminate bare awareness, then determinate cognition by universal and other features; both are perception (ŚV pratyakṣa 112).
Perception: the identity of the consciousnesses delimited by the knower, the mental mode and the object; affirmative, not grasping difference (Maṇḍana).
Reflective recognition, the word-natured 'grasping back' that makes a cognition determinate; the function of speech in awareness (VP 1.124).

equivalents.note: the Pratyabhijñā's vimarśa (reflexive awareness as supreme speech) develops Bhartṛhari's pratyavamarśa

definitions.definition: The demerit incurred by omitting enjoined (obligatory, occasional) acts; the seeker of release performs them to avoid it (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 110; Tantravārttika).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The adverse result which is not found in the yoga of understanding (2.40).
A cognition or presented content of the mind (1.10, 3.2, 3.19, 4.27); also 'cause' in upāya-/bhava-pratyaya (1.19–20).

The intellectual creation of fifty kinds — five errors, twenty-eight incapacities, nine contentments, eight accomplishments — arising from the inequality of the guṇas (SK 46–51); with the liṅga creation it forms the twofold creation (SK 52).
The teaching or recitation of a Vedic recension by a master, from which its name (e.g. Kāṭhaka) derives (MS 1.1.30).
The 'stream': souls carried along in worldly pursuits, outside both grace and rule.
The beginner's stage, relying on the name and the guru's mantra.
Vedic action done with desire, bringing prosperity and equality with the gods (MDh 12.88–90); the natural activity of beings (MDh 5.56).
The undertaking of action by speech, mind and body (NS 1.1.17), good or bad (NBh 1.1.2).

Rites and penances removing the stain of sin — needed by one who omits the enjoined, does the forbidden or is attached to objects (MDh 11.44); by confession, remorse, austerity, recitation and gifts (MDh 11.227).
The rite that removes sin; the Purāṇas hold the name or remembrance of the Lord to be the best expiation.
Expiatory rite for faults in ritual or conduct.
Rites enjoined on the occasion of a fault or failure in performance; treated in Mīmāṃsā as occasional acts (e.g. MS 6.4).
Rites that make good lapses in ritual and observance.
Expiation for deliberate offences after surrender, which the Vaṭakalai require (or a renewed surrender) and the Teṅkalai do not regard as needed for salvation.
A mark and special quality of the self; eternal in the Lord (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Effort: Rāmdās's watchword, to be joined with devotion in both worldly and spiritual life.
The principal injunction, united with the subsidiary injunctions, that conveys the prompt, uninterrupted performance of the whole rite in a fixed sequence.
The aim with regard to which one acts (NS 1.1.24).
Love for Kṛṣṇa: bhāva grown dense, melting the heart completely and marked by intense possessiveness toward him; the supreme goal, desiring only his pleasure (as opposed to kāma).
Love for the Lord, indescribable, 'like a mute's tasting', free of guṇas and desire, ever-increasing, unbroken, subtlest, of the nature of experience (NBS 51–54).
Love of the Lord — 'the two and a half letters of prem' worth more than all books; its lane is too narrow for two.
Selfless divine love, the goal of the siddha stage, refined out of kāma.
Prem: the love-practice (prem-sādhanā) of the one who has died while alive.
The newly dead before being joined with the ancestors; one whose rites are lacking (e.g. no vṛṣotsarga) or who did great wrong remains a preta, hungry and thirsty, troubling kin.
The newly dead, not yet united with the ancestors, sustained by the first-year offerings until the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa.

literal: one who has gone forth; the departed

cross_language.note: hungry ghosts in Buddhist cosmology (U36)

definitions.definition: Living unwashed, unshaven and ungroomed like a poor madman (the 'preta' of the sūtra being a living man), so that caste and āśrama marks are cut off.
Arising again (NS 1.1.19); established by the eternity of the self (NS 4.1.10).
The pleasant: chosen by the fool for the sake of getting and keeping (KU 1.2.2).
Happiness; what the word 'svarga' denotes (Śabara on MS 6.1.2); what is for the person is that which gives delight (MS 4.1.2).
Cause of the usage 'separate'; in all substances.
Substance possessing smell (with colour, taste, touch); eternal as atoms, non-eternal as products; our bodies are earthy.
The Earth, mother of men (AVŚ 12.1.12), upheld by truth, order, consecration, tapas, brahman and sacrifice (12.1.1), to whom the dead are returned (RV 10.18.10).
Worship of Śiva with mantras, twofold: for oneself (in the liṅga received at initiation) and for others (in temples, for king and realm), preceded by the five purifications.
Ijyā, worship of Bhagavān, the third of the five daily periods.
Arcana of Viṣṇu in a consecrated image with Vedic mantras; the best of the means.
The daily sequence of temple pūjās performed by the śānti under the tantri's authority.
Not with flowers but the firm mind fixed on the great void (VBT 147); the liberated worships Bhairava with the substances of self-awareness (Paramārthasāra 75).
Refusing meat (Kuṟaḷ ch. 26): better than a thousand sacrifices.
Taught in the Tirumantiram's first tantra.
Refusing flesh: Paṭṭiṉattār asks what flesh-eaters will do when Yama seizes them (Tiruvēkampamālai 33).
Dying again in the other world; the Brāhmaṇas promise its conquest ('apa punarmṛtyuṃ jayati') to those who know or perform certain rites — the fire-altar, the Nāciketa fire (ŚB 10.4.3; TB 3.11.8).
Inhalation (HYP 2.71).
Inhalation; inwardly, 'I am Brahman' or scriptural knowledge.
Arthavāda narrating what was done or said in former times.
The 'exterior' genre of Tamil poetry — heroism, kingship, praise; the Āḻvārs turn its praise-forms to the Lord's deeds.
A class of sacred narrative lore, called with itihāsa the 'fifth Veda'; remembered by Brahmā before the Vedas and condensed by Vyāsa in every Dvāpara age into eighteen Purāṇas of four lakh verses.

The preliminary 'going before': a course of a fixed number of repetitions of a mantra (commonly counted by its syllables), with fire offering, libations, sprinkling and feeding brāhmaṇas in fixed proportions, by which the mantra is mastered before use.
The ancient Śaiva saints, above all the Tamil Nāyaṉmārs, whose lives Vīraśaiva hagiography narrates as models for the śaraṇas.
The waste of food: gives support and holds wind and fire (Su Sū 15.5).
The region into which the mind enters in deep sleep, where, lacking contact with the skin-sense, it produces no cognition (commentarial tradition on the Muktāvalī).

Full, complete: 'that is full, this is full; from the full the full arises; taking the full from the full, the full remains' (BAU 5.1.1); the space within the heart is full and unchanging (ChU 3.12.9).
The full Kaula consecration; those consecrated by it are Śaiva avadhūtas (Mahānirvāṇa 14.144).
The 'full consecration' of later Śrīvidyā manuals, conferring the full authority of the tradition after the preliminary initiations.
The 'form' (rūpa) level of the fourfold yoni (Kubjikāmata 11.7).
Where Satī's shoulders and neck fell; the goddess there is Pūrṇeśvarī (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.43, 18.49).
One of the four great seats (pīṭha), which in the Yoginīhṛdaya are transformations of the four fused powers and are located in the subtle body.

notes: Shared with the Kaula pīṭha lists (U24).

definitions.definition: The knowledge 'I am Śiva, I am the guru, I am the whole world' (SSM 14.38–41).
The perfect I-awareness whose essence is light and bliss, the potency of the great mantra (PH 20).

notes: Shared vocabulary with Pratyabhijñā (see brw:pratyabhijna-to-virasaiva).

definitions.definition: The conscious principle: neither producer nor product (SK 3); the opposite of the manifest and the unmanifest in being without guṇas, discriminating, subject, individual and conscious (SK 11); witness, isolated, neutral, seer and non-agent (SK 19); many (SK 18). Its existence is proved because aggregates are for another, etc. (SK 17). It is not truly bound or released (SK 62).

The cosmic Person, thousand-headed, who is all this, of whom one quarter is all beings and three quarters the immortal in heaven, and from whose sacrifice the world, Vedas and varṇas came (RV 10.90); the person in whom the gods dwell 'as cows in a stall' (AVŚ 11.8.32).
The seer, pure consciousness, unchanging, not self-luminous objects' owner but always knowing the mind's activities (4.18); utterly unmixed with sattva (3.35); many (2.22).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the conjunction of mind, self and body, subject-matter of Āyurveda (Ca Sū 1.47); the six dhātus (five elements and consciousness), consciousness alone, or the aggregate of twenty-four (Śā 1.16-17); 'the measure of the world' (Śā 5.3); in Suśruta the union of the five elements and the embodied one (Su Sū 1.22).

The person: the self-born person at creation (BAU 1.4.1; AU 1.1.3); the inner person in the eye or heart; in KU 1.3.11 the highest principle beyond the unmanifest; in MuU 2.1.2 the divine formless person; in ŚU 3.8-15 the great person of the Puruṣa Sūkta.

The beginningless principle that experiences pleasure and pain, seated in prakṛti and bound by attachment to the guṇas (BhG 13.19–21); the perishable and imperishable puruṣas are surpassed by the highest (15.16–18); in the Mokṣadharma the twenty-fifth principle, many according to the Sāṃkhya-Yoga thinkers, one in source according to the Nārāyaṇīya's close (12.338).
The cosmic Person with sixteen parts, source of the avatāras (BhP 1.3.1); spirit as one of the four forms of Viṣṇu (VP 1.2).
The Person with whom the sacrifice is identical (ŚB 1.3.2.1); Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa who surpassed all beings by the human sacrifice (ŚB 13.6.1.1).
The supreme Person, ruler of all, subtler than the subtle, called by many names (MDh 12.122–123).
The person, beginningless, beyond prakṛti, not touched by its qualities, like the sun reflected in water.

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify
as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

equivalents.note: Both name the conscious self; Sāṃkhya's puruṣa is plural, inactive and without properties, whereas Advaita's ātman is one (with Brahman) and Nyāya's ātman bears qualities.

notes: Other lineages (e.g. Sāṃkhya) contribute very different definitions under this term; no equivalence is asserted here.

definitions.definition: Twelfth tattva: consciousness bound by māyā and the five kañcukas; the limited individual subject.
Īśvara's definition: a puruṣa distinguished from others by never having been touched by bondage (1.24, YBh 1.24).
What is done here in this life, which can overcome a weak daiva (Ca Vi 3.30-33).
Human effort, without which fate does not succeed (MBh 13.6.7); defended by Draupadī (3.28–33).
Śrī's role of intercession: she turns the soul toward the Lord and moves the Lord to forgive and receive it.
Mediation of Śrī (and, for the Tiruppāvai's commentators, of Nappiṉṉai): Nammāḻvār surrenders naming 'the lady who says she cannot part from him' (TVM 6.10.10).
Dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa, on all of which the epic claims to contain everything (MBh 1.56.33); for Prahlāda 'puruṣārtha' as human effort is denied as a cause (12.215.15).

The purpose — experience and liberation — for which the instruments act (SK 31, 36), the liṅga plays its parts (SK 42) and prakṛti creates (SK 56); the supreme puruṣārtha is the complete cessation of the threefold suffering (SS 1.1).
The aims of human life — dharma, artha, kāma, and (as the fourth) mokṣa; Manu's settled view is that the good is the triad (MDh 2.224).
Of the three, artha is foremost since the others are rooted in it (Arthaśāstra 1.7.6–7).
The three are to be pursued in their proper ages without harming each other; each earlier is weightier (Kāmasūtra 1.2.1–14).

literal: for the sake of the person

definitions.definition: That which gives delight to a person, the desire for it being inseparable from it (MS 4.1.2); acts done for it are for the person, not for the rite.

notes: Mīmāṃsā sense; distinct from the 'four aims of life' sense of puruṣārtha.

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu, beyond both the perishable (souls) and the imperishable (Lakṣmī).
The Lord, beyond the perishable and higher than the imperishable, who enters and sustains the three worlds (BhG 15.16–18).
Nārāyaṇa, reached by the ekāntins; those on the 'fourth path' go to him (MBh 12.336.3).
The Lord as distinct from and higher than both the bound (kṣara) and the freed (akṣara) souls (Gītā 15.16–18).
The highest person, Kṛṣṇa, above Akṣara Brahman; the goal of grace-devotion.
The 'prior' Kaula view presented in Lakṣmīdhara's commentary on SL 34, on the Goddess as Śiva's body and the shared relation of principal and subsidiary.
The Eastern transmission; in the Kashmir–Nepal scheme usually the Kula/Trika worship of Kuleśvarī and Kuleśvara (moderate confidence).
The first, provisional answer to the doubt, stated in its strongest form before being set aside.
The preliminaries of a performance — songs, instrumental pieces and the benediction (nāndī) — offered to please the gods (NŚ 5).
The unmanifest sign of an impending disease (Mādhava Nidāna 1.5-6).
Inference whose object's class has been seen before (e.g., fire from smoke); with śeṣavat and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa one of the three kinds (commentaries on SK 5).
One of the three kinds of inference named in NS 1.1.5; the Bhāṣya offers more than one explanation.
The subtle body arising from the subtle elements and consisting of mind, ego and intellect, which confines the individual (SK 3.17).
The guide on the paths who leads the dead to the fathers (RV 10.17.3–6).
Grace, the Lord's nourishment (poṣaṇa) of the soul (BhP 2.10.4); the path in which grace alone, independent of means, gives loving service.
Calcination in a pit-fire of measured cakes of dung; the basic process of mineral pharmacy.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: An initiate who has received nirvāṇa-dīkṣā and seeks liberation.
Mercury, the central substance of Siddha alchemy and of the mineral medicines; recorded as a term only.

notes: Restricted subject (mercury): no preparations recorded.

definitions.definition: The true name of the supreme being and of the highest region, revealed by Soamiji; glossed in the Agra literature as Rādhā (the soul/current) and Soamī (the Lord).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Gone from the sage of steady mind (2.56); senses free of rāga and dveṣa lead to serenity (2.64); set with dveṣa in each sense towards its object, a waylayer (3.34).
The tāmasa opposite of dispassion; from passion of the nature of rajas comes saṃsāra (SK 45); meditation is its removal (SS 3.30); it is not quieted by enjoyment (SS 4.27).
Attachment, which follows on pleasure (2.7).
Attachment to the agreeable, arising from false knowledge (NBh 1.1.2); one of the three groups of faults.
Arises from pleasure, absorption, satisfaction, the unseen and particular birth (VS 6.2.12–16 C).
Passion in which even sorrow becomes happiness for the beloved's sake.
Kañcuka: attachment, the sense of lacking something.
A melodic entity: that particular sound adorned with notes and melodic movement which colours the minds of people (Bṛhaddeśī 280–281).

notes: Disambiguated from trm:raga (attachment, passion).

definitions.definition: Devotion that follows the rāgātmikā devotion of the Vraja residents, arising from eager longing (lobha); of two kinds, kāmānugā and sambandhānugā.
Devotion consisting of rāga — spontaneous, intense absorption in the beloved — natural to the eternal residents of Vraja.
The three mantras of the Śrīvaiṣṇava: the tirumantra (aṣṭākṣara), the dvaya and the carama-śloka (Gītā 18.66).
The 'secret sacrifice': the Goddess is worshipped by its sequence and pleased by secret libations (LSN 83). (Interpretations differ; summary only.)

The goal served by haṭha: samādhi, the mindless, supportless state in which mind and breath are dissolved; HYP 4.3–4 lists it first among the synonyms of samādhi (with unmanī, manonmanī, amanaska, sahaja, turyā…). The DYŚ calls it the best of the four yogas, the Śiva Saṃhitā 'free of duality'; the Jyotsnā identifies it with asamprajñāta yoga, the cessation of all mental activity.
The royal yoga, the goal to which haṭha leads; synonymous with samādhi, unmanī, sahaja and the rest (HYP 4.3–4).
The fourth of the four yogas; in the Yogaśikhā the union of rajas and retas.

equivalents.standpoint: the haṭha texts' list of synonyms
equivalents.note: HYP 4.3–4 and GS 7.17 treat rājayoga and samādhi as names of one state

definitions.definition: The front teeth, at whose root the tongue is pressed in some forms of padmāsana and mahābandha (HYP 1.46, 3.22; GŚ 64; ŚS 3.73).
The duties of the king, taught by Bhīṣma in the Śāntiparvan (12.1–128) and by Rāma to Bharata (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100).
'Sovereign of the king of kings': Lalitā as supreme empress, the form worshipped in South Indian Śrīvidyā temples.

literal: queen of the king of kings

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Desire and anger arise from the guṇa rajas (3.37).
A region of space, especially the atmosphere; 'there was no rajas' before creation (RV 10.129.1); the six rajāṃsi propped apart (1.164.6).
The guṇa of passion, arising from thirst and attachment, binding by attachment to action (BhG 14.7); desire and anger are born of it (3.37).
The guṇa that is stimulating and mobile (SK 13), of the nature of pain (SK 12); predominant in the middle world (SK 54); suffering is a modification of rajas (Vācaspati).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): with tamas one of the two doṣas of the mind (Ca Sū 1.57; AHS Sū 1.21); the rājasa mind is faulty, having the part of anger (Śā 4.36); rajas and tamas bind the person to the wheel of births (Śā 1.36, 1.68); their absence is a condition of liberation (Śā 1.142).
The guṇa characterized as attraction and aversion; those in it go to the human state (MDh 12.26, 12.40).

notes: The later guṇa sense is contributed by other units.

definitions.definition: The female generative fluid, counterpart of bindu, retained by the yoginī in the vajrolī passage (HYP 3.99–102) and identified with Śakti (SS 1.92). Not the guṇa rajas.
The royal knowledge and royal secret of ch. 9, supreme purifier, directly perceived and easy to practise (BhG 9.1–2).
The rope–snake: stock illustration of superimposition, sublation and substratum.
The eight passions among the ninety-six principles — desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, haughtiness and egoism (list recalled at low confidence).
Demonic beings who harm the rite and cause disease, driven off by Agni and the healer (RV 10.97.6).
The second tissue: gives clarity of complexion, nourishes flesh and sustains life (Su Sū 15.5); counted with the doṣas by Suśruta (Sū 21.3-4).
Bloodletting, counted by the surgical school among the purificatory therapies. Summary only.
Charm, the quality of colouring the mind with delight, lacking in the unstruck nāda and present in music (ŚR 1.2.166); cognate with rāga.
The Sants' most common name for the formless Lord who 'pervades every body' (ghaṭ ghaṭ rām) — explicitly distinguished from Rāma son of Daśaratha.
Rām as the nirguṇa object of remembrance of the 'lovers of Rām'.

cross_language.note: the Sanskrit name primarily denotes the avatāra

definitions.definition: The Vārkarī mantra, given to Tukārām in his dream-initiation and chanted by all Vārkarīs.
The name 'Rāma', greater than both the formless and the embodied Brahman, mediating between them, the one support in the Kali age and the ferrying mantra Śiva gives the dying at Kāśī.

equivalents.note: the Rāma name is one of the forms the tāraka mantra takes (Kāśī), not the whole of the tāraka doctrine

definitions.definition: Rāma's reign as the pattern of a righteous order, free of bodily, divine and elemental suffering, where all keep their dharma and love one another.
The six-syllable Rāma mantra (rāṃ rāmāya namaḥ) given at Rāmānandī initiation.

notes: Form of the initiation mantra as commonly reported; verify against Rāmānandī manuals.

definitions.definition: A verse form (caupāī stanzas closed by a sākhī) used for doctrine, especially cosmology, in the Bījak.
The pitta that colours rasa (into blood): in liver and spleen for Suśruta (Sū 21.10), in the stomach for Vāgbhaṭa (AHS Sū 12.13).

literal: sap; taste; essence; (in Rasa Śāstra) mercury

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) taste, the object of the tongue, sixfold — sweet, sour, salt, pungent, bitter, astringent (Ca Sū 1.64-65; 26.9); (2) the first tissue (AHS Sū 1.13).
In Rasa Śāstra, mercury, 'the rasa of my body' (Rasārṇava 1.36); rasa as the means of crossing saṃsāra, identified with brahman ('raso vai saḥ', SDS Raseśvara 49).

Aesthetic relish: the stable emotion made relishable by the union of determinants, consequents and transient states, tasted by the sensitive spectator as food is tasted (NŚ 6 rasa-sūtra); eight in drama (NŚ 6.15), nine with śānta; 'twin of tasting Brahman' (SD 3.2).
The emotional flavour that notes, rāgas and dance are to evoke; the music treatises assign notes and rāgas to rasas.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The inner taste for sense-objects that remains when one abstains from them and turns away only on seeing the highest (2.59).
Quality grasped by the tongue; six tastes; in earth and water.
The essence of love tasted in the union of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, located in the Sahajiyā body; the Sahajiyā reads Rūpa Gosvāmī's rasa theory as a guide to embodied practice.

notes: Homonym: in aesthetics and bhakti the relished sentiment.

definitions.definition: The first tissue, the essence of digested food: gives satisfaction and pleasure and nourishes blood (Su Sū 15.5).
Kṛṣṇa's circle dance with the gopīs on the autumn full-moon night (BhP 10.29-33).

literal: the play of the rāsa dance

definitions.definition: Mercury, which like the mind is by nature unsteady; 'bound' mercury and mind are compared in HYP 4.26–27 (an alchemical analogy; no procedure).
