The eighteen processings of mercury required before it can be used; named in the SDS (Raseśvara 19-21) and detailed in the rasa texts. RESTRICTED: names and procedures not recorded.

notes: Homonym: saṃskāra as latent impression and as life-cycle rite.

definitions.definition: The seven obstacles to aesthetic relish listed by Abhinavagupta (lack of credibility, particularity of time and place, absorption in one's own feelings, lack of means, lack of clarity, non-predominance, doubt).
Semblance of rasa: an improper or incompatible mixture of rasas, or rasa in an unfit object.
A liṅga made of processed mercury, whose worship is praised above that of all other liṅgas (Rasārṇava 1.43; RRS 1.24, 6.19). RESTRICTED: its making is not recorded.
The hall for rasa work in a safe, righteous land, spacious and well provided with windows, with a secluded rasa-pavilion beside it (RRS 6.11-14).
The science of processing mercury and minerals for the body's stability, jīvanmukti and medicine; also rasavidyā, rasatantra (Rasārṇava 1.46; SDS Raseśvara 23).
Those who, without abandoning the body, have gained the body born of Hara and Gaurī, whose servants are the mantras (Rasahṛdaya 1.7); twenty-seven are listed in RRS 1.2-5.
Relishing: enjoying the bliss of savikalpa samādhi (or of the calm mind), which prevents going further.
Alchemy — the art (vātam) of transmuting metals and fixing mercury (iracam), in the Siddhar corpus both an outer art and a figure for perfecting the body. Summary only.

notes: 'vātam' also names the wind humour; the homonym is kept apart (see trm:vata). Restricted subject.

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the branch and the means by which the healthy gain long life, memory, intelligence, health, youth, lustre and strength — 'the means of obtaining the excellent rasa and other tissues' (Ca Ci 1.1.7-8; AHS Utt 39.1-2); taken by the hut-entering or the wind-and-sun mode (Ci 1.1.16); useless in an unpurified body (Su Ci 27.4; AHS Utt 39.4).
In Rasa Śāstra: rejuvenation by processed mercury and minerals (restricted), the fourth section of the Rasaratnākara 'for the aged' (Rasakhaṇḍa 1.5).
The empirical person, the aggregate of twenty-four, born of delusion, desire, aversion and karma, in which action, fruit, knowledge, pleasure and pain are established (Ca Śā 1.35-37, 1.53).
A devotee who contemplates the sweet, intimate love-play of Sītā and Rāma as a companion (sakhī).
A connoisseur of the pair's love (rasa) in Vṛndāvana; used of the Rādhāvallabha and Haridāsī poets.
As in the Rādhāvallabha usage: one who tastes the rasa of the nikuñja.
One of the two principal sāmans of the soma rite, forming part of the Vrātya's seat (AVŚ 15.3).
Love or attraction for Kṛṣṇa; the seed-form of the permanent emotion; in bhāva-bhakti it first appears.
Love-feeling (and, in coded usage, its bodily basis) that the practitioner must stabilize and raise into prema.
The Sātvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya saṃhitās, held to issue directly from the Lord's mouth; the Īśvara, Pārameśvara and Pādma are their explanatory expansions.

notes: Not the Buddhist or Jain 'three jewels' (different ids).

definitions.definition: The Rudra-gāyatrī ('tatpuruṣāya vidmahe ...') muttered after impurity and as the chosen verse from which yoga proceeds.
Matter (wealth, substance): paired with breath as the first pair produced by Prajāpati; the moon, and all that has form or is formless (PrU 1.4-5); the southern course (1.9).
A metrical verse of praise, the unit of the Ṛgveda; the verses rest on the syllable in the highest heaven (RV 1.164.39); ṛc is speech (VS 36.1).
Exhalation, one of the three parts of breath-control (HYP 2.71).
Exhalation; inwardly, negation of the world or renunciation of objects.
Seed; desire was 'the first seed of mind' (RV 10.129.4); 'seed-placers' in 10.129.5.
A rite on the way to Paṇḍharpūr in which a horse (held to carry the saint unseen) runs in a circle round the assembled pilgrims.
Style, a special arrangement of words (Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, Pāñcālī); for Vāmana the soul of poetry (KAS 1.2.6).
A separate class of gods fit for the office of Brahmā (Vāyu is among them); only they can reach that office.
A mantra whose division into feet depends on the sense (MS 2.1.35).
The debts with which one is born — to the seers, gods and ancestors (TS 6.3.10.5), and to men (ŚB 1.7.2.1).
The three debts to be paid before seeking liberation (MDh 6.35–37).
The three debts with which, according to scripture, a brāhmaṇa is born; urged as a bar to liberation and answered as figurative (NS 4.1.59–62; NBh).
Heaven and earth as a pair.
The red (rising) sun praised as a creative supreme power in Atharvaveda book 13.
A seer of the hymns; 'a ṛṣi is so called from seeing' (Nirukta 2.11); the seers had direct perception of dharma (1.20); Vāc makes whom she loves a ṛṣi (RV 10.125.5).
One who 'saw' the hymns; Brahman the self-existent came upon them in their austerity (Nirukta 2.11); they had direct vision of dharma (Nirukta 1.20).
The seers are the breaths (ŚB 6.1.1.1; AA 2.2.1).
A woman seer of Ṛgveda verses (e.g. Lopāmudrā, Ghoṣā, Apālā, Viśvavārā, Vāc Āmbhṛṇī), recorded in the Anukramaṇīs.

literal: what is fitting; the true course

definitions.definition: The true order that holds together the cosmos (the courses of sun, dawn, seasons and waters), the sacrifice and right conduct; guarded by Varuṇa and Mitra; born with satya from kindled tapas (RV 10.190.1); the twelve-spoked wheel of the year is 'the wheel of ṛta' (1.164.11).
The order of which food, in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, calls itself the firstborn (TB 2.8.8.1).
What is right, the order: spoken alongside truth (TU 1.1, 1.9); the right side of the self made of understanding (TU 2.4); the knower is 'first-born of ṛta' (TU 3.10.6).

equivalents.note: The later tradition speaks of dharma where the Saṃhitās speak of ṛta and dharman (RV 1.164.50 calls the first sacrifices 'the first dharmas'); the scope differs (ṛta is also cosmic order).

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan aṣ̌a/arta.
alt_notes: U02 adds only a Brāhmaṇa usage; the Saṃhitā concept belongs to U01.

definitions.definition: The insight arising in that clarity, which bears only truth (1.48), has the particular as its object unlike testimony and inference (1.49), and whose impression obstructs others (1.50).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the year has six seasons of two months each from Māgha — śiśira, vasanta, grīṣma, varṣā, śarad, hemanta (AHS Sū 3.1; Ca Sū 6.4).
A season; spring, summer and autumn were ghee, fuel and oblation in the Puruṣa sacrifice (RV 10.90.6).
Regimen by season: the six seasons in the 'taking' (ādāna) and 'releasing' (visarga) halves of the year, with diet and conduct to suit the strength and doṣas of each (Ca Sū 6; AHS Sū 3).
An officiating priest; the full soma rite has sixteen in four groups of four (hotṛ, adhvaryu, udgātṛ, brahmán and their assistants).
Taste for practice itself — the sixth stage.
The fierce archer-god feared for his arrows and loved as the best physician, lord of cattle, 'auspicious' (śiva), praised in hundreds of forms in the Śatarudrīya.
The Lord of the Pāśupata Sūtra, near whom the liberated brahmin does not return and with whom he attains union; gods and ancestors are both in him.
Rudra: 'Rudra is one, they do not stand for a second' (ŚU 3.2); source of the gods, who saw Hiraṇyagarbha born (3.4); his auspicious form (3.5); in MaiU 5.2 the tamas-part of the one.
The third knot, pierced in niṣpatti, when the breath reaches Śiva's seat and flute and vīṇā sounds arise (HYP 4.76).

literal: division (of scripture) belonging to the Rudras

definitions.definition: The eighteen Siddhānta tantras from Vijaya to Vātula, revealed to eighteen Rudras; in Jayaratha's reading dominated by difference-and-non-difference.
The seed-beads born from Śiva's tears at the burning of the Triple City (SSM 7.47–48), one of the eight shields; wearing them frees brāhmaṇa and outcaste alike (7.62).
Bead from Kālāgnirudra's tears, worn with mantras.
The seed worn and used for japa by Śaivas, glorified in the Śiva Purāṇa (Vidyeśvara 25) and the Devī Bhāgavata.
The final and certain attainment of Rudra's proximity, from which no one returns.
Quality grasped by sight alone; seven colours; in earth, water, fire.
The outward human form of man and woman, onto which the divine nature (svarūpa) is superimposed in practice.
A short aphoristic saying (from śabda, 'word') of Gorakh or another Nāth, the main form of the Gorakh Bānī.
Vernacular mantras, often ending in an oath by Gorakh or the Nāths, credited with power without the rules of Sanskrit mantras; the tradition ascribes them to Gorakhnāth.

(1) The subtle element of sound and the quality of space (SK 22, 28). (2) The accomplishment of knowledge arising from hearing words of instruction (SK 51). (3) In the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, verbal testimony = reliable instruction (SS 1.101); sound is not eternal and not sphoṭa (SS 5.57–58).
(1) Verbal testimony: the instruction of a reliable person (NS 1.1.7), of seen or unseen objects (NS 1.1.8). (2) Sound, the object of hearing and a non-eternal quality of ākāśa (NS 1.1.14, 2.2.13).
Sound: a quality of ākāśa, its mark, produced by conjunction, disjunction and sound, non-eternal (VS 2.1.24–27, 2.2.36–37 Candrānanda); verbal knowledge is inference (VS 9.19).
Verbal testimony is a statement produced by true knowledge of the meaning that causes its utterance (Tattvacintāmaṇi); sound is of two kinds, inarticulate and phonemic (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The word, defined in the Mahābhāṣya as that by which, when uttered, the understanding of the thing arises.
The Word: the guru's word that awakens the disciple, and the inner Word/sound by which the Lord is known; also the name of the song genre (śabda, pad).
Shabd, the audible life stream or sound current — the creative power of the Supreme, heard within and followed back to its source.

notes: Philosophical senses (śabda-brahman, testimony) belong to U31/U11/U12.

definitions.definition: Brahman as the Word: the Word-principle (śabdatattva) that appears as the world and permeates all cognition; its highest accessible level is paśyantī (VP 1.1, 1.123, 1.142).

The unmanifest sound arising from the dividing supreme bindu; not the word nor the meaning (both insentient) but the consciousness of all beings, which dwells in the body as kuṇḍalinī and becomes the letters (ŚT 1.11–14).
Word-brahman: of the two brahmans, sound and non-sound, one skilled in the word-brahman attains the highest (MaiU 6.22).

equivalents.note: duplicate id used by U19 for the same term; to be merged
the music treatises' nāda-brahman is described in the same words ('the consciousness of all beings') as the mantra manuals' śabda-brahman

definitions.definition: Words are eternal; utterance only manifests them, and a word is recognized as the same in every utterance (MS 1.1.18–23).
Cognition of an unperceived object from words (śāstra); the Vedic word is independently valid; a human word only when the speaker is reliable and the matter within reach of other means.
Verbal testimony: the Veda, authorless and reproduced by Īśvara at each creation; the only means of knowing Brahman.
The refinement or purification of words through grammar, which is 'the attainment of the supreme self' (VP 1, verse number uncertain).
The cognition of a sentence-meaning produced by words, given expectancy, compatibility, proximity and known intention.
The unstruck sound in which one is immersed to reach the supreme Brahman (VBT 38).
The grammarians' absolute, refuted as final by Somānanda (Śivadṛṣṭi 2).
A different verb, which marks a distinct rite (MS 2.2.1); first of the six means of distinguishing rites.
'Yoga preceded by the word': the path in which correct usage of words and knowledge of their nature lead to union with the Word-Brahman (Vṛtti on VP 1).
The totality of the letters, whose powers bind the unaware and grant perfection to the aware (SK 3.13-16).
The relation of word and meaning, eternal and not made by anyone (Kātyāyana's first vārttika; VP 1.23; 3.3 'fitness', yogyatā).

literal: the relation of word and meaning

definitions.definition: The principle (essence) of the Word: Bhartṛhari's name for Brahman, without beginning or end, which appears as things (VP 1.1).

literal: the word-principle / reality of the word

definitions.definition: The prompter's operation conducive to a person's engaging in action, expressed by the injunctive (liṅ) element; in the Veda it resides in the word itself.
The four samāpattis, which have an external thing as seed, are samādhi with seed (1.46, YBh 1.46).
Initiation after which the initiate must keep the observances (samaya), for those capable of them.
ŚiP 7.2.39.8-10: meditation resting on a form (with seed) and awareness of the formless self (without seed).
VP 6.7.40-42: prāṇāyāma is with a support (the gross form of the Lord as its object) or without.
Being–consciousness–bliss: the three words indicate, by excluding their opposites, the one attributeless Brahman; they are not three attributes.
The 'true region', the fifth inner region reached by the soul on the sound current, where it meets the Sat Purush; beyond it Alakh, Agam and Anāmī.
Practices of the learned (śiṣṭa) done with no visible motive, accepted as indicating Vedic injunctions (MS 1.3.7).
Honest livelihood (kāyaka) and moral life, the fruit of which is shared (dāsōha).
The Vedas, the Mahābhārata, the entire Pañcarātra, the original Rāmāyaṇa, the Purāṇas of that character and whatever follows them.
'Oṃ namaḥ śivāya', in which Śiva who is both partless (revealed by Oṃ) and with parts (revealed by the five syllables) abides (SSM 8.17–22).
The six-limbed yoga of the Maitrī: breath-control, withdrawal, meditation, concentration, contemplative reasoning and absorption (MaiU 6.18).

notes: The Kālacakra six-branch yoga has the same name and a different list (other units).

definitions.definition: Name of the Trika scripture/tradition, placed at the top of the hierarchy of grace (TĀ 13.301).
Cat-acat: the soul's nature as neither the Real (Śiva) nor the unreal (the perishing world) but able to know and join both.

The Sāṃkhya Sūtra's account of error: what appears in error is both existent and non-existent, since it is sublated (as there) and not sublated (as real elsewhere) (SS 5.56), rejecting the rival accounts (5.52–55).
The five-faced form of Śiva (faces Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta) from whom all tantras issue; the 28 Siddhānta tantras are the limbs of his mantra-body.
Third tattva: will predominant; the inward 'nimeṣa' (ĪPK 3.1.3), 'I am this' with the 'I' prominent.
Knowledge, power, lordship, strength, virility and splendour, together constituting the supreme Brahman; knowledge is its very form, the other five its aspects; they are also Lakṣmī's body.

notes: Not the three guṇas of prakṛti; the AS calls Brahman 'nirguṇa' with respect to those.

definitions.definition: An initiate consecrated to master a mantra for supernatural powers and enjoyments (bubhukṣu).
In the Dāsbodh: The practitioner who takes up hearing, reflection and devotion under the guru.
The practitioner's stage, relying on bhāva.
The pitta in the heart that accomplishes desired aims through intellect, intelligence and self-regard (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.13-14).
Devotion as practice, performed with the senses, whose aim is the manifestation of the eternally perfect bhāva in the heart.
The four means: discrimination of eternal and non-eternal, dispassion toward enjoyments here and hereafter, the six virtues beginning with calm, and longing for liberation.
Discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues and longing for liberation.
The woman partner of the Sahajiyā (and Bāul) practitioner, regarded as Rādhā and often as the guru of the practice; recorded without details (restricted context).

Viveka (purity of food), vimoka (freedom from desire), abhyāsa (practice), kriyā (ritual duties), kalyāṇa (virtues), anavasāda (no dejection), anuddharṣa (no excessive elation) — the aids to meditation listed by the Vākyakāra.

Generalization: the process by which determinants and emotions shown in the art-work are freed from belonging to a particular person, time and place, so that the spectator relishes them impersonally (Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka; Abhinavagupta).

A correct word (as taught by grammar), whose knowing use brings merit, as opposed to a corrupt form (apaśabda); 'a single word well known and well used is a wish-granting cow in heaven' (Mahābhāṣya on 6.1.84).
Association with saints — the second stage and one of the five most potent limbs.

literal: probandum; what is to be proved

definitions.definition: What is to be proved, stated in the proposition (NS 1.1.33).
A pseudo-reason that itself needs proof (NS 1.2.8 DCS).
A means that the soul performs (bhakti-yoga, or — for the Vaṭakalai — prapatti) to win the Lord's grace.
The six levels of meaning of the mantra: bhāvārtha, sampradāyārtha, nigarbhārtha, kaulikārtha, sarvarahasyārtha, mahātattvārtha (YH 2.15-16).
The twenty-sixth, stainless, awakened, immeasurable and eternal, which ever knows the twenty-fifth and twenty-fourth; the twenty-fifth attains its state on awakening (MBh 12.296.7–12).

equivalents.note: the Mokṣadharma's twenty-sixth above the twenty-fifth parallels the Gītā's highest person above the perishable and imperishable

definitions.definition: The conduct of the good, to be followed always with mindfulness; it yields health and mastery of the senses at once (Ca Sū 8.17-18); it includes worship, cleanliness, truthful and gentle speech, non-covetousness, avoiding bad company and being devoted to continence, knowledge, giving, friendliness, compassion, joy, equanimity and calm (Sū 8.18-29; AHS Sū 2.20-47).
Liberation at once at death, as opposed to the gradual ascent.
Immediate liberation of the knower of the attributeless Brahman, whose prāṇas do not depart (contrasted with krama-mukti).
The two kinds of sahita retention in the GS: with the seed-syllables a, u, m and meditation on Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, or without seed.

equivalents.note: Both divide breath-control by the presence or absence of a support; the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's support is the Lord's form, the Gheraṇḍa's the seed-syllables with the three gods.

definitions.definition: With attributes: Brahman as associated with māyā — Īśvara, omniscient and omnipotent, object of worship and meditation; real at the empirical level.
The embodied Rāma: the formless becomes embodied, overcome by the devotee's love; not different from the formless.

The Lord with qualities and form — the avatāras and the images of temple worship; for the Sants not the final object of devotion (Kabīr: the son of Daśaratha is praised, but the secret of Rām's name is other).
The aikya sub-stage in which guru, Śiva and disciple are remembered as one's own nature (SSM 14.34–36).
The innate, natural state: sahaja-samādhi, in which the mind sees the mind, is liberation (AmŚ 54); sahajā is a synonym of rājayoga and samādhi (HYP 4.4).
The innate principle abiding in the heart (KJN 17.5, 17.21); the innate Kaula path abiding in samarasa, as against the 'made' (kṛtaka) path of kuṇḍalī (Akulavīra B.43).

The natural state (sahajāvasthā), a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4), which arises of itself when śakti is awakened (4.11) but is hard to obtain without a true guru's compassion (4.9); 'natural bliss' in the paricaya stage (4.75).
The natural, innate state: the Lord realized without forced austerities, with eyes open, every act worship; 'sahaj samādhi'. Kabīr also warns that all speak of sahaj and none knows it.
The innate: the ultimate nature of man and woman as Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā and the state of union beyond the two; the goal of the Sahajiyā path.
The natural Man and the natural way (sahaj mānuṣ, sahaj pathe) found in the body under the guru.
The sahaja mānuṣa, the Master hidden in the human, and the sahaja religion revealed by Āulcānd.
'Natural, innate': the divine pair (sahaja jorī) are eternally together by nature, never joined and never parted.

cross_language.note: also the Sahajiyā sense
the Buddhist Sahajiyā sense (the innate as the union of wisdom and means), see U44

equivalents.note: HYP lists sahajā among the names of the one highest state

notes: Haridāsī sense only; not the Sahajiyā or Nāth sense.

definitions.definition: The innate Man, the divine as present in the human person (Kṛṣṇa in man, Rādhā in woman); 'the truth of man is above all'.
The natural Man within, to be worshipped in the human (mānuṣ bhajan).
The Master hidden in the human form, revealed by the Kartā.
Natural absorption: absorption without closing the eyes, stopping the ears or torturing the body, in which walking is circumambulation and lying down prostration.
A variant of vajrolī involving ash; said to succeed only for the virtuous and envy-free (HYP 3.92–95). RESTRICTED: summary only.
A variant of vajrolī named in the haṭha texts; restricted, not described.
The auxiliary or instrumental cause: Śiva's single power (śakti).
The thousand-petalled lotus, the first inner region above the eye centre, seat of Jot Nirañjan, where the bell and conch sound and a flame is seen.

cross_language.note: in haṭha texts the crown lotus (sahasrāra); in Sant Mat the first region above the eyes

definitions.definition: The thousand-petalled lotus of the crown where the Goddess unites with her consort (SL 9; LSN 39); for the Samayins the Śrīcakra is the moon-disc there (Lakṣmīdhara).
The thousand-petalled lotus at or above the crown, seat of Śiva (Kailāsa, SS 5.151–157; Paramaśiva, ṢCN 40–49), where kuṇḍalinī dissolves and nectar flows.
The thousand-petalled lotus above the centres where Śakti unites with Śiva.
Retention joined with inhalation and exhalation, practised until kevala (retention alone) arises; in the GS the first of the eight retentions, of two kinds, sagarbha and nirgarbha.
'One with heart': the sensitive, cultivated spectator or reader whose mind, polished by repeated study of poetry, can become one with the work and relish rasa (NŚ 6.32–33; DhĀ 1.1).
'Master': title of a Bāul-Fakir guru (Lalon Sāṃi, Sirāj Sāṃi).
The third mode: Śaiva worship.
Śiva as having form, worshipped in the image.
A soul bound by all three bonds — mala, karma and māyā — living in the worlds of māyā.
The knower with all three impurities, identifying with body and objects (waking).
Cakalam: the embodied condition with the three malas and the instruments of māyā.
One of the secret scripts in which the Mahānubhāvas long preserved their scriptures from outsiders.
The placing of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) on the deity's body, counted with the invocation gestures.
A branch or recension of a Veda handed down in a teacher-line; Vyāsa's pupils branched the Vedas through their pupils (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.4.23).
The friend's path, corresponding to yoga and exemplified by Cuntarar.
'Witness': the rhymed couplet (dohā) in which the Sants bear witness to what they have seen; arranged in aṅgas.
The heroine's woman friend and go-between, who carries the lovers' longing between Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa and counsels Rādhā (GG).

cross_language.note: the sense 'witness' carried into the genre name

definitions.definition: The devotee's stance as a companion (sahacarī) of Rādhā, serving the pair and delighting in their joy, never seeking union for herself.
The stance of the singer-witness in the grove; Svāmī Haridās is held to be the sakhī Lalitā.
The Rāma-rasik devotee's identity as a companion of Sītā in the inner Ayodhyā.
The mood of Rādhā's female companions, in which the devotee witnesses and serves the couple's eternal play (Harivyāsa's Mahāvāṇī).
The companions' mood; the mañjarī-bhāva is a special form of it centred on service to Rādhā.

literal: the mood of a female friend

definitions.definition: Friendship with the Lord, the eighth form of devotion.
Friendship with the Lord as one of love's eleven forms (NBS 82).
The rasa of friendship: love for Kṛṣṇa as an equal companion, as of the cowherd boys.
Direct realization of the Lord produced by meditation built on hearing and reflection; used interchangeably with aparokṣa-jñāna.
The witness: consciousness that illumines the mind and its modes, the three states and their absence, itself unchanging and never an object.

The soul's own intrinsic faculty of awareness (its 'essential sense'), counted as the seventh kind of perception; it apprehends the self, the mind and its states, time, space and the validity of knowledge, and what it establishes is never sublated.
Puruṣa is witness (SK 19), by direct relation (SS 1.161); the witness of deep sleep and other states (SS 1.148).
The witness distinct from the three states of the intellect (Haṃsa Gītā); the non-eating bird that knows both.
The Self as witness of the elements, body and mind, free and actionless; resting in it is freedom now (Aṣṭāvakra); the Self standing apart as the intellect's witness (Rāma Gītā).
Witness: the Goddess is 'witness of the universe, without a witness' (LSN 84).
The self as its own witness and refuge (MDh 8.84).
Witness: the one God is 'the witness, the knower, alone, without qualities' (ŚU 6.11).
The witnessing consciousness into which, in samādhi, the world dissolves; the Self untouched by states.
The Lord as witness (BhG 9.18); cf. the supreme person as 'upadraṣṭṛ', the one who looks on (13.22).

equivalents.note: The witness of the three states is what the Māṇḍūkya calls the fourth; 'witness' names it in relation to what it witnesses, 'fourth' relative to the three states.

definitions.definition: The Goddess herself as the power of the absolute; without her even Śiva cannot stir (SL 1; Subhagodaya). For Śāktas she is the supreme reality, the Mother, identical with Brahman.
Consciousness-power (citśakti) and also the power of the insentient (LSN 90); the self-awareness (vimarśa) in which Śiva's light knows itself (Kāmakalāvilāsa 2); Lalitā in union with Kāmeśvara.
Power: the world as the power of Brahman like light from a fire (VP 1.22.56); Viṣṇu's threefold śakti (VP 6.7.61); the Goddess herself (DM).
Śiva's power: the pedestal of the liṅga (SSM 11.32), the breath as the liṅga's power (12.2–3), the great power named Umā that lights the supreme self (12.21–24).
Power, never different from its possessor; the door (mukha) through which Śiva is known (VBT 18-21).
Śiva's power, inseparable from him (KJN 17.8); as Will she is Vyomamālinī, Khecarī, Kuṇḍalī, Manonmanī (20.10–11); also the female partner of Kaula rites.
The power supporting the body (piṇḍādhāra) (SSP 4).
Kula: the Goddess as the totality of powers, whose union with Śiva is bliss and liberation (Kulārṇava 5.79; 17.27).
The power without which Śiva is a corpse (Toḍala 1.25); Kālī as the Ādyā Śakti who devours time.
Power: the self-power of God (devātmaśakti) hidden by its qualities (ŚU 1.3); his supreme power is manifold, his innate action of knowledge and strength (6.8).

The denotative power of a word, which is the Lord's convention 'from this word this meaning is to be understood' (Tarkasaṅgraha); causal power as a separate category is rejected, efficacy being explained by the totality of causes and the absence of counteragents.
Śiva's single, conscious power, the instrument (not the material) of his acts; called grace (aruḷ) when it frees, concealment when it drives the bonds.

cross_language.note: loanword

equivalents.note: Śakti is Śiva's self-awareness
Śāktas call māyā the Goddess's own power; Advaita treats māyā as indeterminable and ultimately unreal

notes: Homonym: Śākta and Śaiva units define śakti as divine power.

definitions.definition: The last section of the mantra; the Goddess's body below the waist (LSN 35).
Transformation of the Lord's power (not of the Lord): the world is a real modification of māyā-śakti while the Lord, like a touchstone yielding gold, is unchanged.
Second tattva: the power of Śiva, bliss (ānanda).

The philosophical name of Vīraśaiva doctrine in Śrīpati's Śrīkarabhāṣya (philosophy owned by U16); the SSM's teaching that the liṅga is Śiva with Śakti as its pedestal and the universe their union (11.32) is its root image.
Śrīpati's doctrine: non-duality of Śiva and soul, both qualified by Śakti (in Śiva as power, in the soul as devotion), realised as their union.
The circle of the powers of consciousness; union with it withdraws the universe (Śiva Sūtra 1.6); Śaṅkara is its source (SK 1.1); the established yogin is its lord (SK 3.19).
The mudrā that stirs and raises kuṇḍalinī (HYP 3.104–123). RESTRICTED as an advanced energy practice.
Leading kuṇḍalinī upward; summary only.
Figurative name for Śiva's awakening of the soul by his power, like a teacher waking sleeping pupils; it occurs when the soul's karmas are in equilibrium, and its sign is a distinctive devotion.
Name used by 'those who hold to the āgamas' for Viṣṇu's compassion, his fifth power of grace, by whose glance the soul's karmas become equal and it is lifted from saṃsāra.
The descent of the Lord's power, independent of karma, intense, middling or mild in three degrees each (TĀ 13); its signs in MVT 2.14-16.
Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): until śaktipāta and the cutting of the fetters, understanding of mercury does not arise (Rasārṇava 1.23).
The descent of Śiva's power on a soul whose mala has ripened, qualifying it for initiation.
Catti nipātam, in four grades matched to the four pādas.

equivalents.note: The Ahirbudhnya identifies kṛpā, anugraha-śakti and śaktipāta; the Śaiva texts also treat śaktipāta as the working of grace.

definitions.definition: The empowered means: contemplation with the mind alone, purifying thought (MVT 2.22; TĀ 4).
Treatment of diseases above the collar-bone — ear, eye, mouth, nose (Su Sū 1.8); 'ūrdhvāṅga' in AHS Sū 1.5.
The undistinguished water that 'all this' was in the beginning (RV 10.129.3); the great waters that bore the germ (10.121.7).
Form of liberation: dwelling in the Lord's world.
Liberation as residence in the Lord's world; one of the five that pure devotees refuse without service.
Liberation as residence in the Lord's world; one of five liberations devotees do not accept without service.
Residence in the Lord's world — first of the four kinds of liberation.
Living in Śiva's world; fruit of caryā.
Dwelling in the Lord's world, the first of the four liberations, perishable with the worlds.
Surgery: removal of foreign bodies and management of wounds with instruments, knives, caustics and fire; the first and foremost limb for the Dhanvantari school (Su Sū 1.8, 1.17-18).
Peace or calm, the first gatekeeper: the cooling of the desert of saṃsāra, called the supreme state and the end of delusion.
The intellect fixed on the Lord (Uddhava Gītā's redefinition).
Calm: resting the mind on its goal, withdrawn from objects (VC); control of the mind (Tattvabodha).
Calm, the stable emotion of śānta in the Nāṭyaśāstra's śānta passage and in the Sāhityadarpaṇa (3.245).
The wise who see the same in a learned brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater (BhG 5.18); the yogin who sees the same everywhere (6.29) and the Lord equally present in all (13.27–28).
Concentration: keeping the intellect steadily fixed on Brahman (VC); one-pointedness of mind (Tattvabodha).

As salt dissolves in water, the union of self and mind; the sameness when breath is exhausted and mind dissolved; the union of individual and supreme self with all intention ceased (HYP 4.5–7); sixfold in the GS (7.5–6).
Yoga itself (YBh 1.1); the eighth limb — meditation shining only as its object, as if empty of its own form (3.3); of two kinds, samprajñāta and asamprajñāta; with seed or seedless.
VP 6.7.92: the grasping of the very nature of the object free of imagination, produced by meditation.
The attainment of meditation on Śiva as the self through inner worship; undivided attention on the haṃsa-formed supreme self contemplated as 'I am He' (SSM 12.21–24).

Absorption, collectedness: the one 'not collected' cannot attain it (KU 1.2.24, asamāhita); 'samāhita' among the virtues of BAU 4.4.23; the sixth limb (MaiU 6.18); the happiness of a mind washed by samādhi (MaiU 6.34).
Absorption: the samarasa of breath and mind (GŚ 94); also, among Nāths, the tomb in which a yogī's body is buried seated.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In which the resolute understanding of the ritual-minded is not established (2.44); in which understanding must stand immovable for one to attain yoga (2.53); the one of steady wisdom is 'established in samādhi' (2.54). Commentators gloss the word variously in these verses.
In the Yoga Upaniṣads: the union of jīvātman and paramātman; the forgetting of meditation; distinguished from deep sleep; for the Mahāvākya, realization is not mere samādhi.

The practice of a particular samādhi yields knowledge of truth (NS 4.2.38); obstacles to it are overcome by the continuing effect of prior practice (NS 4.2.41); Īśvara possesses concentration (NBh 4.1.21).
The settled state in which the resolute understanding stands unmoving (BhG 2.44, 2.53), not attained by those attached to enjoyment and power.
Absorption that, cultivated in emergence, becomes ever-present (nityodita, PH 19); the bliss of the world is its joy (Śiva Sūtra 1.18).

notes: Some commentators take samādhi in 2.44 and 2.53 as the mind, or the self, in which one concentrates.
alt_notes: The Gītā's usage precedes and differs from the technical samādhi of the Yoga Sūtra.

definitions.definition: The dwindling of the mind's all-objectness and the rise of one-pointedness (3.11).
The complete set of causal conditions, including the absence of counteragents, which suffices for an effect (no separate causal power needed).
Collective temple singing of the founders' padas in fixed style as worship.
The same practice in Rādhāvallabha temples.
The sixth and weakest means of subsidiarity: a derived name, Vedic or worldly, such as 'the Hotṛ's cup' or 'ādhvaryava' (MS 3.3.14).
A melody sung on a verse by the udgātṛ priests; the Sāmaveda; sāman is breath (VS 36.1).
The name for what is sung (MS 2.1.36).
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at the heart.
The vital air that distributes evenly, operating up to the navel; its mastery gives radiance (3.40, YBh 3.39–40).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the vāyu near the digestive fire, moving through the abdomen, which takes in, digests, separates and releases food (AHS Sū 12.8); it fans the belly-fire (Ca Ci 15.7).
The equalizing breath in the middle of the body, distributing food (PrU 3.5).
The breath at the navel (SS 3.7).
The breath at the navel, distributing food.
The phase before unmanā in the subtle pronunciation of the mantra, lasting one unit (Varivasyārahasya).
The equalizing breath, named with the other breaths in later Vedic lists (low confidence for particular Saṃhitā loci).

queries: local AVŚ/VS/TS grep samāna as breath
checks.note: The term and sense are standard (prāṇo 'pāno vyāna udānaḥ samānaḥ, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.5.3, located), but no occurrence of samāna as a breath was found in the local Śaunaka AV, Vājasaneyi or Taittirīya Saṃhitā texts; the entry's source src:atharvaveda-saunaka is therefore unsupported so far (the entry itself says 'later Vedic lists').

definitions.definition: The application of several words, with different grounds of application, to one and the same object ('the blue lotus'); identity statements like 'tat tvam asi' name one Brahman under different modes, keeping the primary sense of each word.
Co-reference: two words in the same case referring to one thing, the grammatical relation of 'tat' and 'tvam'.
Occurring in the same locus; pervasion is a kind of co-location of probans and probandum.
The two ways of purifying the channels in the GS: samanu, done with seed-syllables (bīja), and nirmanu, done by the act of dhauti.
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the cause of increase — like increases like; it makes for oneness (Ca Sū 1.44-45).
Relative to cognition (VS 1.2.3 C); highest is being; eternal, one, present in many (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The universal vibration on which the particular vibrations (of the guṇas etc.) rest (SK 1.19).
Extraordinary contact by which all instances of a universal (all smoke) are grasped, grounding knowledge of pervasion.
Inference from general correlation, by which things beyond the senses are known (SK 6), such as the senses as instruments (Vācaspati), and both prakṛti and puruṣa (SS 1.103).
One of the three kinds of inference named in NS 1.1.5; the Bhāṣya offers more than one explanation.

The mind's taking on the form of what it rests on — grasper, grasping or grasped — like a flawless crystal (1.41); fourfold: savitarkā, nirvitarkā, savicārā, nirvicārā (1.42–44); also coalescence with the endless in posture (2.47).

cross_language.note: Buddhist 'meditative attainment' (the jhānas and formless attainments)

definitions.definition: The sameness that arises when breath is exhausted and mind dissolved (HYP 4.6; GŚ 94).

Union in which the self is contemplated as dissolved in the stainless sky of consciousness; this is the supreme knowledge called liberation (SSM 14.42–44). In the six-bhakti scheme the devotion of the aikya stage is samarasa-bhakti.
'Equal flavour', fusion: Tripurā is the sāmarasya of prakāśa and vimarśa (Dīpikā on YH 1.6); in the Varivasyārahasya one of the fifteen meanings of the mantra.
Equal taste, one-flavouredness: samādhi is the samarasa oneness when breath is exhausted and mind dissolved (GŚ 94); the samarasa of body and supreme state (SSP 5).
The state in which the Akulavīra is seen everywhere and 'all is samarasa' (Akulavīra A.24, A.41).

notes: Shared term with Nāth and Kashmir Śaiva usage; not asserted equivalent here.

definitions.definition: Offering: everything is used only after being offered to the Lord; the unoffered is to be avoided.
The Śrīvaiṣṇava initiation by the five sacraments, by which one becomes the teacher's disciple.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Equanimity is called yoga: being the same in success and failure (2.48); making pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat the same (2.38); the one who is the same in pain and pleasure is fit for immortality (2.15).
Evenness in success and failure, which is called yoga (BhG 2.48); equality toward friend and foe (6.9, 12.18).
That from which the notion 'here' arises regarding effect and cause (VS 7.2.29 C); one eternal relation of inseparables (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The cause in which the effect inheres (threads for cloth); a substance is an inherent cause (VS 1.1.14 C).
Immersion in Rudra's power, of three kinds - āṇava, śākta, śāmbhava (MVT 2.21-23).
The inner way: worship of the Śrīcakra in the space of the heart; also Śiva as 'Samaya', who has fivefold equality with the Goddess, 'Samayā' (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 8, 41).

Bhāskararāya: imagining the cakra in the dahara-space and worshipping there is called Samaya; the five tantras of Vasiṣṭha and the others are called Samaya; or Samaya is Śiva who shares fivefold equality with the Goddess (on LSN 37).
The pledges and rules binding the initiate; without the samaya discipline there is no perfection (Kulārṇava 5.96).
The pledges which tāmasa disciples fail to honour, becoming 'dead while living' (Kubjikāmata 12.4-9).
The post-initiatory rules binding the initiate; for those unable to keep them they may be purified away, and knowingly breaking them is a great fault.
The observances binding an initiate (TĀ 15); the Mata scriptures reject them (TĀ 4.262).
The first Śaiva initiation, making one a samayin, entitled to worship and study under the post-initiatory observances (samaya).
The first initiation, making one a samayin, entitled to the rules (samaya) and to hear the scriptures.
In Lakṣmīdhara, the Vedic way of Goddess worship taught in the five 'auspicious āgamas', opposed to the Kaula and 'mixed' ways.
The Vedic, inner conduct of Śrīvidyā taught by the five Śubhāgamas and followed by Lakṣmīdhara; rejects outer and Kaula worship.
The Goddess is 'intent on Samaya conduct' (LSN 37); Bhāskararāya notes that the Rudrayāmala teaches samayācāra in ten chapters.

notes: Contribution from U08; U23 owns Śrī Vidyā doctrine.

definitions.definition: The four 'teachers of the religion': Appar, Campantar, Cuntarar and Māṇikkavācakar.
A follower of the Samaya way; for Samayins the worship is of Samayā and Samaya in the thousand-petalled lotus (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 41).
The lowest grade of Śaiva initiate, after samaya-dīkṣā.
The triad structuring Gauḍīya theology: the relation (knowledge of Kṛṣṇa, souls and world), the means (devotion) and the goal (love).
Discussion among physicians, friendly or hostile (Ca Vi 8.15-23).
Proposed as a means of knowledge (e.g. a thousand includes a hundred); included in inference (NS 2.2.2).
Attention fixed on an inner target with the gaze outward and unblinking, kept secret like a woman of good family (HYP 4.35–37); also a name of suṣumnā (3.4; 4.18).
The seal of the open, unblinking gaze with attention on the inner target.
The divine means: immersion without thought through the teacher's awakening (MVT 2.23).
Any of the four groupings of sattras formed after Mādhavadeva (Brahma, Puruṣa, Kāla, Nikā).
The continuous text of a Veda (with sandhi), and the collection itself (Ṛg-, Sāma-, Yajur-, Atharva-saṃhitā).
A revealed Pāñcarātra text; tradition speaks of 108 (the Jayākhya's additional passage), of which the Sātvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya are the 'three gems'.

The recitation of the Veda with all sandhi applied, as distinct from the word-by-word (padapāṭha) and step (kramapāṭha) recitations; its secret meaning is taught in the saṃhitā-upaniṣads (AA 3.1.1; TU 1.3).
Form of liberation: dwelling near the Lord.
Liberation as nearness to the Lord.
Liberation as proximity to the Lord.
Nearness to the Lord — one of the four kinds of liberation.
Nearness to Śiva; fruit of kriyā.
'With fuel in hand': the way a pupil approaches a teacher (MuU 1.2.12; PrU 1.1; ChU 5.11.7, 8.7.2; KauU 1.1).
Concord of mind among people, the subject of RV 10.191.
The intention in which desire is rooted and from which sacrifices and vows arise (MDh 2.3); desire born of right intention is a root of dharma (YS 1.7).
The second form, Śeṣa, identified with the jīva (MBh 12.326.38, 12.326.68).

equivalents.note: the Nārāyaṇīya identifies Saṃkarṣaṇa with the jīva

definitions.definition: The darśana that enumerates the twenty-five principles in order to discriminate puruṣa from prakṛti; its knowledge is the discriminating knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower (SK 2) that removes the threefold suffering.

In the Gītā, the understanding (buddhi) concerning the self (2.39) and the path of knowledge of the Sāṃkhyas (3.3), said to be one with Yoga (5.4–5); in the Mokṣadharma, the system that enumerates twenty-four principles with the puruṣa as twenty-fifth and relies on the teaching of the śāstra (12.289.7; 12.294), proclaimed by Kapila (12.337.60).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The way in which the understanding of 2.11–38 was declared, contrasted with 'yoga' (2.39); the sāṃkhyas are those whose commitment is the yoga of knowledge (3.3). The chunk does not relate the term to a school.

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify
as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

notes: U05's definition (the epic usage); classical Sāṃkhya is defined by U09.
alt_notes: The commentators divide on how far the Gītā's sāṃkhya relates to the classical Sāṃkhya darśana.

definitions.definition: Cause of the usage 'one' etc., from one up to parārdha; duality and higher numbers are non-eternal and produced by an enumerating cognition (apekṣābuddhi).

notes: Id disambiguated from the Sāṃkhya school ('sāṃkhya' → samkhya).

definitions.definition: Harmony in family and community, produced by the Atharvavedic concord hymns (AVŚ 3.30).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Perfection is not reached by renunciation (saṃnyasana) alone (3.4); Arjuna is to renounce all actions in Kṛṣṇa and fight (3.30).

Laying aside actions prompted by desire (BhG 18.2); mere renunciation of action does not bring perfection (3.4), and renunciation is hard without yoga (5.6); the true renouncer neither hates nor desires (5.3; 6.1).
Renunciation of rites and possessions after depositing the fires in oneself (MDh 6.38); the renouncer should never renounce the Veda (VDh 10.4).
Renunciation of household and rites for the wandering life; truly, the union of jīva and Self.
One who has renounced; of four or six kinds.
The tradition handed down; all success comes through tradition and faith (PKS 1.9); the Goddess is 'sovereign of the tradition' (LSN 138).
Samādhi accompanied by reasoning, reflection, bliss or I-am-ness (1.17), with a support (YBh 1.17).
The way the disease comes into being by the vitiated, spreading doṣa (Mādhava Nidāna 1.10).
The serene one: the self that, rising from the body and reaching the highest light, appears in its own form (ChU 8.3.4, 8.12.3); also the state of deep serenity (BAU 4.3.15).
The transfer from a dying father to his son (BAU 1.5.17; KauU 2.15).
Therapy that pacifies the doṣas in place (by fasting, digestives, diet and medicines) without expelling them (Su Sū 1.27; AHS Sū 1.25 'śamana').
The round (of rebirth): the one without understanding goes on in saṃsāra (KU 1.3.7); God is the cause of saṃsāra and liberation (ŚU 6.16); 'the mind alone is saṃsāra' (MaiU 6.34).
The round of death and rebirth, from whose ocean the Lord lifts his devotees (BhG 12.7); the forest of Vidura's parable (MBh 11.5–6).
The soul's own construction of 'I and mine' through ignorance; unreal and to be destroyed — distinct from the world (jagat), which is real.
The relation by which the qualifier is cognized as linked to the qualificand; its property is saṃsargatā.
Doubt: a cognition touching both alternatives (YBh 1.30).
Deliberation awaiting a distinguishing mark (NS 1.1.23); a cognition of one thing as qualified by mutually opposed properties, e.g. 'a post or a man?' (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The doubt about the passage that gives rise to an adhikaraṇa (also called sandeha, viśaya).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The perfection Janaka and others reached by action (3.20).

The three origins of the dispositions (SK 43): innate, as in Kapila at the first creation; natural, as in Brahmā's sons at sixteen or in Āsuri through contact with the supreme sage; acquired, as in ordinary people, with a teacher as occasioning cause.

A latent impression left by activities, producing further activities in a ceaseless wheel (YBh 1.5); impressions of samādhi-insight obstruct others (1.50); impressions of stilling are a mental property (3.9); their direct perception gives knowledge of former births (3.18).
A consecratory rite of passage purifying the body of the twice-born from conception to death (MDh 2.26–28); Gautama counts forty (GDh 8.14–21), later lists sixteen.
Impressions whose momentum keeps the knower embodied after knowledge (SK 67; SS 3.84), exhausted at the fall of the body (Gauḍapāda).
A quality of three kinds: momentum, memory-impression and elasticity (Tarkasaṅgraha); memory arises from self–mind conjunction and impressions (VS 9.22 C).
Latent impressions, exhausted when the mind subsides in the supportless (VBT 82, 'kṣīṇāśaya').

cross_language.note: Buddhist 'formations', a wider sense

notes: Homonym: latent impression (Yoga, Buddhism) is defined by other units.

definitions.definition: Therapy that expels the doṣas (the pañcakarma); doṣas purified by it do not return, whereas those merely subdued may flare again (AHS Sū 4.26; Su Sū 1.27).
Worship of Viṣṇu in a consecrated image, as distinct from formless (amūrta) worship through the fire.
A rival account of liberation rejected by Rāmakaṇṭha: the new production [of the Lord's qualities in the soul].
A 'consistent error' that nevertheless leads to its object, as taking a gem's light for the gem leads to the gem; used for meditation on the attributeless (Pañcadaśī 9).
The year, born from the ocean (RV 10.190.2), the twelve-spoked wheel with 720 sons (1.164.11) or 360 spokes (1.164.48).
Ardor in practice, mild, middling or intense; for the intensely ardent samādhi is near (1.21–22).

cross_language.note: Buddhist 'spiritual urgency'

definitions.definition: The knowledge aspect of the internal power, by which the Lord knows and makes himself known.
Consciousness as the one reality and as each act of awareness; in the Krama the goddess is one's own consciousness (svasaṃvid).
Concentration, meditation and samādhi together on one object (3.4), the 'technical term' of the śāstra (YBh 3.4); its mastery gives the light of insight (3.5) and the powers.
Restraint and moderation — the Nāth middle way ('one crosses over by restraint alone', Gorakh Bānī).
Concentration on an object yielding a power (Śāṇḍilya).

notes: Distinct from the technical Pātañjala saṃyama (dhāraṇā-dhyāna-samādhi together).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The self-restrained, awake in what is night for all beings (2.69).
Prakṛti defined as the equilibrium of sattva, rajas and tamas (SS 1.61); creation proceeds from their inequality.

The conjunction of puruṣa and prakṛti, like that of the lame and the blind, from which creation proceeds (SK 21) and the unconscious appears conscious (SK 20); due to non-discrimination (SS 1.55); though it remains after knowledge, there is no motive for creation (SK 66).
The conjunction of seer and seen, cause of what is to be avoided (2.17), caused by ignorance (2.24), the cause of apprehending owner and owned (2.23); its absence is kaivalya (2.25).
Cause of the usage 'conjoined'; produced by the motion of one or both, or by another conjunction (VS 7.2.10 C).
The true path of knowledge, corresponding to jñāna and exemplified by Māṇikkavācakar.
The 'true path': in the Siddhar songs the path of true knowledge (Kaṭuveḷi speaks of books without caṉmārkkam as not to be sought); later the name of Vallalar's movement.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Epithet of the embodied one (2.24) and, in Arjuna's argument, of the family dharmas (1.40).
The emergence of the principles from the unmanifest in order (Tattvasamāsa 5; SK 22).
Accumulated karma not yet begun to bear fruit; burnt by knowledge.
The existence aspect of the internal power, manifesting the Lord's abode, form and paraphernalia.
The twilight rite in which water consecrated with the Gāyatrī is thrown up against the Mandeha demons and the sun is meditated on as Brahman (TA 2.2).
The obligatory morning and evening worship with bathing, sprinkling, breath-control and Gāyatrī recitation (YS 1.22–25).
The 'twilight' or intentional language of double meanings in which Bāul songs speak of body practice and the Man of the Heart, so that the uninitiated hear only devotional or everyday words.
The coded language of the Sahajiyā manuals and padas.
'Twilight' (intentional) language of the siddhas, shared by Nāth and Buddhist siddha songs; the Nāth vernacular form is the ulaṭbāṃsī.

notes: The term itself comes from the Buddhist tantric commentarial tradition (Caryāgīti; owned by U44).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Attachment: not to inaction (2.47); to be abandoned in action (2.48, 3.9); arises from dwelling on objects and gives rise to desire (2.62); the ignorant are attached to action and to the actions of the guṇas (3.26, 3.29); the knower is not attached (3.28).
The relevance of a topic to the whole śāstra, the chapter and the quarter in which it stands.
Song, instrumental music and dance taken together (ŚR 1.1.21).
A paśu joined to body and organs; its opposite, nirañjana, is a paśu without them.
Living samādhi: the saint, still alive, sits in meditation in a chamber that is then sealed, and is held to remain present there — above all Jñāneśvar at Āḷandī.

equivalents.note: the Tamil Siddhar 'cīva camāti' is described in the same terms; different lineage and context

definitions.definition: The function of manas (SK 27).

Intention: a rung of the ladder (ChU 7.4); the self's intentions are real (ChU 8.1.5, 8.7.1); by intention alone the fathers' world arises (8.2.1); 'intention' is the teaching about brahman with respect to the self (Kena 4.5).
Conceiving or willing by the mind, by which worlds are spun; its cessation is the end of saṃsāra.
Epithet of Śiva as 'maker of all happiness and nirvāṇa'; devotion is to be to none but Śaṅkara.
Name of Śiva in the Spandakārikā's opening: by his unmeṣa and nimeṣa the world dissolves and arises (1.1).

notes: Disambiguated from tch:sankara (the Advaita teacher).

definitions.definition: The title of the pontiffs (jagadguru) who head the āmnāya maṭhas in succession to Śaṅkara.
The vyūha manifesting knowledge and strength; in Śaṅkara's report of the Bhāgavatas, identified with the individual soul.
A 'code' or 'tryst': the threefold saṅketa of cakra, mantra and worship (YH 1.6), explained as the meeting-place of Śiva and Śakti (Dīpikā).
In the Dattātreyayogaśāstra, the 'indications' — points of fixed attention — by which the mind dissolves in layayoga; Ādinātha taught eight crore (DYŚ 14–24).
Congregational singing of the Lord's names, the dharma of the Kali age.
The contraction of consciousness into the individual (PH 4, 9).
A rival account of liberation rejected by Rāmakaṇṭha: the transfer of [the Lord's qualities] into the perfected soul.

notes: Homonym of the Jyotiṣa term for the sun's entry into a sign.

definitions.definition: Closing the ears, eyes, nostrils and mouth with the fingers so that the inner light and sound are perceived.
The contact of sense and object from which perception arises (NS 1.1.4); six kinds (Uddyotakara).
Six ordinary contacts plus three extraordinary ones.
A subsidiary enjoined with reference to a material of the rite (e.g. husking, sprinkling), helping by acting on it.

Renunciation: ascetics purified by 'the yoga of renunciation' (saṃnyāsa-yoga) are released in the brahma-worlds (MuU 3.2.6), an early occurrence of the word; the practice itself is described in BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22.
A holy person who has realized the Truth (sat) and lives by it — used by the tradition for its poet-saints and for any true sādhu; in Sant Mat, a master who has reached the highest region.
The saint, in whom God is present; the saints' company is the true tīrtha and their feet are sought above liberation.
The good person whose company (satsaṅg) gives discernment; greater than the Lord himself in Rāma's teaching to Śabarī.
The three characters of the specific (gross) elements, according to the predominance of sattva, rajas or tamas (SK 38).

The rasa of peace, leading to liberation, whose stable emotion is calm (śama, NŚ śānta passage; SD 3.245), dispassion (nirveda, KP 4) or knowledge of reality — the self itself (Abhinavagupta); denied as a dramatic rasa by Dhanañjaya.
The peaceful devotional rasa, awareness of the Lord's greatness without personal intimacy (as of the sages); the first of the five primary rasas.

equivalents.note: poetics praises the relish of śānta; Gauḍapāda (MK 3.45) calls tasting the bliss of samādhi (rasāsvāda) an obstacle to be given up — the same word, opposite valuations

definitions.definition: Lineage (gotra, maṭhikā); lineage-based restrictions are not enjoined in the Trika and forbidden in the Mata scriptures (TĀ 4.265-270).
The teachers of the lineage: the inner line (Nandi, Sanatkumāra, Satyajñānadarśin, Parañcōti) and the outer line (Meykaṇṭār, Aruṇanti, Maṟaiñāṉa Campantar, Umāpati).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Without cultivation there is no peace, and without peace no happiness (2.66); the one whom desires enter as rivers the ocean, and who abandons all desires, attains peace (2.70–71).
Peace and the appeasing of what is harmful; the peace chants (VS 36.17; AVŚ 19.9).
Resident priests who perform the daily pūjās in a Kerala temple under the tantri's authority.
Not wanting more than the means at hand (YBh 2.32); yields unsurpassed happiness (2.42).
Contentment: not craving the unobtained and enjoying what comes without elation or dejection; the third gatekeeper.
Contentment (tuṣṭi), one of the Uddhava Gītā's twelve niyamas.
What certainly possesses the probandum, e.g. the kitchen.
A kinsman within seven generations (MDh 5.60); defined by shared bodily particles in the Mitākṣarā and by shared piṇḍa-offerings in the Dāyabhāga.
The rite that joins the preta to the three generations of ancestors, ending the preta state; done on the twelfth day or up to a year after death.
The rite (on the twelfth day or after a year) that unites the deceased with his three forefathers, turning the preta into a pitṛ.
The ritual hearing of the Bhāgavata in seven days, modelled on Śuka's recital to Parīkṣit and prescribed in the Bhāgavata-māhātmya.
The powers of Brahmā, Śiva, Skanda, Viṣṇu, Varāha, Narasiṃha and Indra appearing as goddesses who fight beside the Goddess and are absorbed into her.
The seven seers; in RV 10.137 Bharadvāja, Kaśyapa, Gotama, Atri, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni and Vasiṣṭha each contribute a healing verse.
'The seven hundred': the Devī Māhātmya as recited in worship, with its limbs (kavaca, argalā, kīlaka, the three rahasyas).

Rāmānuja's seven objections to Advaita's avidyā: of locus (āśraya), concealment (tirodhāna), nature (svarūpa), indescribability (anirvacanīyatva), means of knowledge (pramāṇa), remover (nivartaka) and removal (nivṛtti).
The eightfold excellence of the tissues (skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, mind) by which a physician judges strength, not by body-size (Ca Vi 8.102-115).

literal: refuge; one who has taken refuge

definitions.definition: The fifth sthala: the aṅgaliṅgī as wife and Śiva as husband, possessed of the bliss of their union (SSM 13.2); also the name of the twelfth-century devotees of Kalyāṇa (fem. śaraṇe).
Śaraṇ: the initiation by which one takes refuge in Kṛṣṇa, the name, the guru and the devotees, given by a sattrādhikār.
Going to the Lord alone as refuge ('mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja', BhG 18.66; 'take refuge in him alone', 18.62); Rāma's vow to protect whoever seeks refuge (Rāmāyaṇa 6.18.33).
Surrendering one who has sought refuge is counted among the gravest sins (MBh 17.3.15).
Six-limbed refuge: resolve to do what pleases, avoidance of what displeases, faith that he will protect, choosing him as protector, laying down oneself, and helplessness.
The same as prapatti: surrender with the limbs of ānukūlya-saṅkalpa, prātikūlya-varjana, mahāviśvāsa, goptṛtva-varaṇa, kārpaṇya and ātma-nikṣepa.

Taking refuge at the Lord's feet with no other refuge: 'I, your servant with no other refuge, have entered beneath your feet' (TVM 6.10.10); 'I have no refuge but your feet', like a child pushed away that still cries for its mother (PT 5.1).
Taking refuge in the Lord or the Goddess, as Gajendra and the gods do; the Goddess is 'intent on saving those who come for refuge'.
Surrender, with six limbs: accepting the favourable, rejecting the unfavourable, faith in his protection, choosing him as protector, self-offering and humility.

equivalents.note: Śrīvaiṣṇava usage treats prapatti, śaraṇāgati and nyāsa as one

definitions.definition: River-goddess, later goddess of speech; the Anukramaṇī gives her as deity of RV 1.164.49.
Primary creation: the arising of the principles (mahat, the elements, the senses) from the unmanifest (BhP 2.10.3; VP 1.5).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The embodied one casts off worn-out bodies like clothes (2.22); it is not slain when the body is slain (2.20); without action even the maintenance of the body (śarīrayātrā) is impossible (3.8).
The substrate of purposive movement, senses and experienced objects (NS 1.1.11); earthy (NS 3.1.27).
Bodies of each element; some beings are not womb-born (VS 4.2.9 C; Tarkasaṅgraha).

Any substance that a conscious being wholly controls and supports for its own purposes and that exists for it alone (as its śeṣa); in this sense all souls and all matter are the body of the Lord, who is their self (śarīrin).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The eternal, indestructible, immeasurable embodied one whose bodies have an end (2.18).
Liberation as equal lordly power with the Lord.
Liberation as equal lordship/opulence with the Lord.
Form of liberation: bearing a form like the Lord's.
Liberation as having a form like the Lord's.
Likeness of form with the Lord — one of the four kinds of liberation.
Having Śiva's form; fruit of yoga.
A name of Rudra, paired with Bhava (AVŚ 11.2).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Epithet of the embodied one (2.24) and of brahman established in sacrifice (3.15).

One claimed to know everything, including dharma, directly; not established by perception, scripture or tradition; an omniscient by all six means of knowledge would not be denied, but none knows dharma by perception (ŚV codanā 110–136).
The fifth mode of the power of seeing: knowledge of everything, said and unsaid, in brief and in detail.
The collection of Madhva's thirty-seven works.
The doctrine that every word, and every letter, primarily designates Viṣṇu, and only secondarily other things.
Being the self of all: liberation is its accomplishment (Kaula Upaniṣad).
'Lady of all': the Goddess after whom the Śrī Sarveśvarī Samūh of Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām is named.

notes: recent

definitions.definition: The whole doctrine that the SK condenses (SK 72): ten fundamental topics and the fifty categories of the creation of cognitions (Yuktidīpikā, Māṭhara, Kramadīpikā); also the name of a lost work.
Being; in RV 10.72 'being was born from non-being'; in 10.129 before creation 'there was neither non-being nor being'.
Being: 'in the beginning this was being alone, one without a second' (ChU 6.2.1); in BAU 2.3.1 and TU 2.6 paired with tyat/tyam as the manifest and the beyond.
Existence/being: that which is never sublated in the three times; Brahman as pure being, present in every cognition 'it is'.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.16: what is (the existent or real), of which there is no non-being (abhāva); what exactly is meant is disputed among commentators.
The 'true name' of the formless Lord, the centre of Satnāmī devotion and the source of the movements' name.
The true Name given at initiation by which the soul passes Kāl.
The sixfold wealth: calm, self-control, withdrawal, forbearance, faith and concentration.
The crown-like vessel bearing the Lord's feet, placed on devotees' heads in Śrīvaiṣṇava temples; named after Śaṭhakopa (Nammāḻvār), who is held to be the Lord's feet.
The litany of homage to Rudra in his hundreds of forms (TS 4.5; VS 16).
The Yajurveda's Rudra litany, whose recitation gives immortality.
The true guru, by whose grace alone the body and the supreme state come to one taste (SSP 5); the 'guru-ful' drink the nectar, the guru-less go thirsty.
The true guru who gives the Name and the Word and opens the inner eye; praised equal to or above God (guru and Govind).
The Sant Satguru: a living master who has reached the highest region and is its embodiment; indispensable for initiation and inner guidance.
The true guru who gives knowledge of the Self and removes doubt, as opposed to givers of mantras for gain or displays of power.
The true guru, the helmsman of the boat of the human body.

equivalents.note: The Sant satguru is the guru who reveals the Name within; outward family or sect gurus are not satgurus.

literal: the relation of wife and husband

definitions.definition: The śaraṇa as wife (satī) and Śiva as husband (pati), the bliss of their union defining the śaraṇa-sthala (SSM 13.2; 13.5–7); lived in Akka Mahādēvi's vacanas; in the Kannada maxim, 'the śaraṇa is the wife, the liṅga the husband'.

equivalents.note: bridal devotion to the Lord in both; the Vīraśaiva form is tied to a named sthala of the ṣaṭsthala path

definitions.definition: The six cleansing acts — dhauti, basti, neti, trāṭaka, nauli, kapālabhāti (HYP 2.22) — needed only by those with excess fat or phlegm (2.21); some teachers hold breath-control alone suffices (2.37); the GS gives them to all as the first means (1.12); later texts count eight.

The six rites of worldly power — pacifying, subjugating, paralysing, dissension, driving away and killing — which the Mahāvidyās are said to accomplish for worshippers (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.132-133). Recorded as a teaching only.

literal: doctrine that the effect is existent

definitions.definition: The doctrine that the effect exists in its material cause before its production, argued with five reasons (SK 9; SS 1.114–118); production is manifestation and destruction is dissolution into the cause (SS 1.121).
The theory that every cognition, even erroneous, apprehends something real; error is incomplete apprehension, explained by the triplication of elements (silver-particles present in the shell).
The true world of the Sat Puruṣ beyond the three worlds of Kāl, the home to which freed souls (haṃs) return.
Sat Lok = Sach Khand, the fifth region, the true home of the soul beyond the reach of Kāl and māyā.
The world Kabīr showed Garībdās.

equivalents.note: Sant Mat itself identifies Sat Lok with Sach Khand.
Same name as the Purāṇic highest world of Brahmā, but the Kabīr Panth places Satlok beyond all worlds of Kāl, including Brahmā's.

literal: what has become one's own; suitability

definitions.definition: That which, used continuously, agrees with a person (Ca Vi 8.118); the unsuitable is 'what does not become one with the self' (Śā 1.127); changes of habit are to be made gradually (Sū 7.36-38).
A reason faced by another reason proving the absence of the probandum.
The good son's path, corresponding to kriyā and exemplified by Campantar.
Company of the holy (sādhusaṅgama), the fourth gatekeeper, from which discrimination arises.
Association with the holy, which wins the Lord more than yoga, Sāṃkhya or austerity; attachment itself, directed to the holy, becomes the open door to liberation.
The first of the nine means of devotion taught to Śabarī.
The company of the good, without which there is no discernment, and which Rāma's grace grants; first of the nine devotions taught to Śabarī.
The saints' company, asked for above liberation.
The company of sants and gathering to sing and hear their words; the purifying association without which the Name does not take root.
The Master's discourse and the gathering of disciples; also, inwardly, contact with the Word.

notes: Also sādhusaṅga, sādhusaṅgama.

definitions.definition: The six stages bhakta, māheśvara, prasādi, prāṇaliṅgi, śaraṇa and aikya (SSM 5.22–23; 5.26; 10.2–3; 11.2; 12.2–3; 13.2; 14.2).
The highest universal, distinct from substance, quality and motion, in which the notion 'existent' arises (VS 1.2.7–8 C).
Being, the great universal (mahāsattā) that all words finally denote, identified with Brahman (VP 3.1).
An Ekaśaraṇa monastery-institution under a sattrādhikār, with a prayer hall, the sanctum holding the book, resident celibate or married devotees, and lay disciples attached to it.
The head of a sattra, who gives initiation (śaraṇ) and guides its disciples.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): in Caraka a name of the mind, one leg of the tripod of life (Sū 1.46; Vi 8.119); the mind named after the quality that predominates (Sū 8.6); the pure (śuddha) mind as against the rājasa and tāmasa (Śā 4.36); of superior, middling or inferior strength (Vi 8.119).

The luminous, stainless guṇa that binds by attachment to happiness and knowledge (BhG 14.6); its sign is the light of knowledge in all the gates of the body (14.11); in the Mokṣadharma also the intellect as distinct from the knower of the field (12.187.39; 12.240.21–22).
The guṇa that is light and illuminating (SK 13), of the nature of pleasure (SK 12); predominant in the upper worlds (SK 54). Vācaspati also uses 'sattva' for buddhi.
The guṇa of illumination; in YS 3.35, 3.49, 3.55 the buddhi-sattva, whose purity equal to the puruṣa's is kaivalya, and whose difference from the puruṣa is discerned in viveka-khyāti.
The guṇa characterized as knowledge; those in it go to the gods' state (MDh 12.26, 12.40).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In nityasattvastha, 'ever abiding in sattva' (2.45), one of the qualities of being free of the three guṇas.

equivalents.note: in Caraka's usage sattva, cetas and manas name the mind

notes: Taken as the guṇa sattva or as 'being, the real'; the commentators divide.

definitions.definition: Time (kāla), the insentient reality lacking the guṇas, which measures change in the realm of prakṛti.
Fourth stage: the mind, from practice of the first three, rests in pure sattva (the state of the Self).
Fourth stage: resting in the Self; the knower of Brahman.
The third kind of therapy: restraint of the mind from unwholesome objects (Ca Sū 11.54); its means are knowledge, understanding, steadiness, memory and concentration (Sū 1.58).
The eight involuntary bodily signs of ecstasy: stupor, sweating, horripilation, faltering voice, trembling, change of colour, tears, fainting.
The eight involuntary states arising from sattva (concentrated mind): paralysis, sweat, horripilation, change of voice, trembling, change of colour, tears, fainting (NŚ 6.22).
Before every act, relinquishing the sense of being its agent, the sense that it is one's own and desire for its fruit, attributing all to the Lord.

literal: relinquishment in the mode of goodness

definitions.definition: Name for the Pāñcarātra's followers and teaching (the 'Sātvata teaching'); in Manu 10.23 a Sātvata appears among the offspring of degraded twice-born, which opponents used against the Bhāgavatas.

equivalents.note: used together in the Āgamaprāmāṇya

definitions.definition: The ancient great dharma given by Nārāyaṇa at the beginning of the Kṛta age and upheld by the Sātvatas (MBh 12.336.27–51).

Truth, the real and the truthful word; upholds the earth (RV 10.85.1; AVŚ 12.1.1); the vow-taker passes 'from untruth to truth' (VS 1.5); Varuṇa's fetters bind the untruthful and release the truth-speaker (AVŚ 4.16.6).
Truth as the nature of the gods, untruth of men; the vow 'I pass from untruth to truth' (ŚB 1.1.1.4–5); truth as the sacrificer (AB 7.10).
One of the common duties; speak truth that is pleasant (MDh 4.138; 10.63).
Speech and mind according to fact, spoken for the good of all beings; truth that harms is a semblance of merit (YBh 2.30); when established, actions and fruits rest on one's word (2.36).

The real, truth: 'the real behind the real' is the hidden name of the self (BAU 2.1.20, 2.3.6); analysed as sa-ti-yam (BAU 5.5.1; ChU 8.3.5); truth-speaking as a virtue (TU 1.11; MuU 3.1.6) and as protection in the axe ordeal (ChU 6.16).
Truth, root of all and higher than any state (Rāmāyaṇa 2.109.13); established in dharma (2.21.40); the highest vow (MBh 3.203.41); part of verbal austerity (BhG 17.15).

equivalents.note: Paired in RV 10.190.1 and AVŚ 12.1.1; satya stresses the real and the spoken truth, ṛta the order.

definitions.definition: The understanding 'this is not I, this is not mine' (Ca Śā 1.153), arising in one who sees the world in himself and himself in the world (Śā 5.7).
The 'true religion': the Kartābhajā self-designation for the sahaja teaching revealed by Āulcānd.
The True Being, supreme Lord of Satlok, from whom the sixteen sons emanated; Kabīr is his incarnation or messenger.
Sat Purush, the Lord of Sach Khand / Sat Lok, the first manifestation of the Supreme in the purely spiritual region.
The highest world within the egg, Brahmā's world, lasting two parārdhas; the yogin who reaches it passes with Brahmā to liberation.

notes: Also: brahmaloka

definitions.definition: Auspicious good fortune and conjugal felicity, the worldly and spiritual blessing the Goddess grants; hence 'Saubhāgya-vidyā' and titles such as Saubhāgyabhāskara.

Outer purity (earth, water, pure food) and inner washing away of the mind's stains (YBh 2.32); yields disgust for one's body and non-contact with others, and purity of sattva up to fitness for seeing the self (2.40–41).
Purity of body, mind and dealings; purity in wealth is the highest; the body is purified by water, the mind by truth (MDh 5.105–109).
Ease of access — 'easy for those who have devotion, hard for others' (TVM 1.3.1); Tamil eḷimai.
The Lord's easy reach, shown above all in his descents and in the temple image.
The Lord's mixing freely with the lowly without regard to his greatness.
Śiva without Śakti: 'with Śakti he is Śiva, without Śakti a corpse' (Toḍala 1.25); hence Kālī stands on him.
A vīra rite performed seated on a corpse in the cremation ground to win the Goddess's vision (as in the account of Sarvānanda). Restricted: named only.
Practice seated on a corpse in the cremation ground, attributed to Aghora and Śākta adepts; restricted — summary only.
Coalescence with subtle objects delimited by place, time and cause (1.44, YBh 1.44).
Absorption in which the mental mode rests in Brahman while the distinction of knower, knowing and known remains.
Perception with a qualifier, e.g. 'this is Ḍittha, a brāhmaṇa, dark' (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The perception that follows the bare awareness and grasps the thing with its universal and other properties; also perception.
Coalescence mixed with the constructions of word, object and cognition (1.42).
The god who impels, to whom the Gāyatrī is addressed (RV 3.62.10) and who first yoked the mind (VS 11.1).
The Gāyatrī verse to Savitṛ (RV 3.62.10) taught at initiation, the 'mother' of the twice-born's Vedic birth (MDh 2.170), recited at the twilights.
A reason that strays from the probandum; common, uncommon, non-conclusive.
Form of liberation in which the liberated enter the Lord's body and come out again, enjoying with him — without identity.
Liberation as union/oneness (ekatva) with the Lord; reached even by Śiśupāla through enmity (VP 4.15.2).
Union with the Goddess, granted to one who merely says 'Bhavāni tvam' (SL 22); the highest of the five liberations in Lakṣmīdhara.
Direct conjunction with Rudra, attained by the ascetic dwelling in the cremation ground.
Union with the Lord — the highest of the four kinds of liberation; Śiva-sāyujya by the tripuṇḍra.
Inseparable union with Śiva; fruit of jñāna; the only final release.
Union with the Lord, the only one of the four liberations that does not perish.

notes: Also: ekatva

definitions.definition: The black woollen cord worn by Nāth yogīs, carrying the nād horn; it takes the place of the brahmin's sacred thread.
That which exists for the sake of another (MS 3.1.2); for Bādari only substances, qualities and purificatory acts, for Jaimini also acts (MS 3.1.3–4). Its correlate is the principal (śeṣin).
That whose nature is to exist for the purpose of another (the śeṣin) and to enhance him; every soul and thing is śeṣa of the Lord.
The soul's essential nature as belonging to and existing for the Lord; its fulfilment is service (kainkarya).
Inference by exclusion (= avīta) (Vācaspati on SK 5).
One of the three kinds of inference named in NS 1.1.5; the Bhāṣya offers more than one explanation.
That for whose sake a subsidiary exists.
Service of the wise, the third way to learn knowledge (BhG 4.34); the Lord is served with unswerving devotion (14.26).
Loving service of the Lord's form: with body (tanujā), wealth (vittajā) and mind (mānasī); the mind flowing to him is sevā itself.
Service in the practitioner's body and in the inner perfected body.
Voluntary service of the Master and the community (physical, financial, mental), a support of meditation.
Sādhu-sevā: feeding and serving the sādhus at melās and ākhṛās.
A body fit for the Lord's service, one of the three fruits of service.
A perfected one — master of yoga who has conquered time and roams the cosmos (HYP 1.9); the Nāths count nine Nāths and eighty-four siddhas.
A perfected one: in Tamil, cittar — the yogin-poets, physicians and alchemists who have attained the powers (citti) and the deathless state, and who stand outside caste and temple ritual.
The perfected masters of haṭha — Ādinātha, Matsyendra, Gorakṣa and the others — who by haṭha broke the staff of time (HYP 1.5–9).
In the Dāsbodh: The accomplished one who abides in the Self, free of doubt, still acting rightly.
The perfected stage, resting in prema and the sahaja state.

cross_language.note: the Tamil Siddhars; overlapping but distinct lineage

definitions.definition: Arises from particular merits (VS 9.28 C).
The perfected body of the Nāth siddha — deathless, unageing, not cut by weapons — as distinct from the Gauḍīya inner devotional body of the same name.
The inner, perfected spiritual body/identity in which the practitioner serves in Vraja, alongside service in the practitioner's body (sādhaka-rūpa).

The transmission by the guru of the disciple's spiritual identity (name, form, age, dress, service, group, residence and the like) for meditation on the divine play; practised in the Nityānanda and Advaita lineages and among Vraja bābājīs, contested in the 20th c.
A settled position; four kinds: common to all systems, peculiar to one, implied, and provisionally accepted (NS 1.1.26–31).
The final answer of an adhikaraṇa, reached after the prima facie view.
The scriptures of the upper stream — the 28 Śiva- and Rudra-tantras and their upāgamas.
Each of the four Pāñcarātra divisions (Mantra-, Āgama-, Tantra-, Tantrāntara-siddhānta), so called because those settled in Mīmāṃsā and other śāstras become eligible for it.
The sixth mode, above the Vāma (Kulārṇava 2.8).
A mantra that needs no preliminary tests; said of the Mahāvidyās by the Muṇḍamālā, a statement Kṛṣṇānanda reads as praise (Tantrasāra).
Yogic power: eighteen are listed (eight chief, ten from the guṇas) plus lesser ones; they are obstacles and a waste of time for one seeking the Lord.

In the Sāṃkhya Kārikā, the eight accomplishments conducive to knowledge: reasoning, words (hearing), study, the three destructions of suffering, gaining friends and giving (SK 51) — not supernormal powers, which Sāṃkhya calls aiśvarya (SK 23).
Powers arising from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity or samādhi (4.1); those from samādhi are obstacles in samādhi but powers in emergence (3.37).
Success in yoga, and the powers that arise (distant hearing and seeing, speed, invisibility, turning metal to gold, flight — DYŚ 89–90) which the yogin must regard as obstacles and hide (DYŚ 91–94).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Success, as against failure, to which one is to be equal (2.48); perfection, not reached by renunciation alone (3.4) but reached by Janaka and others through action (saṃsiddhi, 3.20).
Powers arising from dhāraṇā - eighteen in the Bhāgavata, eight aiśvaryas in MkP and LiP - which are obstacles to the highest goal.
The fifth gain; also the marks of perfection of the yogin (not subject to others, invulnerable, unaging, unobstructed etc.).
A power arising from practice; contrived or spontaneous; an obstacle to hide, or the test of a siddha.
Powers arising in yoga (Śiva Sūtra 1.19-20; SK 3.1-7), which, gained under delusion, fall short of liberation (Śiva Sūtra 3.6).

Tamil citti: the powers won by yoga and kāya-citti — above all the eight great powers (aṭṭamā citti) of the Tirumantiram; Kaṭuveḷi says they come to anyone only by Śiva's action, and Tāyumāṉavar holds them easier than stilling the mind.
The Lord himself as the means, eternally existent and not produced by any act of the soul.
The tuft of hair; abandoned by the paramahaṃsa (knowledge is his topknot) or kept for life by the Vaiṣṇava renouncer.
The instructing guru (may be many), as distinct from the one initiating guru (dīkṣā-guru).
The science of correct pronunciation of the Veda — phoneme, accent, quantity, force, evenness and connection (TU 1.2).

notes: Id disambiguated from Buddhist 'śikṣā' (training).

definitions.definition: Inquiry into Śiva's principle; steady feeling in Śiva; single steadfastness in Śiva-knowledge, like a faithful wife's conduct (SSM 13.30–36).
