The small horn whistle, worn on the black woollen thread (selī), blown by Nāth yogīs before meals and worship; an outward sign of the inner unstruck sound.
The 'vow of the head', which qualifies one to receive the knowledge of brahman (MuU 3.2.10); its nature is not explained in the text (commentators differ).
Its presence makes inference possible even of what is already known (Gaṅgeśa's definition of pakṣatā).
The learned and virtuous whose practice is authoritative where the Veda is silent: free of envy, pride and greed, content with a pot of grain (BDh 1.1.1.5); 'free from desire' (VDh 1.6).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple and asks to be instructed (2.7); Duryodhana calls Dhṛṣṭadyumna Droṇa's disciple (1.3).
Disciple; Arjuna declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple and asks to be taught (BhG 2.7).
The retention with breath drawn in through the tongue and released through the nostrils.
The retention with breath drawn in through the mouth with a hissing sound and released through the nose.
In the Saṃhitās an adjective of Rudra's auspicious, non-terrible form (TS 4.5.1) and a name in 'namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca' (TS 4.5.8); Rudra 'auspicious, go beyond' (VS 3.61).

Śambhu, dense with consciousness and bliss, so called because pure from the beginning, free of the three impurities and the abode of all auspiciousness; the two syllables reveal supreme brahman in their primary sense (SSM 8.8–11); the ocean of consciousness whose waves are the thirty-six tattvas (1.3).
Auspicious; Śiva: 'therefore he is Śiva, present everywhere' (ŚU 3.11); 'knowing Śiva hidden in all beings' (4.14-16); 'Śiva alone' (4.18); the fourth is śiva, auspicious (MāU 7).
Name of the Lord in the closing prayer 'may Śiva be mine, always Śiva'.
The deity of the Kālāmukha temples (e.g. Kedāreśvara at Balligāve).
Pati, the one Lord, eternally free; the efficient cause; not the material of the world; the guru of all.
In the Śaiva and yoga Upaniṣads the supreme Lord and the jīva's true nature: 'the jīva in the body is Śiva alone'; the jīva freed of the twenty faults is called Śiva.
Equality with Śiva: the released soul shares his bliss and powers except world-governance.
First tattva: pure consciousness (cit), the 'I'.

literal: division (of scripture) belonging to the Śivas

definitions.definition: The first ten of the 28 Siddhānta tantras (Kāmika to Suprabheda), revealed to ten Śivas; in Jayaratha's reading they are dominated by difference (bheda).
Regarding all Śiva's devotees as equal irrespective of birth.
The SSM's name for its own doctrine: the śāstra devoted to Śiva's non-duality agreeing with Veda and Vedānta (3.83–87), taught by gurus devoted to Śiva-non-duality (13.24–27).
Qualified non-dualism of Śiva: Śiva with cit-śakti is one, with souls and world as his body.
Civañāṉam: knowledge of Śiva given by grace through the guru — hearing, reflection, clarity, abiding — the true path (san-mārga), leading to sāyujya.
One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the prasādi stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
Direct experience of Śiva; the SSM's author is named Śivayogi from his experience of Śiva in the supreme sky of consciousness-bliss (1.13–24).
The night of Śiva's worship (esp. the great one in Māgha/Phālguna), kept with fast and vigil.
The state of the liberated soul: a 'Śiva', equal to Śiva in omniscience and omnipotence, its innate powers manifest; numerically distinct from Śiva and not an agent of the cosmic acts.
Contemplation of Śiva as the self through inner worship of the prāṇaliṅga, culminating in samādhi (SSM 12.21–24); those who see the world as consciousness through it are Śivayogins (11.37–43).
Yōkam: inner worship and meditation on Śiva (the eightfold or sixfold yoga), the friend's path (sakhā-mārga), leading to sārūpya.

equivalents.note: Vīraśaiva yoga is directed to the liṅga and includes liṅga-gazing and inner worship

definitions.definition: One who sees the world as consciousness through Śiva-yoga, has conquered desire and anger, and is equal to clod and gold, friend and foe (SSM 11.37–43).
Procession of the deity's image around the shrine with offerings to the attendant deities, performed at fixed times of the temple day.
The support or frame of the universe in which tapas, ṛta, vows, faith and truth abide, identified with the highest Brahman (AVŚ 10.7).

equivalents.note: AVŚ 10.7.17 joins knowing Brahman in man, the highest Brahman and Skambha.

definitions.definition: The kapha in the joints that binds them (AHS Sū 12.18).
The epic verse, born, the Rāmāyaṇa says, from Vālmīki's grief (śoka) at the krauñca's death (Rāmāyaṇa 1.2.15–18).
Remembering the Lord, the third form of devotion, and the supreme expiation (VP 2.6.39-40).
Remembrance: the forgetting of the Lord is supreme anguish (NBS 19); remembrance is one of love's eleven forms (NBS 82).
Hari-smaraṇa: the Gīta Govinda is offered to those whose minds delight in remembering Hari (GG 1.3).
Remembrance of the Name, inward and constant, with the breath; repetition on beads without the mind is not sumiran.
Simran: mental repetition of the names given at initiation, to gather the attention at the eye centre.
The dwelling of the fourth stage, not left until the body falls.
Setting of Kāpālika rites in literary portraits.
Kālī's dwelling (Kālī Tantra dhyāna in the Tantrasāra) and the place of the vīra's night worship (Karpūrādistotra). Restricted practices summary only.
The cremation ground, the Aghora ascetic's place of practice and dwelling.
The cremation-ground form of Kālī worshipped by vīra practitioners and in Bengal's burning grounds.

(1) Memory: the not-slipping-away of an experienced object (1.11); memory and impressions are of one form (4.9). (2) In YS 1.20, mindfulness, the third of the five means (faith, energy, mindfulness, samādhi, insight).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Confusion of memory (smṛtivibhrama) follows delusion, and the loss of memory destroys the understanding (2.63).
Texts of human authors learned in the Veda; authoritative because a Vedic source can be inferred from them, but disregarded where they conflict with the Veda or show a worldly motive (MS 1.3.1–4).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): memory arising from eight causes (Ca Śā 1.148-149); its lapse regarding truth is a cause of suffering (Śā 1.101); good conduct is to be followed 'with smṛti' (Sū 8.17); constant present mindfulness (saṃnihita-smṛti) guards from suffering (AHS Sū 2.47).
The dharmaśāstra (MDh 2.10); the recollection of those who know the Veda, a source of dharma second to it.
A quality of the self, the knower (NS 3.2.40), prompted by many causes (NS 3.2.41).
Cognition produced by impressions alone (Tarkasaṅgraha).

cross_language.note: as the faculty of 1.20; Buddhist mindfulness

notes: Homonym: the id trm:smrti is also used for 'remembered tradition'; this entry gives the Yoga senses.
alt_notes: Homonym: smṛti also names the class of remembered (non-Vedic) scriptures.

definitions.definition: In error a memory appears without its 'that' character, as if it were a present experience.
The love that, grounded in knowledge of God's greatness, firm and greater than all other love, constitutes bhakti.
Cause of the cohering of powder etc.; in water only.
Affection/love, the first growth from the seed of devotion, destroying other attachments.
The stage of love above prema in which the heart melts completely.
Internal and external oiling, preparatory to purification and a therapy for vāta.
The identity-formula into which the haṃsa is reversed; the renouncer's worship and meditation.
The sixteen supports (places of fixation) of the body, to be known by the yogī (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2).
The sets of sixteen śrāddhas for the newly dead before and after sapiṇḍīkaraṇa (the 'soiled', 'middle' and 'highest' sixteen).

The person of sixteen parts (kalā): shown by fasting to depend on food (ChU 6.7); in PrU 6 the parts arising from breath (faith, space, wind, light, water, earth, senses, mind, food, strength, austerity, mantras, rites, worlds, name) which vanish into the person as rivers into the ocean.
The sixteen-syllable form of the Śrīvidyā ('the sixteen-syllable vidyā', LSN 118) and the Goddess named by it; the Bahvṛca Upaniṣad names her Ṣoḍaśī.
The third Mahāvidyā, Tripurasundarī of the sixteen-syllable mantra; the Bṛhaddharma lists Ṣoḍaśī and Sundarī separately.
The great sixfold placement of Śrīvidyā in which the worshipper becomes the deity's body; the Setubandha lists its components.

Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): purification of mercury and minerals to remove their inherent impurities, without which mercury is poison (Rasaratnākara, Rasakhaṇḍa 1.30). RESTRICTED: no procedure recorded.
In Āyurveda: purification therapy (saṃśodhana), see trm:samsodhana.
In the SSM the mantra of the supreme self (8.17–22) and the feeling with which the haṃsa-formed supreme self is contemplated in śivayoga-samādhi (12.21–24).
In Basava's vacana the stance the devotee asks to be spared ('do not make me say sōhaṃ'), in favour of dāsōhaṃ, 'I am your servant'.
'I am He': the haṃsa heard in reverse, the natural mantra of the breath (Yogaviṣaya 29).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna, overwhelmed by grief, casts aside his bow (1.47) and sees nothing that would dispel his grief (2.8); Kṛṣṇa: the wise do not grieve (2.11), and since the embodied one is imperishable and death certain for the born, Arjuna should not grieve (2.25–30).
The plant, its pressed juice drunk in the sacrifice, and the god: 'we have drunk the soma, we have become immortal' (RV 8.48.3); but the soma the brahmins know none eats (10.85.3).
In the haṭha texts the moon's nectar: 'drinking soma' with the tongue turned up (HYP 3.44); the body filled with the moon's digit (somakalā) is not abandoned by the soul (HYP 3.45–46; GŚ 66).

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan haoma; the plant's botanical identity is debated by modern scholars and was replaced by substitutes in the tradition.

definitions.definition: Name of the Kāpālika doctrine (Prabodhacandrodaya); the Kūrma Purāṇa lists 'Soma' among non-Vedic Śaiva scriptures.

notes: Etymology as 'Śiva with Umā (sa-umā)' is traditional/uncertain.

definitions.definition: Life-span karma that ripens quickly, like a wet cloth spread out (3.22, YBh 3.22).

The dynamic, vibrant nature of the ultimate - Śaṅkara's opening and closing of the eyes (SK 1.1); the universal vibration on which all particular vibrations rest (SK 1.19); discoverable in intense states (1.22).
Utpaladeva calls consciousness 'sphurattā', the great being, the Heart of the Supreme (ĪPK 1.5.14).

equivalents.standpoint: Kṣemarāja's synthesis of Spanda and Pratyabhijñā
equivalents.note: spanda as the dynamic side of consciousness = vimarśa / svātantrya

definitions.definition: Deliberately shaking the limbs as if struck by a wind-disorder.

notes: Distinct from Kashmir Śaivism's spanda (vibration).

definitions.definition: Quality grasped by the skin alone; cold, hot, neither; in earth, water, fire, air.
The guru, meditating on Śiva, touches the disciple's body (Kulārṇava 14.53).

The grammarians' unitary word-entity distinct from the letters; rejected by Kumārila as superfluous, the letters themselves conveying meaning (ŚV sphoṭavāda); Upavarṣa already identified the word with the letters.

The meaning-bearing word itself, partless and without sequence, distinct from the sounds (dhvani/nāda) that manifest it; it 'bursts forth' as meaning in the intellect when the sounds have planted their seeds (VP 1.44; Mahābhāṣya on P 1.1.70). The later grammarians count eight kinds and hold the sentence-sphoṭa alone real.

equivalents.standpoint: Nāgeśa's placement of the levels of speech in the body
equivalents.note: Nāgeśa identifies the meaning-conveying sphoṭa with speech at the madhyamā level

definitions.definition: A spontaneous vivid manifestation of the Lord or his play in the devotee's heart, short of full direct vision.
Faith and trust that the offering reaches its end: by faith the fire is kindled and the oblation offered (RV 10.151); 'have faith in him — he is Indra' (2.12.5).
The first of the five means (1.20): serenity of mind which, like a kind mother, protects the yogin (YBh 1.20).
Faith as the sacrificer's wife, paired with truth (AB 7.10); the Agnihotra of 'truth offered in faith' (ŚB 11.3.1.4).
The trust by which one may receive good knowledge even from a lower person (MDh 2.238).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who constantly follow Kṛṣṇa's teaching with faith and without carping are freed from actions (3.31).

Faith, threefold by the guṇas and according to one's inner being — 'a person is made of faith' (BhG 17.2–3); the one with faith gains knowledge (4.39); what is done without faith is 'asat' (17.28); the Lord makes each devotee's faith steady (7.21).
The rite of offering food and water to the dead and the ancestors (ekoddiṣṭa for one preta, pārvaṇa for the three ancestors), with feeding of brahmins.
Faith: offered by the gods into the fire of yonder world (ChU 5.4; BAU 6.2.9); 'have faith' (ChU 6.12.2); head of the self made of understanding (TU 2.4); 'give with faith' (TU 1.11).
Faith: firm trust in the words of scripture and teacher, by which the truth is grasped.
Faith — firm trust that by devotion to Kṛṣṇa all is accomplished; the first stage.
In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the bhakta stage. In the SSM's inner worship faith is the incense (12.13–20).

notes: Not to be confused with śrāddha, the ancestral rite (trm:sraddha-ancestral-rite).

definitions.definition: The offering of food and piṇḍas to the ancestors with feeding of brāhmaṇas, monthly on the new moon and on other occasions (MDh 3.122–286).

notes: Id disambiguated from śraddhā (faith).

definitions.definition: In the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, a name of the wind-girdled seers who practised austerity and celibacy (TA 2.7.1).

cross_language.note: In Pali and Jain usage the non-Vedic ascetics

definitions.definition: The solemn Vedic sacrifices performed with three fires and priests of the four Vedas.
Study of the true scriptures and their correct interpretation from a teacher; the first principal means to knowledge, never to be reduced.
Hearing the Lord's names, qualities and deeds, the first form of devotion and the beginning of the path (BhP 1.2.16-21); for the Śiva Purāṇa the first of the three great means.
Hearing: ascertaining, under a teacher and by the six marks of purport, that the Upaniṣads teach the non-dual Brahman; for the Vivaraṇa the principal means.
Hearing the Lord's qualities and stories: with singing, a means to devotion even in worldly life (NBS 37); Garga's definition of devotion is attachment to hearing his stories (NBS 17).

notes: Bhakti hearing (of the Lord's names, qualities and deeds), distinct from the Vedāntic śravaṇa of the Upaniṣads recorded by U13/U15.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna sees no good in killing kin (1.31), holds living on alms better (2.5), and asks what is better (2.7) and for the one thing by which he may reach the good (3.2); by nourishing one another gods and humans attain the highest good (3.11); one's own dharma is better (3.35); nothing is better for a kṣatriya than a dharmic battle (2.31).
The good, the better: chosen by the wise over the pleasant (KU 1.2.1-2).

term: śrī rām jay rām jay jay rām

definitions.definition: The thirteen-syllable (trayodaśākṣarī) Rāma mantra of the Samartha sampradāya.

native: श्रीराम जय राम जय जय राम

literal: offering to the Lord's attendant beings

definitions.definition: Offering of cooked rice to the deity's attendants (bhūtas and guardians) placed around the shrine.

The 'king of cakras', Lalitā's dwelling (LSN 182): nine interlocking triangles — four of Śiva, five of Śakti — with the central point, forty-three angles, the eight- and sixteen-petalled lotuses, three circles and the square of three lines (SL 11); it arises when the supreme Śakti beholds her own vibrancy (YH 1.9-10); the body itself is the Śrīcakra (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
For the Samayins the Śrīcakra is worshipped only in the inner space and is the moon-disc in the crown lotus (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 10).
The yantra of Tripurā; the body contemplated as it.
The 'family of Śrī': the Śākta division centred on Tripurasundarī (Śrīvidyā), contrasted with the Kālīkula.
The Śrīcakra built in raised, three-dimensional form (meru-prastāra), as distinct from the flat form (bhū-prastāra).
Lalitā's city on the central peak of Meru (LSN 22), with its enclosures described in the Lalitopākhyāna and the Āryādviśatī.
Lalitā's city (Śrīnagara) with its enclosures and the Cintāmaṇi palace at the centre.

notes: Also: Śrīnagara

definitions.definition: A member of the community of Rāmānuja's tradition, worshipping Nārāyaṇa with Śrī.
Both the fifteen-syllable mantra of Lalitā (with its sixteen-syllable form) and the tradition of her worship; the Goddess is herself 'Śrīvidyā, the sixteen-syllable vidyā, three-peaked' (LSN 118).
The name of the supreme as never apart from Śrī (Lakṣmī); the Lord is known and approached as her consort.
Making signs of desire toward a young woman from a distance so as to be thought unchaste; the act is feigned and must not violate the restraints.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the channels that carry the tissues undergoing transformation; there are as many as there are embodied kinds of things in the person; thirteen are named (of prāṇa, water, food, rasa, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, urine, faeces, sweat), and for the mind the whole conscious body is its channel (Ca Vi 5.3-7); vitiated by excess flow, obstruction, knotting or wrong course (Vi 5.22).

A stream of Śaiva revelation issuing from one of Sadāśiva's five faces: Siddhānta (upper), Gāruḍa (east), Vāma (north), Bhūta (west) and Bhairava (south); the Kāmika also counts twenty-five by the five faces each being fivefold.

notes: Homonym: in the Śaiva Mantramārga a 'stream' of revelation.

definitions.definition: Learned in the Veda; with brahmaniṣṭha, the double qualification of the teacher.
The periodic origination of the world, initiated by Maheśvara's desire to create, through motion in atoms caused by the selves' adṛṣṭa (Praśastapāda).
The doctrine that creation precedes perception: the empirical world, created by Īśvara, exists whether or not it is perceived (majority Advaita view).
The Veda (MDh 2.10), the supreme authority for those seeking to know dharma (MDh 2.13).
One of the twenty-two audible pitch-divisions of the octave, produced in twenty-two channels at the heart (ŚR 1.3.8–9); the basis from which the svaras arise.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In śrutivipratipannā (2.53): the understanding perplexed by what it has heard, which is to stand immovable in samādhi; cf. nirveda towards what is to be heard and what has been heard (2.52).
The Veda as heard revelation, transmitted by hearing from teacher to pupil.
The Veda, as distinct from smṛti; also, in the theory of application, direct statement (see trm:sruti-mimamsa).
The first and strongest of the six means of determining subsidiarity: an independent word (case-ending, expression or single word) that directly states the relation (MS 3.3.14; Arthasaṅgraha).
A station of the path defined by its dharma and its qualified aspirant; the Vīraśaivas are sixfold by the sthalas (SSM 5.22–23), elaborated as 101 sthalas (1.28–31).

notes: The derivation of 'sthala' as that in which all things abide (sthā) and dissolve (la) is common in later exposition; not verified in the SSM here.

definitions.definition: Local temple or place legend in Purāṇic form, often claiming to belong to a Mahāpurāṇa such as the Skanda.
A place sanctified by the presence or touch of one of the incarnations, visited and venerated by Mahānubhāvas.
The fifth means of subsidiarity: sameness of place in the text or in performance; also a means of fixing sequence (MS 3.3.14).
A levelled ground-altar used as a support of worship, e.g. for one's own worship.
The fixed and built — temple, image, installed liṅga — which in Basava's vacana 'shall perish', against the moving (jaṅgama) that endures.
An installed liṅga of a temple or shrine; the SSM forbids Vīraśaivas to use its nirmālya but bids them protect such liṅgas even at the cost of life (9.33–35).
The permanent emotion underlying a rasa; in bhakti-rasa, love for Kṛṣṇa (kṛṣṇa-rati) in one of five primary or seven secondary forms.
The stable emotion that becomes rasa: love, laughter, grief, anger, energy, fear, disgust, wonder (NŚ 6.17), and for śānta calm, dispassion or knowledge of reality.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Synonym of sthitaprajña in Arjuna's question (2.54); the sage whose mind is unshaken by sorrow and pleasure and free of passion, fear and anger (2.56).

The person whose wisdom is established: content in the self, free of desire, passion, fear and anger, the senses withdrawn like a tortoise's limbs, awake where others sleep, in the brāhmī state (BhG 2.54–72).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The person described in 2.55–72: gives up all desires that enter the mind, content in the self by the self (2.55); his wisdom is firmly established when he is unattached, withdraws the senses and masters them (2.57–68); his state is the brāhmī sthiti (2.72).
One of steady wisdom (Gītā 2.55–72), identified in Advaita with the jīvanmukta, whose wisdom is the non-conceptual mode apprehending the identity of self and Brahman (VC 427).

equivalents.note: the Gītā's descriptions of the one of steady wisdom (ch. 2), the one beyond the guṇas (ch. 14) and the dear devotee (ch. 12) share many marks
the later term 'jīvanmukta' (liberated while living) is applied by Advaita commentators to the sthitaprajña; the Gītā itself does not use the word

definitions.definition: The impression that restores a thing (e.g. a mat) to its former state.
The gross body, made of the quintuplicated elements, seat of experience in waking.
Non-lexical syllables or words (e.g. hāu, hoyi, ā) inserted in a sāman.
The function of arthavāda: praising the enjoined act so as to prompt a person held back by laziness (MS 1.2.7).
Dullness: the mind's unfitness for work (YBh 1.30).
The five 'auspicious āgamas' (saṃhitās of Vasiṣṭha, Sanaka, Śuka, Sanandana and Sanatkumāra) that teach the Vedic Samaya way (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 31).
The Vasiṣṭha, Sanaka, Śuka, Sanandana and Sanatkumāra saṃhitās, which in Lakṣmīdhara's account teach the Vedic Samaya way.
The support of the mind in yoga: Viṣṇu's form, the ground of all powers, which alone purifies (VP 6.7.45-78).
First stage of knowledge: the wish, preceded by dispassion, to leave foolishness and turn to scripture and the good.
First stage of knowledge: the wish for liberation.
The Lord's will-power (saṅkalpa) — his resolve 'may I be many' — personified as his discus; the Ahirbudhnya's central principle, of which even the Sāṃkhya is said to consist.
Cuttam: the purified condition in which the soul, by grace, turns to Śiva.
A self-luminous insentient substance free of rajas and tamas, of which Vaikuṇṭha and the divine forms of the Lord and the freed are made.

The creation proceeding directly from the six qualities — the vyūhas and their realm — as distinct from the 'other-than-pure' creation from prakṛti; the Jayākhya places the Vaiṣṇava creation before the prādhānika and brāhma creations.
Pure non-dualism: Brahman untouched by māyā is the only reality, and the world is its real form.
Fifth tattva: action predominant; the co-reference of 'I' and 'this' in balance (ĪPK 3.1.3); its rise gives mastery of the wheel of powers (Śiva Sūtra 1.21).
The accomplishment of receiving knowledge from a friend who has it (SK 51; Gauḍapāda).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Pleasure and pain come from sense-contacts (2.14) and are to be made the same (2.38); for one without peace there is no happiness (2.66).
What all experience as agreeable; a quality of the self; bound up with pain and so to be relinquished like food mixed with poison (NBh 1.1.2).
The Vājasaneyi Yajurveda, whose Saṃhitā holds the mantras apart from the Brāhmaṇa; received by Yājñavalkya from the Sun.
The seventh tissue, whose supreme essence is ojas (Su Sū 15.19; AHS Sū 11.37); from it the embryo arises as its essence (Ca Ci 15.16).
A good deed; the dead go to the world of those who have done well (RV 10.16.4).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One joined with understanding casts off both here (2.50).

literal: the world of those who have done well

definitions.definition: The heavenly world to which Agni carries the dead man's unborn part (RV 10.16.4).
The subtle bodies, constant, as against the perishing bodies born of mother and father (SK 39); denied by Vindhyavāsin (Yuktidīpikā on SK 39).
The subtle body of seventeen members — five organs of knowledge, five of action, five prāṇas, mind and intellect — made of unquintuplicated elements; it transmigrates.
A hymn of the Ṛg- or Atharvaveda.
Shell–silver: stock illustration of error, superimposition in the form of memory, and of falsity.
Kind and true speech, among the goods asked in the Camaka (TS 4.7).

The void: a name of suṣumnā's path (śūnyapadavī, HYP 3.3–4); the breath dissolves in the void (4.10); the nāda stages pass through śūnya, atiśūnya and mahāśūnya (4.70–75); 'empty within, empty without' (4.56).
The void: the breath's path through the void becomes the royal road (HYP 3.3); the mind made 'void of void' in unmanī (KJN 14.84); in Hindi Nāth sayings 'sunn', the place of the supreme.
Void as an object of contemplation leading beyond itself (VBT 32, 39-40, 43-48, 58): 'by the void power one goes to voidness'.
The void as a limited subject-position (śūnya-pramātṛ), subordinate to consciousness (ĪPK 3.2.12-15).
The void or empty sky (sunn, śūnya-maṇḍal) in the head where the Lord is met — a Nāth-derived name for the highest state, not a Buddhist emptiness.
Sunn (with Mahāsunn above it): the region of the soul's self-realization above Trikuṭī, where the sārangī is heard.
In Allama Prabhu's teaching the void in which liṅga, aṅga and all attainments are no longer two; the 'attainment of the void' gives the Śūnyasampādane its name.

equivalents.note: Allama's śūnya is Śiva's own void-fullness (liṅga as bayalu); interpreters in the tradition reject its identification with Buddhist emptiness, though the word is shared

definitions.definition: The seat of the presiding master of the Anubhava Maṇṭapa, occupied by Allama Prabhu in the Śūnyasampādane.
With the cave, the dwelling of the third stage.
The soul as attention or consciousness-current, a drop of the Supreme scattered through the body; it is gathered at the eye centre and rises on the sound current (surat-śabd).
In Kabīr and the Nāth-influenced Sants: attention or recollection fixed on the Lord (surati-nirati).

equivalents.note: Sant Mat's surat is the individual soul considered as a current of attention.

definitions.definition: The sun in the body: the fire at the navel (GŚ 57) and the right channel; it swallows the nectar that drips from the moon, and so the body ages (HYP 3.77); sun and moon make time, suṣumnā devours it (4.17).
The Sun, eye of Mitra and Varuṇa, 'the self of what moves and stands' (RV 1.115.1).
The sun at the navel, of burning nature, that devours the moon's nectar (GŚ 57–58); the right side (AmŚ 71).
The retention in which breath is drawn in through the right (sun) nostril, held with the locks, and released through the left.

The central channel through which prāṇa and awakened kuṇḍalinī rise; its synonyms are śūnyapadavī, brahmarandhra, mahāpatha, śmaśāna, śāmbhavī and madhyamārga (HYP 3.4); of the 72,000 channels it alone is the śāmbhavī śakti (4.18); it 'devours time' (4.17).
The upward channel carrying breath, divided within the palate, through which, joined with breath, Om and mind, one goes upward (MaiU 6.21) — the earliest use of the name in these texts.
The central channel of fire, through which awakened kuṇḍalinī rises (GŚ 31); the 'middle path' the breath must enter (HYP 4.114).
The central channel, path of liberation, 'devourer of time', the supreme tīrtha.
In BhP 2.2.24 the brilliant path by which the departing yogin rises to Vaiśvānara.
Tamil cuḻumuṉai: the central channel, between iṭakalai and piṅkalai, named in the Siddha invocations and among the ten nāṭis.
The central channel meditated as fine as a lotus fibre (VBT 35).
The path in which the in- and out-breaths set (SK 1.24); Śiva Sūtra 3.44 makes the inner centre prior to the three channels.

equivalents.note: HYP 3.4 lists brahmarandhra among the synonyms of suṣumnā; elsewhere (SS 2.18, 5.123–130) the brahmarandhra is an aperture within or at the end of suṣumnā

definitions.definition: Deep sleep: where one desires no desire and sees no dream (BAU 4.3.19; MāU 5); one has merged with being (ChU 6.8.1); one lies in the hitā channels (BAU 2.1.19).
Deep sleep: the state in which the self, as prājña, rests in ignorance without objects, experiencing bliss; the memory 'I slept happily, I knew nothing' shows the witness and ignorance.
Dreamless sleep, in which there is no affliction — the analogy by which liberation is shown possible (NS 4.1.63); explained as the mind's contact with purītat.
Deep sleep is non-discrimination, māyā (Śiva Sūtra 1.10); a void absorption like deep sleep is not the goal (SK 1.12-13).
Deep sleep, in which the self rests in the Lord in the heart with knowledge contracted, persisting as 'I'.
The bardic reciter of Purāṇa; Romaharṣaṇa and his son Ugraśravas are 'the Sūta' of the Purāṇic frames at Naimiṣa.
Ritual impurity; the teacher who has become Śiva is not tainted by it (SSM 14.16); the vacana tradition rejects such pollution for all liṅga-wearers.
The director-narrator of an aṅkīyā nāṭ who sings, dances, introduces and explains the action and stays on stage throughout.
A married woman honoured as the Goddess; she is 'pleased by the worship of suvāsinīs' (LSN 178).
One's inherent nature: it is svabhāva that acts (BhG 5.14); the varṇa duties arise from it (18.41); for Prahlāda all states arise and cease by svabhāva (MBh 12.215.15).
Inherent nature: a candidate cause (ŚU 1.2); those who say it is the cause are deluded (6.1).
One's own nature, the spanda principle, from which the perceiver never departs (SK 1.3, 1.11).
Yādavaprakāśa's form (as reported by Rāmānuja): Brahman by nature becomes Īśvara, souls and matter; difference and non-difference are both natural.
Name of Nimbārka's doctrine: the relation of Brahman to souls and world is naturally both difference and non-difference, not due to adjuncts.
Inherent power by which That One breathed (RV 10.129.2) and the immortal moves (1.164.38); also the call and food offered to the fathers, who rejoice in svadhā (10.14.7).
The exclamation with which offerings go to the ancestors, their 'drink' (ŚB 2.4.2.2; 11.5.6.2).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna should not waver when he looks to his own dharma as a kṣatriya (2.31); abandoning it incurs sin (2.33); one's own dharma, even imperfect, is better than another's well performed, and death in it is better (3.35).

The duty proper to one's own nature and station, better even when imperfect than another's dharma well performed (BhG 3.35, 18.47); for Arjuna, the kṣatriya's duty to fight a righteous war (2.31); worship of the Lord by one's own work leads to perfection (18.46). In the Vyādha Gītā, the inherited occupation of the meat-seller done rightly (3.198).
The duty proper to one's class and stage; better done imperfectly than another's done well (MDh 10.97); it leads to heaven and endlessness (Arthaśāstra 1.3.14).
The second centre at the genitals, six-petalled, of water (VAṂ); GŚ 14 derives the name from 'sva' = prāṇa.
The centre at the genitals.
Repetition of purifying formulas such as the praṇava, or study of scriptures on liberation (YBh 2.1, 2.32); brings contact with the chosen deity (2.44).
The Veda of one's own branch; the injunction to study it is the starting point of Mīmāṃsā in the Prābhākara account.
Daily Vedic self-study, the sacrifice to Brahman, praised as bringing concentration and joy (ŚB 11.5.6.3; 11.5.7.1).
Recitation (study) of one's Veda: 'do not neglect study' (TU 1.11); all duties 'with study and teaching' (TU 1.9); the householder keeps reciting (ChU 8.15).
The fourth daily period: study of scripture and recitation.

notes: Contribution from U08 (Pāñcarātra sense); Yoga's niyama sense is U10's.

definitions.definition: Difference within Viṣṇu (between him and his qualities, acts, forms or avatāras), declared unreal; apparent distinctions are explained by viśeṣa.
The call with which oblations are given to the gods.
Wedded love; Jīva holds the gopīs to be Kṛṣṇa's own (svakīyā) in truth, appearing as parakīyā in the manifest play.
One's own glory, in which the realized abides and for which the categories of dharma, duality, time, states and samādhi no longer apply.
'Mistress': Rādhā (and the gopīs) as Kṛṣṇa's beloved, emphasised by Viṭṭhalanātha.
The Lord's being the owner of all, which gives him the right and the will to save what is his.
The Lord's own plenary expansions (Viṣṇu forms), non-different from him.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): dreams are sevenfold — of what was seen, heard, experienced, desired, imagined, portending, and born of doṣas (Ca In 5.43); in Ca Sū 11.35 'svapna' = sleep as a support.

Dream: the junction between this world and the other, where the person is his own light and creates chariots and roads (BAU 4.3.9-10); the field of taijasa (MāU 4); where the mind experiences its greatness (PrU 4.5).
Dream: the state in which the self, as taijasa, experiences mental impressions; its creation is 'mere māyā' (BS 3.2.3); the model for the waking world's falsity (GK 2).
Dream cognition is like memory and imagination (NS 4.2.34); the notion of dream-objects is destroyed on waking (NS 4.2.35).
Arises, like memory, from self–mind conjunction and impressions (VS 9.23 C); a form of non-knowledge (Praśastapāda).
Dream is thought-constructs (Śiva Sūtra 1.9).
Dream, whose objects the Lord creates for the dreamer to experience minor fruits of karma.
Dream-waking: a dream taken as waking and grown into great waking, as in a dream-body sustained for long.
Cognition (saṃvid) manifests itself without another cognition; the self and the object are manifested by it.
Self-luminous: not requiring another cognition to be revealed; defined by Citsukha as being fit to be called immediate while not being an object of cognition.
Vedic pitch-accent (udātta, anudātta, svarita) and, in the Sāmaveda, the seven notes of chant; a mantra wrong in svara harms the sacrificer (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 52).
The Vedic pitch accents — udātta (high), anudātta (low), svarita (combined) (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.29–31); also 'vowel'. Error in accent turns a mantra against the sacrificer (PŚ 52).

A note: that which arises right after the śruti, smooth and resonant, and of itself delights the listener (ŚR 1.3.24–25); seven — ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, madhyama, pañcama, dhaivata, niṣāda (sa ri ga ma pa dha ni).
In the svara science, the flow of breath through the left, right or both nostrils and the elements arising in it (Śiva Svarodaya).

notes: The musical sense belongs to lin:sangita (U31).

definitions.definition: The sovereignty over all beings attained by Brahman when it offered itself in all beings (ŚB 13.7.1.1).
The self-rule attained by the one who sacrifices to the self (MDh 12.91).
Later Vīraśaiva devotional songs composed for singing, as distinct from the prose-rhythm vacanas.
Heaven (svar), the world of light reached by sacrifice, gifts and tapas (RV 10.154.2).

The fruit of rites for 'one desiring heaven'; where no fruit is stated, heaven is understood (MS 4.3.15). Śabara concludes that the word denotes happiness (prīti) itself (on MS 6.1.1–2); a later cited verse describes it as happiness unmixed with sorrow, not followed by loss, brought by longing.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's faintness does not lead to heaven (2.2); a dharmic battle is an open door to heaven (2.32) and heaven is gained if slain (2.37); the Veda-delighters are intent on heaven (2.43).

equivalents.note: The Mīmāṃsā treats heaven as the highest human end of ritual; the Upaniṣads and later schools hold heaven impermanent and distinct from liberation.

definitions.definition: The falling (circumflex) accent following an udātta.
Inference in one's own mind, from having grasped pervasion by repeated observation and then seeing the mark.
The inner divine nature of every person: Kṛṣṇa in the man, Rādhā in the woman.
Liberation as the manifestation, not the creation, of the soul's own nature, freed from karma.
Definition by own nature: satyaṃ jñānam anantam / existence–consciousness–bliss.
The seer's abiding in its own form (1.3), and kaivalya as the power of consciousness established in its own form (4.34).
A relation that is nothing over and above its relata, e.g. that of absence to its locus.
A soul's innate, beginningless capacity, which fixes its destiny and the office, worship and vision it may attain; to desire what one is unfit for leads to a fall.
The bliss intrinsic to each soul, enjoyed unobstructed in liberation in the measure of its fitness.
Drawing in outer air and expelling inner air (YBh 1.31, 2.49); disturbed, they accompany distraction (1.31); the cutting off of their movement is prāṇāyāma (2.49).
One's own awareness, unbounded and complete, to be realized (the Mata line quoted at TĀ 4.263a).
One whose doṣas, fire, tissues, wastes and functions are balanced and whose self, senses and mind are clear (Su Sū 15.41).

The whole regimen by which the healthy keep their health — measure in food, daily and seasonal routine, urges, exercise and good conduct; one who follows it lives a hundred years free of disease (Ca Sū 8.31; 11.4).
Abiding in oneself, not attained by study of scriptures without 'forgetting everything'.
Validity of knowledge belongs to it by itself (and is apprehended by the witness); invalidity comes from extraneous defects.

All means of knowledge are valid of themselves, since a capacity not present in a thing cannot be given by another (ŚV codanā 47); invalidity is established only by a cognition that the object is otherwise or by knowledge of a defect in the cause (ŚV codanā 53). The Veda, having no author, has no source of defect.
Validity is intrinsic but is grasped by the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) of the first cognition (as reported by Gaṅgeśa).
That which depends on nothing else for its being, knowledge and activity: Viṣṇu alone.
The absolute freedom of consciousness - its primary sovereignty, identical with reflexive awareness (ĪPK 1.5.13); by it the world is manifested (PH 1-2).

equivalents.note: ĪPK 1.5.13 identifies reflexive awareness as the primary freedom

definitions.definition: Awareness of oneself, declared the goal of human life (PKS 1.6).

equivalents.note: knowledge of the self as the goal

definitions.definition: The Lord himself — Kṛṣṇa — of whom all other forms are portions (BhP 1.3.28, the governing statement).
A Kaula term for menstrual blood as a sacred substance in certain rites. Restricted: named only.

notes: Named in several late Kaula tantras (e.g. Yoni and Mātṛkābheda Tantras) as reported in secondary literature; not checked.

definitions.definition: The liṅga in the root centre around which Kuṇḍalinī lies coiled (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa).
Self-luminous: in dream 'here the person becomes his own light' (BAU 4.3.9, 4.3.14); the self is the light of a person when sun, moon, fire and speech are gone (4.3.6).
The liberated renouncer's freedom from rule.
Moisture of the skin and its softness (Su Sū 15.5); the waste of fat (Ca Ci 15.18).
Inducing sweat, preparatory to purification; thirteen kinds with fire and ten without (Ca Sū 14).
The island north of the milk ocean where the white, one-pointed devotees dwell and where Nārāyaṇa reveals himself to Nārada (MBh 12.323.23–26; 12.321–326).
Bengal's name for Dakṣiṇakālī (the Tantrasāra's Śyāmā section); the 'Śyāmā' of the devotional songs.

equivalents.note: in Bengal Śyāmā usually denotes Dakṣiṇakālī

definitions.definition: The Bengali devotional song genre addressed to Kālī, founded by Rāmprasād and continued by Kamalākānta.
Śyāmā or Rājamātaṅgī, Lalitā's minister (Mantriṇī) who rides the Geyacakra chariot and slays Viṣaṅga (LSN 26-29); her worship is the sixth section of the Kalpasūtra.
Tacakāriyam: the ten acts — form, sight and purification of tattvas, of the soul and of Śiva, then Śiva-yoga and Śiva-bhoga.
That One which breathed windless by its own power before creation (RV 10.129.2), was born by tapas (10.129.3), and 'has become all this' (8.58.2).

equivalents.note: Vedānta reads That One as Brahman; the hymn itself does not name it, and the ritual (Mīmāṃsā) reading posits no such single referent.

definitions.definition: Offering all one's conduct to the Lord — the other half of Nārada's definition (NBS 19; cf. 65).

equivalents.note: the Gītā and Mīmāṃsā-Vedānta offering of acts to Īśvara; NBS makes the offering a mark of love, not a purificatory means

definitions.definition: 'His own': devotees belong to the Lord, and so no distinction of caste, learning, beauty, family, wealth or occupation holds among them (NBS 73).
The Lord's own people, the devotees, whose servants are one's masters (TVM 3.7.9).
A name of brahman, to be venerated as 'tadvana'; all beings long for one who knows it so (Kena 4.6); the sense of the word is disputed.
The form of Viṣṇu that, abiding in the mind, creates the soul's dreams.
Ahaṃkāra in its rājasa aspect, from which both groups (organs and subtle elements) proceed (SK 25).
'The brilliant one': the second quarter of the self, whose field is dream (MāU 4).
The self as experiencer of dream, identified with the subtle body (counterpart of Hiraṇyagarbha).
A medicated oil, for internal use or external application.
Fever, especially the recurring fever, sent away by Atharvavedic charms (AVŚ 5.22); Prāṇa is also called takman (11.4.11).
Rhythm and metrical cycle measured by claps and beats; the subject of the fifth chapter of the Saṅgītaratnākara.
The guṇa born of ignorance, deluding all beings, binding by negligence, sloth and sleep (BhG 14.8).

(1) The guṇa that is heavy and enveloping (SK 13), of the nature of delusion (SK 12), predominant at the root of creation (SK 54). (2) The first of the five kinds of error (viparyaya), eightfold (SK 48): taking the eight non-selves (prakṛti, buddhi, ahaṃkāra, the five subtle elements) for the self (Kramadīpikā; Gauḍapāda).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the second doṣa of the mind (Ca Sū 1.57); the tāmasa mind has the part of delusion (Śā 4.36); sleep born of tamas is the root of sin (Sū 21.59).
The guṇa characterized as ignorance; those in it go to the animal state (MDh 12.26, 12.40).
Not a substance but merely the absence of light (VS 5.2.21 C).
The guṇa of darkness: one who hates all people, always makes 'I' and holds untrue notions is tāmasa, and its removal by the guru is a sub-stage of the śaraṇa (SSM 13.17–19).

notes: Homonym: distinct from the Sāṃkhya guṇa tamas.

definitions.definition: The fourth error, eighteenfold: aversion or resentment concerning the eight powers and ten objects (SK 48; commentaries).
Souls whose nature destines them for eternal blinding darkness: daityas, rākṣasas, piśācas and the lowest humans.
A verse of homage to a teacher or text recited before the Prabandham and the teachers' works.
The five non-specific (aviśeṣa) elements — of sound, touch, form, taste and smell — produced from ahaṃkāra as bhūtādi (SK 25, 38), from which the five gross elements arise (SK 22).
Subtle (unquintuplicated) elements arising from Brahman-with-māyā in the order space, air, fire, water, earth (TU 2.1), material of the subtle body.

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify

definitions.definition: Absorption in or identity with the object of constant attention; reached by any strong emotion directed at Hari.
Being full of him: the one-pointed devotees are 'tanmaya' (NBS 70); absorption is one of the eleven attachments (NBS 82); having love one sees, hears, speaks and thinks only of him (NBS 55).
A revealed scripture, so called because it expands (tanoti) matters of the principles and mantras and protects (trāyate).
Performing a subsidiary once so that it serves several principal rites together, e.g. the prayājas for the several main offerings (adhyāya 11).

notes: Mīmāṃsā sense; distinct from 'tantra' as a class of scripture.

definitions.definition: The account of how the one knowledge was divided and taught by Śiva to Śivas and Rudras and handed down through chains of divine, semi-divine and human recipients.
The devices of exposition by which a treatise is understood — thirty-six in Caraka (Si 12.41-45), thirty-two in Suśruta (Utt 65.3).
The hereditary Nampūtiri brahmin ritual authority of a Kerala temple, who alone performs installation, festivals and major purifications.
A state of the afflictions (2.4): Weakened by cultivating the opposite (YBh 2.4); kriyā-yoga thins the afflictions (2.2).
Third stage: non-attachment to sense-objects arising from the first two, desire having become thin.
Third stage: the mind made subtle.
Branding of the upper arms with the discus and conch, first of the five sacraments.
Not undergone by Vaikhānasas, who hold that they are Vaiṣṇavas from the womb.

notes: Distinct from trm:tapas (austerity).

definitions.definition: Generative heat and ascetic effort: That One was born by the power of tapas (RV 10.129.3); ṛta and satya were born from kindled tapas (10.190.1); the ancients reached heaven by tapas (10.154.2); the seers first undertook tapas and dīkṣā (AVŚ 19.41.1); the one whose body is unheated does not attain soma (RV 9.83.1).
Austerity: bearing the pairs of opposites, with vows as suitable (YBh 2.32); to be practised without disturbing the mind's clarity (YBh 2.1); destroys impurity and perfects body and senses (2.43).
The creative heat by which Prajāpati and the primal waters brought forth the worlds (ŚB 11.1.6.1; AB 5.32); the seers' austerity during which Brahman came upon them (Nirukta 2.11).
Austerity as the root of all happiness; for each class its own work is its tapas — knowledge for the brāhmaṇa (MDh 11.234–235); breath-control is the highest tapas (MDh 6.70; VDh 10.5).

Austerity, heat: by tapas Prajāpati and brahman create (TU 2.6; PrU 1.4; MuU 1.1.8); Bhṛgu seeks brahman by tapas — 'tapas is brahman' (TU 3.2); a branch of dharma (ChU 2.23.1); sickness and cremation as the supreme tapas (BAU 5.11).
Austerity, threefold — of body, speech and mind (BhG 17.14–16) — and sāttvic, rājasic or tāmasic (17.17–19); terrible austerities not enjoined by scripture, tormenting the body, are demonic (17.5–6).
Austerity, for which (not for sense-pleasure) the human body is meant (BhP 5.5.1).

cross_language.note: the Buddhist texts reassess tapas

definitions.definition: Suffering from oneself (body and mind), from other beings, and from divine/natural powers (VP 6.5.1-6).

The second Mahāvidyā; Akṣobhya is her Bhairava because he drank the poison without agitation (Toḍala 1.4-6); the Toḍala makes her the Fish avatāra; linked with Mahācīna and the Buddha (Rudrayāmala 17; Tārā Tantra 1).

cross_language.note: the Buddhist saviour goddess Tārā; the Hindu tantras themselves place Tārā worship in Mahācīna with the Buddha

definitions.definition: Knowledge born of discrimination as arising from one's own intuition, not from instruction (3.54, YBh 3.54); also a name of intuition (YBh 3.33).
(1) The light between the brows and the yoga of targets that carries across saṃsāra; (2) the mantra Rudra gives the dying at Avimukta (Oṃ, the Rāma mantra or the Nārāyaṇa mantra).
What saves (carries across), which those confused by Āgamas, Vedas and logic do not know (HYP 4.40); in the Yoga Upaniṣads a form of rājayoga.
The Rāma name as the ferrying mantra Śiva gives those who die at Kāśī.
The beginningless, unalterable gradation of souls in nature, knowledge, bliss and office, from the lowest to Brahmā and Vāyu, with Lakṣmī above and Viṣṇu infinitely above; it continues in liberation.
Reasoned consideration of what fits, about a thing whose nature is unknown (NS 1.1.40); neither a means of knowledge nor included among them, but their helper (NBh 1.1.1).
Superimposition of the pervader through superimposing the pervaded ('if there were no fire there would be no smoke'); classed as a non-valid cognition that assists (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Reasoning: 'this understanding is not to be gained by reasoning' (KU 1.2.9); yet in MaiU 6.18 and 6.20 tarka is a limb of yoga, contemplative reasoning by which brahman is seen.
In the Amṛtanāda's six limbs, reasoning not opposed to the āgamas.
Reasoning, unstable when unsupported by scripture: what is inferred by the skilled is refuted by the more skilled (VP 1.34).
The kapha in the head that nourishes the senses (AHS Sū 12.17).
Libation that satisfies the deity; the Goddess is 'gratified by libation into the bindu' (LSN 178) and 'by secret libations' (LSN 83).
The water-offering to the ancestors (and gods and seers), the daily sacrifice to the ancestors (MDh 3.70).
Being happy in his happiness — the mark that distinguishes the gopīs' love from a paramour's (NBS 24).
'You are that' (ChU 6.8.7): the teaching sentence whose word-meanings, purified by exclusive-non-exclusive implication, indicate the identity of the inner self and Brahman.

literal: defining mark standing on the bank

definitions.definition: Incidental definition: Brahman as the cause of the world's origin etc., pointing to it as the crow points out the house.
The marginal power: the souls, 'on the border' between the internal and external powers, able to turn to either.
The intended import of a text, known by the marks (opening and close, repetition, novelty, result, praise, reasoning); the 'great purport' of all scripture is Viṣṇu's supremacy.
The speaker's intention, knowledge of which is a condition of verbal cognition (Tātparyavāda).

The intended sense of a passage, settled by the rules of interpretation; the determinants listed in Vedānta manuals as six marks (upakrama–upasaṃhāra, abhyāsa, apūrvatā, phala, arthavāda, upapatti) draw on Mīmāṃsā rules.
Purport: Dhanika and others hold that rasa and implied senses are conveyed by the purport of the sentence, making a separate power of suggestion unnecessary.
The six marks of a text's purport — opening and close, repetition, novelty, fruit, praise, demonstration — by which hearing determines that the Upaniṣads teach the non-dual Brahman.
'Their happiness': the sakhī's joy lies only in the pair's joy, never in her own union.
Whatever is real, i.e. not superimposed (anāropita) and an object of valid knowledge; twofold, independent (Viṣṇu) and dependent (everything else).

Each of the twenty-five principles: mūlaprakṛti, mahat (buddhi), ahaṃkāra, manas, the five sense capacities, the five action capacities, the five subtle elements, the five gross elements, and puruṣa (SK 3, 22; SS 1.61). Knowledge of them liberates.
A principle of the Sāṃkhya enumeration: twenty-four together with prakṛti, the twenty-fifth beyond them (MBh 12.294.42); listed in the field of BhG 13.5.
The thirty-six principles, which are the waves and bubbles of Śiva as the ocean of consciousness (SSM 1.3).
(1) Reality, to which the mind is joined and dissolves (HYP 4.59). (2) In the svara science, the five elements present in the flow of breath (Śiva Svarodaya).
One of the thirty-six levels of manifestation from Śiva to earth (Paramārthasāra 11; PH 7).
Tamil tattuvam: the principles of the embodied person, counted in the Siddha tradition as ninety-six; realization burns them away (Aḻukaṇṇi 36).
A principle or level of reality in the ascending scale of 36 from earth to Śiva; the lower 31 (or so) are products of māyā, the pure five of bindu.
Tattuvam: 36 tattvas (24 ātma, 7 vidyā, 5 śiva), elaborated to 96 in the Tamil lists.

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify

definitions.definition: The circle in which the participants realise 'all is Brahman' (Mahānirvāṇa 8.208).

The repeated contemplation of the principles from which the liberating knowledge arises (SK 64); described by Vācaspati as long, reverent, uninterrupted meditative cultivation after hearing and reasoning, and by the Sāṃkhya Sūtra as renouncing each with 'not this, not this' (SS 3.76).

equivalents.note: Vācaspati's description of tattvābhyāsa (long, reverent, uninterrupted) echoes Yoga's definition of firm practice (YS 1.14); Sāṃkhya's practice has the principles as its content.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The seers of truth (tattvadarśibhiḥ) have seen the conclusion (anta) about the real and the unreal (2.16). (The knower of truth at 3.28 is called tattvavit: trm:tattvavid.)

Knowledge of the true nature of the categories — in the science of the self, of the self and the rest (NBh 1.1.1); it removes false knowledge (NS 1.1.2, 4.2.35) and arises from the practice of samādhi (NS 4.2.38).
Knowledge of the similarities and dissimilarities of the categories, arising from dharma (Praśastapāda).
Knowledge of reality, which Abhinavagupta makes the stable emotion of śānta: it is the self itself (Abhinavabhāratī).
The presence of the memory of truth from which all the means of liberation proceed; 'the one path shown by the liberated' (Ca Śā 1.146-150).
The three real categories: cit (souls), acit (insentient matter) and Īśvara (the Lord).
The three realities: cit, acit and Īśvara, established by scripture (Daśaślokī 7).
The adherents' own name for Madhva's system: the doctrine that what is known through valid means is real (tattva = not superimposed), above all the reality of difference.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The knower of the truth about the division of guṇas and actions, who is not attached (3.28).
Austerity: bearing pain and not harming others (Kuṟaḷ ch. 27).
Substance with hot touch and colour; bodies of fire in Āditya's world; includes gold (mineral fire).

Heat, radiance: the first emanation of being, which produced water (ChU 6.2.3); its finest part is speech (6.5.4); in dying breath goes into heat (6.8.6); in deep sleep the mind is overcome by tejas (PrU 4.6).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) the fire element, the person's heat (Ca Śā 5.5); (2) 'essence' — ojas is the supreme tejas of the tissues (Su Sū 15.19; AHS Sū 11.37); (3) listed with ojas, the fires and the prāṇas among what depends on the body's fire (Ca Ci 15.3).

notes: The grouping 'ojas, tejas and prāṇa' as a doctrinal triad is not found as such in the classical texts checked; Ca Ci 15.3 lists them among things dependent on agni.

definitions.definition: One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.
The first of Lakṣmī's five acts, the concealing power by which souls are bound.
Śiva's concealing power (rodha-śakti), called a bond by figure because it impels the bonds until the soul is ripe.
Tirōtāyi / tirōtam: fifth of the five malas; 'na' of the five letters.
Concealment, the fourth cosmic act, done as Īśvarī (LSN 64).
A holy place of pilgrimage and bathing; the virtues are inner tīrthas and the purest mind the supreme tīrtha; devotees are living tīrthas.
A sacred ford; Vidura calls the self a river with sacred fords whose water is truth, in which one is purified (MBh 5.40.19).
Pilgrim place; the Sants deny that bathing at tīrthas purifies — the true Gaṅgā is in a pure mind.
The pilgrimage is within: 'the original Mecca is in this human body'.
The Pāśupata teachers of the line from Lakulīśa to Rāśīkara saluted daily; Jain doxographers list eighteen.
Śrī — the Goddess inseparable from the Lord; also the prefix 'sacred' (tiru-) before names of places, works and parts of the Lord.
The Lord with Śrī (Tiru) — Viṣṇu/Nārāyaṇa as the Āḻvārs name him; supreme, dark-hued, bearing discus and conch, with Śrī on his chest.

literal: the great one with Śrī; the sacred dark one

equivalents.note: the Āḻvārs use Tirumāl and Nāraṇaṉ of the same Lord

definitions.definition: 'Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya', the eight-syllable root mantra, teaching the soul's exclusive belonging to the Lord and its prayer for service.
'Sacred word/speech': a sequence of hymns, usually in decads, as in Periya Tirumoḻi, Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi, Nācciyār Tirumoḻi; Tiruvāymoḻi is 'the sacred word of the mouth'.
The Lord's sacred feet — the Āḻvārs' constant object of refuge, service and contemplation ('his radiant feet that end sorrow', TVM 1.1.1).
The 'third eye' or eye centre behind and between the eyebrows, where the scattered attention is gathered by simran and the inner journey begins.

equivalents.note: Located at the brow like the ājñā cakra, but Sant Mat places it above the six lower cakras as the door out of the body.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna is told to endure (titikṣasva) the impermanent sense-contacts that give cold and heat, pleasure and pain (2.14).
Enduring the transient contacts that give pleasure and pain (BhG 2.14).
Forbearance: enduring heat and cold, pleasure and pain and all afflictions without retaliation or lament.
Siddha therapeutic massage and manipulation, practised in several kinds.
Worship with joined palms; adoration and bowing ('toḻutu eḻu', 'worship and rise', TVM 1.1.1).

equivalents.note: toḻutal includes the gesture and attitude of worship, not only prostration

definitions.definition: The ninety-six principles that make up the embodied person in the Siddha tradition (see cpt:ninety-six-tattvas).
Service to Śiva and his devotees; the Nāyaṉmārs are 'toṇṭar', servants.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The domain of the Vedas (traiguṇya-viṣayāḥ vedāḥ, 2.45).
The three guṇas taken together, of which prakṛti and the manifest consist (SK 14; Tattvasamāsa 4).
The domain of the three guṇas, which is the Vedas' domain; Arjuna is told to be free of it (BhG 2.45).
Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ and Svar - the region dissolved in each occasional dissolution and within which the hells lie.
Gazing without blinking at a small target until tears fall; one of the six acts, and in the GS a way to śāmbhavī.
The three Vedas (Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman) as the knowledge of the śrauta rite; the Atharvaveda's place beside them was debated.
The second age, in which sacrifice (yajña) is the principal means.
One who has laid down the rods of speech, mind and body (MDh 12.10); outwardly, a renouncer carrying three staves.
Renouncer with the triple staff (Vaiṣṇava mark); inwardly, restraint of speech, body and mind.
The tenth, three-part mudrā of Śrīvidyā worship; the Goddess is 'lady of the trikhaṇḍā' (LSN 180).
The central downward triangle of the Śrīcakra, the eighth enclosure, seat of Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī and Bhagamālinī (in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad the unmanifest, mahat and ahaṃkāra).
What the yogin sees in the stage of paricaya: the 'three peaks' of his karma (SS 3.61).
The second inner region ('three prominences'), seat of Brahm/the universal mind and source of the Veda, sounding like thunder or drum; the causal region.
In Kabīr and the Nāth-influenced Sants, the meeting place between the brows (trikuṭī) where Gaṅgā, Yamunā and Sarasvatī meet.
The 'triple peak' between the brows where the three channels meet (Hindi Nāth and Sant usage).
The three aims (inner, outer, middle) of the yogī's attention (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2).
The one Lord as Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva for creation, maintenance and destruction (VP 1.2.66); in Śākta Purāṇas the three receive their power from the Goddess.
The Lord's transcendent three quarters beyond māyā.
The three horizontal lines of ash on the forehead and body; the SSM's qualified guru is eager to wear it (6.1–6).
Three horizontal lines of ash, each with its correspondences.

The Goddess as she who is prior (purā) to every triad — abodes, principles, seats, liṅgas, letters — the fusion of light and self-awareness (Amṛtānanda on YH 1.6); she 'whose city is threefold' (triangle, circle and square; the three-part mantra) in Bhāskararāya's gloss.
She who existed before the three lights (Naṭanānanda's Cidvallī on Kāmakalāvilāsa 2).

literal: she of the three cities / prior to the three

definitions.definition: 'The beauty of the three cities': the Goddess of Śrīvidyā; as Mahātripurasundarī the queen of Mahākāmeśa (LSN 57).
As a Mahāvidyā, worshipped with the five-faced Śiva as her Bhairava (Toḍala 1.7-9) and matched with Paraśurāma (10.10); her full cult is Śrīvidyā (U23).

literal: beautiful one of the three cities

definitions.definition: The triad of knower, known and knowing, all manifested by every cognition, which is self-luminous (tripuṭī-pratyakṣa).
'True in three': the one for whom devotion alone is greatest (NBS 81); read as true in body, speech and mind, or in the three times.
The metre of four eleven-syllable lines, the commonest of the Ṛgveda.
A Vedic metre of 44 syllables in its standard form (Piṅgala; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya); in the Brāhmaṇas correlated with deities and classes (TS 7.1.1.4–6).
Āyurveda as knowledge of cause (hetu), sign (liṅga) and remedy (auṣadha), for the healthy and the sick; eternal (Ca Sū 1.24).
Dharma, artha and kāma, of which dharma is the root (MBh 18.5.49); each to be pursued at its time (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100).
Dharma, artha and kāma taken together (MDh 2.224); later texts add mokṣa to make the caturvarga.
The confluence of the three channels (iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā — Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī), which mahābandha brings about (HYP 3.24).
Making threefold: being made each of heat, water and food threefold (ChU 6.3.3-4); the later Vedānta name for the teaching (the text says 'trivṛt').
The third, 'beyond the highest' (parātpara) liṅga of the SSM's triad, after the gross iṣṭaliṅga and the subtle prāṇaliṅga.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): craving consisting of desire and aversion arises from pleasure and pain and is again their cause, grasping the seats of feeling (Ca Śā 1.134-135); the ignorant takes it from objects as the silkworm its deadly threads (Śā 1.96).
Thirst from which, with attachment, rajas arises (BhG 14.7).

cross_language.note: cognate; defined in the Buddhist units

definitions.definition: The god (Rudra) of the verse 'we worship Tryambaka … may I be freed from death, not from immortality' (RV 7.59.12; TS 1.8.6; VS 3.60).
The 'three-eyed' Śiva of the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya verse (RV 7.59.12), whose mantra, with added seed-syllables, is repeated for protection from death and disease.

literal: triad; the mote in a sunbeam

definitions.definition: The product of (three) dyads, the smallest visible substance — the mote seen in a sunbeam (later manuals).

notes: The 'three dyads' formula is from later manuals (recalled).

definitions.definition: The first great gift: gold (or other goods) equal to the donor's weight.
The necklace of tuḷsī (basil) beads put on at initiation into the Vārkarī way; its wearer (māḷkarī) vows vegetarianism, abstinence, the Ekādaśī fast and the name.
'Sleeping without sleeping': the yogic sleep of Śiva-yoga, in which the senses are withdrawn but awareness stays (Pattirakiriyār 1–2).

equivalents.note: both name a sleep-like state with awareness; texts and traditions differ

definitions.definition: Renunciation (Kuṟaḷ ch. 35): cutting 'I' and 'mine'.
Renunciation: Paṭṭiṉattār ranks the renouncer far above the giver and the renouncer-in-mind higher still (Tiruvēkampamālai 1).
The form of Viṣṇu at the dvādaśānta, attained by the liberated and occasionally seen by the fully concentrated with direct vision; it gives the liberated their knowledge and activity.
The fourth quarter of speech, the only one humans speak; the other three are hidden (RV 1.164.45).
The fourth, the Lord in whom one abides beyond the intellect's states of waking, dream and sleep, of which the jīva is the witness.
The fourth: not a fourth state beside waking, dream and sleep but the self that pervades and transcends them, non-dual, peaceful, auspicious; the Lord able to end all sorrow (GK 1.10).
The fourth state beyond waking, dream and sleep; the Goddess is 'turyā' (LSN 63); in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad the fourth state is the prostration of inner worship.
The fourth: beyond waking, dream and deep sleep; neither inward- nor outward-knowing, the stilling of the world, non-dual (MāU 7, 12, where the word is caturtha); turya in MaiU 6.19 and 7.11.
The fourth state beyond waking, dream and deep sleep; placed between the brows (Triśikhi) or at the head.

notes: The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad's turīya (the fourth state) is contributed by U03; any link between the two is interpretive and not asserted here.

definitions.definition: (1) A fifth state beyond turīya, located at the brahmarandhra; (2) the name of the highest renouncer who lives like a cow, naked, the body as a corpse.
The state beyond the fourth, reached by firmness in the fourth; the Goddess is 'devoid of all states' (Bhāskararāya on LSN 63).
The fourth state, whose enjoyment arises amid the three (Śiva Sūtra 1.7) and which is to be poured like oil into them (3.20).
The fourth abode in which emission, maintenance, withdrawal and the three states shine without covering it (Paramārthasāra 34-35).
The fourth state, a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4); the place between the brows where mind dissolves and time does not exist (4.48).

equivalents.note: the Māṇḍūkya's fourth; the Kashmir Śaivas add turyātīta and require the fourth to pervade the three

definitions.definition: Seventh stage: with no difference perceived, abiding solely in one's own nature; the turya state of those liberated while living.
Seventh stage: no difference; one's own nature.

equivalents.note: the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha itself calls the seventh stage the turya state of the jīvanmukta (3.118.16); turyagā names the stage, turīya the state

literal: the one gone to the fourth

definitions.definition: The state beyond the fourth, the domain of those liberated without a body (videhamukta), lying beyond the seventh stage.
Turīyātītam: the fifth state beyond the fourth, in the Siddhānta account of the five avasthās.
The state beyond the fourth, in which the fourth pervades all states completely (Tantrāloka 10; Kṣemarāja).

Nine contentments (SK 50): four internal — resting content with nature, with outward means (such as the triple staff and water-pot), with time, or with luck — and five external, from abstaining from objects for seeing their faults; they do not bring liberation and, with error and incapacity, are the curb on accomplishment (SK 51).
The messenger poem: the love-sick heroine sends birds, clouds or the wind as messengers to the Lord.
The divine craftsman who shapes forms and grants long life (RV 10.18.6).

Relinquishing the fruit of all actions (BhG 18.2), threefold according to the guṇas (18.7–9); the embodied cannot give up all action, and so the one who gives up the fruit is the relinquisher (18.11); one of the 'three horses of Brahman' (MBh 11.7.19; 5.43.14).
The soul at the stages of bhakta and māheśvara, in the vacana and manual scheme correlated with the gross body and the iṣṭaliṅga.
A renunciant Rāmānandī ascetic, as distinct from the householder and the rasik.
The twofold character of Brahman in all scripture: opposition to all that is defiling and possession of infinite auspicious qualities.
The Sanskrit Upaniṣads and the Tamil Prabandham (above all the Tiruvāymoḻi) as one Vedānta of equal authority.
The first āṇava support: the breath contemplated in its movement (MVT 2.21; TĀ 5).
The remainder of the sacrifice, praised as the ground in which name and form and all the world rest (AVŚ 11.7).
The familiar instance possessing the property to be proved, or its opposite (NS 1.1.36–37).
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at the throat.
The vital air that leads upward, operating up to the head; its mastery gives non-adherence to water, mud and thorns and departure at death at will (3.39, YBh 3.39).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the vāyu seated in the chest, moving in nose, navel and throat, governing speech, effort, energy, strength, complexion and memory (AHS Sū 12.5-6).
The up-breath, which through one channel leads upward at death — to a world of merit, of evil or of humans (PrU 3.7); identified with heat (PrU 3.9).
The breath in the throat (SS 3.7).
The breath in the throat.
The up-breath, named with the other breaths in some Saṃhitā and Brāhmaṇa lists (low confidence for particular Saṃhitā loci).

checks.note: Located in the Śaunaka AV: 'vyānodānau vāṅ manaḥ' (AVŚ 11.8.4, 26) — the low-confidence Saṃhitā locus now exists.

definitions.definition: A state of the afflictions (2.4): Operating on an object (YBh 2.4).
Puruṣa, indifferent, which appears as agent through conjunction (SK 20); on knowledge it is the indifferent onlooker (SK 66).
Indifference to what opposes the Lord: acting in the world and in the rites only as is favourable to him (NBS 9, 11).
The raised (high) accent.
Naming the things to be examined — the first activity of the śāstra (NBh 1.1.3).
The abdominal lock by which prāṇa 'flies up' suṣumnā; best of the locks, giving liberation naturally when firm (HYP 3.55–60).
The abdominal lock between genitals and navel, 'the lion to the elephant of death' (GŚ 35).
The priest who sings the sāmans.
The central portion of a sāman, sung by the udgātṛ.
The loud chant of the Sāman singer, venerated as Om and as breath (ChU 1.1-1.12; BAU 1.3).
'The upsurge is Bhairava' (Śiva Sūtra 1.5).
The fierce form of Tārā whose five-syllable mantra perfected Buddha and Vasiṣṭha (Tārā Tantra 1.3-4).
The accomplishment of reflecting on 'what is true, what is highest, what is the final good' until the difference of puruṣa and pradhāna is known (SK 51; Gauḍapāda).
The adaptation of a base melody to new verses in the order of the rites.
Adapting transferred mantras, chants and purificatory acts to the ectype, e.g. replacing 'to Agni' by 'to Sūrya' (adhyāya 9).
The secret (rahasya) song-book applying forest melodies to ritual verse-groups.
'Upstream': going against the current, the direction of Bāul practice, as the fish swims upstream.
The retention with breath drawn through both nostrils so that it sounds from throat to heart, held and released through the left.
The letter 'u', which in the Tirumūla ñāṉam is supreme consciousness (ciṟparam), paired with akāram.
Fate, the ordained outcome of former deeds (Kuṟaḷ ch. 38), mightier than any device.
Upside-down speech: paradoxical riddles (the well upside down in the sky, the woman enjoyed by two) used by the Nāths and after them by Kabīr to point to reversed practice.
'Upside-down speech': riddling songs of impossible images (the lion grazing cows, the son born before the mother) whose inversion points to the reversal of ordinary perception.

equivalents.note: Both are coded, paradoxical registers; the Sant form is a genre of songs, the Buddhist/Bāul form a language of double meanings.

definitions.definition: The seven degrees of inner exhilaration in the Kula rite — ārambha, taruṇa, yauvana, prauḍha, tadanta, unmanā, anavastha (Kulārṇava 8.4); the first five are 'waking', unmanā is 'dream', the equal state is 'deep sleep' (8.94-95). The Kulārṇava's chapters are also called ullāsas.
'Reverse practice': turning the downward, outward flow (of desire and bodily substance) back upward and inward; recorded here as a doctrine only (restricted).
The Sahajiyā reversal by which kāma is turned into prema.
Reversed practice: turning the downward flows (breath, bindu, nectar, mind) upward — the viparīta-karaṇa of the Sanskrit texts (GŚ 59).

equivalents.note: Both describe an upward reversal of the vital substance; the Bāul form is a couple's practice and is framed devotionally.

definitions.definition: The ascetic livelihood of gleaning grain left in the fields; the gleaner's gift outweighs a horse sacrifice (MBh 14.92–93) and a gleaning sage attains the highest (12.340–353).
Derangement of mind, fivefold (from each doṣa, all three, and exogenous); the exogenous kind is caused by prajñāparādha and treated by the divine therapies (Ca Ni 7.10-17).
The last and timeless phase in the pronunciation of the mantra's final sound, beyond samanā (Varivasyārahasya).
The sixth ullāsa, called 'dream' (Kulārṇava 8.94).
The final, 'beyond-mind' phase in the subtle utterance of Oṃ, where sound dissolves into the supreme.

equivalents.note: the haṭha unmanī is the mind-free state of samādhi; the Kaula unmanā is a named stage of ullāsa

definitions.definition: The state in which the mind is transcended; it cannot arise while the channels are impure (HYP 2.4); a synonym of samādhi (4.3); through it duality is not perceived (4.61) and the body becomes like a log (4.106).
The mind-less state beyond mind, in which one is not roused even by drums (KJN 14.83–85); a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.3).
The mind 'beyond mind' by which one is liberated here (KJN 13.5); the fourth mind beyond the guṇas (Jñānakārikā 2.8).
The state in which the mind has dissolved; 'unmanībhāva'; beyond merit and sin.
The 'no-mind' state beyond the mind, a Nāth term used by Kabīr for absorption in the Lord.

equivalents.note: listed as synonyms in HYP 4.3
listed as synonyms in HYP 4.3–4
Both name the mind-less state; amanaska is the later part of tāraka-yoga, unmanī the state reached by nāda.

definitions.definition: The madman's guise the ascetic adopts, wandering alone so that people call him mad and foolish.
The opening-out of spanda: that from which a new thought arises in one absorbed in one thought (SK 3.9); with nimeṣa, the pulse of creation and dissolution (1.1).
Īśvara is the outward unmeṣa, Sadāśiva the inward nimeṣa (ĪPK 3.1.3).
Two modes of absorption: inward, eyes-closed absorption and outward absorption in which the world is seen as consciousness; 'again and again there is merging' (Śiva Sūtra 3.45, Kṣemarāja).

notes: Pairing of the two samādhis follows Kṣemarāja's commentaries (low confidence on details).

definitions.definition: A service offered to the deity; the Goddess is 'rich in sixty-four services' (LSN 58); the Kalpasūtra lists them (PKS 4.5); the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad interiorizes them.
The second daily period: gathering flowers and other materials for worship.
The material cause of the world: māyā (and bindu for the pure universe) — never Śiva.
In MS 1.1.5, the (Vedic) instruction that is the means of knowing dharma.

literal: grasping; craving as the basis of suffering

definitions.definition: The supreme cause giving suffering and the seats of suffering; its total renunciation removes all suffering (Ca Śā 1.95).
A fault of disposition; the life-stages yield merit according to its absence (VS 6.2.3–5 C).

cross_language.note: Pali upadhi, 'substratum (of rebirth)'

definitions.definition: Secondary products of the tissues: from rasa breast-milk and menstrual blood, from blood tendons and vessels, from flesh muscle-fat and the six layers of skin, from fat ligaments and joints (Ca Ci 15.17).

notes: Ref from the local Devanāgarī e-text of Ca Ci 15; the term 'upadhātu' itself is the later commentarial name.

definitions.definition: What pervades the probandum without pervading the probans (e.g. contact with wet fuel when smoke is inferred from fire); its presence makes the reason unestablished as to pervasion.
Limiting adjunct: something that makes a thing appear with characteristics not its own without changing it (the red flower near the crystal; the pot delimiting space; body and mind for the self).
The Advaita notion that the soul is Brahman limited by adjuncts, refuted in the Upādhikhaṇḍana: ignorance cannot belong to the all-knower, and adjuncts cannot account for it.
A limiting adjunct — body, senses, intellect — that really delimits Brahman as the individual soul; real, not imagined, and removed only at liberation after death.

notes: Advaita also uses upādhi but holds the adjuncts to be products of avidyā (not ultimately real); Bhāskara insists they are real — same word, different status.

definitions.definition: One who teaches a part of the Veda or its limbs for a living (MDh 2.141).
The supreme person in the body as witness (BhG 13.22).
The fourth portion of a five-part sāman, sung by the udgātṛ.

A subsidiary scripture attached to one of the 28 mūlāgamas; the Kāmika calls them upabheda ('sub-divisions') and lists 206 by the counts it gives (the usual traditional total is 207); the Kiraṇa says a division within the divisions is an upabheda.
The six-limbed offering: laughter, song, dance, the ḍuṇḍuṅ sound, prostration and muttering.
The beginning of a passage; its relative strength against the conclusion (upasaṃhāra) is argued by Appayya Dīkṣita in the Upakramaparākrama.
Establishing what is to be established through similarity to the well known (NS 1.1.6).
Yields knowledge of the name–named relation from cognition of similarity (the gavaya example).
Not a separate means; included in inference (Praśastapāda).
Similarity producing knowledge of an unperceived object: seeing a gavaya one cognizes the similarity in the remembered cow (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
Comparison: knowing the similarity of a remembered thing to one now perceived (the cow is like the gavaya).
Whispered repetition, lips moving slightly, barely audible; a hundred times better.
Restating the subject as 'so' or 'not so' with reference to the example (NS 1.1.38).
Initiation of the student by the teacher (AVŚ 11.5.3, 'upanayamāna').
Initiation in which the boy gives himself to studentship and the teacher, 'becoming pregnant', brings him to birth with the Sāvitrī (ŚB 11.5.4).
The sacrament of initiation at 8, 11 or 12 years for the three classes — the second birth (MDh 2.36, 2.169; ĀpDh 1.1.1.9).

Secret teaching, hidden connection or name: 'its upaniṣad is the real behind the real' (BAU 2.1.20); the upaniṣad of the asuras (ChU 8.8.4); 'we have told you the upaniṣad about brahman' (Kena 4.7); what is done with the upaniṣad is more powerful (ChU 1.1.10).
Knowledge of Brahman, so called because it loosens and destroys the seeds of saṃsāra and leads to Brahman; secondarily the texts.
A lesser seat added to the lists of the major pīṭhas (Pīṭhanirṇaya and Bengali lists).
A Purāṇa outside the eighteen, said to have been told by sages or Vyāsa's disciples; the Kūrma lists eighteen; any Purāṇa taught apart from the eighteen has issued from them (Matsya 53.64).
The apparent coloring of puruṣa by buddhi's modifications, through which agency seems to belong to it (SS 1.164); not real coloring like the red flower's on a crystal but misidentification (SS 6.28).
Withdrawal: the mind's not leaning on external things (VC 23); defined by the Tattvabodha as performance of one's own dharma, and by others as renunciation of works.
Worship of Hari with the qualities appropriate to one's fitness — Brahmā with all qualities, humans as bliss, knower and the ever-existing Self.
The 'knowledge' the Upaniṣads enjoin for liberation: repeated, continuous meditation on Brahman, which, when it becomes loving and vivid, is bhakti.
Veneration, meditation: venerating X as brahman (ChU 7; BAU 4.1); 'one should venerate it as the self' (BAU 1.4.7); 'not this that people venerate here' (Kena 1.5).

Meditation/worship: sustained mental activity directed to a prescribed object (the qualified Brahman, a symbol), an act that can be enjoined; purifies and steadies the mind and leads to the Brahma-world.
Meditation on a thing as something else ('let one meditate on the Real as Brahman'), by which one becomes what one meditates on (ŚB 10.6.3).
What the powers are within samādhi, because they oppose seeing (3.37, YBh 3.37).
