Obstacle-powers that arise after the gross obstacles are overcome: in MkP longings for rewards and five states (prātibha, śrāvaṇa, daiva, bhrama, āvarta); in LiP/ŚiP six siddhis (pratibhā, śravaṇa, vārtā, darśana, āsvāda, vedanā).
The agreeable effect of medicine, food or conduct used contrary to the cause or the disease; it is sātmya (Mādhava Nidāna 1.8-9).
The three supports of the body — food, sleep and continence — by which, rightly used, it continues strong for its full span (Ca Sū 11.35); 'as a house by its pillars' (AHS Sū 7.52).
Fasting as part of a vow.
The means to liberation; the five in Arthapañcaka are karma, jñāna, bhakti, prapatti and the teacher's regard.
The means to immersion: anupāya, śāmbhava, śākta, āṇava; liberation is one whatever the means (TĀ 1.165-170).
Residence, observance, muttering-and-meditation, constant remembrance of Rudra, and grace.
Samādhi arising from means (faith etc.), that of yogins (1.20, YBh 1.19–20).

Equanimity, disregard cultivated toward the non-virtuous, one of the four attitudes that clarify the mind (1.33, YBh 1.33). Vyāsa: equanimity toward the wicked is not a cultivation and yields no strength (YBh 3.23).

cross_language.note: one of the four brahmavihāras (immeasurables); in Buddhism radiated to all beings

definitions.definition: The goal: the Lord (with Śrī) himself and eternal service to him.

literal: goal, what is to be attained

definitions.definition: The Upper transmission, declared highest and the direct means to liberation (Kulārṇava 3.15-19).
The upright forehead mark of the Vaiṣṇava, made with gopīcandana clay; praised as purifying and required for rites to bear fruit.
Vaiṣṇava vertical mark of gopīcandana.
The vertical forehead mark of white clay with the central line (śrīcūrṇa) for Śrī; U-shaped among the Vaṭakalai, Y-shaped with a line down the nose among the Teṅkalai.
One whose seed flows upward — a sign of the nectar-filled yogī's body (GŚ 65; KJN 14.57).
The melting of the heart in love — the 'wick' of Pūtattāḻvār's lamp and the state of the love-sick heroine.

notes: Cf. Madhusūdana's definition of bhakti as the mind melted (druta) by the Lord's qualities (tea:bhaktirasayana:1.3).

definitions.definition: The Dawn, ever returning while generations of mortals pass (RV 1.113.11).
The body (also uṭampu, kāyam, tēkam): for the Siddhars both a leaking pot of filth to be seen through (Aḻukaṇṇi 8; Paṭṭiṉattār) and the Lord's temple to be preserved and perfected (TM 724–725).
The knower's departure from the body through the crown channel, when the tip of the heart lights up, aided by the grace of Hari in the heart.
Departure from the body at death, undertaken at will by one who has mastered udāna (3.39, YBh 3.39).
The departure of the living being from the body at death; for the yogin a controlled departure through the crown.
An injunction that conveys only the form of the act, e.g. 'he offers the Agnihotra'.
The annual temple festival (mahotsava) with flag-hoisting and processions.
The annual festival conducted by the tantri.
Livelihood of the second stage: food cast away or given out of pity or curiosity.
The highest, pure devotion: favourable cultivation of Kṛṣṇa, free from other desires and uncovered by knowledge, works and the like.
The 'later' Kaula view, in which there is no Śiva-principle apart from the Śakti-principle and she alone is worshipped (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 23, 35).
Sins before the attainment of knowledge or surrender, which are destroyed, and those after it, which do not cling (if unintentional).
The Northern transmission: the cults of Kālī (Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, Guhyakālī) and the Krama.
The six months of the northern course, part of the bright path (BhG 8.24); Bhīṣma holds his breath until it comes (MBh 6.114.89–98).

Speech as goddess and power: she proclaims herself queen and self of all (RV 10.125); four quarters of her, three hidden (1.164.45); she revealed herself to some like a bride (10.71.4); the gods begot her and all animals speak her (8.100.11).
Speech as Prajāpati's own and second, sent forth to pervade all (PB 20.14.2); yoked with mind to carry the sacrifice (ŚB 1.4.4.7); speech as consecration (KB 7.1).
The object of grammar and phonetics; in the Mahābhāṣya the 'great god' who enters mortals, identity with whom is the aim of grammar.
Speech as the consciousness of beings, within and without, moving them to all activity; when it departs a being is like a log (VP 1, from memory).

equivalents.note: Bhartṛhari's 'Brahman as word' is a later philosophy of sound that draws on the Vedic exaltation of Vāc; the Saṃhitās do not use the term.

definitions.definition: A short rhythmic Kannada prose-poem spoken from experience, usually closing with the author's signature name for the Lord; the scripture of the śaraṇa strand.
An author of vacanas.
'A verbal handle': the modification is a verbal handle, a name; the reality is clay (ChU 6.1.4).
'A matter of speech': the Chāndogya's description of modifications as mere names (the clay alone being real), the basis of the non-difference of effect from cause (BS 2.1.14).
Audible repetition with correct tones and clear syllables; ten times better than ritual sacrifice.
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): disputation with another based on the science, of two kinds, jalpa and vitaṇḍā (Ca Vi 8.28).

Debate in which both sides prove and refute with the means of knowledge and tarka, without contradicting tenets, using the five members (NS 1.2.1); undertaken with teachers, pupils and seekers of the good (NS 4.2.48).
Debate aimed only at ascertaining the truth, as between teacher and disciple.

notes: Homonym in Rasa Śāstra: 'vāda' = alchemy (dhātuvāda).

definitions.definition: The first section of the mantra, 'born of speech'; the Goddess's face (LSN 35).

The eight goddesses of speech (Vaśinī, Kāmeśvarī, Modinī, Vimalā, Aruṇā, Jayinī, Sarveśvarī, Kaulinī) of the eight-cornered enclosure, composers of the Lalitā Sahasranāma; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad cold, heat, pleasure, pain, desire and the three qualities.
The word-nature of awareness: eternal, it makes recognition (pratyavamarśa) possible; without it light would not illumine (VP 1.124).
Devotion by rule: practice impelled by the command of scripture, where spontaneous attraction (rāga) is not yet present.
A brahmin following the Sūtra of Vikhanas; the Vaikhānasa Sūtra is held to be the first and best of sūtras and 'Vikhanas' to denote Nārāyaṇa.

notes: In Dharmaśāstra the word also names a class of forest hermits.

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta and Aniruddha, the five forms invoked in Vaikhānasa worship.

equivalents.note: both are sets of divine forms for worship; the Vaikhānasas do not present theirs as vyūhas

definitions.definition: Articulated, audible speech, produced when breath strikes the places of articulation, whose letters are grasped by the hearer (Vṛtti on VP 1.142); for Nāgeśa, speech in the throat and mouth.
Spoken speech coming forth through the palate.
Ahaṃkāra in its sāttvika aspect, from which the eleven organs proceed (SK 25).
The eternal realm of the Lord, made of pure sattva, the goal of the freed.

Dispassion: the consciousness of mastery of one free of thirst for seen and scriptural objects (1.15); the higher is freedom from thirst for the guṇas (1.16); dispassion even toward the highest powers leads to kaivalya (3.50).

A sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23); by itself it leads to absorption into prakṛti (SK 45), not to liberation; Gauḍapāda distinguishes external dispassion (from seeing the faults of objects) and internal (seeing even pradhāna as like a dream). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra makes it a support of meditation (3.36).
Dispassion, which with practice restrains the mind (BhG 6.35); dispassion toward sense-objects is a mark of knowledge (13.8).
Freedom from attachment; the supreme dispassion by which the upasarga-powers are renounced (LiP 1.9.52-56).
Dispassion toward the enjoyment of results of action in this world and the next.
Dispassion, the condition of renunciation ('the very day one becomes dispassionate'); the oil of the lamp of knowledge (Dakṣiṇāmūrti).

cross_language.note: Buddhist dispassion

definitions.definition: Narsinh Mehta's 'true Vaiṣṇava': one who knows others' pain, helps without pride, speaks ill of none and is free of greed, deceit, lust and anger.
The second mode: devotion to Viṣṇu with vegetarian purity.
In the Yoga Upaniṣads the inner target held with the outward unblinking gaze — the same definition the HYP gives for śāmbhavī.

equivalents.note: Defined in identical terms (antarlakṣya, bahirdṛṣṭi, nimeṣonmeṣa-varjitā).

definitions.definition: 'Common to all men': the self conceived as the cosmos with sky as head etc. (ChU 5.11-18); the first quarter, waking (MāU 3); the digestive fire within a person (BAU 5.9.1).
The fire of digestion that the Lord becomes in living bodies (BhG 15.14); the fire within whose seven tongues are the senses, mind and intellect (Anugītā 14.20).
The terrible river on the road to Yama, a hundred yojanas wide and full of pus and blood, crossed easily by those who gave the Vaitaraṇī cow; also one of the hells of BhP 5.26.

The branch of virilization: that which gives offspring and delight and keeps semen fruitful into age, for the continuity of lineage here and endlessness hereafter (Ca Ci 1.1.9-12; Su Sū 1.8). Summary only.
'Making adamantine': the practice in the bone-circle by which 'a man becomes like a thunderbolt' and the body has no dissolution (KJN 15, 'paramavajrīkaraṇa').
The channel within suṣumnā, enclosing citriṇī (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa).
A mudrā for retaining and drawing up bindu (and rajas), with the variants sahajolī and amarolī (HYP 3.83–103; DYŚ 137–143). RESTRICTED: summary only.
A seal for drawing up and preserving bindu, in the context of which the HYP states that death comes by the fall of bindu (HYP 3.83–89); restricted, summary only.
Speech: one of the vital functions contending with breath (BAU 1.3; ChU 5.1); fire becoming speech entered the mouth (AU 1.2.4); in the inner agnihotra speech is offered into breath (KauU 2.5).
Oblique, striking expression; for Bhāmaha the basis of all figures, for Kuntaka the life of poetry.
A sentence is one when it has a single purpose and its parts need each other (MS 2.1.46); as the third means of subsidiarity, joint utterance (samabhivyāhāra) of subsidiary and principal words.
The sentence, for the grammarians the primary indivisible unit of meaning (vākya-sphoṭa); Bhartṛhari lists eight rival definitions (VP 2.1–2).
A group of words (Tarkasaṅgraha); Vedic sentences are valid as spoken by the Lord, worldly ones when spoken by a reliable person.
The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by understanding (VS 6.1.1).
Taking one utterance as several sentences, a fault to be avoided in interpretation (MS 2.1.47; Śabara on 1.1.1).
The meaning of the whole sentence, conveyed by the word-meanings (Bhāṭṭa) or by words expressing meanings already connected (Prābhākara).
The meaning of the sentence, grasped as a flash of pratibhā distinct from the word-meanings (VP 2.143).
The remainder of the passage, which settles a doubtful meaning (MS 1.4.29).
The young goddess (Bālā), the Siddhars' Śakti worshipped at the root with three syllables; identified with Maṉōṉmaṇi.
The eleven supplementary hymns printed as RV 8.49–59.
Scriptures of the left/northern stream centred on Tumburu and his four sisters (e.g. Vīṇāśikha).
The left-hand conduct, contrasted with the right; Lakṣmīdhara assigns it to those not eligible for the Vedic way.
The fifth mode: 'left-hand' worship with the Kaula substances, reserved for the vīra (summary only).
Therapeutic emesis, the chief remedy for kapha (AHS Sū 1.25).
The genealogies of gods, sages and kings - the third mark of a Purāṇa.
The narratives of the kings of the solar and lunar dynasties - the fifth mark of a Purāṇa.
The forest-hermit, entered when one sees wrinkles, grey hair and grandchildren (MDh 6.2).
Bowing to and praising the Lord, the sixth form of devotion.
Bowing, adoration with joined palms (Tamil toḻutal): 'O mind, worship his feet and rise' (TVM 1.1.1).
The 'utterance' of a saint — his or her collected words, treated as scripture by the panth.
Lalitā's general (Daṇḍanāthā, Daṇḍinī) on the Kiricakra chariot who slays Viśukra (LSN 26-30); her worship is the seventh section of the Kalpasūtra; in the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad she is 'the father'.

The regular walking pilgrimage to Paṇḍharpūr, above all for the Āṣāḍhī and Kārtikī ekādaśīs, made in singing companies (diṇḍī) behind the saints' palanquins; keeping it for life is what makes one a Vārkarī.
One who keeps the vārī to Paṇḍharpūr; a member of the Vārkarī sampradāya, marked by the tuḷsī necklace, vegetarianism, the Ekādaśī fast and the name.

Vital points of the body where life-breath concentrates; injury to them harms or kills and pressure on them heals. The Siddha tradition counts 108 (12 'striking' paṭu varmam and 96 'touching' toṭu varmam) and ascribes the lore to Agastya.

equivalents.note: Āyurveda's 107 marmas: overlapping idea, different counts and uses

definitions.definition: A phoneme — sixty-three or sixty-four, declared by Svayambhū (PŚ 3); the first topic of phonetics (TU 1.2).
Each of the four social classes — brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra — with their duties (MDh 1.31, 1.88–91; 10.4); stated by the tradition as created from the Person's mouth, arms, thighs and feet.
In the Brāhmaṇas the classes are correlated with metres, gods, chants and animals (TS 7.1.1.4–6) and with the three Vedas (TB 3.12.9.2).

The four classes, created by the Lord according to guṇa and action (BhG 4.13), their duties arising from their nature (18.41–44); Bhṛgu teaches that the whole world was of Brahman and came to varṇa-division by actions (MBh 12.181.10); conduct makes the brāhmaṇa (3.177.16).
The eternal letters are the word: 'gauḥ' is g, au and ḥ (Upavarṣa); meaning is conveyed by the letters through their impressions, without a sphoṭa.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The social orders whose mixture (varṇa-saṅkara) Arjuna fears (1.41).
Letter or sound as object of contemplation (VBT 30, 40, 81, 90) and as an āṇava support (MVT 2.21).
The letter: for the grammarians not a real part of the word, which is partless (VP 1.73).
The letters as the manifestation of śabda-brahman through kuṇḍalinī (ŚT 1.14); gathered as the fifty mātṛkās.

notes: Homonym: phoneme (Vedāṅga) and social class (Dharmaśāstra) kept as separate definitions.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument it arises when the women of a family are corrupted after adharma prevails (1.41), leads the family and its destroyers to hell (1.42) and uproots the jāti- and kula-dharmas (1.43); Kṛṣṇa says that if he did not act he would be the maker of saṅkara (3.24).
The mixture of varṇas that Arjuna fears will follow the ruin of families (BhG 1.41) and that the Lord says would follow if he did not act (3.24).
Sovereign guardian of ṛta and the vows, all-seeing judge who binds with fetters and forgives (RV 7.86–89; AVŚ 4.16).

A technical term for the disciple's eight faculties of learning while living with the teacher (grasping, retaining, inferring, rejecting, understanding, speaking, service, right application); the first means.

Latent tendency: the grasping of an object through firm conception without reflection; one of the two seeds of mind; impure vāsanās bind to rebirth, pure ones (friendliness and the like) are to be cultivated before all are given up; bondage is bondage to vāsanā.

Latent tendencies from past experience that manifest only when suited to ripening karma (4.8), continuous across births (4.9), beginningless because the will to be is eternal (4.10), and ceasing when cause, result, substrate and support cease (4.11).
One of the two causes of mind (with breath): if either is destroyed both are (HYP 4.22); laya is forgetting objects when vāsanās no longer arise (4.34).

Latent tendency: the impressions of past experience and action that incline the mind; the three vāsanās (world, scripture-learning, body) obstruct knowledge; their destruction is a discipline of the jīvanmukta.
Impressions of past experience; the material from which dreams are really produced (dreams are therefore not false).
Latent tendency that sustains mind; pure or impure; its destruction (vāsanā-kṣaya) with dissolution of mind and knowledge gives jīvanmukti.
Exhaustion of latent tendencies; the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha equates it with liberation ('mokṣaḥ syād vāsanākṣayaḥ').
Destruction of latent tendencies, practised with knowledge and mind-dissolution for the stable freedom of the jīvanmukta.
The hotṛ's exclamation at the moment of offering.

The breath treated as a horse to be mastered: the Siddhar breath-yoga (vāci yōkam) that stills and turns the breath inward and is held to perfect the body and lengthen life (summary; see prc:vasi-yoga).

cross_language.note: horse

equivalents.note: vāci is the breath as the object of mastery

definitions.definition: The defining mark of lower dispassion (1.15); in Vācaspati the fourth of four stages of dispassion.

literal: son of Vasudeva; the indwelling god

definitions.definition: Name of Kṛṣṇa; 'Vāsudeva is all' is the realization of the rare great soul (BhG 7.19); 'among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva' (10.37).
The supreme of the fourfold form, the knower of the field without guṇas, dwelling of all, entered by the liberated (MBh 12.326.38; 12.332.17).
The supreme Lord and first vyūha, full of all six qualities.

equivalents.note: the Nārāyaṇīya identifies Vāsudeva as the knower of the field

definitions.definition: The doṣa of movement: dry, cold, light, subtle, mobile, clear and rough (Ca Sū 1.59); fivefold as prāṇa, udāna, samāna, vyāna and apāna; unprovoked it upholds the body's structure, impels all movement and guides the mind, and in the world upholds the earth and drives the seasons (Ca Sū 12.8); chief seat the colon (AHS Sū 12.1).
Tamil vaḷi or vātam: the wind humour, first of the three (Kuṟaḷ 941 names the three 'beginning with vaḷi'); built of air and ether; in Siddha pulse-reading the strongest beat.

equivalents.note: vāta is vāyu as a bodily doṣa; Āyurveda uses vāyu, anila, māruta, samīraṇa as synonyms

definitions.definition: The easier mode of rasāyana, taken without withdrawing from ordinary life (Ca Ci 1.1.16; 1.4.28).
The Lord's love that overlooks — or, for the Teṅkalai, relishes — the faults of the dependent, like a cow's for its calf.
Parental love: love for Kṛṣṇa as one's child, as of Yaśodā and Nanda.
Truthfulness: speech that harms no one (Kuṟaḷ ch. 30).

equivalents.note: defined by the Kuṟaḷ by its harmlessness

definitions.definition: The deity Vāyu, highest soul, giver of liberation by Viṣṇu's permission, whose three avatāras are Hanumān, Bhīma and Madhva.
The breath as wind: ten vāyus move in the channels as the living soul's vehicles (GŚ 23–25; SS 3.4–8); when the wind moves the mind moves (HYP 2.2).
Substance with touch and without colour, inferred from touch; within the body it is breath.
The Wind, 'the breath of the gods, germ of the world', whose sounds are heard, not his form (RV 10.168.4).
In the Siddha ninety-six principles, the ten vital winds (Tamil vāyu, with Tamil names pirāṇaṉ, apāṉaṉ, viyāṉaṉ, utāṉaṉ, camāṉaṉ, nākaṉ, kūrmaṉ, kirukaraṉ, tēvatattaṉ, taṉañcayaṉ).
The authorless (apauruṣeya), beginningless body of sentences, the sole means of knowing dharma; it comprises injunction, mantra, name, prohibition and arthavāda.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who delight in the words of the Veda and say there is nothing else proclaim a flowery speech aimed at heaven, enjoyment and power (2.42–44); the Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain (2.45); for a knowing brāhmaṇa all the Vedas are of as much use as a well in a flood (2.46).
The first mode: Vedic ritual conduct.
Learning the Veda from a teacher by the injunction 'one's own Veda is to be studied'; every such study presupposes a teacher's study, without first beginning (ŚV vākya 366).
Each of the six auxiliary sciences — śikṣā, kalpa, vyākaraṇa, nirukta, chandas, jyotiṣa — pictured as the Veda's nose, hands, mouth, ear, feet and eye (PŚ 41–42).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who delight in vedavāda say 'there is nothing else' and proclaim flowery speech offering heaven, power and rebirth as fruit of works (2.42–43).
The rarest initiation, in which the guru's power pierces the disciple's centres; rare is the guru who can give it (Kulārṇava 13.79; 14.66).
The altar ground strewn with grass between the fires.

Natural urges (of urine, faeces, semen, flatus, vomiting, sneezing, belching, yawning, hunger, thirst, tears, sleep, breath after exertion) which must not be suppressed; and the urges of greed, grief, fear, anger, pride, envy, passion and rash acts which must be restrained (Ca Sū 7.3-4, 7.26-29; AHS Sū 4.1, 4.24).
The impression that keeps a moving thing moving (Tarkasaṅgraha; VS 5.1.17 C on the arrow).

The open, empty space — the supreme as boundless void-expanse beyond the crown; 'for those who hold the open space to be the truth, what need of a title-deed?' (Kuṭampai 1); Kaṭuveḷi speaks of 'the open space of pure Vedānta'.

equivalents.note: space as image of the supreme
the Siddhar 'void' is not the Buddhist emptiness; resemblance only

definitions.definition: The quality that destroys conjunction.
The Lord's descents; the Ahirbudhnya counts thirty-nine, beginning with Padmanābha.
The Lord's descents (avatāra) — principal ones like Rāma and Kṛṣṇa in bodies of pure sattva taken by his will, and secondary ones by empowerment of souls — for the protection of the good.
The excitants of rasa: the object and substratum (ālambana: Kṛṣṇa and his devotees) and the stimuli (uddīpana: his qualities, flute, dress, places).
Determinant: the cause of an emotion in drama or poetry — its object and support (ālambana) and its excitants (uddīpana) (NŚ 6–7).

literal: that which causes to be felt
notes: Disambiguated from trm:vibhava (Pāñcarātra 'vibhava', the Lord's descents); U16's aesthetic use of trm:vibhava belongs here.

definitions.definition: Separated parts: the souls, parts of his marginal power.

The Lord's manifestations in the best of every class — Viṣṇu among the Ādityas, the sun among lights, Oṃ among words, japa among sacrifices, Kapila among the perfected — all sprung from a fragment of his splendour (BhG ch. 10).
Holy ash, one of the eight shields; called vibhūti because it causes prosperity (SSM 7.4–5).
The powers treated in the third pāda (Vibhūti-pāda) that arise from saṃyama.
One of the five names of sacred ash.
Sacred ash from the dhūnī, smeared on the body and given as blessing; in the common legend Gorakh is born from Matsyendra's ash.
Ash of the cremation ground smeared on the body.

notes: In yoga texts vibhūti also means yogic power; the Gītā's sense is the Lord's glory.

definitions.definition: Inquiry: discriminating reflection, guided by scripture and the wise, into what one is and what the world is; the second gatekeeper and the lamp by which the real is seen.
The mind's subtle engagement with its support (YBh 1.17); coalescence with subtle objects (1.44).

cross_language.note: first-jhāna factor 'sustained thought'

definitions.definition: Second stage: taking up right conduct through contact with scripture and the good, with dispassion and practice.
Second stage of knowledge: inquiry with scripture and the wise.
A state of the afflictions (2.4): Appearing again and again in alternation, e.g. anger not active while attachment is (YBh 2.4).
Beings who experience a state like kaivalya without a body; Vyāsa calls them gods (YBh 1.19); Bhoja: those who rest content in bliss-samādhi (RM 1.17).
Bodiless liberation, the domain beyond the fourth (turyātīta).
Bodiless liberation at the fall of the body, when prārabdha is exhausted; nothing is gained that was not already the case.
Liberation at the fall of the body when prārabdha is exhausted, like wind becoming still.

The part of the Veda that makes known an unknown purposeful object; fourfold as originative, applicatory, performative and eligibility injunction (Arthasaṅgraha); also classed as apūrva, niyama and parisaṅkhyā injunctions.
An injunction conveys a command (niyoga), 'what is to be done' (kārya), which prompts the qualified person by itself.
Activity that produces merit: primary (the observance - vows and the six 'doors') and secondary (re-bathing and the like); it begins with ash, has censure in the middle and ends with feigned folly.
A Vedic statement that enjoins (NS 2.1.64 DCS).
The cleft: the suture at the top of the skull through which the self entered the body (AU 1.3.12).

notes: Later traditions speak of the brahmarandhra.

definitions.definition: Renunciation by one who has realized.
Renunciation by the knower, for the stable enjoyment of liberation while living.
The knowledge of the correspondences (and of the self) by which one reaches the world beyond desire where fees and uninformed austerity do not reach (ŚB 10.5.4.16).
The lower knowledge (aparā vidyā) includes the four Vedas and six Vedāṅgas; the higher is that by which the imperishable is reached (MuU 1.1.4–5).
A quality of the paśu, part of the effect: either cognitive (discriminating or not) or non-cognitive (merit and demerit).

Knowledge: what is done with knowledge is more powerful (ChU 1.1.10); the world of the gods is won by knowledge (BAU 1.5.16); paired with avidyā (Īśa 9-11; KU 1.2.4; ŚU 5.1); the higher and lower knowledge (MuU 1.1.4).
Undefective cognition (VS 9.27 C): perception, inference, memory, seers' knowledge (Praśastapāda).
A feminine mantra and the goddess it embodies; the ten 'great vidyās'.
Kañcuka: limited knowledge ('only this I know').
A mantra whose deity is female (ŚT 2.58); e.g. the Śrīvidyā.
The division of the Bhairava tantras centred on goddesses and feminine mantras (vidyā), comprising Yāmala and Śakti tantras.
The Vidyāpīṭha sādhaka's observance in Kāpālika style (cremation ground, skull) while mastering a goddess-mantra; recorded in summary only.

The eight Lords of Knowledge (Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, Śikhaṇḍin), liberated souls in office in the pure universe who act for Śiva; Ananta governs the impure creation.
Embodiment of the deity, which Śabara holds is not established: statements implying it are mantras and arthavādas not meant to assert it (on MS 9.1.9).
Understanding: a rung in Sanatkumāra's ladder (ChU 7.7, 7.17); the self made of understanding (TU 2.4; BAU 4.3.7); brahman is understanding and bliss (BAU 3.9.28).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: With jñāna, what desire destroys (3.41); commentators differ on the distinction.

cross_language.note: Buddhist sense: consciousness as an aggregate

notes: The commentators distinguish jñāna and vijñāna variously.

definitions.definition: A soul bound by mala alone, free of karma and māyā; the highest of these are raised by Śiva to offices as mantras, mantra-lords and Vidyeśvaras.
The knower of pure awareness without agency (ĪPK 3.2.6-7).
Made of understanding: the self within the mind-self, with faith as head and yoga as trunk (TU 2.4); the person made of understanding among the breaths (BAU 4.3.7).
The sheath of intellect: intellect with the organs of knowledge, the agent-ego that transmigrates.
An activity that follows on verbal knowledge but has no real object (1.9); in samāpatti, the mixing of word, object and cognition that marks savitarkā coalescence (1.42).
Conceptual cognition by exclusion of an opposite (ĪPK 1.6.5); dream is vikalpa (Śiva Sūtra 1.9); its dissolution is a means (PH 18) and its purification the śākta way (TĀ 4).

literal: the capacity of acting without organs

definitions.definition: Unsurpassed lordship even with the instruments withdrawn; Kauṇḍinya calls it the Pāśupata's distinction over others' isolation (kaivalya). The Sūtra lists 'vikaraṇa' and 'dharmitva' separately.

notes: SDS text reads 'vikramaṇadharmitva'.

definitions.definition: Action of a contrary or forbidden kind, which must be understood along with action and inaction (BhG 4.17).

notes: Commentators differ: prohibited action (Śaṅkara) or the various kinds of action (others).

definitions.definition: The morbid state of the patient, examined second in the tenfold examination (Ca Vi 8.94); the deviations from normal that signal disease or approaching death (Ca In 1.6-7); disorder as imbalance of the dhātus (Sū 9.4).
A principle that is a product only and produces no further principle: the sixteen (manas, ten capacities, five gross elements) (SK 3; Tattvasamāsa 2).
The eight 'modified' recitations built on the krama: jaṭā, mālā, śikhā, rekhā, dhvaja, daṇḍa, ratha, ghana.
The eight elaborated recitations (jaṭā, mālā, śikhā, rekhā, dhvaja, daṇḍa, ratha, ghana) built from the step recitation.
Distraction in meditation, from which one must turn away (SS 6.30).
Distraction: the mind's turning to external things; also the projecting power of ignorance.
The projecting power of māyā that creates the gross and subtle world.
The projecting power of ignorance, which projects the world and the subtle and gross bodies on the self, as ignorance of the rope projects the snake.
The distracted mind; samādhi in it, subordinate to distraction, is not yoga (YBh 1.1).
The self-reflective awareness that is the very nature of manifestation (ĪPK 1.5.11), supreme speech and the Lord's primary freedom (1.5.13); pure knowing and acting are the Lord's vimarśa (1.8.11).
Self-awareness, the Goddess as the mirror in which Śiva knows himself (KKV 2); 'whose form is vimarśa' (LSN 112).
The stringed instrument of Sarasvatī and Nārada; demonstration device for the śrutis (ŚR 1.3.11–22); one who knows its playing goes the way of liberation (YājS 3.115).
The ritual application of a mantra, stated with its seer, metre and deity before recitation.
The declaration before recitation of a mantra's seer (ṛṣi), metre (chandas), deity (devatā), seed, power and pin and the purpose for which it is applied.
An injunction that conveys the relation of subsidiary and principal, e.g. 'he offers with curd'; assisted by the six means (śruti etc.).
The fruition of karma: birth, life-span and experience (2.13), bearing joy or anguish (2.14).
The taste a substance takes after digestion, threefold: sweet, sour, pungent (AHS Sū 1.17).
What certainly lacks the probandum, e.g. the lake.
The 'reversed practice' — navel above, palate below, sun above, moon below — by which the nectar is saved from the sun; obtained from the guru's mouth (GŚ 59).
The practice that puts the sun above and moon below so the nectar is not swallowed by the sun, learned only from the guru's mouth (HYP 3.77–82; GŚ 59).
Error apprehends a thing as other than it is: the related items are real, only the relation that appears is unreal (Śāstradīpikā).

(1) The opposite of knowledge, from which bondage comes (SK 44). (2) The first class of the creation of cognitions, fivefold — darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, blind gloom — with sixty-two subdivisions (SK 47–48); the Tattvasamāsa calls it 'five-jointed avidyā'.
Error, false knowledge resting on a form not the object's own, sublated by valid cognition; as five-jointed ignorance it is the five afflictions (YS 1.8, YBh 1.8, 2.3).
False cognition, e.g. 'this is silver' of mother-of-pearl (Tarkasaṅgraha).
One of the forms of non-knowledge (avidyā) (Praśastapāda).

equivalents.note: The five errors are identified with the five afflictions (avidyā, asmitā, rāga, dveṣa, abhiniveśa) by the Yoga Bhāṣya on YS 1.8 ('these same, by their own names, are darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, blind gloom'), and implied by the Tattvasamāsa's 'five-jointed avidyā'.

definitions.definition: An inspired poet or priest (RV 1.164.46; 10.114.5).
Love in separation, which nourishes and intensifies union (sambhoga); in Caitanya's last years the dominant mood.
Love-in-separation as a phase of love's play (śṛṅgāra), the ground of most of the Gīta Govinda.
The 'hero' — the qualified Kaula adept, truthful, free of anger, knowing the Śakti born of the body and formed by non-dual conduct (KJN 20.18–22).
The 'hero', the qualified practitioner; the Goddess is 'mother of heroes' (LSN 156) and the knower of the mantra becomes 'lord of the circle of heroes' (YH 2.85).
The Kaula adept of the heroic disposition; fearless, beyond shame and doubt (Kulārṇava 5.82).

One who delights in Śiva-knowledge and keeps māyā away (SSM 5.17–18); in SSM 5.20–21 the Māheśvaras are those devoted to outer worship (the sacrifice of action), not ultimately different from the Śaivas who worship within.
The second disposition, of the fearless adept who worships with the Kaula substances and in the cremation ground (summary only); by the Kālīvilāsa's account proper to the Tretā–Dvāpara ages.
Love in separation from the beloved Lord, which keeps the mind constantly on him (BhP 10.47.34).
Love in separation, which Vallabha holds to be the highest state of devotion (the gopīs' state).
Separation (vipralambha), exemplified in the Śikṣāṣṭaka 7 and in Caitanya's last years.
Separation-longing voiced by the Āḻvārs as the love-sick girl, her mother and friend, and as the grieving parent (Kulaśekhara as Daśaratha); ended in Nammāḻvār's final union (TVM 10.10.11).
Supreme separation (parama-viraha) is the last of love's eleven forms; supreme anguish on forgetting the Lord is Nārada's own definition of devotion (NBS 19, 82).
The mutual longing of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in separation, carried by the friend, which is most of the Gīta Govinda (GG 2–9).
The pain of separation from the Beloved, praised as 'the sultan' and as the sign of true devotion; the body without it is a cremation ground.
The longing for the Man of the Heart who comes near and cannot be held.
The anguish of separation from Giridhar, the wound only the wounded know.
Not real in the eternal play, where the pair are never apart; felt only within union.
The feminine principle from whom the Puruṣa was born and who was born from him (RV 10.90.5); in the Atharvaveda she was all this in the beginning and was milked by gods, men and others (AVŚ 8.10).
The river at the boundary of prakṛti and the eternal realm; crossing it the soul sheds its subtle body.
The 'Virajā' initiation of the Śiva Gītā, in which the body is smeared with ash while reciting the Virajā mantras, taking the Pāśupata vow.
Purificatory oblation in the renunciation rite.
The celibate renunciant order of Liṅgāyata maṭhas, associated with the Basava-centred tradition and the lineage of Toṇṭada Siddhaliṅga.

equivalents.note: renunciant life within a liṅga-wearing, non-Vedic-sannyāsa order

literal: 'heroic' Śaiva; by the tradition's derivation, one who delights (ram) in the knowledge (vī) of Śiva–jīva oneness

definitions.definition: Those who delight in the knowledge that awakens the oneness of Śiva and the jīva (SSM 5.15–16); the name of the tradition as a whole and the preferred self-designation of its Pañcācārya strand.
The Goddess's cosmic form, shown to the gods and worshipped in Vedic worship.
The cosmic gross being: consciousness identified with the aggregate of gross bodies, collective counterpart of viśva.
Therapeutic purgation, the chief remedy for pitta (AHS Sū 1.25).
The obstacles to liberation, fivefold: to knowing the self, the Lord's supremacy, the means, the goal, and to attainment.
A reason pervaded by the absence of the probandum ('sound is eternal because produced').
Brahman as the locus of contradictory attributes, all true of it.
(1) Energy, the second means (1.20); (2) the vigour gained by one established in celibacy (2.38).
The active potency of a substance, twofold as hot or cold (AHS Sū 1.17).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's condition: overcome by compassion and sinking into despondency (viṣīdan, 1.28, 2.1, 2.10).
Arjuna's despondency on seeing his kin, which gives the first chapter its name (BhG 1.28–47).
In the Bhāgavata, the secondary creation by Brahmā (the Puruṣa's creation) from the imbalance of the guṇas (BhP 2.10.3).
The emissive power of the Goddess (VBT 24) and the letter ḥ at whose end awareness is placed (VBT 91).
The sun's southern course (rains to early winter) in which the moon is strong and strength is given back; cool (Ca Sū 6.4-7; AHS Sū 3.4-6).

notes: Homonym: visarga is also the aspirate sign and, in the Purāṇas, secondary creation.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The sense-objects: they turn away from one who abstains, though the taste remains (2.59); dwelling on them breeds attachment (2.62); the self-governed move among them with mastered senses (2.64).
The Vedic passage under discussion in an adhikaraṇa.
The property of being the content of a cognition, analysed into qualificandness, qualifierness and relationness.
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the cause of decrease — the unlike reduces; it makes for separateness (Ca Sū 1.44-45).
The gross elements (SK 38); the specifics are threefold: subtle bodies, bodies born of parents, and gross elements (SK 39).
The first level of the guṇas: the sixteen particularized products — five elements, ten senses and mind (2.19, YBh 2.19).
Residing in eternal substances and distinguishing them from one another; endless in number (Tarkasaṅgraha).

In Madhva's usage a 'substitute for difference' (bheda-pratinidhi): the capacity that allows a thing to be spoken of as distinct from its lasting properties (or God from his qualities and forms) where there is no real difference.
In several Siddhānta sources a name for the initiation (often identified with or following samaya-dīkṣā) that qualifies for personal Śiva-worship.
The 'special' initiation qualifying the initiate for the daily worship of Śiva (details vary among manuals).
That which qualifies and distinguishes a substrate (viśeṣya); the soul is a qualifier of Brahman and so an 'aṃśa' of it.
A property qualifying a thing; the qualifier–qualified relation (viśeṣaṇatā) is the contact by which absence is perceived.
The sixth ordinary contact, by which absence and inherence are perceived.
What a cognition is about as qualified; its property is viśeṣyatā.
The relation in which a qualifier stands to what it qualifies — in perception, the contact for absence.
The doctrine that Brahman, qualified by souls and matter as its inseparable modes, is one without a second; also read as the non-duality of Brahman in its causal (subtle) and effected (gross) states.
The one independent reality, full of infinite auspicious qualities and free of defects, the Brahman of the Upaniṣads and the primary meaning of all words.
The god of the three strides, whose highest step the wise ever see (RV 1.22.20, 1.154).
The second knot, pierced in the ghaṭa stage, when a kettledrum sound is heard in the extreme void (HYP 4.73).
Prenatal saṃskāra in the eighth month of pregnancy dedicating the child to Viṣṇu.
Servants of Viṣṇu who protect a dying person who has uttered the Lord's name from Yama's messengers.
Repose: drama gives rest to the afflicted (NŚ 1.114); in Abhinavagupta's aesthetics rasa is consciousness at rest in itself.
The throat centre, sixteen-petalled, of space (HAṂ) (ṢCN).
The absolute removal of each impurity: of ignorance, demerit, what causes attachment, falling away, and the paśu-state.
The throat centre.
The form of Viṣṇu that presides over the soul's waking state.
The self as experiencer of waking, identified with the gross body (microcosmic counterpart of Virāj/Vaiśvānara).
Where no fruit is stated for an enjoined rite, heaven is understood as its fruit (MS 4.3.15); used widely, e.g. by the Prakaraṇapañcikā.
The All-maker who forged heaven and earth, with eyes, faces, arms and feet everywhere, the one name-giver of the gods (RV 10.81–82).

The Lord's sovereign form shown to Arjuna with the divine eye: the whole universe in one body, with countless faces, brighter than a thousand suns, devouring the warriors as Time (BhG ch. 11); seen only by undivided devotion (11.54).
Faith or trust; validity 'consists above all in faith' (PKS 1.10).
Inference proceeding by agreement, establishing its object; divided into pūrvavat and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa (Vācaspati on SK 5).
Wrangling without establishing a counter-thesis (NS 1.2.3); the caviller who states a purpose thereby adopts a thesis (NBh 1.1.1).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): merely finding fault with the other side (Ca Vi 8.28).
Debate that only attacks the opponent's position, one of the three kinds of debate.

(1) The mind's gross engagement with its support, the mark of the first samprajñāta samādhi (1.17, YBh 1.17). (2) A distinct sense in 2.33–34: harmful thoughts such as violence, to be countered by cultivating their opposites.

cross_language.note: first-jhāna factor 'applied thought'

notes: Homonym within the YS itself; do not merge the two senses.

definitions.definition: The Lord of Paṇḍharpūr (also Viṭhobā, Pāṇḍuraṅga, Viṭhāī 'mother Viṭṭhala'), a form of Kṛṣṇa who stands on the brick Puṇḍalīka threw him, hands on hips; for some saints one with Śiva as well.

literal: (popularly) 'standing on a brick' (viṭ + ṭhala); other derivations exist

definitions.definition: Release, liberation: the Lord is 'the one who owns release' (TVM 1.2.1); Nammāḻvār, his longing ended, 'attained release' (TVM 10.10.11).
Release, liberation — the fourth aim, not a separate book in the Kuṟaḷ but implied in its chapters on renunciation and truth.
Release, 'the house': Kaṭuveḷi's pun — burn the forest of the senses and you will see the house (14); to know the root is the house of liberation (13).

equivalents.note: the Tamil word for liberation

definitions.definition: Marriage, of eight forms (MDh 3.21), performed with the customs of region and village (ĀśGS 1.7.1).
Apparent transformation: a change in appearance without change in the substance, as the rope appears as a snake; the world is Brahman's vivarta and avidyā's pariṇāma.
The Advaita doctrine that the world is an apparent transformation of Brahman; rejected because the witness establishes the world's reality.
The 'turning out' or unfolding by which the Word-principle appears as things (VP 1.1); whether this means an unreal appearance (as later Advaita) or a manifestation is debated.
Bhavabhūti: the one rasa, compassion, takes different forms (vivarta) as water takes the forms of eddies, bubbles and waves (UR 3.47).

Discriminating knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower (SK 2), which buddhi accomplishes (SK 37); it is accomplished through practice of the principles, renouncing each with 'not this, not this' (SS 3.76).
Discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal: the firm conviction 'Brahman is real, the world is false' (VC 20); also the discernment of self from not-self.

The cognition of the difference between sattva and puruṣa (YBh 2.26); unwavering, it is the means of avoidance (2.26); the light of knowledge grows up to it (2.28); complete, it yields the cloud of dharma (4.29).
The non-apprehension of the difference between the two cognitions that makes up error.
Knowledge from saṃyama on the moment and its sequence (3.52), discerning even indistinguishable things (3.53); the deliverer, all-embracing and without sequence (3.54).

The discernment of the distinctness of puruṣa and prakṛti (sattva), culminating in the knowledge 'I am not, not mine, not I' (SK 64); called the direct realization of the distinctness of sattva and puruṣa (Vācaspati).

notes: The compound is standard in Yoga (YS 2.26); the SK uses vijñāna/jñāna, Pañcaśikha 'khyāti'.

definitions.definition: The desire to know (Brahman), produced (per the Bhāmatī) by sacrifice, gifts and austerity (BĀU 4.4.22).
Renunciation in order to realize, keeping the insignia.
Renunciation by one who desires knowledge, as a means to it.
The binding ordinance of a god (Varuṇa 'of firm vratas'), and a vow undertaken by a person ('Agni, lord of vows, I shall undertake the vow', VS 1.5).
A religious vow for a set period or day (fast, vigil, worship, gifts), with its story and fruit (e.g. Ekādaśī, Śivarātri, Navarātra, Kātyāyanī vrata).
The primary observance of ash-bathing, lying in ash, the sixfold offering, muttering and circumambulation.
Vow, observance: the vow of breathing (BAU 1.5.23); the food vows (TU 3.7-10); the head-vow (MuU 3.2.10); Prajāpati's vow (PrU 1.13).
The observance taken by the sacrificer on entering a rite (ŚB 1.1.1).
The vows of the Vedic student and the observances (fasts and rules) prescribed in the smṛtis and digests.

literal: one bound by a vow / of a band

definitions.definition: The vow-bound wanderer of Atharvaveda book 15 who stirs Prajāpati, becomes Mahādeva and Īśāna, and is honoured as guest.
A member of groups living outside the Vedic sacrificial order, who may be admitted by the Vrātya rites (PB 17.1–4).
A twice-born whose initiation has lapsed ('fallen from the Sāvitrī', MDh 2.39).
The beginningless usage of elders, observing which children learn the meanings of words (as connected with action).
Crooked conduct, which Varuṇa and the Ādityas see beside the straight.

checks.note: Located: the Ādityas are 'avṛjināḥ' and 'antaḥ paśyanti vṛjinota sādhu' (RV 2.27.2–3).

definitions.definition: The rite of setting free a consecrated bull on the eleventh day, without which the preta state becomes fixed.
The serpent who enclosed the waters and was slain by Indra (RV 1.32).

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cf. Avestan vərəθraγna (victory).

definitions.definition: An activity (modification) of the mind; five kinds — valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep and memory — each afflicted or unafflicted (YS 1.5–6); the seer, when not in its own form, conforms to them (1.4).
The three livelihoods: alms, discarded food, and what is obtained.
A mode or modification of the inner organ; in perception it goes out and takes the form of the object; the mode in the form of Brahman removes ignorance.

cross_language.note: rare in this sense in Pali

notes: Homonym of Yoga's citta-vṛtti.

definitions.definition: The seer's taking on the form of the mind's activities when not stilled (1.4).
The earlier commentator whose exposition of MS 1.1.3–5 Śabara reproduces.
A relation by which one thing can occur in another (e.g. conjunction, inherence), as opposed to relations that do not ground occurrence.
The thirty-three transient states that move within the stable emotion, from despondency (nirveda) to deliberation (NŚ 6.18–21).
The thirty-three transient emotions that move within the permanent emotion.
Illness: imbalance of the bodily elements, fluids and organs (YBh 1.30).
The body's power to resist the arising or growth of disease (Ca Sū 28.7).
The utterances bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, recited before the Gāyatrī (VS 36.3; cf. 3.5).
The three utterances bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, spoken by Prajāpati to create earth, atmosphere and sky (ŚB 11.1.6.3), drawn from the three Vedas (AB 5.32).
The utterances recited before the Sāvitrī and in breath-control (MDh 2.76–81; YS 1.23).
The calls bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ (and mahaḥ): meditated on as worlds, lights, Vedas and breaths (TU 1.5); flowed from the Veda at creation (ChU 2.23.2).
The soul's act (surrender) that the Lord's free grace takes as its occasion so that he is not partial.
Grammar, 'the mouth of the Veda' and chief of its limbs (PŚ 41–42; Mahābhāṣya), studied to protect and understand the Veda.
Grammar as the nearest to Brahman, the highest austerity, the door to liberation and remedy for the impurities of speech (VP 1.11–16).

The evolutes of prakṛti, from mahat to the gross elements: caused, impermanent, non-pervasive, active, many, supported, merging, composite and dependent (SK 10), consisting of the three guṇas, non-discriminating, object, common, unconscious and productive (SK 11).
Conduct openly displayed while the sign is hidden.
The first stage, in which the Pāśupata sign is made manifest by ash-bathing and the rest; lived in the temple under the teacher.
A concrete thing that is the substrate of particular qualities (NS 2.2.69 DCS).
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at the joints.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the vāyu seated in the heart and moving swiftly through the whole body, governing movement, flexion, extension, blinking — nearly all the body's actions (AHS Sū 12.6-7).
The diffused breath, moving through the channels (PrU 3.6); the right side of the self made of breath (TU 2.2).
The breath pervading the whole body (SS 3.7).
The diffused breath, the third of the breaths named in the Saṃhitās (TS 4.7; AVŚ 15.15–17).
The breath pervading the body.

The power of suggestion, a function of words beyond denotation (abhidhā) and indication (lakṣaṇā) by which the implied sense and rasa are conveyed; denied by Mahimabhaṭṭa (inference) and by Mīmāṃsakas and Naiyāyikas.
Accepted by Nāgeśa as a third power of words beside denotation and indication.
The rule of co-presence 'wherever there is smoke there is fire' (Tarkasaṅgraha); defined precisely after rejecting five provisional definitions (Tattvacintāmaṇi).
The relation between mark and marked on which inference rests (term prominent from Uddyotakara and Vācaspati on).
Consuming absorption or 'addiction' to Kṛṣṇa, the culmination of the growth of devotion.
Litigation and the law of the eighteen titles, which arose when dharma declined among humans (Nāradasmṛti Mātṛkā 1.1–2).
Empirically real: valid for all practical dealings and sublated only by knowledge of Brahman — the waking world, Īśvara, scripture and the path.
A determinate cognition; 'vyavasāyātmaka' in NS 1.1.4 denotes determinate perception (Vācaspati).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Here it is one, whereas the understandings of the irresolute are many-branched and endless (2.41); it is not established in samādhi for those carried away by enjoyment and power (2.44).
The single, resolute understanding of the yogin, contrasted with the many-branched minds of the irresolute (BhG 2.41, 2.44).
Bodily exertion for steadiness and strength, to be done in measure (to half one's strength); excess causes disease (Ca Sū 7.31-35; AHS Sū 2.10-14).
Space as a place of the subtle body: the 'space-wheel' (vyomacakra) of khecarī between sun and moon (HYP 3.37, 4.45); the five voids (vyomapañcaka) of the Nāth body-map.
The five voids or spaces to be known in the body (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2).
The HYP's name for the place where the reversed tongue meets the junction of the three paths in khecarī, and for the space between sun and moon where the inner khecarī abides.
One of the five spaces seen in the intermediate target (ākāśa, parākāśa, mahākāśa, sūryākāśa, paramākāśa).
The fourfold form (caturmūrti) of the Lord — Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha — each arising from the prior (MBh 12.326.68–69).
The four emanated forms of the Lord — Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha — each manifesting a pair of the six qualities while possessing all six.
The four emanations Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha, each manifesting the six qualities or pairs of them, for creation, maintenance, dissolution and for the meditation of seekers.
The fourfold form of the Lord (Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) in the Triśikhi's concentrations and the Mudgala.

notes: The word 'vyūha' for the fourfold form is the later Pāñcarātra term; the Nārāyaṇīya speaks of the Lord's four forms (mūrti).

definitions.definition: The mind's outgoing, non-concentrated state, whose impressions are overpowered in stilling (3.9); powers count as powers only in it (3.37); kriyā-yoga is for the emergent (vyutthita) mind (YBh 2.1).
Chance: listed among the candidate causes in ŚU 1.2.
The principal enjoined act, the giving up of a substance with reference to a deity; it is what produces the apūrva and fruit (MS 9.1.1, 9.1.9).

notes: The definition 'giving up a substance with reference to a deity' is the standard manual formula, from memory (moderate).

definitions.definition: The patron of the sacrifice who bears its cost and receives its fruit.

The sacrifice: offering into fire to the gods with mantra, the rite that sustains gods and world; the gods first sacrificed the Puruṣa, 'sacrificing to the sacrifice with the sacrifice' (RV 10.90.16).

The Vedic offering-rite performed with fire, mantras and priests; in the Brāhmaṇas it is identified with the cosmic Person, with Prajāpati, with the year and with Viṣṇu ('puruṣo vai yajñaḥ', ŚB 1.3.2.1; 'yajño vai viṣṇuḥ').
Any of the prescribed offerings of the householder — the daily great sacrifices, the cooked-food, oblation and Soma sacrifices counted among the forty sacraments (GDh 8.14–21).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Action other than for the sake of sacrifice binds (3.9); Prajāpati created beings together with sacrifice, by which gods and humans nourish one another (3.10–12); rain arises from sacrifice and sacrifice from action (3.14); the all-pervading brahman is ever established in it (3.15).

Sacrifice, action done for whose sake does not bind (BhG 3.9); the wheel of sacrifice between gods and men (3.10–16); widened to many kinds — of material things, austerity, yoga, study, knowledge, breath (4.25–30) — the sacrifice of knowledge being highest (4.33); inwardly, the seven priests of the senses offering into the fire within (Anugītā 14.20).

cross_language.note: reinterpreted as giving and virtue in the Pali texts

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan yasna.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The good who eat the remainder of the sacrifice are freed from all faults (3.13).
The sacrificial thread; for the renouncer the Self, Brahman or praṇava is the true thread.
A (mostly prose) sacrificial formula spoken by the adhvaryu while acting; the Yajurveda; yajus is mind (VS 36.1).
The name for the remaining mantras, neither metrically divided by sense nor sung (MS 2.1.37).

The wondrous presence, 'endowed with self' (ātmanvat), within the golden sheath or nine-gated lotus, known by the knowers of Brahman (AVŚ 10.2.32, 10.8.43); the mind is the unprecedented yakṣa within creatures (VS 34.2).
A wondrous being, the form in which brahman appears to the proud gods (Kena 3).
Consumption or disease generally, driven out by Atharvavedic hymns (AVŚ 3.7).
Yama son of Vivasvant, first mortal to die, who found the path for many and is king of the dead in the highest heaven (RV 10.14).
The five restraints: non-harming, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, non-possessiveness (2.30); universal, the great vow (2.31).
The first limb: in the VP and ŚiP non-harming, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, non-possession; in MkP 41.16 the ascetic's five vows (non-stealing, celibacy, renunciation, non-greed, non-harming).
Non-harming, celibacy, truthfulness, non-dealing and non-stealing (with the five niyamas also counted as yamas).
Ten restraints (non-injury … purity), each with an outer and an inner meaning; moderate diet is chief.
The means of dharma common to all life-stages (NBh 4.2.46).
Without restraint, pure food does not bring prosperity (VS 6.2.9 C).
Tamil Yamaṉ, Namaṉ, Kālaṉ: death, who carries off the sinner (Kaṭuveḷi pallavi) but has no hold on knowers (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 10) or on those who conquered him (Kuṭampai 26).

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan Yima.

definitions.definition: The fearsome servants of Yama who bind and drag the dead to Yama's city; they appear to the dying.
A class of Vidyāpīṭha tantras named for the union of Bhairava and the goddess (e.g. Brahmayāmala, Jayadrathayāmala); the Śrīkaṇṭhīya's second group of eight.
Yama (Dharmarāja, Vaivasvata), king of the ancestors, who judges the dead according to their deeds under the Lord's command; he has no authority over the Lord's devotees.

notes: Also: Yama, Dharmarāja

definitions.definition: The body, born of one's deeds and not of parents, in which the dead is bound and suffers on the road and in hell.
Livelihood of the fourth stage: whatever comes unasked to one staying in the cremation ground.
Ascetic, striver: the yatis who have ascertained the meaning of Vedānta (MuU 3.2.6).
The renouncer-ascetic; the texts address him as yati.
A sorcerer or demon; Vasiṣṭha swears he is none (RV 7.104.15).

literal: yoking; (from yuj 'to concentrate', per Vyāsa and Bhoja) concentration

definitions.definition: The stilling of the activities of the mind (YS 1.2); Vyāsa: 'yoga is samādhi', a property of the mind at all its levels, counting as yoga only in the one-pointed and stilled mind.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Equanimity is called yoga (2.48); yoga is skill in actions (2.50); the understanding 'according to yoga' (2.39); one attains yoga when the understanding stands immovable in samādhi (2.53); karmayoga is the commitment of the yogins (3.3).

In the Gītā: evenness of mind in success and failure (2.48), skill in action (2.50), and the disconnection from union with sorrow (6.23); also the discipline of action as distinct from sāṃkhya (3.3). In the Mokṣadharma, the path relying on direct perception and a Lord, as against Sāṃkhya (12.289.3–7).
The conjunction of the self with the Lord (through the mind); twofold - in action (muttering, meditation) and in the cessation of action.

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda, Caraka): the state in which, the mind being steady and established in the self, pleasure and pain cease and mastery arises in the embodied — it leads to liberation (Śā 1.137-139); its eight powers (Śā 1.140-141); also 'yoga' = right combination/application of drugs (Sū 1.123).

The discipline by which the self is seen (YS 1.8) and by which the faults that burn beings are removed (ĀpDh 1.8.23); the renouncer's practice of breath-control, fixation, withdrawal and meditation (MDh 6.70–74).
The union of the jīva and the Self (Devī Gītā).
Not union with wealth, kin, powers, heavens or divine ranks, but the undivided understanding regarding Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śakti, the Sun and Gaṇeśa (Gaṇeśa Gītā).
One-pointedness of mind on the Lord by stopping other modifications, with eight means (Īśvara Gītā).

VP 6.7.31: the joining with Brahman of the special, effort-dependent movement of the mind; LiP 1.8: restraint of citta's activities, and the word means nirvāṇa, Maheśa's state; ŚiP 7.2.37.6: the mind's steady activity fixed on Śiva.

Yoga: 'the firm holding of the senses' (KU 2.3.11); the method taught by Death (KU 2.3.18); the trunk of the self made of understanding (TU 2.4); the chapter on posture, breath and signs (ŚU 2); the six-limbed yoga (MaiU 6.18).
The state in which, the mind abiding in the self, the embodied one has no pleasure or pain (VS 5.2.17 C).
A means to liberation, practised in forests, caves and sandbanks, with the method of the inner self learned from the Yoga śāstra (NS 4.2.42, 4.2.46; NBh).
Tamil yōkam: the Siddhars teach the eight-limbed yoga of the Tirumantiram and vāci yoga, yet Kuṭampai asks what need of yoga the realized has.
The power gained by yoga, by which the yogin checks sense-objects as an elephant stems a current and enters other beings at will (MBh 12.289.23–24).
The one who falls away from yoga before perfection; he is not lost but reborn among the pure or in a family of yogins and continues (BhG 6.37–45).
The five faults to be cut off in yoga: desire, anger, greed, fear and sleep (MBh 12.232.4; 12.266.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna is told to be free of concern for acquiring and keeping (niryogakṣema) (2.45).
Gain and security, whose burden the Lord bears for those who worship him with undivided minds (BhG 9.22); Arjuna is told to be free of acquiring and keeping (niryogakṣema, 2.45).
The Lord's yoga-māyā by which he is veiled and not manifest to all (BhG 7.25).
The Lord's internal power that arranges his play, e.g. making the gopīs appear married to others and veiling his majesty.
The soul at the stages of śaraṇa and aikya, correlated with the causal body and the bhāvaliṅga.
In the HYP the state to be practised for through khecarī: for one who attains yogic sleep 'there is never time' (4.49).
The Lord's sleep on the waters between creations; in the Devī Māhātmya the Goddess as Viṣṇu's sleep who leaves him so he can wake.

literal: one who has ascended to yoga

definitions.definition: One who has ascended to yoga, for whom quiescence is the means; attached neither to objects nor actions, having renounced all intentions (BhG 6.3–4).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 3.3 the yogins are those whose commitment is the yoga of action.

In Śrīvidyā the classes of attendant goddesses of the nine enclosures — Prakaṭa, Gupta, Guptatara, Sampradāya, Kulottīrṇa, Nigarbha, Rahasya, Atirahasya and Parāparātirahasya yoginīs; the Tripurā Upaniṣad (2) names nine yoginīs.

The goddesses of the Kula — sky-going, mother and earth-going — through whom Kaula knowledge descended; in Kāmarūpa the Kaula scripture is 'in every yoginī's house' (Kaulajñānanirṇaya 9.11-15; 22.10).
Goddesses of the six centres of the Kubjikā system (Kubjikāmata 15).
The Kaula of the yoginīs, the name the Kaulajñānanirṇaya gives itself in its colophons, brought down by Macchaghnapāda from Candradvīpa.
The meeting with the yoginīs — a sign and power of Kaula practice (KJN 7.22; 16.8).
One born from a Kaula union, by nature a vessel of knowledge, Rudra (TĀ 29.162-163).
Perception of the self and other substances from a special conjunction of self and mind (VS 9.13–14); of yogins in concentration (yukta) and out of it (viyukta) (Praśastapāda).
The perception of one engaged in yoga arises from samādhi (NBh 1.1.3).
Yogaja, one of the three extraordinary contacts.
Non-contradiction of the meaning ('sprinkle with fire' lacks it).
Fitness: the natural capacity of a word to express its meaning, the eternal relation between them (VP 3.3).
The Goddess's yoni fallen at Kāmagiri, worshipped at Kāmākhyā; Kāmākhyā is 'the great vidyā in the form of the yoni' (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.42; Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.4).
The supreme primal yoni of the supreme, fourfold (Kubjikāmata 11.6).
The triangle as womb of the universe: the triangles of the Śrīcakra are yonis; the yoni-mudrā is the ninth mudrā; the Tripurā Upaniṣad calls the Goddess's Śakti the womb of all.

In the GS, closing the senses, joining prāṇa and apāna and raising the goddess through the centres to union with Śiva; in the ŚS the contraction of the 'yoni' between anus and genitals with meditation on the flame in the brahma-yoni; also the name of a hand-gesture in Śākta worship.
The five-year cycle of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, presided over by Prajāpati (Ṛk 1).

The four world-ages Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali, of 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 divine years with twilights, in which dharma declines foot by foot (MDh 1.68–86); named already as states of a man in AB 7.15.

An age: the Lord comes into being age after age (BhG 4.8); Brahmā's day and night last a thousand ages each (8.17); the four ages and their decline taught by Hanumān (MBh 3.148) and Nārada (Rāmāyaṇa 7.74).
An age or generation; 'in the earliest age of the gods being was born from non-being' (RV 10.72.2).

An age of the world: Kṛta (Satya), Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali, of 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 divine years with junctions (sandhyā) of a tenth of that length before and after, so 4,800 + 3,600 + 2,400 + 1,200 divine years; dharma declines through them.

notes: The later cycle of four yugas is contributed by other units.

definitions.definition: The divine couple Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, worshipped together (yugala-upāsanā).
Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa as the object of service in mañjarī-bhāva.
The divine couple (Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa) and the human couple in which they are realized.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One should sit disciplined, intent on Kṛṣṇa (2.61); the undisciplined (ayukta) have no understanding or cultivation (2.66); the knowing one acts disciplined (3.26); one joined with understanding (buddhiyukta) casts off good and evil deeds (2.50).
Fitting detachment: using things without attachment in Kṛṣṇa's service, as opposed to 'futile' renunciation (phalgu-vairāgya) of what relates to him.

Caraka's fourth means of knowledge: the understanding that sees things produced by the conjunction of many causes, valid for the three times, by which the three aims are achieved (Ca Sū 11.25); also the right application of medicine to place, time and person (Sū 1.123-127).
The planned use of diet and medicines (Ca Sū 11.54): purification and pacification (Vi 8.87).
The post to which the victim is tied in the animal sacrifice.
